title: Creator of ‘We Do Not Care Club’ describes first video, response from followers
text:
(Aging Untold) — Melani Sanders is a social media sensation now, but there was a time when the creator of the popular “We Do Not Care Club” wasn’t one to be in front of the camera.
That changed one day when she decided that she had reached capacity. She was already tired and still had so much to do. Instead, she recorded a video from her car in the parking lot of her local Whole Foods.
In it, she announced a new club — the WDNC, the We Do Not Care Club — and asked if anyone wanted to join her.
After posting it to all of her social platforms, she learned that people did!
Now millions have watched Sanders’ videos that address perimenopause, menopause and life after menopause.
She described the community as “that sisterhood that we need.”
Her book, “The Official We Do Not Care Club Handbook,” is a New York Times bestseller, and Sanders has gone on a nine-city, sold-out tour.
“And I did everything scared,” she said.
How the club started
In an interview with Aging Untold’s aging well coach Katherine Ambrose and board-certified physician Dr. Rhea Rogers, Sanders said she had gone to Whole Foods for ashwagandha.
In the parking lot after that shopping trip, she looked in the mirror and thought of all the things she had to do, including laundry, cooking dinner and taking a book to the library.
“And then I just said, you know what? No, you don’t,” Sanders said. “I am at capacity. I’m tired. My body is tired.”
Sanders said she’d had a hysterectomy some months before and thinks her body went into shock.
“But at that moment, in that car, I was just tired,” Sanders said. “I had had it with myself. I had it with my family, with my friends. I just had it and I was over it.”
So she hit record to see if anyone wanted to join her.
In the 20 minutes between posting that video to all of her platforms and arriving home, Sanders was gaining hundreds of thousands of followers, she said.
Response from followers
Sanders said she was “a little confused” by the response. She has been a creator for years and has had viral content before, but she said, “this was just something different.”
Within a few weeks, millions of people were following Sanders.
She said she became scared and for a while, she turned off her computer. Then, she decided to read the comments.
“One of the main things that women were saying was, ‘me too, me too,’ and ‘thank you for speaking up, thank you for using your voice,’” Sanders said. “All of this is just with Melani just being Melani.”
That was enough in that moment, Sanders said, and over the past year she is “slowly coming to grips with I’m enough.”
Menopause and perimenopause experience
What has surprised Sanders most about the menopause or perimenopause experience is that nobody was talking about it, she said.
Sanders said she had a great surgeon for her hysterectomy but was not told anything about perimenopause or menopause. She had to figure it out on her own.
Community and announcements
A big part of the We Do Not Care Club is Sanders’ funny “special announcements.”
She said members send ideas for them in the comments.
“‘Everyone, we’re all putting the world on notice of what we ‘simply just do not care much about anymore,’” Sanders said.
Sanders said the support from the “We Do Not Care Club” gives her courage.

title: What we know about the cost of Maine’s latest ranked-choice count
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
The ranked-choice count that sealed U.S. Rep.-elect Paul LePage’s win over Democrat Matt Dunlap in Maine’s 2nd District will cost less than the nearly $246,000 spent on June’s primary count, state officials said Thursday.
The main reason is overtime. Secretary of State Shenna Bellows’ office did not pay staff to work extra hours on a race that Dunlap already conceded last week.
But it is the second time in two years that blank ballots have pushed an effectively decided 2nd District race into a count. That has added fuel to a long-running debate over the system. Republicans have opposed it since voters adopted it in 2016, and U.S. Rep. Jared Golden’s 2018 win was the first congressional race decided by the method.
A final price tag isn’t available yet. But officials “know it will be lower than the June cost report as we are not having staff work overtime for this round,” Jana Spaulding, a Bellows spokesperson, said before the count was finalized.
Rep. David Boyer, R-Poland, who pushed for changes to the process due to blank ballots two years ago and sits on the Legislature’s voting committee, said he expects this count to cost $40,000 to $45,000. He said that’s about what the 2024 count cost, when the race between Golden and state Rep. Austin Theriault, R-Fort Kent, dragged on for several days.
Most of a count’s cost comes from overtime and travel. Paper ballots and thumb drives holding results have to be retrieved from towns across the sprawling district, with help from state troopers, and driven to Augusta so officials can reconcile them. In a district that is the biggest east of the Mississippi River, that means a lot of miles.
The June count came under more pressure. Minor technical problems and clerical errors delayed results by at least a day and set off a debate over how they would be released to the public and the candidates. This time, the tabulation only confirmed a result both sides had accepted. LePage, a former two-term governor, declared victory.
“I appreciate [Bellows] using her discretion to not bring in staff for overtime,” Boyer said. “The guy already conceded; there’s no rush.”
State law still required the count. LePage led Dunlap in first-choice votes, but more than 6,000 blank and write-in ballots kept him short of a majority. He ended up winning by almost 5,500 votes. The 2024 race played out the same way, with more than 12,000 blank ballots keeping both Golden and Theriault under a majority in the first round. Theriault asked for a recount.
Boyer has argued that a count shouldn’t be required in a two-person race when blank ballots are the only thing keeping a candidate from a majority. He said he doesn’t believe ranked-choice voting is stacked against Republicans, but in those cases, “it seems a little too much.” He said he is unlikely to bring his proposal back in the new session, though he would back a Democrat’s bill written with good governance in mind.
“I just think we have to be better stewards of our tax dollars,” Boyer said. “Unfortunately any reform proposed to RCV is taken as a way to undermine it or not make it work.”

title: Falling gas prices aren’t proof gas companies inflated prices to hurt Trump
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Falling gas prices aren’t proof gas companies inflated prices to hurt Trump
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
Falling gas prices in the week after the Nov. 3 election created online speculation about the shift.
“Gas prices are dropping, which means the gas companies purposely increased the prices so you would blame Trump and vote blue,” read several social media posts, including one from an Instagram account called Republican Party (which is not an official GOP account) and from conservative influencer David J. Harris Jr. “It had nothing to do with the Iran war,” Harris posted.
But prices have been falling since late September, well before the election. Energy market experts attribute the decline largely to seasonal shifts and increasing Middle East oil exports.
The U.S. average gas price dropped below $4 for the first time since July on the week of Nov. 9. The nationwide average on Nov. 11 was about $3.94, more than $0.50 below the peak of $4.48 on Sept. 21.
The average on the West Coast was $5.11 on Nov. 9, compared with $5.60 on Sept. 21.
Gas prices generally drop in the autumn. People drive less, which reduces demand, and gas stations switch over to a wintertime gasoline blend that is cheaper than gasoline sold in the summer, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for the gasoline price tracker GasBuddy.
Hugh Daigle, a University of Texas at Austin associate professor of petroleum and geosystems engineering, said recent prices have fallen a little more than what’s normal for this time of year, but the change is still in line with seasonal trends.
“I think the overall trend is mostly normal seasonal fluctuations,” Daigle said, adding that more oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz helps, too.
Average U.S. gas prices have gone down every week since Sept. 21, according to Energy Information Administration data. The current price is still higher than it was at this time in the last four years.
The Iran war is the main cause of this year’s spike in gas prices. After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping route, restraining global oil supply.
Changes in the global oil flow and Trump’s posture on Iran have also helped ease prices, De Haan said. Trump said on Nov. 9 he didn’t see a need for more military strikes. Despite continuing attacks from Iran on commercial tankers in the strait, oil exports from the Middle East have increased through the strait and alternative routes, like oil pipelines, increasing oil supply.
Some analysts have also said Democrats’ election win had an effect on oil prices, even though no policy has changed yet. Oil prices are based partly on expectations, and the next Congress could affect how the war is funded and conducted.
There’s no reason to believe gas companies purposely inflated prices, De Haan said.
Oil is traded on a global market, and American gas companies have little ability to dictate the price of oil and gas. And Democrats tend to regulate the oil and gas industry more than Republicans, so there’s no clear incentive for oil companies to tip the scale for Democrats, De Haan said.
“There’s never going to be a shortage of these conspiracy theories, but ultimately, as an analyst that’s been covering markets for 20 years, I see all the numbers behind the scenes, and I’m not worried about conspiracies,” De Haan said.
Our ruling
Social media posts said falling gas prices mean “the gas companies purposely increased the prices so you would blame Trump and vote blue.”
Gas prices are following normal seasonal trends, and new developments around the Iran war are bringing down oil prices. The decrease began before the election, and there’s no evidence it was coordinated by gas companies to hurt Trump.
We rate the claim False.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com. It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Angus King is standing by Chuck Schumer in challenge for Senate leadership
text:
WASHINGTON — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that is why he is running.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate majority leader.”
Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race, which will be the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
Sen. Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats and will vote in the leadership election, is among those who have said they will support Schumer.
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins for Maine’s other seat, said throughout his campaign that he wouldn’t support Schumer.
A Jackson spokesperson said in a statement that the senator-elect “looks forward to speaking with Senator Van Hollen in the coming weeks.”
“The next Senate majority leader needs to be ready to do what’s right for working families and the people of Maine,” the spokesperson said.
The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote, even before Van Hollen entered the race. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election and many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal.
Making the pitch for his reelection, Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer opened discussion on a broad plan for their first 100 days in power that included healthcare and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war.
“I’m going to win it,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.
In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.
“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
Divisions over Schumer have simmered since 2025
While Schumer is favored to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025, when Schumer was put on the defensive after he sided with Republicans on a spending vote.
Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.
Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.
While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least two backers: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, and progressive standard-bearer Bernie Sanders.
El-Sayed posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.”
“I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, held a news conference Tuesday announcing he would not support Schumer. He posted Thursday night that the American people “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats.”
Van Hollen has not yet laid out his own agenda, but he has criticized Schumer for his ties to Israel and other special interests.
While Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, he has strongly criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza.
Schumer says he has broad support
Several senators besides King have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week. Beyond the election wins, those who support him say being the leader is a difficult job, experience is necessary and Schumer has proven himself with legislative successes when they held the Senate under President Joe Biden.
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” King said in a statement Thursday. “Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible.”
Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., also posted her support Thursday evening:
Cortez Masto said Schumer was key in “securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader.”

title: ‘I literally was a walking stroke’: A growing need for organ donations among Black Americans
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (InvestigateTV) — Black Americans face a critical need for organ transplants, yet they experience longer wait times and lower donation rates.
In 2026, African Americans accounted for more than a quarter of those on the organ transplant waiting list.
But at the same time, they made up only about 12% of all donors and nearly a quarter of total transplant recipients nationwide.
Health experts say the need is driven by higher rates of conditions like diabetes and high blood pressure. If those conditions are unmanaged it can lead to organ failure, especially kidney disease.
In fact, kidney disease is often called a “silent killer” because people can live with the condition for years without noticeable symptoms.
If you’ve ever tuned into a College of Charleston men’s basketball game, you’ve heard Everett German’s voice. That’s because he’s their official play-by-play announcer.
“So I announce all the games on the radio and our local TV games. In my 20th year of doing that. So this is a place that I’m familiar and comfortable with here at TD Arena,” German said.
He calls the love for his play-by-play work the why behind his why. But about 20 years ago, he faced a season of shakeups.
“I’m an account executive, so I’m constantly staring, you know, at a computer screen. And just one day I just started having blurry vision. I mean like my eyes, I’m like, ‘Oh, maybe again it’s time for me to get glasses.’ Wear and tear, so forth and so on,” German said.
So he went in for a visit with his optometrist. German said even though his tests didn’t appear abnormal, the doctor recommended he get his blood pressure checked.
“My blood pressure was 220 over 160. I literally was a walking stroke and the only symptoms I had was blurred vision,” German said.
He was immediately admitted to the hospital. His kidneys were failing with only 12% function left. For about five years, he was able to manage his condition with medication. But once his kidney function dropped to 5%, he needed a new organ. So he reached out to those who knew him best.
“It was something I blasted out to all my family, kind of letting them know what was going on and you know if anybody had interest in terms of being tested to be a donor,” he said.
After a year of being on dialysis, on June 8, 2011, German got the gift of life in the form of a transplant. His youngest sister, Charlene, became his kidney donor.
“She knows that if the roles were reversed, I would do the same. And you know, when you have that brother-sister connection, it’s just something that’s unbreakable and she didn’t hesitate. She did the testing and everything and everything she needed to do on her end and then when the time came, she was here and came through like my true hero,” German said.
This is the kind of success story that We Are Sharing Hope SC wants to see more of, especially in communities of color. The federally designated organization facilitates organ, eye and tissue donations throughout South Carolina.
“We currently have over 1,900 people that are on the waitlist and over 56% of those are African-American. So, a lot of that is based on the lack of education around it and lack of trust,” Krystal Cau, director of communications for We Are Sharing Hope SC, said.
Cau said the organization actively works to dispel myths about organ, eye and tissue donations in order to offer clarity and establish trust with community members.
“One of the biggest things that we hear is if there is a heart on my license, you fall ill, you’re in an accident, the medical professional won’t help because an organization like Sharing Hope would want to retrieve organs. So there’s no truth to it,” she said.
German works alongside We Are Sharing Hope SC to share his story of kidney donation and to encourage others to register.
Cau explained the conversations surrounding organ donation can be scary, but they’re important.
“People don’t want to speak about death and what happens when we are no longer here. The fact of the matter is, is that it’s a decision that can change someone’s life. You can save up to eight people’s lives just by saying ‘yes’, and to enhance their tissue donations up to 75 people’s life. So the impact that that has alone is incredible,” she said.
It’s a kind of impact that’s giving German, a now 51-year-old husband and father of two, a second shot at life on and off the court.
“It’s just a new outlook on life. It just makes you more appreciative of the things I used to take for granted, you know,” he said.

title: UMaine Extension 4-H offers educational workshop on invasive species in Blue Hill
text:
BLUE HILL – University of Maine Cooperative Extension will offer Seaside Invasion, a free, hands-on learning activity for youth ages 5 to 13, from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 18 at Blue Hill Public Library, 5 Parker Point Road. The library is hosting the event as part of the 4-H Coastal Kids Science Series.
Participants will explore the challenges invasive species create for coastal ecosystems through a hands-on population survey. Youth will investigate how invasive green crabs affect native marine life and learn how human interventions can help protect and restore local habitats. UMaine Extension 4-H Youth Development Professional Leah McCluskey will lead the activity.
The event is free, and no registration is required. Additional information is available on the event webpage.
For more information or if reasonable accommodation is needed, please contact Leah McCluskey at 207-667-8212 or leah.mccluskey@maine.edu.

title: Styling for the holidays and the rest of winter
text:
The holiday season has a way of inspiring us to layer in warmth, sparkle and sentiment, but the key to decorating well this time of year is creating a look that still feels fresh and inviting long after the last cookie has been eaten. The best seasonal styling doesn’t expire on Dec. 26; it shifts gracefully into the quieter months that follow. With a thoughtful approach to color palette, texture and placement, your home can feel festive now and effortlessly cozy all winter long.
Start with a cohesive theme and color palette
Rather than collecting bits and pieces of holiday decor, choose a theme or palette that guides your decisions. Whether it’s soft winter whites, traditional red and green, organic minimalism or modern metallics, consistency is what creates visual harmony. Sticking to one palette also makes it easier to remove explicitly holiday-themed elements later while keeping the core winter decor intact.
Create a welcoming glow
Lighting is the heart of winter coziness. Layer lighting at different heights to create depth and warmth: string lights along a banister, candles on the mantel, lanterns on the floor near a fireplace (placed safely) or small lamps on side tables. The goal isn’t brightness; it’s softness and atmosphere. Lighting that flickers or diffuses creates the feeling of being wrapped in a blanket.
About the author
Jacqueline Kennedy is the owner and lead designer at Spruced Interiors, which works with homeowners and Realtors to transform houses into highly desired homes. With 10 years of experience in high end design and color consultations, Kennedy’s style is timeless, deploying vibrant color to catch a potential buyer’s eye.
(207) 899-7841
spruced-interiors.com
Instagram: @sprucedinteriors
Incorporate nature (and keep it simple)
Winter decor shines when it feels connected to the season. Think pine cones, evergreen clippings, holly sprigs or dried citrus garlands. These elements not only bring texture and warmth but also feel timeless beyond the holidays. Local greenery is both cost-effective and more visually authentic than plastic substitutes.
Craft nostalgic vignettes
It can feel overwhelming to decorate the whole house. Instead, focus on meaningful vignettes, such as small, curated decor groupings on a mantel, coffee table, entry console or windowsill. Choose one to three items that tell a story: a candle, a family keepsake or a seasonal branch. These clusters draw the eye naturally and keep your space feeling thoughtful rather than cluttered.
Lean into winter textures
A mohair throw draped over the bed, heavier cotton or flannel sheets, layered pillows in wool or velvet. These subtle swaps instantly transition a home from summer-light to winter-warm. On coffee tables, pair candles and books with an organic accent: evergreen cuttings, winter berries, pine cones or even a simple grocery-store bouquet.
The magic of winter styling lies in warmth, simplicity and intention. Let your decor carry the glow of the holidays into the quiet beauty of the months that follow by keeping things simple and understated.

title: This woman and her dog have taken to the motorcycle life
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, SC (InvestigateTV) - Paige Parlato kicks her motorcycle alive, and her Doberman mix, Han, is ready to ride.
“He’s very laidback, he really likes to be where I’m at, but he really can have some energy if he wants to,” Parlato said.
Parlato and Han cruise weekly through the Grand Strand, turning heads everywhere they go.
“Normally, they’re in shock when he’s on the back, and they just want all of his attention,” Parlato said.
Parlato, a vet tech, adopted Han at 12 weeks old.
“He came in as a surrender with a broken jaw,” Parlato said. “The people couldn’t care for him, and I took him on in, and he’s been with me ever since.”
By day, the two clock in at the clinic.
“He goes, and he helps technicians learn new skills,” Parlato said.
The pair then turns to riding for their shared escape.
“Whenever he heard bikes, he associated them with friends,” Parlato said. “So whenever the bikes showed up, his friends showed up, and he got to play and have fun, and he was not scared of the sounds. He was out there with everyone.”
She recorded Han’s excitement for the open road before they suited up for safety. Han slipped into his adventure backpack and goggles before getting strapped onto Parlato’s back.
“We try to keep off the busier roads. Places where he can enjoy and we don’t have to go too fast,” Parlato said.
The pair posts their adventures on social media.
“It just makes people smile, so I want more people to see them; he makes people happy,” Parlato said. “I just enjoy being with him, and he enjoys being with me, so it’s just a happy experience all around.”
Han also enjoys hiking, rock hunting for fossils and paddleboarding.

title: Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado loses House seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher
Ketamine infusion therapy could offer hope for chronic pain patients
text:
(Aging Untold) — Millions of Americans live with chronic pain. The epidemic is often hidden behind closed doors as patients suffer in silence, according to research published in the “Journal of Primary Care & Community Health.”
Chronic pain, such as back pain, arthritis and headaches, including migraines, is often described as aching, burning, shooting or throbbing.
For those who cannot get relief from traditional pain management methods, some in the medical community are promoting ketamine infusion as a possible solution. The treatment works by slowing down pain-sensing nerves that send messages to the brain.
Elanor Koch of Nebraska said she has seen improvement since starting the therapy.
In 2020, doctors found a tumor on her cervical spine that had eroded and compressed her spinal cord by more than 60%.
“Before, I would wake up in pain and live life in pain, and I’d only have so much in me I could give a day until I would push myself into a flare that would leave me in bed for a handful of days,” Koch said.
She went through neck fusion surgery, then had to relearn to walk and use her left arm. Still, she experienced debilitating pain.
“Couldn’t get a hold of or a grasp on how to manage my pain in a way that felt safe or effective,” Koch said. “Opioid pain therapy didn’t feel like a good long-term solution, and other alternative pain-management areas were not working.”
Finding relief through ketamine treatment
In 2023, Koch found ketamine infusion therapy at Mind and Body Wellness Center.
The off-label treatment is said to help the brain process thoughts and emotions more effectively.
“When I’ve went through ketamine, I had a perspective that I’d never been able to force myself into,” Koch said. “To see it for what it is and understand that that’s part of the experience of why we’re here and it didn’t feel like my pain was as daunting.”
During the hour-long sessions, patients experience dissociation.
“You’re not fully aware of your physical body and you’re kind of just hanging out in your head for a while,” Koch said.
After six treatments in one month, Koch said she experienced significant improvement.
“I was like pain free for three months,” she said. “I had minor flares every once in a while, but they weren’t long lasting, and they weren’t very common or close together.”
Koch requires maintenance infusions about every few months.
Cost barriers limit access
Infusions cost $400 to 500 per session and are not covered by insurance.
Dr. Stephen Salzbrenner at Nebraska Medicine said the price keeps more people from accessing the treatment.
“It’s pretty widely accepted in the scientific community that it’s effective and so it’s offered,” Salzbrenner said. “Now it’s not often covered by insurance ‘cause it’s not approved. If it was FDA-approved for depression, then insurance might cover it as a treatment.”
FDA-approved alternative available
Salzbrenner offers an alternative treatment that is FDA-approved and accepted by insurance for depression.
Esketamine is a nasal spray that’s chemically related to ketamine but has a distinct chemical makeup.
“It can happen within hours, it’s really pretty remarkable,” Salzbrenner said. “Because a lot of the traditional antidepressants we have take six weeks, eight weeks, before you really know if it’s going to help.”
Salzbrenner said it’s essential to combine the treatment with talk therapy.
“Therapy is really indispensable,” he said. “You can’t replicate that with a medicine.”
Koch agrees with that approach.
“I have a psychiatrist and a talk therapist,” she said. “I’m no longer taking any antidepressive medications. If my word counts for anything as somebody who could barely get out of bed two years ago, I’d say try it.”

title: Ask 8 Investigates: Can you drive with handwritten license plates?
text:
Ask 8 Investigates: Can you drive with handwritten license plates?
Temporary plates may be needed if your license plates are lost or damaged
Ask 8 Investigates: Can you drive with handwritten license plates?
Temporary plates may be needed if your license plates are lost or damaged
A viewer who saw a handwritten license plate on the road asked 8 Investigates whether it was legal.
According to the Maine Secretary of State’s Office, handwritten temporary plates are allowed. They may be needed if plates are lost, such as in a crash, or become unreadable from wear and tear.
State law requires drivers to report lost plates within 24 hours. While waiting for replacement plates to arrive by mail, drivers must use temporary plates that conform as closely as possible to the originals. The Secretary of State’s Office recommends keeping a copy of the lost plate form in the glove box.
A spokesperson for the office said of the plate in the viewer’s photo: “This does not appear to be someone who just lost their plates and ordered new ones – this isn’t a normal number pattern of our plates, and it looks like they have a metal plate underneath the paper.”
If you have a question you want answered, email 8investigates@wmtw.com. The team reads every email.

title: Microsoft explains what caused global outage, Outlook to go down for millions of users
text:
REDMOND, Wash. (Gray News) - Microsoft has apologized for a global service outage that has disrupted millions of users this week.
The tech giant took to social media on Friday to offer an apology to its users while explaining the cause of the outage that appeared to have started on Thursday.
“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” Microsoft shared.
The Microsoft outage disrupted business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and left multiple businesses across the world without access to Outlook emails and other platforms.
On Friday, Microsoft said it was making headway as it worked to restore services.
“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” the company said.
According to Microsoft, the outage was related to a technical issue that was not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” Microsoft said.
The company added that it has been restoring services gradually while validating stability at each stage, a process that has taken longer, but it has helped ensure a stable restoration.
The total number of people affected by the outage was not immediately shared, but the company stated earlier this year that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

title: ‘General Hospital’ actor releases statement after son is charged in fatal hit-and-run
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Jack Antonio Sabàto appeared in court Thursday for a hearing in the case stemming from a hit-and-run that killed pedestrian Carl Simmonds.
Sabàto, 32, is charged with the felony crime of leaving an accident without assisting and a misdemeanor count of leaving the scene of an accident involving injury or death.
Statement from Sabàto’s father
Sabàto is the son of actors Antonio Sabàto Jr., of “General Hospital,” and Virginia Madsen, known for roles in movies like “Candyman” and “Sideways.”
In a statement posted to his Facebook page Wednesday, Sabàto Jr. offered condolences to the family and loved ones of the person killed, said his love for his children remains unconditional, and asked the public and media to respect his family’s privacy.
“I also wish to extend my heartfelt condolences to the family and loved ones of the gentleman who tragically lost his life. My thoughts and prayers are with them as well,” Sabàto Jr. said.
What the charging document says
According to the charging document filed Nov. 10, Anchorage police and firefighters responded around 5:48 a.m. Monday to a body on the sidewalk along Airport Heights Drive near the Blood Bank of Alaska.
Officers identified the person as Simmonds and found broken vehicle parts nearby.
Prosecutors said surveillance video from the blood bank shows a white Chevrolet Tahoe hitting Simmonds around 5:35 a.m. The charging document says no braking was observed before or after the collision.
Police traced a registered white Tahoe to Sabàto and found the vehicle at an Amazon warehouse around 12:45 p.m. with fresh damage to its front-right corner, according to the document. Officers obtained a warrant to seize the vehicle.
The document says Sabàto called police at 2:46 p.m. and reported that he had struck an animal. When officers spoke with him, he said he had been doing late-night DoorDash deliveries and was on his way home when something appeared in the road.
He said he knew he had hit something, but did not know it was a person, according to the charging document.
Prosecutors said Sabàto told officers he did not stop to check because he was scared and did not have insurance. He also said he called police after his girlfriend told him the Tahoe had been taken, according to the document.
Tuesday’s hearing
At Tuesday’s hearing, a defense attorney challenged the state’s characterization of the case and argued that Sabàto had contacted police and cooperated. The attorney also asked for lower bail and a no-driving condition, citing Sabàto’s lack of criminal history.
The court set bail at $5,000 cash performance and $5,000 unsecured appearance, meaning the second amount does not have to be posted, but could be assessed if Sabàto fails to appear.
The judge also ordered him not to drive, sit in a vehicle’s driver’s seat or possess vehicle keys.
The charging document said the Alaska Public Safety Information Network showed no prior state convictions for Sabàto.
Blood bank video and family
The Blood Bank of Alaska is checking with police and its board of directors to determine whether footage of the crash can be publicly released.
KTUU also reached out to Simmonds’ family, who declined to speak.
In a Nov. 9 Facebook post, Crystal Tickett asked for help finding Simmonds, saying he left Alaska Regional Hospital around 5 a.m. that morning. Tickett wrote that she filed a missing persons report. A spokesperson for Anchorage police said the department does not have a record of the report.
The judge set Sabàto’s next pre-indictment hearing for Dec. 3.

title: Hermon football stifles Greely in Class C semifinal
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
CUMBERLAND — In consecutive late-season losses at Greely and against Leavitt, the Hermon Hawks learned what it would take to win playoff football games against the southern powers in Maine’s statewide Class C.
Friday night in a rematch against Greely, the Hawks showed they not only had learned, but they could also apply those lessons with impressive physical effort from start to finish in a 17-10 semifinal victory.
“We learned after that game that we lost that we had to be tougher and stop making mistakes,” said Sam Hopkins, Hermon’s leading rusher. “And we learned that the North can play with anybody. People write us off because we’re from the North, but we’re just small-town kids who love to play.”
Hermon’s defense bottled up the second-seeded Rangers and standout senior quarterback Luke Piper for nearly the entire game. Hermon had three fourth-down stops — including on fourth-and-2 at the 3. The Hawks, led by linebacker Dylan Yeo (three tackles for loss, including a sack), also forced three turnovers.
Hermon wasn’t perfect. Hopkins fumbled on Hermon’s first offensive play. The second half started with Greely recovering an onside kick. In the third quarter, Hopkins and quarterback Griffin Dunton botched an exchange, and Greely took over at the Hermon 16. The defense held Greely to a 32-yard field goal by Jack Carthy, however, and the Hawks’ offense responded with an eight-play, 72-yard touchdown drive.
Greely beat Hermon 28-14 in a Week 7 game in Cumberland. In that contest, the Rangers’ held Hermon to 136 yards and pulled away from a 14-14 halftime tie. The next week, Hermon led undefeated Leavitt 10-0 at halftime but lost 14-10.
“I said to our team, losses like that can sometimes blossom to better things,” Hermon coach Kyle Gallant said.
Hermon (9-2) will face Leavitt (11-0) in the state championship game next Saturday at Lewiston High. Hermon lost to Fryeburg Academy, 28-0, in the 2024 state final — the Hawks’ only previous title game appearance.
“We’re not done. We have one more week. Let’s go,” Hopkins said.
Another difference for Hermon is that Dunton, a sophomore, is now sharing snaps at quarterback with junior Ethan Curtis, a move Gallant made after the two losses.
“He’s a great athlete. We weren’t giving him the ball enough,” Gallant said. “When you have Hopkins and Dunton in the backfield together, it’s hard to figure out who has the ball.”
Dunton scored both Hermon touchdowns on runs of 8 and 26 yards, the latter with 7:34 remaining to give the Hawks a 17-3 lead. He finished with 83 yards on 15 carries. Hopkins was the workhorse, with 23 carries for 161 yards.
For Greely’s seniors, the result was a rare loss. Those players went to three straight state championship games. They won the 8-man Large School title in 2024 and were unbeaten Class C champs last season in the school’s return to 11-man football. Greely’s record over the last three season is 29-3.
“This senior class, all they’ve known is competing in state championships,” said Greely coach Caleb King. “And that wasn’t an accident. They love football. They worked hard every day. We just fell a little bit short this year.”
The Rangers’ running game was held to 105 yards on 32 carries, with just one run going for more than 10 yards. Piper, a dangerous runner, gained 37 yards on 12 carries, and fullback Noah Allen had 13 carries for 26 yards.
That forced Piper to go to the air. The passing game was inconsistent, with Piper completing 12 of 28 passes for 221 yards. A good chunk of those came on an 87-yard touchdown pass to Jackson Justice with 35 seconds to play.
Yeo recovered the onside kick to seal Hermon’s win.
“It’s a great ride. Whatever you get out of the game is what you put into it, and all the boys, all four years, we’ve put everything into this game and we’ve gotten everything out of it,” Piper said. “Obviously, you want to win your senior year, but it can’t always happen.”
STATISTICS
• Hermon: Sam Hopkins (23 carries, 161 yards), Griffin Dunton (15 carries, 83 yards, 2 TDs; 2 for 2 passing, 26 yards), Dylan Yeo (6 carries, 15 yards; 3 tackles for loss, 1 sack)
• Greely: Luke Piper (12 for 28 passing, 221 yards, 1 INT; 12 carries, 37 yards), Jackson Justice (5 carries, 26 yards; 4 receptions, 108 yards, 1 TD), Noah Allen (13 carries, 26 yards; 4 catches, 61 yards), James Tyll (3 catches, 58 yards)

title: Housing market in Maine eases as sales volume and prices drop
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing market in Maine eases as sales volume and prices drop
There are more homes on the market now than a year ago, but experts say mortgage interest rates are having an impact.
Housing market in Maine eases as sales volume and prices drop
There are more homes on the market now than a year ago, but experts say mortgage interest rates are having an impact.
The housing market is easing in Maine. A report from the Maine Association of Realtors on Thursday found that the total number of single-family homes that sold in October was down 6.58% compared to October of 2025 and the median sales price was down 5.63 percent.
The median sales prices for the state in October was $402,500. In October of 2025, the median sales price in Maine was $426,500.
If you compare the three-month period of August through October, however, the median sales price is unchanged from a year ago, holding steady at $415,000. The number of homes sold for that three month period dropped 6.75% from a year ago.
“As we move into the fourth quarter, buyer demand has softened as mortgage interest rates are shaping market dynamics,” said Judy Oberg, 2026 President of the Maine Association of Realtors. “Statewide, buyers have more homes to choose from than last year and more room to negotiate. Sellers are facing more competition from other listings and that’s reflected in the median sold prices.”
The sales volume drop is in line with national and regional trends, with overall sales across the country down 8.6% in October compared to a year ago. Sales across the northeast United States were down 4.1%. However, while the median price dropped in Maine, prices across the country were up 0.4% to $421,900 and prices across the northeast were up 3.2% to $519,600.
The highest home prices in the state continue to be in Cumberland County, where the median price for the last three months was $600,000. York County is second at $560,000, followed by Lincoln County at $522,500 and Hancock County at $505,000.
The lowest prices continue to be in Aroostook County, where the median sales price for the last three months was $168,250. The next lowest median price is in Washington County, where the price was $241,500. Piscataquis County came in at $242,000 and Somerset County was at $252,500.
The biggest sales price increase, by percentage, was in Franklin County, where prices rose 22.41% compared to a year ago to a current median sales price of $355,000. There were also double-digit percentage gains in Hancock and Lincoln Counties.
The biggest drop in sales prices, by percentage, was in Washington County, where prices dropped 14.51%.

title: Batesies: Take a Stand Against Bigotry in Lewiston Mayoral Runoffs
text:
When I first came to Bates in 2023, I was impressed that a small city in this predominantly white state could have overcome such vitriolic xenophobia to have a thriving community of immigrants involved across the community. Of course I knew that racism and bigotry was still real here in Maine, just as anywhere else. But I also found great appreciation in the community efforts to bring Lewistonians together, whether they were originally French, Somali, Angolan, Thai or from anywhere else in the world.
Much of this progress could be reversed if Rick LaChapelle is elected the next mayor of Lewiston.
After the midterm election results were finalized, there was no clear winner of the Lewiston mayoral race. The top two candidates in this technically nonpartisan race were self-identified Republican Rick LaChapelle, with 6,164 votes or 45.7%, and current mayor and self-identified Democrat Carl Sheline, with 4,766 votes or 35.3%. By contrast, Democratic senator-elect Troy Jackson received 7,730 votes, or 53.8%, in Lewiston.
You may not know much about LaChapelle; I certainly did not until recently. Everything I have learned about him, though, has struck me with disgust and fear for the Lewiston community should he be elected.
Mayors in Lewiston serve a part-time role. They can rarely vote in city council matters and largely act as a presiding figurehead. This means that they need to be community-oriented and focused on uniting people, not driving them apart.
On Sept. 15, LaChapelle advocated for greater ICE enforcement at a city council meeting. Publicly available minutes from this meeting describe LaChapelle as expressing concern that “There is an active warrant for someone who assaulted a police officer. ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] picked up the person, but ICE cannot work with LPD [Lewiston Police Department] per city ordinance, so they had to let him go.”
In a video of the meeting posted on social media by Sheline, LaChapelle’s rhetoric is even worse.
“I implore this council to change their view,” LaChapelle said, speaking to a city ordinance that prevents LPD from cooperating with ICE. “This is no longer a sanctuary city. [LPD], start cooperating with ICE.”
ICE, of course, has allowed 32 people to die in its custody this year as of Oct. 29, and has murdered several others on the streets, including Johan Sebastián Guerrero of Biddeford on July 13. Protecting our fellow Lewistonians from ICE should be the mandate of the city government. But this is not an article about ICE.
Lewiston has a long and unfortunate history of anti-immigrant sentiment, according to the Maine Memory Network. In the late 1800s, French Canadians arriving in the city were segregated from the rest of the population, forcing many to live in impoverished conditions. Speaking French in schools was made illegal in 1919 and only ended in 1969.
Less than a century later in 2002, then-mayor of Lewiston Laurier Raymond wrote a letter in the Sun Journal imploring Somali immigrants to “exercise restraint” in moving to the city. After Raymond’s letter, people formed the “Many and One” coalition to show support for Somalis, many of whom are refugees.
In 2012, then-mayor Bob MacDonald said of Somali Lewistonians, “don’t try to insert your culture, which obviously isn’t working, into ours, which does.”
To elaborate upon the entire history of Lewiston’s relationship with its Somali community, both the ups and downs, would take thousands of words. It is clear that many Lewistonians believe, rightly, that Somali immigrants make the city richer. And it is also true that many do not. I fear it is the latter’s voices who may prevail in this mayoral election, but not if we actually turn out and vote.
It concerns me deeply to see how LaChapelle voters discuss immigration issues in Facebook threads, such as these below.
“Will ICE be there?? May cut down on some illegal voting,” reads one comment on LaChapelle’s post about the upcoming runoff.
“How many more BMW’s and Mercedes do the Lewiston people have to supply refugees that will never work a day in their life?” reads another comment under a post of Sheline’s.
“I myself demand a recount, and to reject all ballots that were manipulated by interpreters, or anyone that can’t read English,” says another.
We cannot ignore this. Allowing xenophobia to rule this city is a thousand steps backward, and we cannot let it happen.
Carl Sheline stands for immigrant rights and unity. His platform includes increasing public safety through more youth programs and local school investment, building more affordable housing and encouraging small businesses to come to Lewiston, and of course, maintaining Lewiston as an immigrant-friendly city.
The election is on Dec. 15 and registered Lewiston voters can cast their ballots at Longley School on 145 Birch Street. Early voting starts on Nov. 16 at Lewiston City Hall in the City Clerk’s Office, 27 Pine Street, second floor.
Batesies, do not sit this election out. Elect Carl Sheline for another term as mayor and send a message against bigotry.

title: How to reset when stress becomes chronic
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many people, stress feels like a bigger part of everyday life. When stress becomes chronic, it can bring physical effects.
According to the American Psychological Association, most Americans say their stress has increased, and about 75% report physical or emotional symptoms as a result.
We are sharing what people can do about it when stress becomes chronic.
When normal stress crosses the line
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the stress response itself is normal.
“If you have a tiger running at you, you’re going to run,” Rogers said. “You have to have that response so you can stay focused.”
However, stress becomes chronic “when you can’t turn it off.”
“But you can’t run from the tiger all day long,” she said.
How chronic stress shows up in the body
Rogers said physical effects of chronic stress can include a faster heart rate and higher blood pressure.
“Immune system takes a hit,” she said.
Rogers said many people now deal with ongoing stressors because of multitasking. When it lingers, there can be detrimental effects, she said.
“It’s a constant influx of information and interaction where there’s not any downtime,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said, adding that adrenaline and cortisol levels stay high as a result.
Rogers said children are affected too.
“We’re also seeing a greater increase of stress-related diseases happening in younger people,” Cradduck said.
Rogers said the body doesn’t know the difference between the types of stress.
If a person’s gut is off or insulin is high, Rogers said, the body reacts the same way and cortisol increases.
Cortisol is the body’s primary stress hormone, according to Mayo Clinic.
Rogers said swelling and fluid retention can also be signs that the body is under stress.
For menopausal women who have good control with hormones, Rogers said, hot flashes returning can be the “number one” sign that stress is present.
Why a break matters
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a personal story about stress. Her mother was sick and dying, and there was no end in sight. Friends convinced her to leave for a trip to Chicago and visit museums.
“I didn’t want to go. It just felt so wrong and bad,” O’Rourke said. “I went and then I went back to see her, and I felt like a totally different person.”
You might not think you need a break, but go ahead and take it, she said.
“Go for a walk. Get a good night’s sleep. Do something that brings you joy or comfort or happiness, because it really will offset the stress that you’re under,” O’Rourke said.
Quick ways to calm the body
The goal is to activate the parasympathetic nervous system, Rogers said, which she described as the “rest and digest” state, rather than the fight-or-flight response of the sympathetic nervous system.
Rogers and O’Rourke listed several options:
- Box breathing: Inhale for four seconds, hold for four seconds, exhale for four seconds, hold for four seconds
- Mudra
- Humming, singing and gargling, which Rogers said activate the vagus nerve
- Alternating nostril breathing
“It’s a very quick way to drop your stress,” Rogers said of activating the vagus nerve.
Cradduck also suggested a release. “Go sit in your car and roll up your windows and scream.”
Cradduck said family caregivers may not be able to step away for a museum visit.
“Sometimes they’re in that so deeply that they can’t,” Cradduck said. For them, she recommended box breathing, centering, “anything that can allow your body to have that release.”
O’Rourke said that when a client starts crying and stops out of embarrassment, she tells them to let it go.
“I know how much relief they’re going to get from just sitting there and sobbing,” she said.
The experts also shared the SEEDS method:
- Sleep
- Exercise
- Engagement
- Diet
- Active Stress Management
Key takeaways
- Do not normalize high stress. “What your mind suppresses, your body expresses,” Rogers says.
- Ignoring stress will not stop it from physically damaging the heart, brain and immune system.
- SEEDS method: Sleep, exercise, engagement, diet, active stress management

title: Angus King backs Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
U.S. Sen. Angus King will back New York’s Chuck Schumer to lead the U.S. Senate.
That puts the soon-to-be senior senator from Maine at odds with U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who affirmed late last week that he wouldn’t support giving Schumer the gavel.
King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, credited Schumer with Democrats’ stunning success in last week’s election, which handed them at least a 55-seat majority in the upper chamber after Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi and at least a 255-seat majority in the U.S. House of Representatives. Just under a dozen House races have yet to be called, while results are outstanding just in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, where Democrat Mary Peltola has a narrow lead.
“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” King said in a Friday statement.
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” he said.
But the Democratic caucus is divided over whether to anoint Schumer U.S. Senate majority leader. U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland on Thursday announced that he would jockey with Schumer for the gavel, saying that “the American people called for change” in the midterm election.
In Maine, Schumer was instrumental in convincing outgoing Gov. Janet Mills to run for the Democratic nomination in the U.S. Senate race.
Her loss to insurgent candidate Graham Platner was seen as a repudiation of Democratic powerbrokers like Schumer. And when Platner’s campaign imploded after an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape, Schumer notably kept to the sidelines as Maine Democrats scrambled to find a replacement, telling Politico back in July, “I’m staying out of Maine.”
One anonymous Democratic strategist bluntly told Politico at the time that Schumer’s influence was “toxic.”

title: Calais businesses invite shoppers downtown for ‘Ladies’ Day Out’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CALAIS, Maine (WABI) - Business owners in Calais are inviting shoppers downtown this weekend as the community continues to adjust to fewer Canadian visitors.
Calais and St. Stephen, New Brunswick, are neighboring communities separated by an international border.
“One of the things about Calais and St. Stephen is that when there are no such thing as international borders, they really would be one community,” said Economic Development Director Bob Wheeler.
St. Croix Tap and Table owner Jayna Smith says recent tariffs and impacts from the pandemic have presented unique challenges for cross-border shopping.
As a Calais business owner and dual citizen, Smith says an upcoming event is helping to engage Calais locals in the downtown atmosphere.
“It’s my hope that with this event, people will come down to Calais, meet the new owners of these businesses, find a gift that they didn’t know they could buy here locally, and maybe come back another day,” said Smith.
This Saturday, an event called “Meet Me Downtown: A Ladies’ Day Out” aims to reintroduce shoppers to local women-owned businesses, some of which have opened over the last year.
“One of the biggest challenges is actually getting people through the door and just being able to talk to them. I think things like what Jayna is doing really helps us overcome that barrier,” said Harley Sanford of Divine Ink & Beauty.
Shoppers can pick up hand made “passport cards,” get them stamped at participating businesses, and turn them in for a chance at a grand prize.
Smith says that space in St. Croix will also be set aside for crafters as part of a Holiday Mini Mart.
“We do miss the shoppers we used to have from Canada. Many don’t come over anymore or fewer and fewer come over. We hope this will help let them know that we’re still here. We’re still welcoming to our Canadian friends and family,” said Smith.
Wheeler says the event is an example of the community’s entrepreneurial spirit.
“I think a lot of times people, a lot of the businesses, particularly here on Main Street, don’t get enough attention. So it’s hard to get them visible. This is a great example of getting people down here to make them visible,” said Wheeler.
The event runs until 3 p.m. Saturday. The first participating business opens at 8 a.m., and the others open at 10 a.m.
Passport cards must be turned in by 3 p.m.

title: Presque Isle students perform ‘Anastasia’ musical this weekend and next
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - A school musical about finding a family opens Friday in Presque Isle. Students in the production are also finding a family of their own behind the scenes.
Cast finds family in theater
In the musical “Anastasia,” the character Anya spends the show looking for her home. For Jada Cyr, who plays Anya, home is the theater family she has had over the last three years.
“I feel like we’ve all supported each other so much that it’s very easy to kind of slip into roles where you’re like, this is my family, you know?” Cyr said.
Cyr said the performance is challenging. With many costume and scene changes, students on and off stage have spent many hours keeping the story moving from start to finish.
Crew and director on years together
Savannah Daniels, the set director, said actors and stage crew work together to bring each scene to life.
“Everybody sees the actors, but we have a group of superheroes backstage, too, making it so all of that is happening for the actors as well,” Daniels said.
Working together comes from years of experience, which many of the students have.
“A lot of these kids I’ve had for, you know, five, six, seven years at this point,” said Julie Stephenson, the director. “So it’s been amazing to just see how they grow and get more confident in themselves as the years go by and all the different roles they get to play and how they do them.”
A final show for seniors
For Cyr, the end of the show will be the end of an era.
“And I’m very grateful for the cast,” Cyr said. “They’re some of my closest friends, and so it’s very nice to like share the show with them, especially as my last one.”
For the seniors, the show is the finale with a theater family that has been together for years.
Show dates and tickets

title: VIDEO: Frankie Muniz says he's recovering after crash at Daytona International Speedway
text:
"I'm doing OK': Frankie Muniz recovering after crash at Daytona International Speedway
Actor and racecar driver Frankie Muniz is recovering after a crash at Daytona International Speedway that sent him to the hospital on Wednesday.
"First of all, I wanna say I'm doing OK. I'm extremely sore, but fortunately no major injuries. I'm not 100% sure how that's the case, but that's just a testament to how well-built the Ford Mustang Dark Horse R cars are," Muniz said in a video shared on X.
Muniz, who gained fame as a child actor and is well known for his role as Malcolm in "Malcolm in the Middle" and several films including "Agent Cody Banks," "Big Fat Liar," and "My Dog Skip," said he is grateful to be walking and plans to head home to Phoenix for the time being, adding he plans to return to the track soon. 
The crash occurred Wednesday while Muniz was practicing for the Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic event.
Van Richmond, a spectator, said that he witnessed the crash during practice.
"It's one of the hardest hits I've ever seen," Richmond said. "(...)They cut the entire roof of the car off and pulled him out."
According to his driver profile on NASCAR's website, Muniz "drives the No. 33 Team Reaume Ford full-time in the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series." Muniz and NASCAR driver Austin Cindric were set to represent Team Air Force in an exhibition race that benefits six nonprofits that support military and veteran communities through the Proud to Honor Fund, according to a NASCAR release.
A dozen Ford Racing drivers were split into six teams to race head-to-head in Mustang Dark Horse cars in honor of a branch of the U.S. military.

title: Obituary: Ernestine Marie Stoddard
SpaceX aims for first double catch of Starship in its most ambitious test flight yet
text:
SpaceX is launching Starship into orbit on Friday in its boldest test yet: a 22-hour flight that aims to recapture the entire rocket in a move meant to accelerate moon and Mars travel.
If all goes well, the massive booster will return to its Texas pad six minutes after blasting off and the bullet-shaped spacecraft will steer there the next day. Both will be plucked from midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower.
Everything was on track for Friday’s planned late afternoon launch of the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket, pending Federal Aviation Administration approval.
If Elon Musk and his team succeed, it will be the first time every single piece of a rocket that is launched into orbit gets retrieved for the purpose of recycling. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.
“It’s hard to describe how I’m going to feel when we pull this off,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center. “It’s so incredibly exciting. It’s such a feat of engineering.”
Once in orbit, Starship will deliver 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX has already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. This will be the first attempt to capture the upgraded version that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars travel. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters).
The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.
SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” Dontchev said.
SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.
Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said.
NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.
During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.

title: ‘Quiet the Sirens’, Colonial Theatre teams up with Upwell Psychiatry for a Robbins Lumber fire recovery fundraiser
text:
BELFAST – The Colonial Theatre is partnering with Upwell Psychiatry to present “Quiet the Sirens”, a documentary film focusing on psychedelics-based treatment of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder in first responders. All proceeds from ticket sales will go directly to first responders recovering from this year’s fire at the Robbins Lumber Mill.
This one-night special presentation will take place at 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 17 at the Colonial Theatre, located at 163 High St. in downtown Belfast. Tickets cost $15 and are available at the box office or in advance through the Colonial Theatre’s website. The evening will include a screening of the documentary and a post-screening community discussion.
“Quiet the Sirens” is a feature-length documentary by Mike Bernard that follows the journeys of three firefighters as they confront and recover from the effects of PTSD. Their quests for wellness lead them to an innovative Canadian mental health program that combines group therapy, peer support and psychedelic-assisted ketamine treatment, offering new options for individuals who have not found relief through conventional care.
“I chose to bring this film to communities here in Maine because, as a culture, we’ve become accustomed to suffering alone,” Jaclyn Burskey of Upwell Psychology said. “And I think this film offers another perspective: Perhaps the real medicine is found in coming together, where we can find ways to bear what feels unbearable, expand our understanding of what’s possible, and reconnect with something fundamental about being human: that we all suffer, that none of us are meant to go it alone, and that community is essential. My hope is that this film creates space for that kind of remembering.””
“Jaclyn had reached out to us prior to the Robbins Lumber Mill fire to organize this screening,” Cam Howard, Colonial Theatre Program Director, said. “We are really hoping that hosting this film screening will provide a setting where we can continue to process the impacts of the fire on our community.”
The Colonial Theatre is owned and operated by Hawthorne Arts Collaborative, a nonprofit organization rooted in the preservation of the century-old theatre and its continued operation as a cinema and arts hub. For more information, visit colonialtheatre.com.

title: Ex-Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleads guilty to lesser charge in 1997 killing
text:
(AP) - Former Oklahoma death row prisoner Richard Glossip, who spent nearly 30 years incarcerated and was on the brink of execution three times for a 1997 killing, pleaded guilty to a lesser charge, his attorney said Thursday.
Glossip had been sentenced to death over the killing in Oklahoma City of his former boss, motel owner Barry Van Treese. Van Treese was beaten with a baseball bat in what prosecutors have alleged was a murder-for-hire scheme.
Another man, Justin Sneed, admitted robbing and killing Van Treese, but testified that he did so after Glossip promised to pay him $10,000. Sneed was the state’s key witness against Glossip and was sentenced to life in prison.
The U.S. Supreme Court previously threw out Glossip’s conviction, and he was released on bond in May to await retrial. His longstanding claims of innocence have drawn support from Kim Kardashian and other prominent figures.
With Glossip’s plea to a lesser accessory charge, the murder charge was dismissed, said Don Knight, Glossip’s attorney. He said Glossip will be sentenced in December, when he could be released or sent back to prison for another 15 years.
“We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society by spending nearly 30 years on death row, during which time he was served three last meals and came within minutes of being executed for a crime he did not commit,” Knight said.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond had previously said the state would seek to retry Glossip on a murder charge but would not pursue the death penalty again. In a statement sent to media outlets, Drummond said prosecutors would seek more prison time.
Accepting the plea to a lesser charge “was a difficult decision for me and, more importantly, the Van Treese family. We both recognize that this path ensures a conviction related to Mr. Van Treese’s killing and gives us the best chance to secure additional prison time for Glossip,” Drummond said.
By pleading guilty to being an accessory, Knight said Glossip acknowledged the prosecution’s allegations that he helped place plexiglass over a broken window at the motel. Van Treese’s body was inside the room, but Glossip did not know it was there and never saw it, Knight said.
The prosecution also said Glossip did not immediately tell police that Sneed had told him he killed Van Treese. Knight said Glossip did not believe that was true at the time.
“He had nothing to do with the murder, none of the planning, or carrying it out,” Knight said.
During his time on death row, courts in Oklahoma set nine different execution dates for Glossip, and he came so close to being put to death that he ate three separate last meals. In 2015, he was even held in a cell next to Oklahoma’s execution chamber, waiting to be strapped to a gurney and die by lethal injection.
But the scheduled time for his execution came and went. Behind the walls of the Oklahoma State Penitentiary, prison officials were scrambling after learning one of the lethal drugs they received to carry out the procedure didn’t match the execution protocols. The drug mix-up ultimately led to a nearly seven-year moratorium on executions in Oklahoma.
Van Treese’s family had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to leave Glossip’s conviction and sentence intact.
Glossip’s case attracted international attention after actress Susan Sarandon — who won an Academy Award for her portrayal of death penalty opponent Sister Helen Prejean’s fight to save a man on Louisiana’s death row in the 1995 movie “Dead Man Walking” — took up his cause in real life. Glossip’s case was also featured in the 2017 documentary film titled “Killing Richard Glossip.”
___
This story has been corrected to show Glossip did not see the victim’s body.
