text:
State lawmakers to introduce new data center regulations
Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a bill that would have introduced a moratorium on data centers last session.
State lawmakers to introduce new data center regulations
Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a bill that would have introduced a moratorium on data centers last session.
On the campaign trail, Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree has said repeatedly that she would have signed the bill to put a moratorium on data centers that Gov. Janet Mills vetoed last year.
"We have talked about implementing a moratorium until we have rules in place, to protect ratepayers, to protect the environment and ensure community benefits. And that will continue to be my position," Pingree said in a press conference earlier this week.
She might have the chance to do just that.
"We have two pieces of legislation that we're speaking about broadly are two vehicles. One Senator Grohoski is introducing basically that, reintroduction of the moratorium," Rep. Sophie Warren, D-Scarborough, said.
Warren has proposed this legislation for next session, when she will be sworn in as a state senator, and she and her fellow Democrats are looking to regulate data centers.
Her bill would implement recommendations from the Maine Data Center Advisory Council and ensure companies that want to create data centers here would be paying their fair share.
"[We're] bringing forward legislation that is robustly protective, is consistent with our climate, clean energy goals and is also putting affordability at the center, especially in light of so many ongoing discussions about whether our utilities are profiting on the backs of Maine people," Warren said.
Earlier this week, the developers at the Jay mill data center project updated their permit request.
The project is currently on track to be up and running by early 2029. Warren said proposals like this one in Jay should not get a carve-out in a moratorium, as Mills proposed last session.

title: Inside Lewiston, According to Peter Santenello
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
“Inside the Most Dangerous City, in America’s Safest State” is the title that Peter Santenello chose for his latest documentary-style vlog about Lewiston. Santenello is an independent documentarian, YouTuber and media personality with about 4.3 million YouTube subscribers. He travels across the United States, creating long-form “documentaries” about communities whose cultures are often misrepresented or underrepresented in mainstream media.
Currently, Santenello is working on a series about Maine, where he has so far toured Portland, Northern Rural Maine, Millinocket and Lewiston. Published from July to October of 2026, the series covered Lewiston for a total of 71 minutes, in an episode posted on July 18th 2026.
Independent of media outlets or political organizations, Santenello presents himself and these videos as providing unfiltered perspectives on the communities. He conducts informal, spontaneous interviews with locals and documents his experiences in these areas while recording on a GoPro.
In his YouTube biography, Santenello claims, “I make videos showing you a world that the media fails to capture. No BS polarization or political angle—just pure authentic interactions with the locals. I present the story. You present your own opinion.” Throughout his videos, he echoes this mission repeatedly. While he does have authentic encounters with locals, I found that in his coverage of Lewiston, he framed the interviews through specific questioning to enforce a negative perspective.
The documentary starts with a series of clips introducing themes and interviews from later in the video. Santenello includes a voice-over of himself before and between the clips. His first words are, “Today we are going to a different Maine.” This statement is immediately followed by interview snippets, most of which contain the most negative observations made in these interviews. For example, the first interview features a local calling Lewiston “the Dirty Lew” and claiming, “There’s nothing to do around here.”
While Santenello does sprinkle in the occasional clip of him enjoying food or having a friendly interaction, I found this introduction to be the start of an inaccurate story of Lewiston. Santenello promotes the Lewiston stereotype of a distressed, unconnected community, where government services and Bates College in particular are worsening the crisis that the city is experiencing.
Following the documentary’s introduction, Santenello steps out of his car into Lewiston and briefly points out a meal drive hosted by Prince of Peace Parish. Following this, he records a woman using drugs. As he films the woman, Santenello narrates, “I’m just showing you what I see, guys,” before describing her as “just sticking her vein right there… with something.” This immediately sets up the narrative that Lewiston is dangerous and unfairly shines a light on the city’s hardships. This image establishes an idea of crisis before exploring the broader realities of the city.
It’s no secret that Lewiston is facing serious social changes, including poverty, drug use, and homelessness. This stands in contrast with the city’s industrial growth in the 19th century, when it became one of the state’s most famous and largest textile production centers. However, manufacturing jobs moved overseas in the early 2000s, leaving Lewiston with job-quality and income issues. This shift, along with broader economic and population changes, has resulted in a poverty rate roughly double Maine’s and the country’s averages.
In his documentary, Santenello provided important context for how Lewiston’s industrial past has shaped the city. The current situation in Lewiston, however, is far more complicated than the documentary makes it out to be.
Santenello is not wrong to highlight Lewiston’s struggles, but his narrative seems uninterested in offering a more complex view that looks beyond the city’s plights or into their roots. The piece is inevitably filtered through the subjectivity of a high-profile protagonist navigating Lewiston as a poverty tourist. Visibly recording the entire time, Santenello asks the question “So what is Lewiston like today?” to locals who are evidently experiencing hardship. By doing this, he forces binary answers.
In one interview, he asks a group of men who came to Maine from Florida, “What’s Lewiston like compared to Florida?” One man responds, “Trash, high-quality garbage.” They all laugh, and Santenello laughs with them. Then he asks a woman talking to one of the men, “What’s your take [on Lewiston]? How is it?” She says, “Get me out of here.” Laughing again, he responds, “I’ve been here ten minutes, that’s what everyone’s saying. Why?” She then lists her grievances with the city and its struggles.
In the spontaneity and directness of his approach, his subjects seem to choose their words to emphasize the struggles they are experiencing within Lewiston. The suddenness of the interaction, coupled with the perception of his identity as a “known” figure with a potentially large public platform, appears to force a negative perspective meant to elicit sympathy from a large audience. Additionally, by laughing with, or agreeing with his interviewees’ perspectives, Santenello encourages them to double down on their frustrations.
His approach sensationalizes and flattens a story about drugs and poverty, while displaying his ability to navigate difficult situations. Throughout the documentary, Santenello acknowledges the piece’s flaws, particularly its lack of journalistic integrity, while emphasizing his confidence in his own journalistic instincts.
I spoke with Councilmember Joshua Nagine about his thoughts on the documentary. He appreciated that Santenello highlighted the affordable housing opportunities, saying, “I thought [the interview] around the Picker House and the affordable housing options that were available out there was really good.” What I found most interesting in our conversation was the idea that Lewiston’s appearance can create a misleading impression. Nagine explained, “The visual imagery of the conditions in the blight reinforces a stereotype that doesn’t necessarily exist.”
The city has invested a lot of money in downtown Lewiston, but much more is needed to create a sense of community in that area. The documentary is obviously a visual experience and Lewiston is at a disadvantage when it comes to that type of coverage.
The city’s infrastructure was designed for efficiency in the mill era, which isn’t ideal for what the city needs today. Nagine stated, “We [Lewiston] literally have created infrastructure that at one point in time favored the industry that existed here, all the one-way streets, the reason why those exist is so that people could get quickly to the mills and get quickly out of the mills. Mills are no longer running. Why are the streets still that way?”
The city’s planning has created an environment poorly suited to the needs of present-day Lewiston. Nagine reinforced this idea by explaining that “We’ve framed much of our physical infrastructure in a way that contains these neighborhoods. Those are physical infrastructure pieces that are almost intended to segregate neighborhoods. It’s not built for a lived environment that is thriving.”
Nagine’s perspective emphasized the disconnect between the city’s appearance and the reality of its residents’ lives. Throughout the documentary, the sentiment that the “Tree Streets” neighborhood is dangerous was repeated often. Nagine pushed back against the perception that the neighborhood’s appearance reflects its residents, saying that good, hardworking people live there and that, like any city, people are just trying to get by.
I also spoke with Councilmember Chrissy Noble, who acknowledged that Lewiston does face real challenges, but those challenges do not represent the city. Noble said, “I don’t think that what he was… showing isn’t true, but I definitely don’t think that that’s the whole story of our city.”
Noble recognized that Lewiston has “its fair share of negative things that are happening right now.” She added, “There are wonderful people that live downtown… that just go to work, that, you know, take care of their children, that live here and call this their home.”
This idea was echoed by Councilmember Michael Roy, who wrote in an email exchange with me, “I understand people try to get an unbiased opinion in videos, but the Lewiston I know is different. I have been here all my life and the people in Lewiston that love Lewiston are the strength of Lewiston.”
Nagine said, “This is a community that has a very hard time telling its own story, right? We just do not know how to tell our own story. So people from outside are always telling our story.”
The video’s YouTube comment section further explains why Santenello’s portrayal is dangerous. The comments were riddled with negativity and racially charged opinions. Viewers blamed the city’s residents rather than the broader conditions that shape it. One commenter wrote, “It isn’t the city, it is the people. They can all move to the nicest city, and they would ruin that one too.” Another said, “Those First Ladies blaming everyone else but themselves. Go back the big city then if you hate the area. They are the real problem”
This kind of response reduces the complexity of the problems in Lewiston and puts blame upon its residents. These comments do not represent every viewer, but they demonstrate how incomplete coverage can create harmful biases.
The struggles Santenello’s video highlights are very real, but those issues represent a fraction of a much more complex culture.
In his YouTube bio, Santenello commits to portraying “a world that the media fails to capture.” He captured the parts of Lewiston that are easy to see but failed to document the city’s complexity, creating an unbalanced narrative.
Lewiston is the second-largest city in an otherwise extremely rural state. As a result, the contrast between Lewiston and the rest of Maine will always be evident. However, the documentary’s portrayal of the city is an incomplete part of the full story.

text:
IRS announces new 401(k) contribution limit for 2027
The IRS on Thursday announced a new contribution limit for 401(k) plans for 2027, increasing it to account for inflation.
Related video above: How the Nvidia selloff hits your 401(k)
The amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans next year will increase to $25,500, up $1,000 from 2026, the IRS said in a news release Thursday.
The annual contribution limit for those who participate in 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan will also increase by $1,000 to $25,500 for 2027.
IRA remains unchanged
The limit on annual contributions to an Individual Retirement Account (IRA) will remain unchanged for 2027, staying at $7,500.
Catch‑up contributions
The limit for catch‑up contributions — that can be made by employees aged 50 and over who participate in most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the Thrift Savings Plan — will increase by $500 for 2027.
The limit will increase to $8,500 next year, up from $8,000 for 2026. Therefore, those who are eligible could contribute up to $34,000 starting in 2027.
Employees aged 60 to 63 who participate in these plans will have a higher catch-up contribution limit of $11,750 for 2027, which makes the maximum contribution $37,250 for next year.
The IRA catch‑up contribution limit will remain unchanged at $1,100 for next year.

title: Philosophy, Public Health Panel Examines Right to Health Care
text:
Do all people have the right to health care? If so, what roles do government and other institutions play in ensuring access to that said right?
On Thursday, Nov. 5, “The Moral Basis of Care: Understanding the Right to Health” event organized by the Bates Philosophy Forum and Public Health Initiative invited students to discuss these issues with distinguished faculty.
The panel featured professors Frank Chessa, Susan Stark, and Heidi Taylor, who each brought unique perspectives on health care. Each professor was given 10 minutes for their individual presentation. Then, the event opened up to questions from the audience of Bates students.
Frank Chessa, Director of Clinical Ethics at Maine Medical Center, began by discussing health care spending in the United States. He argued that the country’s poor health outcomes are not from a lack of funding.
“The problem isn’t that we don’t spend money on health care,” Chessa said.
Chessa added that while the United States spends nearly $6 trillion annually on health care, Americans have a lower life expectancy than people in many developed countries that spend less. He argued that this discrepancy comes from how health care is funded through a mix of for-profit and not-for-profit institutions in the United States.
“The way we mix for-profit and not-for-profit ends up in an inefficient spending of health care dollars,” Chessa said.
He emphasized that health care companies prioritize more expensive treatments over preventative care due to financial incentives. Procedural care such CT scans, chemotherapy, and surgery are significantly more profitable than primary care visits. Chessa also educated the audience about the fee-for-service model, where health care providers are compensated directly based on the services they provide.
He argued that the overarching financial pressure could lead to unnecessary but profitable procedures being performed. Chessa emphasized that prioritizing preventive care, like managing cholesterol and blood sugar, would help patients avoid developing more severe conditions.
Susan Stark, Professor of Philosophy at Bates College, focused her remarks on reparations and material mortality in the United States. She opened by explaining the United Nations’ framework for reparations, including acknowledging wrongdoing, delivering compensation, and working to prevent future harm.
Stark claimed that this ideology could be applied to the high rates of material mortality among Black Americans. She cited the fact that material mortality in the United States has increased from 11 deaths per 100,000 live births in 1985 to 22 in 2022, adding that Black people giving birth face significantly higher mortality rates than the national average.
Stark emphasized that addressing these disparities starts with acknowledging the current and past problems in the healthcare system.
“That’s the first step for repair. It’s the precursor to all others,” Stark said.
She claimed that health care providers do not always listen to their patients, specifically women giving birth. Stark discussed tennis player Serena Williams as an example, as she experiences a blood clot after giving birth and had to repeatedly speak up before receiving medical attention.
She questioned the power structures within health care institutions, stating that they can contribute to existing inequalities.
“These power structures need to change in order for us to really make reparations for these harms that are connected to the past and ongoing,” Stark said.
Heidi Taylor, Professor of Sociology at Bates, discussed healthcare from a sociological perspective, focusing on the relationship between human rights and health.
Taylor encouraged that human rights begins with “respecting the worth and dignity of every human being.”
She argued that health care disparities are not a simple result of medical conditions, but rather that broader issues like racism, economic inequality, and discrimination play a key role. Taylor also highlighted the importance of viewing health care from a human rights framework.
“Pay attention to suffering. Suffering isn’t just something that happens to people. It is brought upon by other people. Suffering is an actionable injustice,” Taylor said.
Taylor mentioned the concept of structural violence, and how discrimination and inequality can affect one’s physical health over time.
She used diabetes as an example, highlighting that it is more than a medical diagnosis. While the medical approach to diabetes focuses on insulin prescription, Taylor claimed that a public health approach may focus on improving widespread access to healthy food.
Taylor also questioned why health care access in the United States is tied to employment, highlighting issues with the idea that people should work to deserve coverage. She brought up that many Americans work jobs that don’t provide health insurance options.
Taylor concluded her remarks by underscoring that improving healthcare access requires people to take action and actively challenge the ideology behind existing systems.
“Change is not inevitable,” Taylor said.
After the initial presentations, the panel opened up to questions from the audience. In light of the recent midterm elections, The Bates Student asked the panelists what they would prioritize if they could add a provision to a future health care reform bill.
Chessa prioritized bringing back health insurance marketplace subsidies and revising Medicaid changes from the “One Big Beautiful Bill” act, expressing his frustration with the work requirements and administrative barriers that he argued could prevent individuals from applying for Medicaid.
Taylor focused on marginalized communities.
“I would look for reproductive access. I would look for gender-affirming care. I would look for coverage for immigrant communities,” Taylor said.

title: Paul LePage Wins Maine's 2nd Congressional District After Ranked-choice Tabulation
text:
Maine Republican Paul LePage Wins Congressional Seat
After ranked-choice tabulation, Paul LePage is declared the winner of the 2nd Congressional District seat.
Maine's Ranked-Choice Tabulation Determines Paul LePage is the Winner
Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matthew Dunlap faced off in a close race that required first a recount and then a ranked-choice tabulation.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says the final result of the tabulation is as follows:
- Paul LePage - 170,80 votes 50.81%
- Matthew Dunlap - 165,432 votes 49.18%
The ranked-choice tabulation concluded early Thursday afternoon.
LePage will replace Congressman Jared Golden, who chose not to run for re-election.
Maine's Paul LePage Wins 2nd Congressional District
In ranked-choice voting races, the winner must receive a majority - more than 50% - of the vote.
Matthew Dunlap conceded the race before tabulation, but Bellows said that the process still had to be conducted for legal reasons.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest district east of the Mississippi River and includes the following counties:
- Androscoggin
- Aroostook
- Franklin
- Hancock
- Oxford
- Penobscot
- Piscataquis
- Somerset
- Waldo
- Washington
This includes the municipalities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne, and Winthrop in Kennebec County.
Official results will be posted on the Election Results page within 20 days after the election.
Congressman Paul LePage Has a History in Maine Politics
Paul LePage is well-known in Maine politics.
He served as the state's 74th Governor from 2011 to 2019 and as Mayor of Waterville from 2004 to 2011.
Election results are unofficial until they are officially communicated to Governor Janet Mills.

title: Ex-Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleads guilty to lesser charge in 1997 killing
text:
(AP) - Former Oklahoma death row prisoner Richard Glossip, who spent nearly 30 years incarcerated and was on the brink of execution three times for a 1997 killing, pleaded guilty to a lesser charge, his attorney said Thursday.
Glossip had been sentenced to death over the killing in Oklahoma City of his former boss, motel owner Barry Van Treese. Van Treese was beaten with a baseball bat in what prosecutors have alleged was a murder-for-hire scheme.
Another man, Justin Sneed, admitted robbing and killing Van Treese, but testified that he did so after Glossip promised to pay him $10,000. Sneed was the state’s key witness against Glossip and was sentenced to life in prison.
The U.S. Supreme Court previously threw out Glossip’s conviction, and he was released on bond in May to await retrial. His longstanding claims of innocence have drawn support from Kim Kardashian and other prominent figures.
With Glossip’s plea to a lesser accessory charge, the murder charge was dismissed, said Don Knight, Glossip’s attorney. He said Glossip will be sentenced in December, when he could be released or sent back to prison for another 15 years.
“We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society by spending nearly 30 years on death row, during which time he was served three last meals and came within minutes of being executed for a crime he did not commit,” Knight said.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond had previously said the state would seek to retry Glossip on a murder charge but would not pursue the death penalty again. In a statement sent to media outlets, Drummond said prosecutors would seek more prison time.
Accepting the plea to a lesser charge “was a difficult decision for me and, more importantly, the Van Treese family. We both recognize that this path ensures a conviction related to Mr. Van Treese’s killing and gives us the best chance to secure additional prison time for Glossip,” Drummond said.
By pleading guilty to being an accessory, Knight said Glossip acknowledged the prosecution’s allegations that he helped place plexiglass over a broken window at the motel. Van Treese’s body was inside the room, but Glossip did not know it was there and never saw it, Knight said.
The prosecution also said Glossip did not immediately tell police that Sneed had told him he killed Van Treese. Knight said Glossip did not believe that was true at the time.
“He had nothing to do with the murder, none of the planning, or carrying it out,” Knight said.
During his time on death row, courts in Oklahoma set nine different execution dates for Glossip, and he came so close to being put to death that he ate three separate last meals. In 2015, he was even held in a cell next to Oklahoma’s execution chamber, waiting to be strapped to a gurney and die by lethal injection.
But the scheduled time for his execution came and went. Behind the walls of the Oklahoma State Penitentiary, prison officials were scrambling after learning one of the lethal drugs they received to carry out the procedure didn’t match the execution protocols. The drug mix-up ultimately led to a nearly seven-year moratorium on executions in Oklahoma.
Van Treese’s family had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to leave Glossip’s conviction and sentence intact.
Glossip’s case attracted international attention after actress Susan Sarandon — who won an Academy Award for her portrayal of death penalty opponent Sister Helen Prejean’s fight to save a man on Louisiana’s death row in the 1995 movie “Dead Man Walking” — took up his cause in real life. Glossip’s case was also featured in the 2017 documentary film titled “Killing Richard Glossip.”
___
This story has been corrected to show Glossip did not see the victim’s body.

title: Portland will install holiday tree at Monument Square next week
text:
The holiday tree will be installed in Portland’s Monument Square next week.
The 50-foot-tall red spruce, currently rooted at the Rabbit Run cul-de-sac, was selected for this year’s holiday tree, according to Jessica Grondin, a spokesperson for the city.
The tree will be harvested and installed in Monument Square on Wednesday. Crews will cut down the tree about 8:30 a.m. and then depart with a police escort for Monument Square about 9 a.m. The tree is expected to arrive at the square by 11 a.m.
Crews will then begin installing lights on the tree Wednesday or Thursday, with a target finish date of Nov. 24.
You can watch the tree’s arrival on an online live feed.
If the weather is inclement, the tree will make its journey Thursday instead.
The tree lighting will happen at 5:45 p.m. on Nov. 27. Other festivities will include live performances, including from Pine State Pitches, and a free showing of “How the Grinch Stole Christmas” at 3 p.m.

title: Anna Bullett wins Portland City Council District 4 race after recount
text:
Anna Bullett wins Portland City Council District 4 race after recount
Bullett defeated Jacob Viola by 12 votes following a hand recount Friday
Anna Bullett wins Portland City Council District 4 race after recount
Bullett defeated Jacob Viola by 12 votes following a hand recount Friday
Anna Bullett has been confirmed as the winner of Portland's City Council District 4 race following a recount Friday.

The recount included a hand count of all ballots cast in the race.
Although the final totals differed slightly from the original electronic count on Nov. 3, Bullett maintained her lead, winning by 12 votes.

title: FAA halts flights nationwide
text:
WASHINGTON — Airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that canceled thousands of flights Saturday, stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers, spread ripple effects around the world, and forced pro and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.
New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.
Planes were taking flight and landing Saturday, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said/ But the effects could be felt for days. Officials say the system will likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday’s stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Jetport tells passengers to check with airlines
The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:19 p.m., according to Zachary Sundquist, assistant airport director at the Portland International Jetport.
Around that time, Sundquist said 17 flights to and from the jetport were canceled and 12 delayed.
In an update at 10 p.m., Sundquist said two grounded flights had taken off from the jetport, but 19 flights had been canceled, including six Saturday departures.
The airport was on standby for any flights that needed to divert there, but none did, Sundquist said. He noted airlines have issued travel waivers for impacted passengers, and that passengers should check with their airline for up-to-date flight information.
Sundquist said the jetport would provide more information when it receives updates from airlines.
Thousands of flights delayed and canceled
At airports, passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations.
Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours Friday at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were traveling to surprise her daughter’s best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Brown said.
“She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she’s planned this whole weekend,” Brown said. “Now we’re not sure when we’re gonna be able to go.”
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent greeted passengers at Dallas Love Field at dawn Saturday with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to expedite the process and help keep flights moving.
Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses. No. 19 Mississippi’s game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday. Start times for some other games were pushed back hours.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 4,100 flights had been canceled. Cirium, a similar site, put that number above 3,200 flights.
Corbyn Wascher’s flight was on the tarmac at the Charlotte, N.C., airport for four hours Friday on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. The 37-year-old high school teacher paid $100 to take an Uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find a flight until Saturday afternoon to Chicago.
At London’s Heathrow Airport, several flights to and from the U.S. were listed as delayed or canceled Saturday.
“While U.S. flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to rebook affected passengers and get all services back to normal,” said Tim Johnson, consumer director at the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the failure involved old equipment and was not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system, which the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky.
The problem was due to updating a system that can never shut down, Charlton said.
“What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Charlton said. “It’s a 24/7 operation. And to make changes on the fly, if you’ll pardon that pun, is incredibly complex and dangerous.”
The FAA already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
It differed from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: Carole J. Mosher (1946-2026)
May we return to pre-2016 normative behavior
text:
In the aftermath of Nov. 3, the vindictive, Old Testament corner of my brain yearns for impeachment, investigation and punitive retribution directed toward our current federal government. These people have violated their oaths of office, engaged in corrupt and self-serving behavior and been cruelly inertial in addressing the problems caused by their action and inaction.
Vilifying them however, no matter how deserved, serves no constructive purpose. My few remaining rational neurons trump (pun intended) that impulse. What I yearn for from our elected and appointed officials is the high road; a return to pre-2016 normative behavior.
I ask them to fulfill their fiduciary duty to us, their constituents. I expect them to cease and desist with the juvenile behaviors of the last 10 years, display empathy and civility, speak the truth and solve problems.
James Russell
Cape Elizabeth

title: Flights halted at airports across US due to air traffic control communications problems
text:
Trump administration blames 'overloaded' systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated systems and caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted Friday night after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the United States.
Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected from coast to coast. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn't happen again.
Mullin said the Federal Aviation Administration was installing "new equipment, new technology" and "it was overwhelming the older system." There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, Mullin said.
A limited number of domestic flights began departing Friday evening after the ground stop was lifted, but it would likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Video below: What should you do if you have a flight this weekend?
Mullin says no sign of nefarious act
Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said: "There's nothing completely certain right now. It doesn't appear that way." He said there are no "footprints" showing an attack and that it appears to be "mechanically driven," adding that officials were still looking for the cause.
At least 827 flights had been diverted. As of 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
The airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted included Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
Video below: What are your options, rights after Friday's FAA groundstop?
At the time of the ground stoppage, 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.
"And last time I looked, we had less than 400 in the airspace," he said. He said it's going to be slow getting air traffic back to normal.
At Chicago O'Hare Airport on Friday afternoon, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board.
Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there.
"There's not really any information being passed to me," said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. "I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I'm like, that would be miserable."
Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend's baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago.
They had boarded a flight to Denver from O'Hare International Airport when they were told to get off the plane.
"We did see them taking luggage off our plane and others, so we're assuming it's going to be a pretty substantial delay," Curtis said.
They were unsure whether to get a hotel room or keep waiting out the delay at the airport. With care already in place for their two young children at home, they might stay the weekend in Chicago, he said.
Sports teams stranded and cargo flights delayed
NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
"I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move" to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world's largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.
U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.
Despite the ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon in its latest test flight.
Past problems have also been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them," said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
Friday's ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
Video below: What passengers can expect now that nationwide ground stop has lifted
Weather radars are not down, NWS says
Nationwide weather radars are not experiencing an outage Friday night.
That is according to the National Weather Service, which put out a statement on social media debunking the fast-moving rumor.
"In case you heard otherwise, there is no radar outage and https://radar.weather.gov is fully operational!" NWS wrote. "Outdated content from isolated webpages stating otherwise has been circulating, but NWS radars are operating normally."
Are the Microsoft Outlook outage and FAA ground stop connected?
The world-stopping news comes just a day after a massive Microsoft outage left thousands of users without access to Outlook, the company's email platform.
According to Downdetector, reports peaked at 130,000 users impacted, though other estimates say it was closer to millions.
These two events, both stemming from apparently complicated technological issues, happened so close together that many are wondering whether they are connected.
However, Microsoft and the federal government have denied any connection.
Hours after the ground stop was put in place, Microsoft released a statement on social media.
"We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company wrote.
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also rejected the link.
Responding to questions Friday afternoon outside the White House, Mullin said they are "separate issues," and that he didn't see “any reason to connect those two at all.”
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; and Alex Veiga in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

title: US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
text:
President Donald Trump’s administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.
The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won’t have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.
Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they’ll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school or volunteering.
The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.
“I think these extra six months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures” resulting from states’ inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told The Associated Press.
Still, she said it’s not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.
Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders “appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing.”
There’s political pressure over the requirement
The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress to consider changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.
The news comes after Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, of Oregon, and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, wrote to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.
“The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements,” the letter states. “The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their health care coverage.”
Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don’t have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over 64, caring for kids under 14 or deemed too medically frail to work.
Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.
The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.
Critics worry that the paperwork part will be the biggest issue
A few states have launched the work requirements early.
The first of them was Nebraska, where they started in May.
Preliminary data presented to the state’s Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than 9 in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.
But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn’t show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.
Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.
Among both groups, it’s not clear how many people didn’t provide information because they weren’t working — or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.
“There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it,” said Amy Behnke, the CEO of the Health Care Center Association of Nebraska.

title: Former nonprofit employee who helped foster children arrested on child endangerment charges
text:
WACO, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) — An employee of a nonprofit group that helps abused and neglected foster children navigate the court system was arrested Wednesday with his wife after authorities searched their Texas home and found the conditions in which they and their two children were living.
John Moorman, 51, director of advocacy at CASA of McLennan County, and his wife, 48-year-old Leslie Moorman, were expected to be released Thursday from the county jail on $5,000 bonds each. Both were arrested on state felony charges of endangering a child.
Employment status
John Moorman, a former Child Protective Services worker, was placed on administrative leave Wednesday from his job, said CASA Executive Director Ashlee Knutson.
“Moorman is no longer employed by CASA of McLennan County,” Knutson said Thursday.
CASA, or Court-Appointed Special Advocates, recruits, trains and supports volunteers who assist children in the foster care system.
Knutson said the arrests of John Moorman and his wife had nothing to do with his role as a CASA staff member.
“Anyone who serves a CASA program goes through a comprehensive, multi-layered background screening process – whether they are a staff member, volunteer, or board member,” Knutson said in a statement. “The process includes FBI fingerprinting as well as child protective services, national sex offender registry, and criminal background checks. Because these background checks are fingerprint-based and given the responsibility CASA programs hold, ongoing monitoring continues once someone begins serving in any of these roles.”
Search warrant at China Spring home
According to arrest affidavits, Waco police investigators served a search warrant Wednesday at the Moormans’ home in the 10000 block of Barton Creek Drive in China Spring. Authorities had received a “CyberTip concerning child sexual abuse material,” the affidavits state.
During the execution of the search warrant, officers “immediately noticed a foul odor commonly associated with human or animal excrement, such as feces and urine,” the affidavit states.
The detective wrote that while going through the home, investigators found trash, food, feces, soiled diapers and other materials ‘throughout the entire residence in a way that made it impossible to walk through without stepping on it."
The affidavit alleges that while there was food in the refrigerator, the kitchen was not in a state in which anything could be cooked and “there were bugs throughout the residence.”
The affidavit also alleges there was a rat’s nest in the kitchen and officers saw rodents in a child’s room.
“In the (detective’s) training and experience, the state of the residence presents a clear and present danger to the welfare of the children,” according to the affidavit.
Children placed with family
Child Protective Services workers took custody of a 15-year-old boy and a 6-year-old girl and placed them with other family members, said Cierra Shipley, Waco police spokesperson.
Investigators also seized “technology” from the Moormans’ home as the investigation continues, Shipley said.

A Bucksport man was arrested Thursday morning after he allegedly became belligerent in the Bangor police station lobby.

title: Cloudy and cool into the weekend
text:
Cloudy and cool into the weekend
Weekend trending drier but still quite chilly
Cloudy and cool into the weekend
Weekend trending drier but still quite chilly
Most of Maine is staying dry this morning as a coastal storm offshore fails to push moisture far enough north. Only far southern communities around Portland are seeing a brush of light precipitation, while towns farther up the coast and inland remain completely dry.
Whatever dampness lingers in southern Maine will wrap up quickly before lunchtime. A steady north wind is sweeping drier air across the state, breaking up the clouds while keeping a noticeable chill in the air.
High pressure takes control for the weekend, locking in quiet and dry weather. Daytime temperatures will sit a couple of degrees below average, while clear skies and light winds at night will cause readings to tumble well below normal.
A warming trend will finally break the chill early next week. As the high-pressure system moves out, temperatures are expected to climb back toward above-average territory by midweek.

title: Down the Rabbit Hole: Where children’s stories come to life
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — Reading is crucial for young children, helping them to build their vocabulary and their imaginations. But the joy and love of reading among kids is slipping away. Federal data shows fewer children are reading for fun today compared to years past. That’s also true for adults.
But The Rabbit hOle, a Kansas City museum based on children’s literature, aims to bring that love for literature back, by bringing your favorite stories to life.
Sprawling more than 40,000 square feet, life-size exhibits at The Rabbit hOle include classic titles such as “Madeline,” “Frog and Toad” and “Curious George.” Newer titles include “My Garden” and “I Want My Hat Back.” There’s even a total recreation of the “great green room” from the book, “Goodnight Moon”, complete with a bed, fireplace, an oversized rocking chair, and a moon that actually moves in the sky.
At each of the exhibits, you can find the book that correlates with it. It’s not unusual to see a child reading “The Fire Cat” or “I am a Bunny” in a tunnel or a chair situated in the exhibit.
Since opening in 2024, the museum has drawn more than 300,000 visitors from all 50 states and other countries, including Italy, Sweden and Singapore. The museum has roughly 45 exhibits.
One exhibit features a 16-foot giant panda named Stillwater from the book “Zen Shorts” by Jon J. Muth. The displays are made in house at The Rabbit hOle factory.
Founder Peter Cowdin and his wife Deb Pettid ran a bookstore for 28 years before opening the museum. Cowdin said while he did not grow up in a “rich environment of children’s books”, he fell in love with the stories as an adult. And the idea behind The Rabbit hOle had been brewing for years.
“We wanted to do something that celebrated children’s literature in a way that had nothing to do with marketing and sales, but had everything to do with the history and culture and the books,” Cowdin said.
“Creation and generative activity is really at the soul of the Rabbit Hole,” he said.
Reading competes with screens
Abbey Mecca visits the museum regularly with her three children.
“Reading is like a non-negotiable from the start. When they first come home, that’s just part of our culture,” Mecca said. “It’s not an option to not read at our house.”
Screens, including tablets and smartphones, compete for children’s attention.
In the 1980s, more than half of 9-year-olds read for fun almost every day. The latest data from the Nation’s Report Card (needs a new hyperlink, this is not correct) shows that figure is down to 37%.
The statistics get worse as kids age. Only 14% of 13-year-olds regularly read for fun, according to the data. The number of children who never or hardly read is also growing.
Meanwhile, 65% of children ages 8 to 13 watch TV daily and average 5½ hours of screen time a day.
Idean Bindell, a mother of three, said the museum helps keep her children interested in reading.
“It’s really made my kids fall in love with the art of storytelling and not just see that there’s just books on a shelf. They see every step of the process,” she said.
Cowdin said getting children off screens was not the museum’s goal, but he said it has been a result.
“I never run into a kid wanting to be on a phone or a tablet in here ever,” Cowdin said.
Part of the reason he thinks children are so captivated by the books and displays at the museum, is because It’s not turning reading into a chore or homework.
“There’s this sort of overreaction, in my opinion, of, you know, really drilling and reading as a skill rather than a pleasure. And so our counterbalance to that is that exactly The Rabbit hOle is really emphasizing the joy of reading,” Cowdin said.
Cowdin hopes the museum inspires more people to follow its approach to reading.
Admission and exhibit permissions
Cowdin and his wife needed permission for every exhibit.
The authors or their estates had to agree to give them the rights for free to keep admission costs affordable.
Tickets are $16 per person. Admission is free for children 2 and younger.

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss case against Eddington mother accused in baby’s overdose
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A judge on Friday denied a request to dismiss the case against Brittany Wood, an Eddington woman and RSU 63 school board member charged in connection with her baby’s apparent near-fatal overdose.
Wood’s attorney, David Walker, argued investigators overstepped in their search of a phone used by his office. Wood had the phone because she was working for Walker as a paralegal at the time of her arrest.
Phone search at issue
Walker accused prosecutors of improperly accessing both privileged and personal communications.
An investigator testified the state did not improperly access Walker’s personal phone or communications. The investigator said what Walker was accusing them of was “impossible.”
The judge also denied a separate defense motion seeking sanctions against prosecutors. He called the case “most unusual,” and the situation “embarrassing, awkward, and intrusive,” but found no violations by the state.
Wood remains held
Following her arrest on new drug charges this week, Wood remains held without bail in the underlying assault case.
She is due back in court next month.

title: Patriots need to bounce back against Lions in Germany
text:
MUNICH — Heading into international games, NFL coaches typically talk up the niceties of “growing the game” globally.
Not this week.
The New England Patriots (5-4) have lost two of their past three games and have a slew of injury concerns, including running back Rhamondre Stevenson. The Detroit Lions, even with a 6-2 record and four straight victories, are trying to keep pace in the tight NFC North.
Sunday’s game in Munich is a big one for both teams.
Lions coach Dan Campbell wasn’t focused on the international implications.
“Well, if I’m being honest, I just haven’t thought that far into it. I’m like, ‘We’ve got to get prepared,’” Campbell said.
The Patriots were embarrassed at home by the Green Bay Packers last week, losing 45-27, with Drake Maye throwing three interceptions and the secondary struggling to contain the Packers passing game.
Campbell expects a much-improved New England team on Sunday.
“You look at the totality of what this team is capable of, the firepower they have, and they’re a good team. They’re dangerous,” he said. “And they’re going to clean a lot of things up.”
The Lions slogged through a 19-9 win over the rebuilding Miami Dolphins last week, relying on four field goals from Jake Bates. It was also just one week after a neck injury to All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell.
Detroit’s bye week is in the rearview mirror and after Munich the team will host Tampa Bay and then Chicago on Thanksgiving Day.
“It’s a good thing to be tested during the season,” Campbell said. “It really is. And to have to go through some of these tough stretches because that’s what the playoffs are. That’s what it is. And certainly if you got to go on the road. So, that’s what this is. This is about us. This is the next obstacle we have. Told the team we’re not going to clear it. Our objective is to go through it and that’s the mindset.”
Injuries are a top concern for New England. Before traveling Wednesday night, the Patriots ruled out LG Ben Brown (knee), CB Carlton Davis III (knee) and RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness).
Stevenson, the team’s leading rusher with 399 yards on 102 carries, has been limited in practice due to a knee injury.
That could put second-year running back Corey Kiner in line for the bulk of the carries.
“Corey has done a really nice job, but there are also some things that Corey has to be able to improve on,” coach Mike Vrabel said, citing “recognition of the pressure and then the ability to block the pressure.”
The coach said “a lot of contending teams” are 5-4.
“We’ve got to start putting ourselves in position to play meaningful games in January or in the middle of January,” Vrabel said. “It’s usually what happens in the National Football League; a bunch of teams get bunched up and they go in different directions, and I know the direction that we’re going to head in, and that’s going to be the one that’s forward, positive and winning.”
Need to know
New England (5-4) vs. Detroit (6-2) in Munich, Germany.
When/where to watch: 9:30 a.m. Sunday, FOX
Latest odds: Lions by 2 1/2
Against the spread: Patriots 3-5-1; Lions 4-4
Last week: Patriots lost to Packers 45-27; Lions beat Dolphins 19-9
Last meeting: Patriots won 29-0 on Oct. 9, 2022, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass.
Series record: Patriots lead 8-5
Matchup to watch
Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez against Lions receivers Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown. Gonzalez, who signed a lucrative contract extension in September, is hoping to bounce back from struggling against Green Bay last week. According to the NFL Next Gen Stats, he gave up 105 yards to Matthew Golden and 82 yards to Christian Watson. St. Brown, who typically lines up in the slot, leads the Lions with 61 receptions for 657 yards. He’s scored five touchdowns. Williams has 468 yards on 28 receptions — though just one last week in Miami — and five TDs.
Stats and stuff
• Detroit running back Jahmyr Gibbs leads the NFL with 60 scrimmage touchdowns (48 rushing, 12 receiving) and ranks second with 6,161 scrimmage yards since entering the NFL in 2023.
• With a touchdown Sunday, Gibbs can tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Terrell Davis (61 touchdowns) for the most touchdowns by a player in his first four seasons in NFL history.
• This is Detroit’s first international game since 2015. The Lions are 1-1 internationally.
• The Patriots won three international games with Tom Brady at quarterback. They lost 32-16 to Jacksonville in London in 2024 in Drake Maye’s second NFL start; and lost 10-6 to the Colts in Frankfurt in 2023 with Mac Jones at the helm.
• Entering Week 10, Maye is tied with Justin Herbert for most interceptions (11). He’s tied for fourth in touchdown passes (18).

title: 'A change from status quo': Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announces bid for Senate Majority Leader
text:
'A change from status quo': Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announces bid for Senate Majority Leader
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, has entered the race for Senate Democratic leader, challenging incumbent Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-New York, highlighting growing divisions within the party ahead of a secret ballot election in December.
'A change from status quo': Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announces bid for Senate Majority Leader
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, has entered the race for Senate Democratic leader, challenging incumbent Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-New York, highlighting growing divisions within the party ahead of a secret ballot election in December.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, announced his candidacy for Senate Majority Leader following Democrats' sweeping win in the midterms.
His bid challenges incumbent Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-New York, who says he already has the votes to win re-election. Still, the race highlights growing divisions among Democrats that could impact the future direction of the party.
Schumer, currently the Senate Minority Leader, responded to Van Hollen’s announcement expressing confidence in his re-election bid.
"I welcome any discussion about the future of the caucus," Schumer said in a statement Thursday. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
But while some progressives have publicly called for Schumer to step aside, many Democrats have declined to say how they will vote.
Van Hollen has stepped in to claim voters are seeking change from President Donald Trump’s policies and Democrats' leadership status quo.
"They want to turn the page on Trump's corruption and his wars and his cruelty and his complete disregard for their economic pain but that wasn't an embrace of Democrats," Van Hollen said. "We've been given an opportunity and we need to make sure that we use it in a way that meets the needs of the country."
Van Hollen's announcement marks the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades.
The closed-door, secret ballot vote is expected to take place in early December.

title: Brother of slain Mexican cartel leader is sentenced to 22 years in prison for drug trafficking plot
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A man whose slain brother led one of Mexico’s most violent drug cartels was sentenced Friday to more than 22 years in U.S. prison for his part in a sprawling drug trafficking conspiracy that brought cocaine and methamphetamine to American streets.
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, the brother of the Jalisco New Generation co-founder known as El Mencho, pleaded guilty to drug trafficking charges in July after the Mexican government handed him over to U.S. authorities last year alongside other high-ranking cartel leaders.
His case is part of a broader Trump administration effort to crack down on powerful cartels such as Jalisco New Generation, also known as CJNG, that have helped fuel America’s drug epidemic.
“Oseguera Cervantes’ sentence sends a clear message to criminals around the world that the Department of Justice is committed to the total elimination of drug cartels and transnational criminal organizations, including the CJNG,” Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva, who leads the department’s Criminal Division, said in an emailed statement.
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 68, of Michoacán, Mexico, worked for cartels with his brother Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, the drug lord known as El Mencho, who was killed by the Mexican army in February, according to federal prosecutors.
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes was a leader of the Milenio Cartel and later reported directly to his brother after El Mencho became the CJNG’s top leader, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors in Washington’s federal court had recommended a 30-year prison sentence, noting that his duties included receiving CJNG drug proceeds, managing the cartel’s money laundering activities and supervising meth laboratories.
“Rival cartels rarely settle disputes through diplomacy alone,” prosecutors wrote in court papers. “And while there may be no nonviolent drug cartels in Mexico, (Oseguera Cervantes) was a member of particularly brutal cartels.”
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes’ attorneys requested a 20-year prison sentence, saying in court documents that he accepts full responsibility for his crimes and “blames no one except himself.” They noted that he already has spent several years behind bars in Mexico for essentially the same conduct to which he pleaded guilty in the U.S.
He expressed remorse in a letter addressed to the court, saying he is “deeply sorry for my actions and for the harm they caused.”
“One of my greatest fears is that I will die far away from my family,” he wrote. “I love my children and my family very much, and I hope that I may one day have the opportunity to spend the remaining years of my life with them.”
_____
Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: Nurse practitioner opens wellness practice in Brewer
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - A local nurse practitioner has opened a practice in Brewer offering care for respiratory and sleep conditions, along with weight management and other wellness services.
Jackie Foraker grew up in Dedham and followed her mother into nursing. After years working in a local intensive care unit, she became a nurse practitioner specializing in respiratory and sleep medicine.
Foraker said she opened Foraker Wellness to spend more time getting to know patients while offering personalized care.
“I’m huge on education, prevention, being able to really sit with a patient and get to know them,” Foraker said. “I want to know things about their family, what they’ve got going on in their life and have them feel relaxed.”
Sleep treatment
Foraker said she worked to bring Inspire, a treatment for sleep apnea, to Bangor. She said it had previously been available only south of Augusta.
“I wanted to have alternatives for patients,” she said.
The practice is on South Main Street in Brewer. It also offers wellness services, including IV therapy.

title: Decoding hidden meanings behind some emojis and acronyms
text:
(Aging Untold) — Certain emojis and acronyms beyond LOL and BRB used in text messages carry hidden meanings that parents and grandparents may not know.
Jill Story said it is tough to stay on top of the abbreviated language her three daughters use.
“They have a whole language that they use that I’m constantly having to, like, figure out,” Story said.
Story said some of the acronyms her daughters use are even more difficult to decipher.
Chart lists coded emoji meanings
A chart from For Working Parents went viral.
The group’s founder, a former vice principal, detailed what he described as sinister emojis, symbols that could represent something different from what parents might think. The meanings range from drugs to sex to extremism.
Mothers guess at meanings
Neither Story nor two of her mom friends knew that Code 9, or CD9, means “parents are around.”
Aside from a few good guesses, none of the mothers knew all of the potential secret meanings.
One of the mothers said she felt somber and shocked after learning what some of the messages meant.
GNOC: Get naked on camera
Screen Sanity co-founder offers advice
Tracy Foster, co-founder and CEO of Screen Sanity, an organization that helps parents navigate the digital world as parents raise children, said one acronym she feels strongly about is KYS. Foster said it stands for kill yourself.
Foster said it is up to parents to help kids understand the weight of their words, whether explicit or coded.
“You don’t want them to become desensitized,” Foster said.
Foster said parents can start by showing interest in what their children know.
“So often, if you just start to show curiosity and an appreciation for their knowledge, they’ll start to open up,” Foster said.
Story said every generation has a coded language.
“As a mom, I would like to be up on those things,” she said.
