title: Team Reviewing MaineHealth Labor and Delivery Decision Introduced at Forum
text:
The team tasked with evaluating MaineHealth’s decision to close the labor and delivery unit at Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta introduced themselves and laid out the framework of their review at an online forum on Wednesday, Nov. 4.
In a Monday, Oct. 26 press release, MaineHealth Vice President of Communications and Public Affairs Kathleen Taggersell said the team will assess whether alternatives considered by the hospital’s management were “reasonable, feasible, and sustainable.” The results from the review are due to MaineHealth on Friday, Dec. 11.
“We are not beginning this review with the assumption that closure or regionalizing is the right answer,” said Jeni Stolow, the review team’s process lead. “We are not also beginning with the assumption that keeping the unit open is the right answers. We’re beginning with the questions; with an obligation to examine the evidence and with a commitment to reaching conclusions that are supported by the science we used and data we analyze.”
On Aug. 6, the system voted to close the unit, effective Friday, Dec. 18. The decision came after two other votes from the MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital Local Board and the Coastal Region Board. MaineHealth said the decision the system will not close any additional labor and delivery programs anywhere in the health system during the next two years.
Under the new regional model, the Damariscotta and Brunswick-based hospitals will operate as “one coordinated regional OB-GYN and certified nurse midwife team,” hospital officials said in the announcement. Patients will be transitioned to MaineHealth Mid Coast Hospital in Brunswick.
The review team comprises five experts from backgrounds in maternal healthcare, rural healthcare delivery, workforce sustainability, clinical quality and safety, and community engagement. The meeting was opened by Carol Kelly, an independent Portland-based consultant from Pivot Point.
The upcoming work was summarized by Stolow, a public health researcher based in New Orleans, La. and an associate professor at Tulane University School of Public Health and Tropical Medicine,.
Stolow said she has spent the past decade specializing in public health, accessibility to reproductive and maternal child healthcare, participatory research, and workforce capacity strengthening. Before moving to Louisiana, Stolow work in Maine on the Rural Maternity and Obstetrics Management Strategies, often referred to as RMOMS, which assessed the obstetric workforces in the state’s rural hospitals.
In the presentation, Stolow said forum is the beginning of a long line of work, research, and evaluation. The review is only in its formative stage and the team looks forward to hearing feedback from different community members.
Stolow also gave kudos to the Miles Delivers Actions Coalition, a grassroots efforts that advocated for the unit to stay open before the decision was made, for reaching out with ideas.
Stolow recognized that many attendees were probably frustrated with the decision to close.
“We recognize that this is not simply a conversation about a hospital unit,” Stolow said. “This is a conversation about families, mothers, babies, partners, and loved ones. It’s about health care professionals who have dedicated their careers for caring for thing community.”
The team has been tasked with conducting an independent review after the Maine Legislature’s Health Coverage, Insurance, and Financial Services Committee’s Aug. 27 hearing, during which committee members suggested a third-party review of the assessment that led to the decision to close the unit.
Findings will be presented directly to MaineHealth in December and the final report will be publicly available. Stolow said the purpose of the engagement is to determine if that data and process that MaineHealth used to assess options before decision to close the unit is fair and reasonable.
While reviewing, the team will look at the information considered, the options evaluated, and feedback from stakeholders. Additionally, they will also take recommendations from others external entities.
A major point of concern brought up heading into this evaluation is independence. Stolow said the team is responsible for reaching their own conclusions, even if they different from the ones of MaineHealth, the coalition, or any other stakeholder.
Even if the review team finds information differing from MaineHealth’s, Stolow said it is solely up to the hospital system to decide if the unit remains open.
“We cannot promise that everyone will agree with our conclusions, but we can commit to a process that is thoughtful, systematic, fair transparent and guided by evidence,” Stolow said.
The review process was broken up into three steps during the presentation. Step one will be examining the process and data used by MaineHealth in making the decision to close. Step two is to review materials prepared by the coalition, along with other data sets, literature, and professional guidance. The third step is to interview MaineHealth administration, clinicians, coalition members, community members, and others to collect further data.
Some of the key points to be evaluated include whether proposed alternatives for the closure are reasonable, whether the unit can be safely staffed while also meeting an appropriate standard of care, and if these alternatives are sustainable.
The planned closure date is not contingent upon the review and is still set to happen at the end of the year, Stolow said.
The maternal-fetal medicine lead in Ann Borders, a physician working at Evanston Hospital in Evanston, Ill. Borders is also the executive director of the Illinois Perinatal Quality Collaborative, where she works with birthing hospitals in Illinois to improve the quality and safety of care.
Borders compared the rural hospitals in Maine to her own personal experiences in her hometown in Iowa. She said she was born in a small rural hospital where her parents still receive their care.
The staffing models and continuity lead is Daisy Goodman, a certified nurse-midwife and associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth Health in Hanover, N.H. Her role is split between clinical practice, program implementation and evaluation, and research.
Before starting at Dartmouth, Goodman practiced as a nurse midwife in Maine, first at Rumford Hospital and then at Franklin Memorial Hospital in Farmington. Since her time there, Rumford Hospital has closed its labor and delivery unit.
“On a personal note, I’m someone who’s not only attended many births in rural community hospitals but also has delivered in them myself,” Goodman said.
The financial, operational, and quantitative lead is Alec McKinney, co-founder and principal of public health and healthcare consulting firm Population Health Strategies. McKinney said he is not a clinician but a program evaluator, assessor, and researcher. In his job, he is responsible for community assessment, program assessment, and planning activities, especially surrounding primary care, behavioral health, and specialty care services.
McKinney has worked on assessments on populations in rural communities, including those with unstable housing conditions, mental health disorders, and who deal with substance abuse.
In this project, McKinney will be responsible for assessing the quantitative data that MaineHealth used to form their decision to close the unit.
“I’ll be looking at the drive time analyzes, as well as validating a lot of the different data and data sources, looking at both what has been said and what has been included in the assessment and the white paper, as well as sort of what has not been included,” McKinney said.
The final team member is Sanam Roder-DeWan, the obstetric quality and safety lead. Roder-DeWan is a family physician who is also an associate professor of community family medicine at Dartmouth Institute, as well as obstetrics and gynecology at Dartmouth Health.
For a decade of her career, Roder-Dewan was a full-spectrum family doctor who delivered babies, as well as a maternal child health director. She eventually switched over to more research-oriented work that she said has driven her “health equity perspective.”
“I just want to express my, I guess delight, but it just feels like an honor to be part of a process that includes a community that is as active as this,” Roder-DeWan said.
At the end of the forum, Kelly said one of the most frequently asked questions was regarding how the team got selected and what ensures their independence.
According to Kelly, after the coalition and legislative committee asked for the neutral third party, MaineHealth agreed to initiate the review. MaineHealth’s Katherine Campbell and Katie Fullam Harris were responsible for recruitment and spent weeks identifying people for the team. MaineHealth is paying for the review.
Other questions included how the team applied the skills they plan on using in this review in their other lines of work. One question asked if the team plans on using artificial intelligence during the review. Stolow said AI “does not belong” in the review and it will not be used.
In a Monday, Nov. 9 interview, Lincoln Hospital President Cindy Wade said the forum was a great opportunity for the community meet the review team and see what the upcoming work looks like.
“I think it went well,” Wade said.
Questions and more information can be found by emailing [email protected] or going to lincolnmidocastobgyn.mainehealth.org.

title: 1 dead, 6 injured after school bus and SUV collide in crash
text:

title: Old Orchard Beach on state funding list for new school
text:
The Maine State Board of Education voted Thursday to place an Old Orchard Beach school on the state’s Approved Projects List for major school construction.
Loranger Memorial School, which serves grades 3 through 8, was called “the worst” still-operating school in the state last year.
The aging school, with one wing built in 1936 and the other in 1968, has a host of issues: The two main levels are only accessible from the outside for people with disabilities, the 60-year-old boiler poses a fire risk and the parent pickup system is chaotic.
Because of those problems, Loranger was ranked third out of 95 schools that applied for approval this year.
In a news release Thursday, Regional School Unit 23 Superintendent John Suttie said that ranking is a recognition of the real needs in the building and years of steady work by staff, the school board and the community.
“This is an important first step in a longer process,” Suttie wrote.
OVER A DECADE IN THE MAKING
For over 10 years, RSU 23 has been working toward building a new school to replace Loranger, Suttie said.
Since 2014, the district has erased a $1.5 million deficit, restored an A1 bond rating, built capital reserves and invested steadily in its buildings, he said.
The district also completed facility assessments, an enrollment study and site testing to ensure RSU 23 is prepared for construction of a new school.
WHAT COMES NEXT
Next steps are already underway, Suttie said Thursday. An Educational Visioning Committee made up of teachers, parents, students, residents, school board members and administrators has been meeting since September to outline what students need from their schools.
A second committee focused on building plans will be formed in the spring, Suttie added.
The town has also invited architecture and engineering firms to submit qualifications for a feasibility and planning study. Those submissions are due in January.
It’s definite that a brand-new school will replace Loranger, Suttie said Friday, but the scope, size, grade levels and cost of the project are still unknown.
“As the study progresses, we will share what we learn and seek your input along the way, so the decisions are shaped by the voices of our community,” Suttie wrote.

title: Play at Waldo Theatre depicts fictional conversation between JFK and painter Jamie Wyeth
text:
WALDOBORO, Maine (WABI) - A famous portrait of President John F. Kennedy is inspiring a new play at the Waldo Theatre.
Writer Shannon Mullen decided to bring the story of the portrait to life, and she thought a play would be the best way to tell it. Her version, “An Addition of One,” depicts a fictional conversation between Kennedy and painter Jamie Wyeth, who was tasked with painting the late president after his death.
How the play began
Mullen said the idea came from an interview with Wyeth.
“He mentioned that he had done this posthumous portrait of President Kennedy. Jamie was only 20 at the time, and he said that the process had gotten so real to him of getting to know this martyred president, that he created a memory of having met him for about a half an hour,” Mullen said. “And I remember listening to my recording of the interview a few days later, is when I first really heard that, and I thought, ‘That’s a play. I have to hear that conversation, and I guess I’m going to have to write it.’”
The portrait
Wyeth was hesitant when he was given the opportunity to create a portrait of Kennedy.
“I turned it down thinking, ‘How can I do it if he’s not alive?’ But then I started thinking about it, as I was taken up as everybody was with Kennedy at that point,” Wyeth said. “And so then I went myself and decided to do this, and I created a painting which was very romantic and so forth, and then I felt the need to get some life into it.”
To draw inspiration, Wyeth used his creativity and also leaned on other members of the Kennedy family, in particular Kennedy’s two brothers.
The portrait is popular now, but it was not a hit when it first came out.
“The portrait was hated when it was first reproduced in Look Magazine, life-sized,” Wyeth said. “Because at that point, he was this demigod with blue eyes and blonde hair, neither of which he had. Now it’s sort of reversed. It’s now the national stamp of Ireland, it’s reproduced a lot, it’s in the Boston Museum.”
One performer, two roles
Mullen wrote and directed the play, produced it and is the only actress in it. She plays both Wyeth and Kennedy.
Mullen said a table reading led her to take both roles.
“At that table reading, we asked the small audience we had, ‘Did you mind that it was two women reading these roles?’” Mullen said. “A friend of mine read Jamie and I read Jack, and they said no, they found it liberating because, as I hoped, they weren’t focused on or distracted by the fact that I don’t look like Jack Kennedy or sound exactly like him. So after that I said, ‘I think I’m just going to do them both myself.’”
Speaker series follows the show
The roughly 45-minute show is followed by a speaker series featuring artists, journalists and writers who explore the play’s themes.
Waldo Theatre leaders said the interactive format and post-show Q&A build on the theater’s reputation for fostering a close-knit community.
“We’re trying to get as many different kinds of people through the door, and to develop a program that has, like, a lot of legs. Maybe it’s a centipede,” Cooney said. “We’re trying to bring everybody in the doors and offer programming that can speak to people, but also resonates long after.”
The show premiered November 7th and will continue this Saturday, November 14th and Sunday the 15th at 4 o’clock.
There will be an additional two shows November 21st and 22nd at the same time.

title: Nationwide ground stop lifted after flights halted for hours across US, FAA says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.
Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
EN ESPAÑOL | Gobierno federal ordena la suspensión de todos los vuelos a nivel nacional
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.
A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Mullin says no sign of nefarious act
Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.
At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.
Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
The stoppage affected thousands of flights
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.
At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.
“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”
Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.
Sports teams stranded and cargo flights delayed
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.
U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.
Past problems have also been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
___
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

Cooler temperatures and passing clouds will highlight the weekend
How’s the weather looking for your weekend? Get the latest Maine’s Total Weather video forecast from Chief Meteorologist Roger Griswold.
A chilly pattern will remain in place through the weekend as an upper-level low moves across northern New England. High temperatures will run slightly below normal, while overnight lows dip well below normal, with many areas falling into the 20s. Periodic snow showers are expected around and north of the mountains Saturday and Sunday, with the best chance Saturday into Saturday night as the upper low moves overhead. Most accumulations will be light, although a few higher peaks in northern New Hampshire and northwest Maine could pick up 1-2 inches.
The upper-level system will gradually move east on Sunday, allowing snow shower chances to taper off through the afternoon. High pressure then builds in for the start of next week, bringing a gradual warm-up. Highs will climb from the 30s and 40s Monday to the upper 40s and 50s by midweek, with a few lower 60s possible across southern areas. Dry weather is expected for much of next week.

title: High levels of lead found in drinking water at midcoast school
text:
Bristol Consolidated School is under a “do not drink” order after elevated levels of lead were found in a faucet at the farthest end of the building.
Facilities Director John Carroll said the date the lead was identified is unknown; the school was informed Oct. 26. Carroll provided an update during the Bristol School Committee meeting on Thursday, Nov. 5.
A semiannual testing conducted by Water Quality and Compliance Services Inc., of Wiscasset, found a faucet with an elevated lead count of 166 parts per billion, according to Carroll.
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the standard for lead in drinking water is 15 parts per billion.
The company reported the results to the state immediately after the testing, according to Carroll.
“We tested the water, the faucet was removed, we did other work on the plumbing, (and) had it retested,” Carroll said. “It was not above the threshold, but still elevated to the point where we’re in a no-drink situation.”
According to the EPA, there is no safe level of lead exposure for children, a very small amount of lead can harm their health, and the current “reference level” is a screening threshold, not a safety limit.
“Before the 2020s, brass had a lot of lead in it because when they milled it and machined it, it made it smooth and nice brass. But they can’t do that anymore, because that’s one of the areas that lead leaches into the waters from brass fittings,” Carroll said. “One hundred years ago, when you put in a well, you put in a lead line because lead never goes bad, as we all found out.”
According to a document from the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, the school is required to collect source water samples and test for lead and copper from each active entry point to the distribution system within six months. It must also collect one source water sample for lead and copper from each active entry point to the distribution system within 60 days.
After the school was alerted, water fountains were covered with signs, and the kitchen was instructed not to cook with water.
According to Carroll, there is bottled water and coolers spread throughout the school.
“The next step will be retesting,” Carroll said. “Before we retest we have to do some work on the system.”
Carroll said he is unaware what the date retesting is going to begin.
“The school has softeners and a filtration system going through the water softening system, the softener heads were not at 100% so they were rebuilt, and had new beds, so they are back to fully operational, and there is a system to lower the potential of hydrogen, but the PH levels are fine,” according to Carroll.
Carroll hopes to have the school “lead free” by the beginning of December.
“The school remains in a no-drink situation until you’re back to zero,” he said.
The Bristol School Committee will next meet at 5:30 p.m. on Thursday, Dec. 3 at BCS, at 2153 Bristol Road. For more information, go to johnsbayschools.org or call 886-8358.

title: UMaine women’s basketball’s upset bid thwarted by Oregon
text:
Brooklynn Haywood and Katie Fiso combined for 23 points in the fourth quarter as Oregon rallied for a 79-72 victory over Maine in a women’s basketball game Friday night in Orono.
Maine (2-1) built a 19-11 lead after one quarter and held it until the fourth, when Haywood scored 13 of her 24 points and Fiso added 10 of her 32 points. Haywood made 10 of 14 shots overall, including 4 of 7 from 3-point range, and Fiso was 14 for 21 as Oregon improved to 4-1.
Lala Woods led the Black Bears with 21 points. Maddie Fitzpatrick recorded 19 points and nine rebounds.

title: Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about her cancer recovery
text:
Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about her cancer recovery
Catherine, Princess of Wales, shares new details about her health.
In a Country Life interview with Robert Macfarlane, the princess opened up about how nature played a significant role in her cancer recovery.
"I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time," she said in the interview. "This is the same in nature. It shows us that periods of rest, reflection and renewal are equally as important as moments of growth."
Related video above: Kate Middleton greeted by Italian crowds
Catherine originally disclosed that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy in a video announcement in March 2024.
In September 2024, the mother of three announced she had completed her chemotherapy treatments. Catherine said that her cancer was in remission after she spent the day supporting other cancer patients at the hospital where she received treatment in January 2025.
She launched a quarterly short film project in May 2025 titled "Mother Nature" on the official The Prince and Princess of Wales YouTube channel.
The project, narrated by Catherine, features landscapes throughout the U.K. and is her "deeply personal, creative reflection." The series takes viewers through the seasons: Spring (May 2025); Summer (2025); Autumn (November 2025); and lastly, Winter (January 2026).
Catherine said in the interview that she finds hope in nature's lessons.
"Nature reminds us that change is inevitable. We might not be able to have certainty or control every outcome, but we can do the small things, and those small things add up and do make a difference, if we nurture what is around us and have faith," she said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Lincoln Theater will wind down its year-long 150th anniversary celebration with a special fundraising concert on Saturday, Nov. 21 at 7 p.m. featuring Heat Wave: The Linda Ronstadt Experience, starring vocalist Kelly Caufield.
Caufield’s soaring soprano has previously graced Lincoln Theater’s stage as Annie in the LCCT production of "The Bikinis," and as Crystal in "Little Shop of Horrors." title: May we return to pre-2016 normative behavior
New England Republicans should stand up for their heritage
text:
The Republican Party has given up on New England and I can’t understand why.
It’s not as if it can’t win. It’s like the party doesn’t even want to try.
Perhaps it’s best to start with the original New England Republican: Maine’s Hannibal Hamlin, a senator who couldn’t stomach his Democratic Party’s nomination of a pro-slavery presidential nominee in 1856. Disgusted at what his party had become, Hamlin joined the brand-new Republican Party instead.
“I love my country more than I love my party,” he said.
The most consequential political decision of his life led to his selection as Abraham Lincoln’s vice presidential running mate in 1860, a position he held for most of the Civil War. He would have kept it too, had Lincoln worried more about securing New England’s votes in 1864.
But since the six Northeastern states never wavered in their support for Lincoln, the president tapped Tennessee loyalist Andrew Johnson instead, the biggest political mistake Lincoln ever made.
For generations after, New England remained solidly Republican, with many powerful members of Congress who promoted fiscal responsibility, minimal taxes and enough social justice to keep the rabble content. They were generally genteel businessmen.
In the 1960s, after Democrats began supporting civil rights while the GOP began cozying up to white Southerners, that era came to a close.
Even in the past half century, however, New England has been reasonably friendly to Republicans. Since 1976, it has elected 29 Republicans to the U.S. House, 27 governors and 16 U.S. senators.
Then came disaster in the form of one man: President Donald Trump.
Since 2016, Maine has been the only New England state to elect a Republican to Congress. It gave Sen. Susan Collins another term in 2020 and allowed Rep. Bruce Poliquin to stay in office in 2016 (before dumping him two years later). This year, the district elected Paul LePage as its next U.S. House representative.
If the GOP’s footing seems shaky in Maine, recall that, since 2016, all five other New England states have rejected every Republican on the ballot for any federal office.
Trump’s xenophobic rants and ugly politics helped raise up a generation of MAGA warriors who, despite residing in a region that long prided itself on its civility, now model their politics on his.
If Republicans still hewed to their party’s heritage, I believe that politicians like Maine’s Olympia Snowe and Bill Cohen or Connecticut’s Lowell Weicker or New Hampshire’s Warren Rudman or Rhode Island’s John and Lincoln Chafee could win today.
I don’t see how they could fit into a party warped by Trump. Candidates like this would have a hard time even getting nominated.
The problem now is one that Hamlin himself faced: the Trump-dominated national party is no longer tolerable to New Englanders. Facing a similar situation in 1856, when slaveholders captured control of the Democrats, Hamlin quit his party, to his eternal credit. Sen. Collins, though, stayed within her party’s fold — and paid the price at the polls this month.
As people try to cope with fresh challenges, political parties change. That will happen with the GOP, too, once it puts Trump in its rear-view mirror.
Maybe when Trump is out of the picture, Republicans can reclaim their legacy in New England and become leaders in shaping our region and our nation once more. In light of all we’ve seen recently, it may seem strange to wish for a rational, competitive GOP. But I do.

title: New hangar project breaks ground at Old Town Municipal Airport
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - A new hangar project is getting off the ground at Old Town Municipal Airport after more than four years of planning.
The primary use of the hangar is for aircraft from Northwoods Air and to allow for expansion of their flight school and other operations.
Northwoods Air owner Cody Anderson says the hangar is intended to accommodate corporate aircraft bringing executives and employees to the area for business.
“Currently at Old Town there’s no hangars big enough to handle a corporate aircraft for a business that might fly their executives or employees in to do business in the area,” Anderson said. “Outside of Bangor there’s really no options that can handle that sort of aircraft so our goal is to be able to do that here at Old Town.”
A place for aircraft and maintenance
Anderson says the heated hangar will provide a place to store aircraft and work on them.
“Having a warm place to put an airplane, do maintenance on it if you need to, it makes a huge difference,” he said, adding that employees have a better experience working in a heated facility.
Northwoods Air also provides aerial surveying and mapping and operates a flight school with students from across the country.
Support from longtime pilots
Retired pilot Ray Gibouleau has flown in and out of Old Town Municipal Airport for 61 years. He says he is impressed by the airport’s growth and Anderson’s work there.
Anderson says support from veteran pilots like Gibouleau has been especially meaningful.
“Ray has been a mentor to me for a very long time here at the airport,” Anderson said. He added that seeing support from older pilots in the community has been rewarding and has helped reassure him that he is doing the right thing.
Anderson credits his crew and the town of Old Town for supporting the project.
We’re told the hangar is being built by Santos Custom Builders of Holden.

title: Hold the elected accountable on accountability
Here’s why some contestants have been forced out of Miss Universe competition
text:
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico because of visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration, while two others are struggling to obtain visas.
Representatives from Zambia and the Republic of Congo have withdrawn from the pageant, which takes place this month in the U.S. territory, after failing to secure visas. Contestants from South Sudan and Zimbabwe are still awaiting theirs.
The United States has imposed sweeping travel restrictions affecting dozens of countries, many of them in Africa, under proclamations issued during Trump’s second administration.
Last December, the administration expanded restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while maintaining a full suspension of entry for nationals of the Republic of Congo and South Sudan.
“She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves,” Miss Universe Zambia organizers said in a statement this week announcing the withdrawal of their representative, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka.
In the Republic of Congo, Georgina Kambongo made history when she was crowned the Central African country’s first Miss Universe representative. National organizers say her inability to travel to Puerto Rico is linked solely to Trump’s travel restrictions.
“American visa challenges have delayed that journey, but the fight is not over,” Zimbabwe’s representative, Roseanna Hall, said in a social media post. “After months of preparation, I am not giving up. I remain confident that God who began a good work in me will bring it to completion.”
In South Sudan, organizers said contestant Adut Deng’s participation remained uncertain despite months of efforts to secure the necessary travel documents and approvals.
“South Sudan deserves to be seen, heard, and represented. Our queen carries the hopes, dreams, beauty, and resilience of a nation,” organizers said in a statement.
The competition’s 75th edition is expected to attract up to 120 contestants. Delegates began arriving in Puerto Rico on Sunday for rehearsals and other preliminary activities.
A national costume competition is scheduled for Nov. 21, followed by swimsuit and evening gown segments the following day. The winner will be crowned on Nov. 24.

title: The Roux Institute’s new campus is a year from completion. It’s already changing Portland.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Against a sky and ocean backdrop of monotone gray, the copper-red columns of the curving, seven-story centerpiece of the Roux Institute’s new campus, the Alfond Center, provided some of the only color Tuesday afternoon.
That was, of course, if one didn’t count the bright yellow and orange of construction vehicles, reflective vests and cones that dotted the sprawling construction site along the water in East Deering.
Over the sounds of a crew of about 220 workers, Mike Pollastri, senior vice provost and interim head of the Roux Institute, said the copper color was chosen as a nod to the former B&M Baked Beans factory, which is undergoing its own transformation.
While construction on Northeastern University’s $500 million high-tech education, research and entrepreneurial hub officially began in November 2024, the general public didn’t get a clear picture of the project until this year, when a parking garage emerged seemingly overnight and the Alfond Center began to take shape.
For native Portlanders, it’s the latest marker of a changing city.
The project is on track to be completed by this time next year, with 600-plus students set to arrive for the spring 2028 semester. Two empty lots remain for future growth, and while they could be used for housing, Sam Reiche, a project manager, said there are no immediate plans for them.
“We have our hands full,” Pollastri said.
The Portland Press Herald walked the site with its developers this week to understand what’s coming and how the work is already transforming a former industrial site into a modern, public-facing technology campus.
HOMAGES TO THE PAST
The Roux Institute, established in 2020 with a $100 million donation from Lewiston native and technology entrepreneur David Roux, welcomed its first class of students in 2020 using offices at the Wex building on Fore Street.
Its founders envisioned a high-tech graduate school, business accelerator and training pipeline to boost Maine’s workforce and economy, and Roux chose the Boston-based Northeastern University as its academic partner. A separate nonprofit was then formed to develop a permanent campus, eventually settling on the 13-acre B&M site in 2021.
The new campus includes firsts for Portland but will also retain mirrors of the city’s past, calls for which project managers heard loud and clear from residents — along with concerns for traffic — during the approval process.
The main features of the development are the 245,000 square-foot Alfond Center; the renovated bean factory, which will be called Lunder Innovation Labs; and a parking garage with an attached childcare center with capacity for about 60 children.
The site was designed to be fully electric and will incorporate geothermal wells, air-source heat pumps, an electric boiler, and a chiller for heating and cooling. Crews drilled down 800 feet for the geothermal wells, which will meet roughly 80% of the heating and cooling demand.
A two-story front section of the Alfond Center was built using mass timber, compressed layers of wood that serve as the load-bearing structure in place of traditional steel or concrete. In addition to lowering a building’s carbon footprint, they’re also more fire-resistant and faster to assemble.
Reiche said the decision to employ the emerging material was made partly to show Maine what can be done with mass timber.
“It could be the future of our forestry industry,” Pollastri said.
On the building’s exterior — with materials sourced from Maine to Italy — the facade went up quickly over the last few months. The front portion is meant to evoke the “cribstone” bridge to Bailey Island in Harpswell.
On each of the large window panes, small circles are etched into the glass in line with Portland’s bird-safe ordinance.
Kevin Kraft, Portland’s planning director, said it’s rare to see this combination of emerging technology and green building features in a single project.
“We’re excited to see this sort of thoughtful approach to architecture and sustainability coming to Portland,” he said.
Despite all of the modern technology and sustainable elements going into the site, developers say the most frequent question from the public is about the seasonal Christmas tree that’s sat atop the former factory for years.
A new version of the “tree” — a tower strung with lights — will soon be lit.
“We’re well aware that it’s a landmark,” Pollastri said. “It’s the first question we get.”
“Anyone who grew up here understands the nostalgia behind it,” Reiche added.
PLACES FOR THE PUBLIC
Beyond a handful of homes and an Interstate 295 underpass, the pavement on Sherwood Street begins to turn brown with dirt from the site. A sign in front of a house tells workers not to park there.
Next year, as part of a $25 million transportation grant, a new interstate exit will empty directly onto the street. The remaining funding is already being put to use: Construction has begun on a perimeter pathway and on a rebuild of the pier facing the Portland peninsula, both of which will be open to the public.
As part of the Maine Department of Transportation’s work, a pedestrian bridge running parallel with Tukey’s Bridge, which carries the interstate, will provide a sought-after connection. Reiche said the bridge is in the design phase now and likely won’t be built for a few years.
While nostalgia often fuels mixed feelings about redevelopment, Pollastri said Roux is excited to transition the property into a place where the public is welcome. While Portlanders may have fond memories of the view — and smell — of B&M, only factory workers set foot on the property for decades.
“We’re really excited by the fact that it will be a way to invite the public into what we’re doing,” Pollastri said.
At the former factory, dozens of workers stood on scaffolding Tuesday as they repaired the exterior of the 1913 building.
Christina Consigli, a senior project manager from construction firm Consigli, said crews have been repointing all of the brick and patching concrete. Inside, they’ve put up structural shoring in order to demolish the rest of the interior.
Reiche said the team inherited tons of old material from the building — beanpots, records and old photos — and they’re working on how to display some of it when the renovation is complete.
The construction team has been working with the city’s historic preservation office on the project. All new windows will be installed in the spring. Pollastri said it’s been registered as a landmark, “so it can never come down.”
Between buildings, the interior of the site will feature a “round,” with native landscaping and gardens. Reiche said those involved are also excited for the coming Casco Bay Trail, slated for the former Berlin subdivision rail line that cuts just past the property, ending at the defunct swing bridge.
While native Portlanders and East Deering neighbors used several public meetings to air concerns over traffic and infrastructure strain, the new campus won’t be full to start. According to Pollastri, it’s being built to accommodate 1,500 students, but when it opens, two floors at the Alfond Center will be empty — shells of spaces that could host partners or new lab spaces depending on future growth.
At a Nov. 2 virtual neighborhood meeting, there were only a handful of attendees, and questions were limited, when the development team gave a quarterly progress update.
PERSPECTIVE
In the Alfond Center, a lift with a 40-person capacity brings workers and equipment from floor to floor. Several classrooms and an event space funded by Joe Wishcamper are going into the sixth floor. There’s a panoramic view of Casco Bay.
Pollastri, who was once a chemistry professor at Northeastern, said Roux’s new campus will “scale up” the work they’ve already been doing: graduate programs, workforce training, experiential learning, and research programs in AI, health, climate technology and more. The institute has large research partners like Jackson Laboratories and MaineHealth, and provides incubator space for startup companies.
The Alfond Center will also feature an advanced manufacturing lab, where students or startups can prototype products in every stage of the process and eventually invite the public in to test or interact with them.
Down near the pier, where new decking is being installed, the clouds began to part to reveal blue sky. Developers envision a water taxi having a berth there, part of a transportation plan they hope will limit traffic worries.
Alex Shepherd, a project manager, said the entire property was raised at least 10 feet to take it out of the 100-year flood plain. Reiche said the factory remains lower, but that the new buildings are “well above the worst, worst case.”
Pollastri mentioned how the view from next to the factory changed the feel of the campus. One could say the same driving across Tukey’s Bridge, or east on Washington Avenue where the sloping roof juts above the tree line.
“Every angle is a little different,” he said.

title: Paul LePage officially deemed the victor of Congressional District 2 race
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Former Governor Paul LePage is officially going to be Maine’s next congressman.
Ranked choice tabulations in Augusta ended just after 1 p.m. on Thursday. LePage, a republican, won with 50.81% of the vote. Democratic challenger Matt Dunlap received 49.18%.
LePage fills the seat currently held by Rep. Jared Golden (D) who opted to not run for re-election. Golden, a democrat, has held that seat since 2019.
Unofficial first-round results showed Paul LePage leading Matt Dunlap. LePage received 49.894% of the vote in the initial results—just short of a majority. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the state was legally obligated to begin ranked-choice tabulation, despite Dunlap appearing to concede.
“It’s not surprising, given that he had 49.89% of the vote going into the process,” Bellows said. “But, it does, under ranked-choice voting, give him a majority plus one. And that is always the goal in ranked-choice voting, is that the winner has the backing of a majority of the voters.“
Tabulation began Monday morning. Bellows said since it seemed unlikely that the ranked choice tabulation would change the final outcome, her office thought it was wise to reduce costs by not requiring staff to work overtime and conduct the process during working hours.
LePage declared victory the day after the election, saying the gap was too much for Dunlap to overcome.
In a concession statement shared with the press on Nov. 5, Dunlap said “This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best. I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard. Your support inspired me, and I’m honored to have worked side by side with you over the past year.”
Congressman-elect LePage has already started orientation in Washington. “
The Maine Ranked Choice Voting process only confirmed what we already knew, Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District,” said Senior LePage adviser Brent Littlefield. “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people. As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”
Local Recounts
Bellows also announced today recounts were requested in four races by the November 10th deadline:
- Senate District 18 in Oxford County
- House District 96 in Lewiston
- House District 106 in Windham
- Kennebec County Commissioner, District 2
Bellows said they will start those recounts Monday.

title: What you need to know about new child car seat standards coming Dec. 5
text:
(Gray Media) – A new update to child car seat safety standards is fast approaching, changing the requirements for newly manufactured seats.
Starting Dec. 5, 2026, updated federal testing standards will affect how covered car seats are tested for side-impact crashes and how child restraints are tested for frontal crashes.
What’s changing?
Side-impact protection: FMVSS 213a
Covered car seats must meet a federal side-impact performance standard designed to reduce injuries and deaths in crashes where a vehicle is struck from the side.
The test uses a simulated vehicle seat and door to assess how a child restraint performs in a side-impact crash. It’s meant to simulate the kind of collision often called a T-bone crash.
The standard generally covers portable child restraints recommended for a weight range that includes children under 40 pounds or a height range that includes children under about 43 inches. That doesn’t mean a seat is exempt just because it can also be used by larger children.
There are exceptions, including car beds, harness-only restraints and qualifying restraints made only for school buses.
Important date distinction: NHTSA issued the side-impact rule in 2022. Dec. 5, 2026, is its mandatory compliance date, not the date the original rule was first issued.
Updated frontal-impact testing: FMVSS 213b
A separate updated standard becomes mandatory for child restraints manufactured on or after Dec. 5, 2026.
The frontal-crash test will use:
- An updated test seat designed to better represent a modern vehicle’s back seat.
- A simulated lap-and-shoulder belt for testing most restraints, rather than the lap belt used in the older test for many seats.
Basically, the government is updating how it tests car seats for front-end crashes while adding a separate side-impact requirement for covered seats.
Do parents need to buy a new car seat?
Parents are not required to replace their existing car seats simply because of the deadline.
A seat purchased after Dec. 5 may have been manufactured before that date, so the manufacture date, rather than the purchase date alone, matters. Some manufacturers also complied with the newer standards early.
Parents should continue to check that the seat:
- Fits their child and their vehicle.
- Is installed and used according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
- Has not been recalled and is within the manufacturer’s stated usable life.
What about weight limits for forward-facing seats and boosters?
The Child Passenger Safety Board overview describes updated manufacturer labeling requirements:
Manufacturers must specify a minimum forward-facing weight of at least 26.5 pounds.
Manufacturers must specify a minimum booster-seat weight of at least 40 pounds.
These are not instructions to switch a child’s seat as soon as they reach those weights. NHTSA recommends keeping children in each stage as long as they fit within the seat manufacturer’s limits.

KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) - A truck driver in Missouri is accused of killing a mother and her two young sons in a crash as they were heading to the airport.
Eldar Skander, 39, was charged Tuesday with three counts of involuntary manslaughter in the deaths of 35-year-old Olga Sorbalo and her sons, 9-year-old Luis Sorbalo and 6-year-old Samir Sorbalo.
On Wednesday, the of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Skander was “an illegal alien from Ukraine.”
Court documents allege Skander was driving a semi-truck at a high speed on northbound U.S. 71 around 3:20 p.m. when he hit three stopped vehicles.
A preliminary investigation found no signs that the truck’s emergency brakes had been applied, authorities said.
An officer found a tablet on the truck’s floorboard open to YouTube.

Skander’s address in the court filing listed him as a Chicago resident. Jail records show he is being held at the Jackson County Detention Center with “an additional hold for ICE.”

title: No Injuries Following a Fire in Fort Fairfield
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WAGM) - No injuries following a structure fire in Fort Fairfield.
According to Fort Fairfield Fire Rescue, the department received a call at 8:50 this morning reporting a structure fire at the intersection of Brown and Depot Street. Upon arrival firefighters found smoke and flames coming out of the second story windows at 36 Brown Street. All occupants and pets were safely outside of the building upon arrival. There were no injuries reported. Fort Fairfield called in the Presque Isle, Caribou, Easton, and Limestone Fire Departments for mutual aid. Firefighters initiated an exterior fire attack while additional personnel and resources responded to the scene. Once sufficient resources were in place, crews transitioned to an interior attack and were able to quickly extinguish the fire. Extensive overhaul operations were conducted to ensure the fire was fully extinguished. Both roads were closed to traffic during response. title: Ford throws open the doors to its new Vault, unveiling 125 rare historic vehicles
text:
ROMULUS, Mich. (AP) — Ford will open the doors to its new Vault this weekend to some lucky gearheads and fans of history.
The 123-year-old carmaker on Saturday will allow select members of the public and employees into the Ford Vault to take a gander at everything from rare concept cars and Hollywood Mustangs to historic police cruisers and even a 1938 ambulance. Tickets were snapped up quickly, but Ford Motor Co. said there will be future showings.
“You don’t create an experience like this and a space like this and then hide it away,” said Ted Ryan, Ford’s Archives and Heritage Brand Manager. “We’re going to find a way to make it available to the car community in Michigan as soon as we can.”
Ford’s collection of historic vehicles once was housed at its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters and other locations. Its vast new home, the Vault, is situated inside a former Amazon fulfillment center in Romulus, another Detroit suburb, and measures 79,000 square feet (7,339 square meters).
“I can tell you, after working here for a couple weeks, I’m averaging about 20,000 steps a day,” said Ryan.
The Vault brings together 125 of the Heritage Fleet’s historically significant vehicles, including race cars, design concepts and vehicles tied to pop culture.
“Here, we can actually have a purpose-built space for the cars,” Ford Archives Manager Ciera Casteel said. “That’s our legacy. That’s what we do here. That is what this company is.”
Some highlights:
— A 2005 Mustang GT proof-of-concept that paved the way for the Shelby GT350. Engineers nicknamed it “Johnny Cash” (inspired by his song “One Piece at a Time,” about an autoworker who cobbles together a car out of mismatched parts). “It’s like Frankenstein. Things have been bolted onto Johnny over the years. This is the first time he’s ever been displayed,” Ryan said.
— The first three cars to cross the finish line at Le Mans in 1966, a race immortalized in the 2019 Matt Damon/Christian Bale film, “Ford v Ferrari.”
— A 1910 right-hand-drive Model T that was built in the U.K. and remained there until 2025, when it was added to the Heritage Fleet.
— A 1973 Mustang convertible used in “The Mary Tyler Moore Show.” The vehicle was sold in 1974, and remained in private ownership until Ford bought it last year. The body underwent a restoration in 1999, while the interior remains original.
The carmaker built the Vault to be a working archive, giving today’s designers and engineers access to the ideas and experiments that shaped the company as they work on what comes next.
“There’s ‘surprise and delight’ moments throughout the building,” Ryan said.

Sanford Police Chief Eric Small will retire in December
text:
Sanford Chief of Police Eric Small announced he will retire on Dec. 25 this year.
Small announced his retirement from law enforcement in a Facebook post Friday morning, where he thanked his community for 18 years with the Sanford Police Department, just over two of them as chief.
In his announcement, Small said he was unsure what he would do next but that he was “looking forward to finding out.”
“I plan to spend more time with family, more time around horses, and a lot more time doing things that don’t involve a police radio,” he wrote.
Small said he was planning to put more time into the Unbroken Children’s Foundation, a non-profit he founded that partners with local horse farms and facilities to use equine therapy to assist children experiencing grief and trauma and strengthen their confidence.
“I’m not leaving Sanford,” he wrote. “You’ll still see me around town, probably wearing a cowboy hat, Birkenstocks, and corduroy rather then (sic) a police uniform… And I hope you’ll still stop and say hello.”
In an email Friday, Small said serving as chief of police for Sanford has been an honor, and that he was incredibly proud of the men and women at the department and what they had all accomplished together.
Small said he was looking forward to having more time to spend with his wife, their children and grandchildren.
“I may be hanging up my badge on Christmas Day, but I’m certainly not retiring from life,” he said.
Small ran for state representative as a Republican in House District 143 before withdrawing in June, saying his beliefs no longer aligned with either political party.

title: Aging Untold: How to reset when stress becomes chronic
text:

Some medical professionals are promoting ketamine infusion as a possible solution for patients who cannot get relief from traditional pain management methods.
Elanor Koch of Nebraska said she has seen improvement since starting the therapy.
She said a tumor eroded and compressed her spinal cord by more than 60%, and she would wake up in pain. A flare would leave her in bed for days.
Then, Koch said she found ketamine infusion therapy and experienced significant improvement after six treatments in one month.
People with certain medical histories might not be good candidates for ketamine infusion, including those with mental health conditions such as schizophrenia, uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease, kidney or liver disease and substance use disorder.

title: SpaceX’s attempt for a Starship double catch is thwarted when the booster ends up in Gulf
text:
STARBASE, Texas (AP) — SpaceX’s attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.
Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.
It’s the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk’s company missed out on a double catch.
The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.
Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday’s miss all the more surprising.
“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.
This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.
The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.
SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.
SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.
Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said ahead of Friday’s launch.
NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.
During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.
“We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.

title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce, lawyer says, ending long marriage
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce from his wife, Angela, one of his lawyers said Thursday.
It comes nearly a week after Paxton, a Republican, lost his U.S. Senate race by double digits to Democrat James Talarico in one of the most expensive contests of the midterm elections that saw a wave of victories for Democrats across the country.
Angela Paxton, a state senator, cited allegations of adultery when she sought to end their 38-year-marriage. She filed the divorce after her husband had launched his run for Senate, posting on social media that she was doing so on “biblical grounds.”
Jared Julian, a lawyer for Ken Paxton, said the terms would remain private.
“From my observation, however, they share a mutual respect for one another,” Julian said. He added that both appeared to be looking forward “to the next chapters of their lives.”
An attorney for Angela Paxton did not immediately respond to phone and email messages Thursday. The finalized divorce was first reported by The New York Times.
After Paxton entered the race, some Republicans considered Paxton a potential drain on GOP resources because of legal, ethical and personal questions he has faced for years.
Angela Paxton had stuck by her husband through a decade of legal troubles that included state and federal corruption investigations and a 2023 state impeachment trial that publicly exposed an extramarital affair.
The Senate race that seemed like a longshot for Democrats when the year began became partly a referendum on Paxton’s history. Despite beating the long-seated incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, in a primary and gaining President Donald Trump’s endorsement, Paxton struggled to find traction in the general election against Talarico.
In October, less than a month before the election, Angela Paxton urged voters to back the Republican ticket but did not mention her estranged husband by name.
“It’s not as much about the individual players on the team. It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” she said in a campaign advertisement.
Democrat Nathan Johnson was elected attorney general and will take office in January.

title: Homeland Security secretary says no indication yet of nefarious act behind FAA communications issue
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security secretary says no indication yet of nefarious act behind FAA communications issue.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story is below.
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.
But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
___
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: Nationwide Ground Stop: FAA Halts All Flights Over Communications Issue
text:
Ground Stop Ordered for All Airports Nationwide
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday for all all airlines and all airports (including those in our area) for what they're describing as "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
The FAA issued the stop at 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday afternoon. It is unclear how long it will be in effect, according to reports from ABC and other outlets.
“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the advisory states, “all airports are ground stopped.”
The FAA issued the group stop due to a communications issues that impacted all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, according to a post from Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy on social media. He said that FAA technicians are currently investigating the issue.
Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis, the FAA said.
In the moments leading up to the alert from the FAA airports across the country including Chicago O'Hare and Newark, NJ were reporting delays.
Ground stops of the entire airspace are very rare. The most recent one took place in Janaury 2023. That's when a pilot notification system went down resulting in a ground stop. Prior to that one was issued after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
This is a developing story.

title: WATCH: Historic SS United States completes its final voyage – at the bottom of the Gulf
text:
WATCH: Historic SS United States completes its final voyage – at the bottom of the Gulf
The historic S.S. United States made its final voyage Wednesday, sinking beneath the Gulf off the coast of Florida and beginning a new chapter as the world’s largest artificial reef.
A slow final voyage
The nearly 1,000-foot luxury liner was deliberately sunk about 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida, where it is expected to attract divers and fishing enthusiasts while providing habitat for marine life.
The sinking took several hours longer than expected.
Much of the massive ship could still be seen in the dark water by nightfall after the sinking began on a cloudy Wednesday afternoon. Organizers had predicted the process could take as little as an hour.
Around 9 p.m., the vessel leaned to one side before quickly disappearing beneath the water.
“She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight,” Coleen O’Malley, president of Coleen Marine, the company sinking the ship, said before the vessel disappeared.
From speed record to reef
The controlled sinking was part of a long-planned $13.5 million project intended to create a major artificial reef and draw more divers and anglers to the area.
Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, said crews filled 128 fuel and lubricant tanks aboard the ship with water to help the vessel settle evenly on the ocean floor.
The process took longer than expected, Tomecek said.
“She’s a big ship,” he said.
The S.S. United States was once the fastest passenger ship to cross the Atlantic, setting the record in 1952. The liner crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times and is longer than the Titanic.
Now, the ship is destined to rest on the Gulf floor, where it will become a permanent underwater attraction and artificial reef.
The Associated Press and CNN contributed to this story.

title: 'The new bank robbery': What is ATM 'jackpotting'?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
'The new bank robbery': What is ATM 'jackpotting'?
'The new bank robbery': What is ATM 'jackpotting'?
Investigators call it a new way to rob a bank: Thieves target ATMs and get the machines to spit out hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash.
Video obtained by Hearst sister station WISN shows men pulling up to ATMs at two different banks in Wisconsin in March. Video shows them using a key to get inside the ATM. Once they come back later, it spits out cash.
Investigators call the crime "ATM jackpotting," because when it's successful, it is referred to by criminals as "hitting the jackpot."
Search warrants and a police report show the thieves got away with roughly $230,000 from ATMs in Greenfield, Wisconsin, on March 11 and 12. Search warrants show thieves came back 13 times in a six-hour span, and video shows them taking stacks of cash from the ATM.
In each video, a driver sits in the front seat while a man in the back seat, who appears to be on FaceTime, works with the ATM.
Thieves also got away with roughly $110,000 from ATMs in Glendale on March 4 and 5. Search warrants show the pair showed up six different times in a three-hour span.
In Glendale, video shows one of the suspects taking a selfie and fanning out the cash.
Glendale police told WISN they're working to figure out if the crimes are connected and who the suspects are. Greenfield police said they closed their investigation because they don't have any leads on the case.
"Think of this as the new bank robbery, without the force of violence of a bank robbery," said FBI Milwaukee Special Agent in Charge Alan Karr.
Karr couldn't speak on the two cases directly, but he did share information about ATM jackpotting. The FBI warned banks and the public about ATM jackpotting earlier this year.
FBI numbers show banks have reported 1,900 jackpotting incidents since 2020 across the United States. In 2025 alone, 700 incidents resulted in banks losing more than $20 million.
"Generally, these jackpot cases are done by crews in which people case an ATM; they are looking at the ATM to see what vulnerabilities they can exploit," Karr said. "'Hey, what's the security measures around this ATM? Are there cameras? Can we get into this ATM? Do we have a key to get into it to access the hard drive?' Then, someone will come back and collect the cash."
Karr said once thieves find their target, they use a key to open the front compartment of the ATM. Then, they connect a hard drive with malware, or their own computers, and hack the machine to give away cash.
"We always encourage the banks to take common-sense approaches and measures, updating software to overcome vulnerabilities, increasing the physical protections of ATMs, cameras in the area," Karr said.
A search warrant shows Glendale police believe one of the suspects may be from Chicago. WISN is not naming him because he has not been charged with a crime.
"UW Credit Union is aware of the March 4 criminal activity involving one of our Glendale ATMs," said Carma Atkinson, vice president of card programs and loss prevention at UW Credit Union, in an emailed statement. "We can confirm that member accounts and funds were not impacted. Protecting our members and the security of our operations are top priorities."
U.S. Bank said none of the cash was taken from customers' accounts.
