title: DHS responds to New York Times report on ICE agent involved in deadly Biddeford shooting
text:
Department of Homeland Security responds to New York Times report on ICE agent involved in deadly Biddeford shooting
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has issued a response to a New York Times report that raised questions about the vetting and training of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent involved in the fatal shooting of a Colombian man that happened in Maine four months ago.
David Brouillette had been identified by The Associated Press as the ICE officer who shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13. Both Brouillette's first ex-wife and his daughter told the AP that Brouillette told them he was the one who shot and killed Guerrero. DHS has repeatedly declined to identify Brouillette as the ICE agent involved in the shooting.
"Attempting to publicize their identities puts their lives and the lives of their families at serious risk," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement shared with Maine's Total Coverage on Friday.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Brouillette's sister, Elizabeth Emen, shared a series of emails with The Times from 2021 in which Brouillette berated Emen and their relatives and criticized her for her longtime relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children.
Emen later spoke about how she reacted to the news of the deadly shooting in an interview with ABC News.
"When I saw his actions on July 13, I just couldn't believe that it had been allowed to get to that point," Emen told ABC News. "I can't believe that he was onboarded into a federal agency and provided a weapon, and I'm really looking for answers around how that was allowed to happen."
The report from The Times also goes into detail about Brouillette's recruiting history, citing an anonymous source who said Brouillette was sped through the vetting process and that he was cleared to work for ICE in December 2025.
In their statement, the DHS spokesperson said that incoming ICE officers are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards.
"Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE," the DHS spokesperson said. "This administration is preserving ICE's reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world."
The DHS spokesperson went on to say that ICE maintains rigorous standards for all personnel.
"We ensure that every applicant is thoroughly assessed through mandatory pre-employment vetting protocols," the spokesperson said. "The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors."
In addition, the DHS spokesperson said that ICE officers go through rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship after they graduate from the academy, and that the additional training is tracked online and closely monitored.
Response from Guerrero family's attorney and Maine lawmakers
Ben Gideon, an attorney representing Guerrero's wife and his estate, has issued a statement in response to The Times' report on Brouillette.
"David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training," Gideon said in his statement. "Johan Sebastian’s death was not an inevitable accident. It was a natural and predictable choice of the policies of our government and its political leadership."
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine's 1st Congressional District, said that she demanded answers from Homeland Security about training and background checks in the days following Guerrero's death, and that Wednesday's report from The New York Times makes a full, independent investigation even more urgent.
"DHS must release Brouillette's hiring, vetting, training, and deployment records and cooperate fully with independent investigators," Pingree said in a statement. "Responsibility reaches beyond the officer who pulled the trigger. It extends to the leadership that armed and deployed him, and to an administration that put its deportation agenda ahead of human life. Every official responsible must be held accountable. Johan Sebastián’s family deserves justice, and I will keep fighting until they get it."
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, the Maine Democrat who defeated five-term Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, told Maine's Total Coverage that he plans to push for hearings or an independent review of ICE's hiring practices.
"I have every faith in legitimate law enforcement. I've respected it and appreciated it. I think in this situation, you're dragging down legitimate law enforcement when you don't have proper vetting and you don't have people that have the training," Jackson said. "This is a stain, and I do think we have to have hearings about it and get this resolved, and weed out these type of people and have a legitimate process to hire immigration officers."
Pingree and U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, have said Guerrero was not the target of the ICE operation that ultimately resulted in his death. King and Pingree also said that Guerrero, the father of a 3-year-old girl, had no criminal history.
In September, another attorney representing Guerrero's family testified before members of Congress. The testimony was part of a public forum examining several deadly shootings involving federal immigration agents.

title: How to reset when stress becomes chronic
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many people, stress feels like a bigger part of everyday life. When stress becomes chronic, it can bring physical effects.
According to the American Psychological Association, most Americans say their stress has increased, and about 75% report physical or emotional symptoms as a result.
We are sharing what people can do about it when stress becomes chronic.
When normal stress crosses the line
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the stress response itself is normal.
“If you have a tiger running at you, you’re going to run,” Rogers said. “You have to have that response so you can stay focused.”
However, stress becomes chronic “when you can’t turn it off.”
“But you can’t run from the tiger all day long,” she said.
How chronic stress shows up in the body
Rogers said physical effects of chronic stress can include a faster heart rate and higher blood pressure.
“Immune system takes a hit,” she said.
Rogers said many people now deal with ongoing stressors because of multitasking. When it lingers, there can be detrimental effects, she said.
“It’s a constant influx of information and interaction where there’s not any downtime,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said, adding that adrenaline and cortisol levels stay high as a result.
Rogers said children are affected too.
“We’re also seeing a greater increase of stress-related diseases happening in younger people,” Cradduck said.
Rogers said the body doesn’t know the difference between the types of stress.
If a person’s gut is off or insulin is high, Rogers said, the body reacts the same way and cortisol increases.
Cortisol is the body’s primary stress hormone, according to Mayo Clinic.
Rogers said swelling and fluid retention can also be signs that the body is under stress.
For menopausal women who have good control with hormones, Rogers said, hot flashes returning can be the “number one” sign that stress is present.
Why a break matters
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a personal story about stress. Her mother was sick and dying, and there was no end in sight. Friends convinced her to leave for a trip to Chicago and visit museums.
“I didn’t want to go. It just felt so wrong and bad,” O’Rourke said. “I went and then I went back to see her, and I felt like a totally different person.”
You might not think you need a break, but go ahead and take it, she said.
“Go for a walk. Get a good night’s sleep. Do something that brings you joy or comfort or happiness, because it really will offset the stress that you’re under,” O’Rourke said.
Quick ways to calm the body
The goal is to activate the parasympathetic nervous system, Rogers said, which she described as the “rest and digest” state, rather than the fight-or-flight response of the sympathetic nervous system.
Rogers and O’Rourke listed several options:
- Box breathing: Inhale for four seconds, hold for four seconds, exhale for four seconds, hold for four seconds
- Mudra
- Humming, singing and gargling, which Rogers said activate the vagus nerve
- Alternating nostril breathing
“It’s a very quick way to drop your stress,” Rogers said of activating the vagus nerve.
Cradduck also suggested a release. “Go sit in your car and roll up your windows and scream.”
Cradduck said family caregivers may not be able to step away for a museum visit.
“Sometimes they’re in that so deeply that they can’t,” Cradduck said. For them, she recommended box breathing, centering, “anything that can allow your body to have that release.”
O’Rourke said that when a client starts crying and stops out of embarrassment, she tells them to let it go.
“I know how much relief they’re going to get from just sitting there and sobbing,” she said.
The experts also shared the SEEDS method:
- Sleep
- Exercise
- Engagement
- Diet
- Active Stress Management
Key takeaways
- Do not normalize high stress. “What your mind suppresses, your body expresses,” Rogers says.
- Ignoring stress will not stop it from physically damaging the heart, brain and immune system.
- SEEDS method: Sleep, exercise, engagement, diet, active stress management

title: Soldier returning home after 84 years following a DNA match
text:
Soldier returning home after 84 years following a DNA match
Robert DuBois survived the Bataan Death March but later died in Japanese POW camp
Soldier returning home after 84 years following a DNA match
Robert DuBois survived the Bataan Death March but later died in Japanese POW camp
The remains of U.S. Army Pvt. Robert Dubois, who died in a Japanese prison camp during World War II, have been identified and are returning to New Mexico after 84 years.
For his niece, Patsy Gutierrez, the discovery has been an emotional experience.
Video above: Untold story of German-American WWII soldier
"Because I wish that his siblings and his parents could be here to see this," Gutierrez said.
Dubois’s parents and eight siblings died without seeing his remains come home.
Dubois joined the Army and was deployed to the Philippines, where he was captured on April 9, 1942, after the Bataan Peninsula fell to Japanese forces. He endured the brutal 65-mile Bataan Death March and was later interned at the infamous Cabanatuan prison camp. He died there on July 4, 1942, at the age of 24 from malnutrition.
"When I think about what has happened to him, could I have survived that? I doubt it," Gutierrez said.
After the war, Dubois never returned home. A few years later, his parents received a letter from the Army informing them of his death.
Dubois’s remains were recovered by the U.S. Army years after the war and sent to the Army’s identification lab in Hawaii, but they could not be identified at the time.
Ten years ago, the Army reached out to Gutierrez, asking for a DNA sample to help identify Dubois’s remains. Three months ago, she received confirmation that the remains were a match.
"I was just in shock for, you know, just in awe that they had found his body," Gutierrez said.
The Army posthumously awarded Dubois the Bronze Star for valor and the Purple Heart. He will be laid to rest this weekend at Mount Calvary Cemetery in Albuquerque, New Mexico, next to his mother and father.
"He's home at last, and that's what makes me happy, that I'm still alive to see it," Gutierrez said.

title: Cargo ship strikes bridge between New Jersey and Philadelphia, causing traffic backup
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — A cargo ship struck a bridge across the Delaware River on Thursday, disrupting traffic between Palmyra, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, according to a Pennsylvania lawmaker.
The collision left the 3,659-foot-long (1,115-meter-long) Tacony-Palmyra Bridge unable to close, causing a major backup on the Philadelphia side, state Rep. Ed Neilson said in a news release. No injuries have been reported, he said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the cargo vessel is currently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where an inspection team is on site. The Coast Guard identified the vessel as the 591-foot (180-meter) Strategic Alliance, which was built in 2013 and sails under the flag of Singapore.
The drawbridge was open for ships to pass through at the time of the collision around 1:15 p.m., according to the Coast Guard. It remained open afterward because another vessel needed to pass through, and has since come back down. The bridge reopened to traffic with a lane closure Thursday evening, the Burlington County (New Jersey) Bridge Commission Police Department said.
The steel bridge carries vehicles along Route 73 between Palmyra and the Tacony neighborhood in northeast Philadelphia. It has three lanes of vehicular traffic, two into Philadelphia and one into New Jersey. Estimates from 2025 show the bridge can carry as many as 76,200 vehicles each day.
Opened in 1929, the Tacony-Palmyra toll bridge was found to be in “fair” condition, according to the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 National Bridge Inventory data released this fall.
Inspectors rated the deck of the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge as in good condition, the substructure as in fair condition and the superstructure — the component that absorbs the live traffic load — as fair.

title: Here’s what Susan Collins can do to improve her legacy
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Chris Kast, a grandfather and avowed rabble rouser, is a writer and marketing professional who lives in Portland.
Last week the so-called Blue Wave hit like a tsunami and people in each state in our incredible — albeit increasingly more fragile — union turned up at the polls and said, “enough is enough.” I know I did.
And as I carefully filled in the first choice circle near Troy Jackson’s name, I did so not because I’m a huge fan — I think Jackson has some weaknesses — but because he was our only real choice to defeat “I’ll only serve two terms if elected” Susan Collins. So, he got my vote. After all, the way I look at it, nearly anyone would have been a better choice than Sen. Collins, who has become a voter of political convenience, seemingly to protect her status as a moderate.
But I saw through what I consider her machinations and pearl-clutching concerns and for months have been writing her in the hopes that she would respond to me not with a form letter telling me about the hard work she was doing, but with more substantive answers to my questions in order to better understand where she stood on issues and not on her impeccable voting record (which I have to admit is impressive).
As I looked at her record and voting, I noticed a pattern of opposition to President Donald Trump when it was convenient and would garner news coverage and then, when it mattered to the MAGA base, she’d step in line and vote for people ( Brett Kavanaugh) and to move forward legislation (the One Big Beautiful Bill) that showed me and many people like me her true colors. Actually it’s one color really — MAGA red.
So as we live through the last few weeks of her long tenure, I have a few suggestions that may help her leave office by making a few moves in her role that could help her maintain respect for the years she spent in Washington, D.C. working on behalf of all Mainers. Those are of course the pre-Trump fealty years.
From the tone of her ads toward the end, I could tell that she and the team felt trouble was brewing as the digs at Jackson were puerile and beneath what I thought was her dignity and ability to always take the high road. But since that notion was completely scrapped from what I saw and heard in ads supporting her campaign, I wanted to suggest a few things that she may be able to do to regain some respect. And preserve her legacy.
She should:
Rebuke Trump for all his bullying, name calling and chaotic brinksmanship that has flipped our republic on its head.
Go back, if only for these fleeting last weeks in office, to your true centrist roots and pave the way for both sides to come together as a collective for the greater good.
Look into the allegations that Darline Graham Nordone’s (you know Lindsey Graham’s sister) husband works for a company that’s connected to a Chinese firm that was reportedly sanctioned in 2024 for supplying military technology to Russia. That’s likely the tip of the iceberg for these types of actions among insiders in Washington.
Apologize for voting in Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and every other judge who seems to believe that white males are the ones who should make decisions for women over their healthcare.
Share again your deep concern that the Epstein files have yet to be released in their entirety and that all who committed crimes regardless of their party affiliation will be tracked down and if guilty, be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.
It’s not a very long list so maybe, just maybe she can still leave a legacy that matters.

title: Lincoln’s conservative bloc loses its majority after voters oust David Ireland ally
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Lincoln has new leadership after last week’s election ousted one member of a conservative bloc that made headlines for pushing steep budget cuts that were ultimately reversed under public pressure.
Lee Rand, a right-wing councilor and supporter of the town’s polarizing Vice Chair David Ireland, lost reelection. He received the fourth most votes in a six-person race for two open seats. Democratic councilor Gordon Street and newcomer Bobbi Stormann won.
Rand’s loss leaves Ireland’s bloc one vote short of the 4-3 majority it has held on the seven-member council since Ireland took office last year. At a Monday council meeting, Street was elected vice chair, replacing Ireland, who remains on the board.
The change comes as the Penobscot County town of about 4,800 people prepares for an economic shift. Its former mill is slated to become home to the world’s largest battery system by 2027. Officials have been planning for an economy that no longer depends on one major employer.
They have been doing so under enormous political strife. Since Ireland’s election last fall, Lincoln has gone through four town managers, fought over a 12.8% budget cut passed in June that was later scaled back to about 3%, and weathered two failed attempts to recall Ireland and his allies.
Ireland won his seat in November 2025 after campaigning for the removal of the town manager at the time, who resigned after the election. Ireland’s bloc, which included Rand as well as former state Rep. Sheldon Hanington and councilor Eric Rojo, pushed through its budget cut in June, following through on promises to cut taxes sharply.
Police and fire departments warned the cut could seriously impact public safety. After weeks of protest by town employees and residents, the council reversed course, with Hanington and Rojo breaking from Ireland to back the town manager’s smaller cuts.
Under the conservative bloc, Lincoln burned through town managers at a furious pace. Andrew Frodahl, whom Rand recruited, backed out days before he was set to start in March. The council then fired his replacement in a 4-3 vote less than two months into the job. Its current interim town manager, Police Chief Lee Miller, is the fourth person to accept the job this year.
Ireland has brought a combative style of political discourse to town, often calling out political opponents on Facebook. His push for steep budget cuts as well as resurfacing allegations that he sexually assaulted his sister and daughter fueled both recall attempts. Ireland has repeatedly denied the allegations.
Rand, like Ireland, is a prolific social media poster. He often shares negative posts about Islam, many of them AI-generated. He also runs a Facebook group about biblical prophecy, with a focus on the end times.
Street said Stormann’s election made it clear locals were “demanding a change.” The two are poised to use their new power to create a social media policy for town officials. Stormann said the social media environment surrounding the council over the last two years may have deterred talent from coming to town.
“I think that Lincoln has a bright future with the mill site,” she said. “We just need to get our house in order, and it’s going to be a great, great community.”
Rand could not be reached for comment. Ireland said he respected the election results but worried what they would mean for taxpayers.
“The election may be over, but my commitment to the people of Lincoln remains unchanged,” he said in a statement. “I intend to continue asking difficult questions, demanding financial accountability, advocating for responsible municipal spending and working to reduce Lincoln’s reliance on property taxation.”
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Eddington school board member held without bail after latest arrest
text:
The Eddington school board member arrested on drug charges this week is being held without bail.
Brittany Wood, 36, was denied bail during a Thursday court hearing, when she entered a not guilty plea to charges of possessing drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violating her conditions of release, CBS affiliate WABI reported.
Those charges stem from a Sunday traffic stop, when deputies seized drugs and stopped Wood from allegedly “destroying potential evidence,” according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
Over the next couple days, deputies unsuccessfully tried to get Wood — who sits on the Regional School Unit 63 school board, which comprises Clifton, Eddington and Holden — to surrender willingly. The sheriff’s office then asked Tuesday night for the public’s help in finding Wood.
She was booked at the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor on Wednesday afternoon. She turned herself into police, WABI reported.
Wood was out on bail for domestic violence aggravated assault and endangering the welfare of a child, charges stemming from the May 31 overdose at a Clewleyville Road home in Eddington that sent a 9-month-old infant into cardiac arrest. The infant was revived after CPR and two doses of naloxone, an opioid-overdose-reversing antidote.
In July, the sheriff’s office asked for the public’s help in locating Wood when she didn’t turn herself in on a previous arrest warrant.
While she had an active arrest warrant out in the overdose case, Wood allegedly was spending time in Boston and at Times Square.
Eventually, Wood returned to Maine, and she was arrested about 7 p.m. on July 14 as she left a Brewer home as a passenger in a white pickup truck.
On Friday morning, Wood was still listed as a member of the RSU 63 school board. Her term expires in June.

title: What Nvidia’s stock drop could mean for your 401(k)

text:
What Nvidia’s stock drop could mean for your 401(k)
Nvidia’s stock fell after its CEO resigned. Here’s how the drop could reach your 401(k) through investment funds.
What Nvidia’s stock drop could mean for your 401(k)
Nvidia’s stock fell after its CEO resigned. Here’s how the drop could reach your 401(k) through investment funds.
Nvidia’s stock fell sharply Thursday after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Because Nvidia is one of the largest companies on the market, its share price can affect major stock indexes and the investment funds some people hold in their 401(k)s.
“One of the reasons a company like Nvidia can move the broader market is it’s a pretty large component of the market,” said Ryan Sterling, CEO of NerdWallet Wealth Partners and a chartered financial analyst.
That market exposure can reach retirement savings even for people who never bought Nvidia stock directly. Funds offered in a 401(k) plan may hold Nvidia shares, including target-date funds, which invest in a mix of assets and are designed for people planning to retire around a certain year.
"For most 401(k) investors, the target-date funds ... are very well-diversified," Sterling said. "And this is why you diversify, is you want to minimize the chance that one story, one scandal is going to have an impact on your retirement."
For people with diversified retirement savings, a decline in Nvidia alone generally isn’t a reason to change their investment plan. Investors can speak with a financial advisor or check their funds’ holdings in a fact sheet or on their plan’s website to see what they own.
Sterling also urged investors to keep short-term headlines in perspective.
"At the core of investing, the reason the U.S. market and markets around the world have gone up over time is because it's really a function of progress and innovation. Betting against progress and innovation is a very dangerous thing to bet against," he said.
If a person is heavily invested in Nvidia stock, Sterling recommended reassessing financial plans. This could involve saving more, cutting expenses or selling shares to diversify holdings.

title: Jails have become destinations for people who need mental health treatment
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Experts say prisons and county jails have become destinations for people who need mental health treatment, not time behind bars.
According to multiple reports, three jail systems are among the largest mental health facilities in the country: Rikers Island in New York, Twin Towers Jail in Los Angeles and Cook County Jail in Chicago.
But some people are looking for solutions, hoping to bridge the gap between police and mental health services.
A 911 call in Michigan
In May 2024, Cynthia Marek called 911 in Ingham County, Michigan, seeking help for her son, Brandon Labrie, who was experiencing a mental health emergency.
Within seconds, the crisis escalated into a stabbing. Labrie was charged in his mother’s death.
His father, Steve Labrie, spent more than three decades as a registered nurse in state-run psychiatric hospitals. He said weeks before the attack, his son had attempted suicide by overdose.
Steve Labrie said the family was told at the time that Brandon would be placed in a long-term mental health facility. He said that never happened.
“I’ve seen a lot of things in my life. It was, in my opinion, preventable,” Steve Labrie said.
He said he does not know what type of mental health treatment his son will receive.
“My guess is, if he gets any, it’s minimal. I wish I had those answers. I wish I knew,” Steve Labrie said.
Jails not built for long-term care
Mental health advocates say stories like this reflect a national reality. In many places, jails have become de facto mental health facilities, even though they are not built or staffed to provide long-term care, advocates said.
According to the National Alliance on Mental Illness, 60% of people with a history of mental illness do not receive treatment while incarcerated. Once people are locked up, it is challenging for them to remain on medication regimens.
William Malcom runs mental health services for the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office in South Carolina.
“We are the largest mental health facility in Charleston County and we really shouldn’t be,” Malcom said.
He said what he is seeing is happening nationwide.
“I don’t think this is really unique to Charleston County. This happens all over the country,” Malcom said.
Malcom said that when communities do not have enough places to take someone in crisis, jail can become the default.
Some police departments and sheriff’s offices are exploring changes to how they respond to mental health calls.
Zach Andrews is the mental health officer for Shelby County, Alabama. He responds to crisis scenes and trains deputies in crisis intervention.
“People experience mental health crisis pretty often, and I think the ones that make the news are those severe cases where potentially it was not handled in the most appropriate situation,” Andrews said.
The approach involves sending a mix of officers and mental health clinicians or peer specialists to de-escalate calls involving someone in crisis, connect the person to treatment and avoid jail.
The first crisis intervention team model was developed in Memphis in the late 1980s. It now exists in more than 2,700 communities across the U.S.
“CIT training is vital. Because what it’s doing, it’s training law enforcement and equipping them with tools and strategies to be able to handle those intense situations,” Andrews said.
A program for people leaving jail or prison
For people already in the court system, a handful of states, including North Carolina, are trying a model called Forensic Assertive Community Treatment, or FACT.
The program provides mental health care, housing help, peer support and court oversight for people with severe mental illness who have been released from jail or prison.
Angel Nelson is a peer support specialist for the FACT team in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. She said she knows how fast a personal crisis can spiral.
“Just being without the things we need, like food, the necessities, I started shoplifting, to get what I need,” Nelson said.
Nelson said trauma at a young age forced her into survival mode, leading to theft, addiction and repeated jail time. She said she started abusing drugs at age 9 and committed her first crime a few years later.
She said the turning point came when a judge gave her a choice: extensive mental health treatment or a lifetime behind bars.
“The first time, I went to the store by myself and didn’t steal nothing. That was the most awesome feeling I had ever felt in my life. I get so emotional because I never knew I could do that,” Nelson said.
Nelson now guides FACT participants through experiences she knows firsthand. She said that type of accountability and treatment saved her life.
“I was diagnosed with anxiety and postpartum depression,” Nelson said. “I was even told in one of my abuse group that the stealing could have come from trying to take back what was taken from me. And that was my innocence.”
Update on Brandon Labrie’s case
In April 2026, Brandon Labrie reached an agreement to plead guilty but mentally ill to second-degree murder. The following month, a judge sentenced him to 25 to 50 years in prison.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. Help is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

title: Teen indicted by grand jury for murder of midcoast paddleboarder
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — A grand jury indicted Deven Young for the July 2025 murder of Sunshine “Sunny” Stewart.
The indictment is dated Nov. 12.
The indictment comes a week after Young waived his right to a bind-over hearing that would have determined whether the 19-year-old would be tried as a juvenile or an adult.
The Maine Attorney General’s Office had filed the criminal complaint of murder against him following that hearing. In Maine, a grand jury must then issue an indictment for the case to proceed to a plea or trial.
The defense and prosecution agreed that Young would be held without bail. He was to be moved from the Long Creek Youth Development Center to the Knox County holding facility, although he may be transferred to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset, with which Knox County has a contract to hold incarcerated people.
As an adult, he will face a minimum of 25 years and up to life in prison if convicted.
Young, 19, has been charged with the July 3, 2025, blunt force and strangulation murder of 48-year-old Stewart, whose body was found on 100-Acre Island in Crawford Pond, Union. Young turned 18 on Sept. 24, 2025, less than three months after Stewart was killed.
Judge Walker ruled April 29 that the defendant was “competent to proceed based on the court’s finding that the juvenile has a rational as well as a factual understanding of the proceedings and a sufficient present ability to consult with legal counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding.”
The probable cause affidavit that led to Young’s arrest remains sealed. Thus, it is not known whether Young made any incriminating statements to Maine State Police or others.
Stewart grew up in the Union area and attended Medomak Valley High School. She bought and restored her circa 1900 home on River Road in Tenants Harbor. Stewart also worked as a waitress, bartender, fisherman and carpenter. Her friends said she was a strong, self-made woman and could do anything she set her mind on.
State Police reviewed surveillance video from the campground. The footage showed Young going out in his aluminum boat before Stewart. The boat had both a motor and oars. Stewart left at 6 p.m. to go paddle boarding on Crawford Pond. Young later was seen returning to the campground in his boat.
Witnesses said that in the two weeks after Stewart’s murder, Young’s behavior did not raise suspicion. He offered to help other campers with loose pets and yard work and made wood crafts that he gave to others.
Young approached investigators and said he had information about the case. He went out on Crawford Pond in a boat with investigators and a game warden, leading them to the opposite end of 100-Acre Island from where Stewart’s body was found. When they returned to the campground, police continued interviewing him.
Investigators left the campground but returned later that night and went directly to the Youngs’ camper. Police interviewed the family for two hours before arresting the son on the night of July 16. Detective Erin James was the arresting officer.
Young is a resident of Frankfort. His family was at the Mic Mac Campground on Crawford Pond, where Stewart was also staying.
Young made his initial court appearance July 18, 2025, via Zoom from Long Creek. The hearing, held at the state court in Knox County, was open to the public at the request of the Midcoast Villager. Young entered a denial of the murder charge. He is represented by attorneys Pratt and Caitlyn Smith. Assistant Attorneys General Lisa Bogue and Suzanne Russell are prosecuting the case.
After that hearing, the defense requested a competency hearing. State law mandates that juvenile cases be sealed for felony and murder cases if a motion for competency determination is made. The entire court file was sealed until Judge Walker’s April 29 ruling that found Young competent to stand trial.
Following that ruling, the Maine Forensic Service in Augusta conducted a diagnostic evaluation of Young on June 16. Results of that evaluation were to have been used at the bind-over hearing to help determine whether he would be tried as an adult or juvenile. That evaluation could also be used to determine whether he can be held criminally responsible for the death if the case goes to trial.
Midcoast Villager successfully challenged in court the denial of access to police records maintained by the Waldo County Sheriff’s Office on calls that department made to Young’s home in Frankfort.
Those records showed that the parents discussed how they had sought services for Young, who spent two stints at Acadia Hospital — a psychiatric facility — in Bangor and how he did well in its day program. They said he had been on a waiting list for more than two years to get home counseling services but had not yet received those services. He was also getting therapy at Hampden Academy, according to the audio recording.
The father said if the teen kept up his actions he would end up in jail when he turned 18.

title: Newly released Ring camera shows Brooklyn building collapsing
text:
Newly released Ring camera footage shows Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight in Flatbush
Newly released Ring camera footage shows the moment a building in Brooklyn collapsed, killing eight people.
The video, submitted to CNN by James Williams, was captured by a camera that appears to be mounted on a wall of a neighboring apartment building, near an apartment’s doorway. It focuses on a staircase.
The building that fell, located in Brooklyn’s Flatbush section, was three stories, but it was unclear at the time of publication exactly what floor the camera was on.
In the video, a loud crashing noise can be heard as the building comes crumbling down. On the right side of the video’s frame, debris can be seen falling as a cloud of dust shoots up in the air.
Seconds later, car alarms can be heard blaring in the background, and people can be heard shouting below.
Then, in a second video captured by the same camera, a New York firefighter can be seen helping a person out of the apartment.
The firefighter guides the person toward a staircase, which has rubble lying next to it and at the bottom of it.
“You’re going to come with me — nice and easy,” the firefighter can be heard saying as sirens blare in the background. See that video in the player below
Investigators on Thursday began searching for a cause for the collapse following NYFD ending its rescue operations after the last victim was freed from the wreckage.
The building gave way while construction workers were digging Wednesday afternoon at an adjacent lot, causing Mayor Zohran Mamdani to order inspections at about 100 building sites involving companies related to the project.
Among those killed were two children, ages 9 and 10. The adults who died ranged in age from 22 to 31, according to the New York City Police Department. There were also 18 injured, including four firefighters, the city’s mayor said. The children were Colombian, as was one of the adults who was killed, according to the country’s consulate in New York.

title: Double murder suspect charged again after witnesses lead investigators to hidden remains
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A suspect in a July double murder in Brookwood, Alabama, has been charged with another murder after skeletal remains were found Tuesday behind a Tuscaloosa apartment complex, the Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit said.
On July 6, Brookwood Police were called to do a welfare check around 1 p.m. The woman who rented the home was out of the country and had a co-worker, 31-year-old Jose Felix Alvarez-Duenas, house and dog sitting.
The woman was unable to reach Alvarez-Duenas for some time between July 5 and 6. She accessed several doorbell cameras and saw a suspect, later identified as 24-year-old De’Kendrick Crawford, acting suspiciously.
When Brookwood Police got to the house, they found Alvarez-Duenas inside the entryway. They also found 22-year-old Jazmine Alexis Bates, a University of Alabama student from Chicago, and a dog, dead inside a closet. All had gunshot wounds.
The VCU took over the investigation. Crawford, the renter of the home, Alvarez-Duenas, and Bates reportedly worked together at Buffalo Phil’s in Tuscaloosa.
Crawford had an outstanding felony warrant for shooting into an occupied building in May 2026. In that incident, Crawford was terminated from a contractor job on campus of the University of Alabama, and as he drove away, fired several shots that hit an occupied office building near Coleman Coliseum, authorities said. Warrants were obtained in that case, and Crawford was said to be actively eluding law enforcement.
Based on the video and other physical evidence found on scene, a warrant for capital murder was obtained, and the US Marshals Task Force was contacted to assist.
Within hours, Crawford was found at a relative’s apartment in Northport. Crawford refused to exit, police said, and the apartment building was secured. After a tactical breach and search of the building, Crawford was found hiding in an attic crawlspace and was taken into custody approximately 10 hours after the victims were discovered.
In early November, the VCU said a witness came to authorities claiming Crawford told them that before he allegedly killed Alvarez-Duenas and Bates, he had also killed an unknown man at a different place in Tuscaloosa.
Investigators were able to find other witnesses who also said Crawford had told them differing accounts of this murder. From there, the VCU said investigators pieced together different details from witnesses, compared them to digital evidence, and corroborated some of the places and events Crawford said to witnesses.
On Tuesday, authorities found skeletal remains partially buried in a wooded area behind River Road Apartments.
“The remains were purposely hidden and were only found by the corroborated details Crawford provided to witnesses,” the VCU said.
Crawford was reportedly interviewed before he allegedly denied involvement again. He was charged with murder in the new case.
The VCU said they have not yet identified the remains of the alleged victim. They believe he is a Black man between 40 and 70 years old, and that he may have a Chevy Cruze that was often seen at 10th Avenue Apartments, but authorities do not know if he was a resident at that complex or not.
The remains are being tested by the Alabama Department of Forensic Sciences in hopes of identifying the victim.
Anyone who knows of anyone who fits this description to be missing or believes they have any information is asked to contact the VCU at 205-464-8692.

title: NFL Week 10 schedule, predictions and more
text:
NFL Week 10 schedule, predictions and more
NFL Week 10 schedule, predictions and more
The NFL trade deadline has come and gone, with some teams featuring all-new looks on both sides of the ball. How will the transactions affect the second half of the season?
Video above: Former NFL coach Rex Ryan accused of hitting two pedestrians with truck in Nashville, leaving scene
Some of the biggest moves included the Chicago Bears pulling off a win-now move by trading two first-round draft picks to the Tennessee Titans for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and Kirk Cousins being traded from the Las Vegas Raiders to the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a third-round draft pick.
Let's see how these moves pay off this week — and for the rest of the season.
Here's a look at what's ahead this week, as Matthew Peaslee of the Hearst National Team continues his predictions. Peaslee went 13-2 in his Week 9 predictions and sits at 87-48-1 on the year.
All game times are in Eastern Standard Time.
Thursday, Nov. 12
Washington Commanders (2-5-1) vs. New York Giants (5-2-1), 8:15 p.m.
The last time these two teams met, it ended in a tie. The Commanders should have been able to hold on, but blew up in the fourth quarter. If Washington had pulled off the win a month ago, the seasons of the Commanders and Giants may have gone in different directions. If the Giants win at home, this should ensure their stay at the top of the NFC East standings.
Prediction: Giants 23, Commanders 17
Sunday, Nov. 15
New England Patriots (5-4) vs. Detroit Lions (6-2), 9:30 a.m.
Can the Patriots cool off the red-hot Lions? Detroit enters this Munich, Germany, contest as winners of four-straight games. New England was humbled by the Packers last week as quarterback Drake Maye threw three interceptions. He actually leads the NFL with 11 interceptions, but maybe a flight across the pond will calm his nerves. The Patriots have won five of their last six games against Detroit, and it's likely they'll make it six of seven.
Prediction: Patriots 28, Lions 21
Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) vs. Atlanta Falcons (3-6), 1 p.m.
Kansas City added wide receiver Josh Downs at the trade deadline, giving quarterback Patrick Mahomes another option for the passing game. An already dynamic offense that has had its running game boosted by Kenneth Walker III, who is second in the league with 872 rushing yards, should roll over the struggling Falcons.
Prediction: Chiefs 37, Falcons 10
Houston Texans (3-5) vs. Cleveland Browns (5-4), 1 p.m.
The Browns are undefeated at home this year and needed a team like the Titans to come to Cleveland this week. The Browns need their steady defense, headlined by linebacker Carson Schwesinger, to slow down Houston's strong passing game, which is third in the league with 269.4 passing yards per game. The promise Cleveland showed at the beginning of the year still has some untapped potential that could lead the Browns to their first playoff appearance since 2023 — and a first postseason victory since 2021.
Prediction: Browns 28, Texans 27
Minnesota Vikings (6-2) vs. Green Bay Packers (6-3), 1 p.m.
The fierce rivalry renews after a memorable Week 1 game. The Vikings have had a couple days of extra rest after a Thursday beatdown at the hands of the Bills. The Packers, meanwhile, might just be the hottest team in the league, led by quarterback Jordan Love. But on the other side is newly acquired Kirk Cousins. It's the Minnesota defense stealing the show, though, and with Josh Jacobs' status in question, the Vikings could prevail on the road — making a big statement.
Prediction: Vikings 27, Packers 24
Miami Dolphins (1-7) vs. Indianapolis Colts (2-7), 1 p.m.
It's the battle of futility as two teams heading in the same negative direction look for a silver lining on a dismal season. The Colts have a slight edge, being the favorites at home, but a loss for either team might be the ideal result for a potential No. 1 draft pick in 2027.
Prediction: Colts 18, Dolphins 10
Carolina Panthers (3-5) vs. New Orleans Saints (3-5), 1 p.m.
As both teams are two games under .500, it's hard to believe they're tied for first place. Such is life in the NFC South. Even the Falcons and Buccaneers, who both sport 3-6 records, aren't out of the running for the division crown, though they are currently in the basement. Chase Young leads the Saints defense with eight sacks and they'll need some big stops to earn this pivotal victory.
Prediction: Saints 24, Panthers 16
Buffalo Bills (7-1) vs. New York Jets (2-7), 1 p.m.
The Bills faced their stiffest competition to date last week and handled their business. Some may look at their trip to the New York City metro as a trap game, so Buffalo needs to make another statement right away this week. Josh Allen needs a game throwing for nearly 300 yards and four touchdowns — without any interceptions — to cement his MVP campaign.
Prediction: Bills 47, Jets 23
Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2) vs. Tennessee Titans (1-7), 1 p.m.
Jacksonville is a double-digit favorite and should pick up the easiest win of the week. The Jaguars have won five of their past six games and have a three-game lead in the AFC South. They've shored up their defense and may just pitch a shutout — the second of this NFL season — as the first came just two weeks ago when the Buccaneers blanked Atlanta.
Prediction: Rams 24, Commanders 0
Los Angeles Rams (5-4) vs. Arizona Cardinals (3-6), 4:05 p.m.
Arizona won this matchup in Week 6, but the Rams have rattled off three straight wins and are finally playing to their full potential. They'll be battling some injuries, but the Cardinals are banged up too. Carson Beck will be making his first career start for the Cardinals and the offensive line has holes to fill. The Rams should steal a road victory and cruise to the top of the division standings.
Prediction: Rams 22, Cardinals 14
Seattle Seahawks (5-4) vs. Las Vegas Raiders (4-5), 4:25 p.m.
Kirk Cousins had been the heart and soul of the Raiders, but he's now in Minnesota. It's now time for Fernando Mendoza to get his shot after leading one of the best college football seasons in recent memory with the national champion Indiana Hoosiers. A big win would be a wonderful first chapter to what should be a storybook career.  
Prediction: Raiders 32, Seahawks 28
San Francisco 49ers (7-1) vs. Dallas Cowboys (4-5), 4:25 p.m.
The San Francisco defense will create problems for Dak Prescott and the Cowboys. Meanwhile, Brock Purdy should torch the Dallas defense. It sure would move the needle if the Cowboys could pull off an upset, but the 49ers seem to be a team of destiny this season.
Prediction: 49ers 30, Cowboys 27
Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) vs. Cincinnati Bengals (6-2), 8:20 p.m.
Joe Burrow might be too much for the Steelers to handle. It's been an unpredictable season for both teams, but Pittsburgh handled the Bengals earlier in the year, and it will be difficult to replicate that performance.
Prediction: Bengals 27, Steelers 17
Monday, Nov. 16
Los Angeles Chargers (0-8) vs. Baltimore Ravens (4-5), 8:15 p.m.
This Monday night matchup isn't exactly what Hank Williams Jr. would want to sing about. It could be seen as an opportunity for Los Angeles to steal its first win with the world watching, but it could also be the opportunity the Ravens need to get back into the playoff picture.
Prediction: Ravens 27, Chargers 7

title: 11-month-old found buried alive in dog crate went home to family the same night
text:
BATESBURG-LEESVILLE, S.C. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) — An 11-month-old boy who was buried alive in a dog crate was released from a South Carolina hospital and is back home with his family after he was dug out of a grave.
Koah Sharp was rescued nearly 24 hours after he was reported missing. He is expected to make a full recovery, according to his medical team.
Koah’s disappearance led to a large law enforcement effort that ended with the arrest of his 25-year-old father, Michael Comer.
The grave
On Wednesday, Koah’s grandfather took WRDW to the grave in a wooded area off Parthenon Road in Lexington County. The area has trees spaced apart, sparse brush and ground covered in pine straw.
The hole has been filled in. The grandfather used a pointed finger to show the edges of the 2-foot-by-2-foot grave, then pulled aside the pine straw to show the dirt below.
Koah was found Tuesday, buried inside a dog crate a foot below the surface, crying “at the top of his lungs,” Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said.
Koon said the wire dog crate was wrapped in a towel that trapped enough air for Koah to survive for about 24 hours. He said the 45-degree outdoor temperature likely slowed the boy’s metabolism.
Koon said “a lot of things were going in Koah’s favor,” including the large response from law enforcement, the searcher who noticed the disturbed ground, the 45-degree outdoor temperature and the towel that created the air pocket.
“The Good Lord looked down on him,” Koon said.
How it unfolded
According to authorities, Comer had Koah for about four days after getting out of jail for other offenses.
Authorities were told of messages Comer sent to Koah’s mother in which he reportedly threatened to keep the child or gain custody, said he felt like killing himself and planned to move to New York.
On Monday, Comer’s mother was caring for the boy in Gaston, according to authorities. She left to run an errand, and another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Authorities said Comer left Gaston around 9 a.m. and was in Batesburg-Leesville around noon. Koon said that is probably when Koah was buried.
A relative filed a missing-person report by 3 p.m. Authorities said Comer went to several locations Monday without a car, which made it difficult to determine where the boy might be.
“We found some video of Michael in and around Batesburg-Leesville with no baby,” Koon said. “So certainly, we got worried, hoping and praying that he dropped the baby with another person. As the day went on and nobody came forward, it was certainly more and more concerning.”
Arrest and charges
Around 10 p.m. Monday, authorities found Comer, without Koah, in a shed that did not belong to him. He was arrested and charged with burglary.
Charges related to Koah were added later: attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child and custodial interference.
Bond was denied for Comer on Thursday morning.
A month earlier, Comer was placed on probation after pleading guilty to aggravated breach of peace. Court records also showed he was arrested earlier this year on a domestic violence count and a weapons-related count.
His next court appearance is set for Dec. 10.
The search and rescue
A South Carolina Law Enforcement Division helicopter logged several flights in the area of Parthenon Road on Monday night and early Tuesday.
Authorities focused on the area where Comer’s father lives.
Around 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, one of about 100 searchers noticed a disturbed section of ground about 50 yards into the nearby woods. Crime scene technicians checked the area.
“You could hear little Koah crying,” Koon said. “As you can imagine, the race was on. Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out.”
Koah was taken to a hospital around 2 p.m. Tuesday. He went home that night.

title: Holiday travelers may be paying more this season. These airports had higher fares in June
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
US domestic flight average hits $445 as holiday travelers face rising airfare
Holiday travelers may be paying more this travel season as average airfares have continued to climb this year, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
The average cost of a domestic flight in the U.S. was $445 in June, up nearly 16% from the same time last year, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
The agency's latest data, released in late September, covers airfare from April to June, and shows the price increase following the U.S.-Iran War, which began in late February. Prices include the cost of the flight and exclude baggage and other fees.
Airfares have risen as jet fuel prices increased after the conflict in the Middle East disrupted a crucial waterway route for global oil supplies. In April, several airlines announced fare and fee increases to offset higher jet fuel costs.
Which airports had fare increases?
Of the nation's 30 busiest airports, 25 saw rises in average domestic airfare from March to June. Daniel K. Inouye International had the largest increase, at $47.
The average fare at San Francisco International Airport went up $44, from $477 in March to $521 in June. Fares for flights from Los Angeles International also rose by nearly $40, bringing the average ticket price to $500.
Only five airports had decreases in average domestic airfares. The average fare from Minneapolis-St. Paul International fell from $519 in March to about $486 in June.
Other airports where average fares decreased were Chicago O'Hare International, Washington Dulles International, Chicago Midway International and Memphis International.
Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International and Orlando International offer the cheapest fares among the 30 busiest airports, at $321 and $329, respectively.

title: Maine sees more wildfires over past decade as officials emphasize prevention
text:
Maine sees more wildfires over past decade as officials emphasize prevention
Maine Forest Service officials highlighted changing wildfire risks, community preparedness efforts and funding opportunities during a Thursday presentation
Maine sees more wildfires over past decade as officials emphasize prevention
Maine Forest Service officials highlighted changing wildfire risks, community preparedness efforts and funding opportunities during a Thursday presentation
Maine has averaged 125 more wildfires each year over the past decade, according to figures presented by the Maine Forest Service on Thursday.
The agency reported 853 wildfires in 2025, burning nearly 515 acres. So far, Maine has recorded 795 wildfires, which burned around 378 acres as of Nov. 10, 2026.
Those fires were said to have damaged or destroyed buildings across the state. This year, 21 residences and 48 other structures have been damaged or destroyed.
According to the Maine Forest Service, equipment and vehicle use has been responsible for 198 wildfires this year, while debris burning has accounted for another 191 fires.
Officials also highlighted the number of Maine homes located in areas where development meets or overlaps with forests and other vegetation. According to figures presented from the USDA Northeast Climate Hub, approximately 78% of Maine homes are in these areas, compared to 32% nationwide.
The presentation highlighted how warmer temperatures, drought conditions, stronger winds and longer periods without snow can contribute to wildfire risks.
The Maine Forest Service is encouraging the development of community wildfire protection plans, which address wildfire risks, identify vulnerable areas and recommend ways to reduce the chances of homes and other structures catching fire.
Residents of Camden, Rockport, Hope and Lincolnville will have an opportunity to learn more about local wildlife protection plans during a public meeting on Monday, Nov. 16, from 5 to 6 p.m. at the Camden Town Office.
The Maine Forest Service is also accepting applications for its Volunteer Fire Capacity Program, which provides federal reimbursement to eligible volunteer fire departments serving communities with fewer than 10,000 residents.
The funding is intended to be used for wildland firefighting equipment and gear. Applications are due Dec. 18.
Officials remind Mainers to take precautions when burning brush and other debris, including obtaining burn permits, keeping fires small and having water and tools nearby.

title: Wiscasset, Boothbay Region school districts’ leaders denounce firm’s report as wrong, misleading
text:
Wiscasset Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson said she knew nothing about Dirigo Strategic Advisors' June 2026 report, "Maine School Budget Analysis Tool Pilot," prepared for Maine Policy Institute and its Maine Education Initiative, until she heard about it recently from Alternative Organizational Structure 98 Superintendent of Schools Robert Kahler.
Kahler didn't know Boothbay Region schools were referred to in it, either, until someone mentioned it to him at a Maine School Management Association conference.
And Wiscasset School Committee Chair Tracey Whitney shared her multiple concerns Nov. 10 about Dirigo's report. Andersson provided Wiscasset Newspaper with it on request Nov. 11.
According to the discussion in the Nov. 10 Wiscasset school committee meeting, after Andersson learned about the report, she sent Whitney it; then Whitney asked Andersson to send it to the rest of the committee. "I felt that it was really important that we address (this) because this is out in the world (and) one part of it is now being used as marketing to other schools ... to do this same pilot," Whitney said.
Andersson, in the meeting, and Kahler, in a phone interview Nov. 12, said the report includes wrong information about their school systems.
Kahler said the report also makes it sound like the pilot tool helped pare the AOS school budget.
"It's a wildly inaccurate statement. And if anyone wanted to go back and look at the very hard work that the trustees did, that the school committee did and that my administrative team did," they could see that, Kahler said. "I know I don't recall seeing that tool used at all. I know I didn't use it during the budget season."
After he looked at the report, he contacted its makers and told them of his surprise and disappointment, and was told they don't need permission because the data included is public information.
Andersson said the data does come from public information, namely numbers on Maine Department of Education's data dashboard, but she said: "The data dashboard runs ... 18 months behind. She said Dirigo's report compared Wiscasset data with a "peer group" of school systems she doesn't consider similar to Wiscasset, including Mount Desert Isle, Winthrop and Islesboro. She said Wiscasset budget numbers are used that date to a January budget draft "that never got off the table," and the report gets wrong Wiscasset's cost per student.
"It's slick," Andersson said of the report. "It's fancy. It's slop, but to someone who didn't know that, they might think it was really the truth," Andersson said.
Wiscasset Newspaper has sought comment from the documents' makers.
Andersson added in the meeting, because the material is "faulty by any sort of measure" and has been around since last spring, it is "probably partially to blame for a narrative, that the quality of education here is not worth the amount of money ... It's disappointing that this may have influenced a couple of budget votes. We'll never know."
The town rejected school budget offers in June and September and passed a third offer Nov. 3.
Whitney said the report suggests Wiscasset's school committee played a part it did not play in the report — a report she said doesn't put Wiscasset in a good light.
"This was nothing that we as a board had approved. We hadn't voted on it. Never came before us. But we do figure prominently in this report."
Whitney said it appears a couple of then-committee members "acted ... without board knowledge (and) worked with this outside group" last spring, on different parts of the report. "The board did not approve this to begin with. The board never saw these reports up until I saw them (from Andersson). I'm concerned about the validity of the report seeing that no one ever worked with our finance group, (and) some of the numbers in here were pulled from budgets that weren't done yet."
The executive summary’s cover page states: “Prepared by Dirigo Strategic Advisors April 2026 DRAFT - FOR BOARD REVIEW, Prepared for: Brycson Grover, Board Member, Jonathan Barnes, Vice Chair.”
The cover page for a “research brief” reads in part: “Teacher Compensation & Staffing Peer Analysis, Wiscasset School Department, Prepared in Advance of FY 2027 Collective Bargaining. Prepared for: Wiscasset School Board; Board, Administration and Legal Counsel Prepared by: Dirigo Strategic Advisors. April 2026. DRAFT - FOR BOARD REVIEW.”
A note at the bottom of that page reads: “This document is prepared by Dirigo Strategic Advisors for informational purposes only. It represents research findings drawn from Maine Department of Education public data, verified Supabase DOE tables. the Maine School Budget Analysis Tool (maineschoolbudgetanalysistool.com), and Maine Revised Statutes. This document is not legal or financial advice, does not represent a negotiating recommendation, and should be reviewed in consultation with district administration and legal counsel. Dirigo Strategic Advisors is a strictly neutral research firm and holds no position on any bargaining outcome.”
The documents also claim Dirigo delivered “ongoing support” for then-Wiscasset School Committee Vice Chair Jonathan Barnes and then-member Brycson Grover.
Responding to email questions Nov. 11, Grover said: "I have not seen that exact report that you sent me before now, but there was parts of it that I have reviewed.
"I reviewed the information that had been provided to me during that time period. As a former school committee member, I have always made an effort to educate myself and review as much information as possible to improve my knowledge and understanding of the school budget, operations, and how different parts of the school district functions.
"I believe it is our responsibility as elected or appointed school committee members to remain engaged, ask questions, and seek information from all available sources. We cannot fulfill that obligation to provide the best quality education for Wiscasset students by simply accepting what is presented to us. It requires asking tough questions, educating ourselves, and taking the initiative to better understand the issues facing our district. That is how we should make educated, informed decisions and help our school district thrive, grow, and become something we continue to be proud of.
"I find it frustrating that there seems to be an issue with me seeking information. The information in these reports is public information and accessible to anyone. I don’t feel any board member have the ability to control what outside individuals or organizations choose to do with publicly available information or how they choose to analyze it. If board members are upset with the information that is displayed in the report I encourage the board to invite who did the report to do a presentation on it. It wouldn’t hurt in my opinion.
"As far as informing the rest of the board, I did not see a reason why an independent review of public information would require formal notice to the entire committee. Seeking information and educating myself does not automatically create an obligation to bring every independent analysis or resource I review before the full board. I also think it is unfortunate that the focus seems to be shifting toward placing blame on former board members rather than addressing the actual information and questions raised in the report."
Wiscasset Newspaper has also sought comment from Barnes.
In the meeting, member Christopher Hart said the report "does represent or (it) suggests that there was school committee endorsement of this project, of this product."
"And we're sitting here publicly and saying that isn't true," member Doug Merrill said.
When resident Chet Grover pressed those at the table for more specifics on what they said was wrong in the report, Hart said that, for one, it says Wiscasset has a pre-K through eighth grade campus and a nine through 12 one, Hart said. Wiscasset has pre-K through five at one campus and the rest at the other.
If the financial data it starts with is wrong, including about a budget draft used, the report's analysis can't be right, Facilities and Maintenance Director Buzz Johnson observed from the audience. When another audience member asked if he'd read the report, Johnson said "No, I don't have time for that kind of garbage."
The committee and Andersson reasoned there was no point to give the report further discussion.
Said Merrill, "We acknowledge it's there and we disagree with it strongly, and move on. It's inaccurate, but if you dwell on something like this, then you're giving it credence."
"And we don't want to give it legitimacy," Whitney agreed.
Merrill also said going to court over the report whose makers "had every legal right to produce" would "waste a lot of resources."
"I don't know about their legal rights, because it is riddled with inaccuracies," Hart said, but he agreed going to court is "not enticing at all."
Everyone has already acknowledged Wiscasset's test scores need improving, Vice Chair John Merry said. "We're working on that in our workshop (sessions), right? And I say we continue to do that."
"Absolutely," Whitney said.
Also Nov. 10, the committee nodded hiring Sarah Stephens as Wiscasset Middle High School's nurse. She was to start Nov. 16, Andersson said.
In a written statement the committee received, Stephens said she graduated from University of North Alabama and was commissioned into the Army Reserves as a nurse. "I moved to Maine after graduating to be close to family and absolutely love it here. Currently I still serve and provide fully funded care to communities in need with my unit during summers," Stephens wrote. "I have a variety of nursing backgrounds including dementia care; medsurg; pre-op/recovery room and most recently occupational health; certified in both adult and pediatric advanced care. I have four 'fur-children' and a supportive husband. I look forward to becoming part of the community and getting to know and care for the students at Wiscasset Middle High!"
"She's got quite a background," Merry noted.
WMHS resource room educational technician III Cheryl Dilts is retiring, effective next July 1, after 48 years in education, "including 20 wonderful years here at Wiscasset Middle High School," Dilts wrote. "I am very deeply grateful for the support of the administration, my fellow staff and teachers, plus the entire Wiscasset community throughout my years here at Wiscasset Middle High School. It has been an extreme honor to serve this school and our students. Thank you for all your guidance and support over the years."
Committee members accepted Dilts' retirement with regret. Whitney added appreciation and thanks for Dilts' years of service, and congratulations on her retirement. Dilts and her husband plan to get a camper and take it on a trip to Alaska, Andersson said.
Whitney read aloud from a card she said Wiscasset Elementary School Principal Stacy Clements handed her, from everyone at WES. Whitney read, "To the school board: Thank you for thinking of us."
And according to a parent in public comment, WMHS' changes this school year, toward keeping students where they are supposed to be, are working, and the school's atmosphere has completely changed.

title: Potential for snow and rain to brush the Maine coast Friday morning
text:
Storm just misses Maine but cold air settles in
Storm just misses Maine but cold air settles in
A coastal storm spinning off southern New England is mostly bypassing Maine this morning, leaving the state largely dry. While light precipitation is brushing far southern areas near York, communities north of that line are missing out on the moisture entirely.
Any lingering morning dampness will shut off quickly during the first half of the day. A brisk north wind will push drier air into the region, clearing out the skies while keeping temperatures on the chilly side.
LIVE WEATHER RADAR | HOUR-BY-HOUR FORECAST
High pressure builds in to keep conditions quiet and dry through the weekend. Afternoon highs will run a few degrees below normal, and clear, calm nights will allow temperatures to drop sharply overnight.
The cool pattern will eventually break as high pressure shifts away. Temperatures will start to rebound toward the middle of next week, bringing a chance for warmer-than-average weather to return to the state.

title: Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.
The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.
Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.
At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.
Federal attorneys say long yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.
But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.
They say his executive order is an attempt to unilaterally “eviscerate” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.
The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, those attorneys argue.
The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

title: Rescues are underway in New Orleans after a tanker hits a river cruise boat on the Mississippi River
text:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A tanker struck the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat in New Orleans on Friday with 129 passengers aboard, partially submerging the boat. Rescues were underway on the Mississippi River, officials said.
Authorities did not immediately release whether there were injuries or deaths.
Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the paddlewheel cruise boat while it appeared to be docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.
More than a dozen people in lifejackets were being dragged from the 66-degree Fahrenheit (19-degree Celsius) river onto nearby ships. Others were standing near the railing as the other side of the American Heritage listed further into the water.
“Surreal — that’s what that was,” witness Jamie Holford told WDSU-TV. “Fifteen minutes from impact to where it rolled over.”
The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
Ships carrying asphalt and bitumen are often heated well above 250 degrees Fahrenheit (120 degrees Celsius) to prevent the asphalt from solidifying on the ship, according to the maritime periodical Marine Insights. It is not immediately clear whether the ship was carrying any materials when the crash occurred.
The 520-foot (160-meter) long vessel had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.

title: Paul LePage Wins Maine's 2nd Congressional District After Ranked-choice Tabulation
text:
Maine Republican Paul LePage Wins Congressional Seat
After ranked-choice tabulation, Paul LePage is declared the winner of the 2nd Congressional District seat.
Maine's Ranked-Choice Tabulation Determines Paul LePage is the Winner
Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matthew Dunlap faced off in a close race that required first a recount and then a ranked-choice tabulation.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows says the final result of the tabulation is as follows:
- Paul LePage - 170,80 votes 50.81%
- Matthew Dunlap - 165,432 votes 49.18%
The ranked-choice tabulation concluded early Thursday afternoon.
LePage will replace Congressman Jared Golden, who chose not to run for re-election.
Maine's Paul LePage Wins 2nd Congressional District
In ranked-choice voting races, the winner must receive a majority - more than 50% - of the vote.
Matthew Dunlap conceded the race before tabulation, but Bellows said that the process still had to be conducted for legal reasons.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest district east of the Mississippi River and includes the following counties:
- Androscoggin
- Aroostook
- Franklin
- Hancock
- Oxford
- Penobscot
- Piscataquis
- Somerset
- Waldo
- Washington
This includes the municipalities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne, and Winthrop in Kennebec County.
Official results will be posted on the Election Results page within 20 days after the election.
Congressman Paul LePage Has a History in Maine Politics
Paul LePage is well-known in Maine politics.
He served as the state's 74th Governor from 2011 to 2019 and as Mayor of Waterville from 2004 to 2011.
Election results are unofficial until they are officially communicated to Governor Janet Mills.

title: Police release names in fatal Hermon crash

The Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office on Friday identified the woman who died after a single-vehicle crash in Hermon on Tuesday night, along with the driver of the car.
The crash was reported at about 8:45 p.m. on Billings Road near Bryant Road.
The driver has been identified as Mark Benningfield, 38, of Hampden. The passenger who died from injuries sustained in the crash was Ashley Benningfield, 37, of Hampden, the sheriff’s office said.

title: Maine woman collects fuzzy socks for cancer patients in sister’s memory
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -A Maine woman is collecting fuzzy socks and other comforting gifts for people undergoing cancer treatment in memory of her sister.
Melissa Marshall remembers her sister, Tiffany Andrews, wearing fuzzy socks to her weekly chemotherapy appointments. Sometimes they were purple, Andrews’ favorite color, and they were always cute.
“They started the chemo, and I said, ‘Wow, those are really neat socks,’ and she goes, ‘Yeah, my feet are freezing. I went to Reny’s the other day and got a bunch,’” Marshall recalled.
Andrews died of breast cancer in 2017. She was 47.
In 2020, Marshall and her coworkers started Operation Fuzzy Socks in her memory. Each year, Marshall collects donations and brings them to the Harold Alfond Center for Cancer Care in Augusta. The gifts have grown to include blankets, lip balm and journals.
Heather Moore, Supervisor for the Center for Hope and Healing at the Harold Alfond Center for Cancer Care, works closely with patients at the center. She said the donations let patients know their community is thinking of them and supporting them through their cancer journeys.
Moore has been through breast cancer treatment herself and knows how much those comforts can mean.
“When I was going through treatment, you’re freezing. You’re freezing,” Moore said. “So, I mean, warm blankets, fuzzy socks, shawls, anything, you know, that is donated. It absolutely makes such a difference.”
For Marshall, each donation is also a reminder of her sister.
“Tiffany was very, very strong. She thought she was going to beat it. She thought she was going to get married. And it didn’t work out that way, but I know she’s up there so happy that people are warm and wearing fuzzy socks,” Marshall said.
Asked what Andrews would think of her work, Marshall said, “She would be like, ‘Miss, great job.’”
Anyone interested in donating can find items on Marshall’s Amazon wish list for Operation Fuzzy Socks.
