title: Cargo ship strikes bridge between New Jersey and Philadelphia, causing traffic backup
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — A cargo ship struck a bridge across the Delaware River on Thursday, disrupting traffic between Palmyra, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, according to a Pennsylvania lawmaker.
The collision left the 3,659-foot-long (1,115-meter-long) Tacony-Palmyra Bridge unable to close, causing a major backup on the Philadelphia side, state Rep. Ed Neilson said in a news release. No injuries have been reported, he said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the cargo vessel is currently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where an inspection team is on site. The Coast Guard identified the vessel as the 591-foot (180-meter) Strategic Alliance, which was built in 2013 and sails under the flag of Singapore.
The drawbridge was open for ships to pass through at the time of the collision around 1:15 p.m., according to the Coast Guard. It remained open afterward because another vessel needed to pass through, and has since come back down. The bridge reopened to traffic with a lane closure Thursday evening, the Burlington County (New Jersey) Bridge Commission Police Department said.
The steel bridge carries vehicles along Route 73 between Palmyra and the Tacony neighborhood in northeast Philadelphia. It has three lanes of vehicular traffic, two into Philadelphia and one into New Jersey. Estimates from 2025 show the bridge can carry as many as 76,200 vehicles each day.
Opened in 1929, the Tacony-Palmyra toll bridge was found to be in “fair” condition, according to the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 National Bridge Inventory data released this fall.
Inspectors rated the deck of the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge as in good condition, the substructure as in fair condition and the superstructure — the component that absorbs the live traffic load — as fair.
___
Associated Press journalists Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Julie Carr Smyth in Columbus, Ohio, and Christopher L. Keller in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed.

Rebecca O'Leary, Central Aroostook, Golf

Emily Lapierre, Van Buren, Soccer

Sadie Trams, Ashland, Soccer

Choose the Three Strongest Seasons
This isn't about picking one favorite.
Take a look at all eight finalists in your division and choose the three athletes you believe put together the strongest overall fall seasons.
Remember:
You must select exactly THREE athletes for your ballot to count.
You can return and vote once per hour through Thursday, November 19 at 11 p.m.
Four athletes will eventually emerge as the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall, but simply making this field means putting together one of the area's standout seasons.
Congratulations to all 32 finalists.
Now it's your turn to help decide the winners.

title: Texas executes man convicted in beheading of 3 children
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A Texas man convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading three young children in a squalid, windowless apartment in 2003 was executed Thursday evening, hours after Oklahoma put another man to death.
John Allen Rubio, 46, was pronounced dead at 6:47 p.m. after a lethal injection at the state prison in Huntsville. The killings of the baby girl and two toddlers so rocked the city of Brownsville on the U.S. border with Mexico that the apartment building was later demolished and the land turned into a park and community garden.
After a spiritual adviser prayed over him briefly, Rubio thanked friends and family for their “love and understanding” and said he was “not the same person I once was.” He thanked prison staff for teaching him how to find God and also expressed love for his common-law wife, Angela Camacho, who is serving life in prison for her role in the slayings.
“I want to say I’m sorry to my wife’s family,” he said. “I can’t change the past but I can tell you my life is going to be over. But that’s not going to make you happy.”
“I’m going to be with my kids in a little bit,” he added. “I’m ready to go to heaven to be with my lord and savior.”
As the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital began taking effect, Rubio took three breaths and began what sounded like snoring. All movement ceased afterward, and a physician pronounced him dead 21 minutes after the injection began.
Earlier Thursday, James Pavatt, 73, received a lethal injection at an Oklahoma prison for the fatal shooting of his girlfriend’s estranged husband in 2001. The victim was killed as he arrived to pick up his two young children before Thanksgiving.
Thursday’s executions were the 36th and 37th this year, with the U.S. on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year — a pace driven by Florida.
The death penalty has drawn renewed attention since the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September. And last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office in January — what experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
Texas victims included a 2-month-old girl
Rubio and Camacho were accused of killing 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the apartment they shared in Brownsville. Camacho drew a life sentence after pleading guilty.
An appeals court overturned Rubio’s first capital murder conviction, ruling Camacho’s statements were improperly admitted as evidence in his trial. At his second trial, Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity but again was convicted and sentenced to death.
According to court records, Rubio wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but treated them as his own.
At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world.
Defense experts diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, a finding prosecution experts rejected. The defense experts also testified his childhood — marked by violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution — damaged him developmentally.
Oklahoma advertising executive killed in garage
When the Oklahoma inmate Pavatt was asked if he had any last words before his execution, he shook his head no. As a chaplain read from the Bible, Pavatt appeared to mouth some words that couldn’t be heard.
Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the killing of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Pavatt attended the same church as the Andrew family and had been having an affair with Rob Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. She was convicted at a separate trial and is the only woman currently on Oklahoma’s death row.
Weeks before the shooting, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.
Pavatt and Brenda Andrew fled to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while reentering the U.S.
Also Thursday, former Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory in a 1997 murder and awaits sentencing in December. Glossip, who had been on the brink of execution three times, was released on bond in May after nearly 30 years in prison. He had been awaiting a retrial after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned his conviction.

title: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US
text:
Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade.
These findings about the longevity of contamination in the nation’s drinking water supplies are especially concerning as climate change and increasingly strong El Niño weather events, which intensify drought conditions, have led to bigger and more frequent wildfires in the U.S. So far in 2026, there have been 68,179 blazes burning more than 9.5 million acres (3.8 million hectares).
After a wildfire sweeps through hillsides and forests, rains carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities alike. Communities are working to adapt, but it can take years and require stopgap solutions.
People in the City of Las Vegas, New Mexico, went without water for months after the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire contaminated the Gallinas River in 2022. In the four years since, they’ve had to give residents bottled water and ship tanks in from nearby towns as they collected funds to build a new treatment plant.
Karen Pettine, who has owned the Hillcrest Restaurant for 50 years, said the water crisis forced them to close, sometimes for a week at a time.
“It’s hard to run a restaurant without good water,” she said. “We used some paper plates at times. They brought in semi-truckloads of bottled water. You could pick up four cases at a time. The water situation is ongoing because when it rains, it floods and it brings dirty water down the stream.”
Las Vegas Mayor David Romero said climate change has made the things that used to be reliable less predictable.
“It’s a scary situation that we’re all going to encounter,” he said.
Sediment from burned landscapes a headache for water-treatment plants
Wildfires are a natural part of forest ecosystems, but an increase in their severity has made areas that capture, filter and regulate the flow of water, known as watersheds, vulnerable, said Amanda Hohner, an assistant professor at Montana State University who specializes in wildfires and water quality.
Forested watersheds provide water to nearly two-thirds of municipalities in the U.S., according to Carli Brucker, lead author of a University of Colorado Boulder study that assessed wildfire-affected water quality in hundreds of burned basins and compared them to unburned areas. Their study found that the impacts can last up to eight years.
Garrett McKay, an assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering at Texas A&M, said utilities are extremely concerned about the impacts wildfires have on water. They’re reaching out to experts like him for help finding different water sources or to learn how to treat the organic matter coming into their plants.
Water treatment facilities that rely on streams and rivers typically treat high quality water, aided by trees and soil that act as a natural filtration system, Brucker said. But wildfires cause spikes in heavy metals or dissolved organic matter, which the plants aren’t built to handle, she said.
This can force treatment facilities to shut off the incoming water and resort to other sources, which may not be immediately available, Brucker said. Some have groundwater or reservoir backups, but even those can be impacted.
Reservoirs can serve as a “sedimentation basin” where particles can settle, said Kyle Shimabuku, an assistant professor of civil engineering at Gonzaga University. But sediments from burned vegetation are rich in nutrients, like nitrogen and phosphorus, and as they sit in still water, algal blooms can grow, he said. The algae can make people sick and kill the fish.
Chlorine, routinely used to treat water, also is impacted by wildfires, said McKay at Texas A&M. When facilities add disinfectants, like chlorine, to water, they react with the dissolved organic matter left behind by the fires to form “disinfection byproducts,” which are regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency because they can cause illnesses, including cancer.
Since plants can’t remove the disinfection byproducts, they must get rid of the organic matter before disinfecting the water, which can cause delays in the water supply.
Implementing new options can cost facilities millions
When a 2020 wildfire burned the area around No Name and Grizzly creeks, the primary water sources for the city of Glenwood Springs, Colorado, officials scrambled to protect against sediment expected to wash down the slopes when spring rains arrived. They sought help from the Colorado Water Conservation Board. Within two months, the board authorized an emergency loan of $8 million for improvements to the treatment system.
Fort Collins faced a similar challenge that year when ash and sediment from the Cameron Peak fire forced the city to close its river intake and pull water from the Horsetooth Reservoir, which was safe to use because it’s fed by a different watershed.
Las Vegas, New Mexico, was hit harder when the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon fire damaged the Gallinas River watershed in 2022. A massive rainstorm swept ash and sludge from the burn scar into the river and reservoirs, forcing the town to shut down its water treatment plant while they installed additional filters and looked for additional water sources.
As they worked on solutions, a massive flood in 2024 carried more burn debris into the town’s two reservoirs, leaving them with only a few days of safe water. As businesses closed and residents bought bottled water, the town hired trucks to bring 2.2 million gallons (8.3 million liters) of water from nearby towns of Santa Fe and Santa Rosa.
They were hit again in February 2025. Burn scar debris coupled with bad weather and equipment failure caused a pressure drop, which resulted in a monthlong boil-water advisory and more water shipments.
“The February event was probably the scariest,” Romero said.
Ultimately, the state and federal governments allocated $148 million to rebuild the town’s treatment plant and help support their efforts to find other options, including drilling wells and reusing water. Groundbreaking on the first phase of their new water treatment plant is slated for Nov. 18, the mayor said.
“We’ve been doing a lot of work for other sources of water and we know with climate change and what we experienced in the past, the Gallinas River is something we can’t depend on forever.”

title: Keeping Maine Pedestrians Safe Is Everyone's Responsibility
text:
As the days get shorter, it's a good time to remind pedestrians and drivers about how to coexist safely.
Maine Pedestrians and Drivers Must Work Together to Keep Everyone Safe
This topic hits home with me because I drive to work early in the morning, when people are out walking before dawn.
More than once, I've encountered pedestrians in dark clothing with few or no reflectors to signal their presence to drivers.
Drivers also have responsibilities, as was proven by a fatal crash earlier this week when a driver struck a bicyclist in Pittsfield.
Road safety is everyone's responsibility, so drivers and pedestrians have to work together.
Safety Tips for Maine Pedestrians Who Often Walk on Dark, Rural Roads
The National Traffic Highway Safety Commission offers several tips for pedestrians:
- Follow the rules of the road
- Walk on sidewalks when they're available. If there's no sidewalk, walk facing traffic and as far from the vehicles as possible.
- Use crosswalks when available and don't cross mid-block.
- Look both ways before crossing the street and make sure the drivers can see you.
- Wear bright, reflective clothing and/or have visible lights to alert drivers to your presence.
- Watch for vehicles entering or exiting driveways or backing up in parking lots.
- Be alert to others' movements, whether they're in a vehicle or on a bicycle.
- Make eye contact with drivers whenever possible and wait for a clear, complete stop before crossing the street.
I would add another suggestion to build on that last tip: Don't assume drivers can see you just because you're standing or walking in a crosswalk.
Being a Responsible Driver Means Keeping Maine Pedestrians Safe
Drivers also have a responsibility to keep pedestrians safe on the roads.
Here are a few suggestions from the NHTSA:
- Slow down because speeding endangers drivers and pedestrians.
- Keep your eyes moving and look for pedestrians everywhere.
- Minimize blind spots and remember to check them.
- Use extra caution at night or in bad weather.
- Yield to pedestrians in crosswalks.
- Watch for pedestrians when turning, especially if you're turning right on a red light.
- Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk.
- Follow the speed limit, including the slower limits in school zones.
- Watch for pedestrians when backing up. Look around instead of relying only on your backup camera.
I would add that drivers need to minimize distractions. Put the phone down and pay attention when you're behind the wheel.
According to the Maine Department of Transportation, 182 crashes this year have involved pedestrians.
8 of those have been fatal.
If we all work together, maybe we can get those numbers down in 2027.

title: Open health insurance enrollment: What it means for your taxes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When you work for yourself, the stakes of open enrollment are much higher than they are for someone on an employer-sponsored plan.
Three decisions you make during the Open Enrollment Period (OEP) affect your tax return:
- Your income estimate: The Marketplace uses your income estimate to set your Advance Premium Tax Credit (APTC). Guess too low, and you’ll have to pay back the excess credit when you file your tax return.
- Your plan: Your premiums may qualify for the self-employed health insurance deduction. The right type of plan can also let you make tax-deductible contributions to a health savings account (HSA).
- Whether you enroll: Some states charge a penalty if you go without coverage.
So how does the ACA tie into your taxes?
Once you have Marketplace coverage, if you get an Advance Premium Tax Credit, it links your health plan to your tax return. When you file, you compare the advance credit paid during the year with the credit you actually qualify for. The numbers come from Form 1095-A.
You have to file a return if you received advance credit payments, even if your income falls below the normal filing threshold, Intuit TurboTax reports.
What’s changing for 2026-27 and why your premium jumped
The enhanced premium tax credits that made Marketplace plans cheaper from 2021 through 2025 expired at the end of 2025. As a result, average out-of-pocket premiums rose 58% in 2026, according to the KFF (Kaiser Family Foundation). Insurance companies also raised health insurance premiums by an average of 20% in 2026 and are proposing an average of 15% for 2027.
Without the enhanced credits, if your household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty level, you don’t qualify for a premium tax credit. Going even $1 over that line costs you the entire credit.
If your income is close to the line, deductions that lower your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) may help you stay eligible for an advance premium tax credit. Learn more about how the premium tax credit works and how to stay eligible.
How your plan choice shows up on your tax return
Form 8962 calculates the difference between the credit you received during the year and the credit you qualify for once you know your actual income for the year. If you’re a W-2 employee with steady paychecks, the gap is usually small. If you’re self-employed, your income might rise and fall from quarter to quarter, so the difference can be big.
Starting with 2026 returns (the ones you file in 2027), you repay any excess advance credit in full, with no cap. So if a strong fourth quarter pushes your household income over 400% of the federal poverty level, you repay the full credit.
To avoid a big bill at tax time, update your income with the Marketplace within 30 days of an income change. You might also consider taking less than the full advance credit and claiming the rest when you file your tax return.
The tax forms you’ll need
If you have a Marketplace plan, the federal platform or a state-based marketplace exchange will mail you Form 1095-A and post it to your online account by January 31 of the following year.
It lists your monthly premiums, the benchmark plan cost, and any advance credit paid on your behalf. All three numbers feed directly into Form 8962.
Check the form before you file. If it has the wrong household members, coverage months, or benchmark premium, ask the Marketplace for a corrected copy. Wrong numbers can affect your credit and trigger an IRS notice.
If your spouse has employer coverage, you may also receive Form 1095-B or 1095-C. You don’t have to wait for either one to file.
Don’t leave this deduction on the table
If you pay for your own health insurance as a self-employed person, you can generally deduct the premiums you pay for yourself, your spouse, and your dependents. You claim the deduction using Form 7206 and Schedule 1, and you don’t need to itemize.
With premiums rising, this deduction can be worth more when you file your tax return. Just keep two limits in mind. First, your deduction can’t exceed your net business profit. Second, you can’t take the deduction for any month you were eligible for an employer-subsidized plan, including one through your spouse’s job.
Driving, delivering, or freelancing through a platform?
In California and Massachusetts, app-based rideshare and delivery drivers may qualify for a health insurance stipend from their platforms.
You can receive a stipend and a premium tax credit at the same time, but the stipend counts as business income, so include it in your income estimate and on your tax return.
Exemptions, penalties, and what happens if you skip coverage
Congress cut the federal penalty for going without health insurance to $0 starting in 2019, so skipping coverage won’t affect your federal return. However, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia may charge a penalty on your state or district return.
If you skipped coverage in one of these states, you may qualify for a state exemption, for example, if your coverage gap was short or the coverage available to you would have cost more than a set share of your income.
Exemptions aren’t automatic. You have to claim them on your state return.
Missed the window or had a life change?
If you miss the enrollment deadline, you must qualify for a Special Enrollment Period to get coverage at a later date. Common qualifying life events include losing health coverage after leaving a job, moving to a new area, getting married, or having or adopting a child.
If you don’t qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you can still apply for Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) any time of year.
Quick reference checklist
During open enrollment
- Enroll by Dec. 15 for coverage that starts Jan. 1 (Deadlines for state exchanges may differ).
- Estimate your household income using net self-employment income, and include any platform health stipend.
- If you want to contribute to an HSA, make sure your plan is a high-deductible health plan (HDHP).
During the year
Update your Marketplace application within 30 days of a significant income or life change.
When you file your tax return
- Watch for Form 1095-A by Jan. 31 and check it for errors.
- File Form 8962 to calculate your premium tax credit and compare it to the Advance Premium Tax Credit you received.
- Report any health care stipends you received as business income.
Mark your calendar
Open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs from Nov. 1, 2026, through Jan. 15, 2027, on HealthCare.gov. If you enroll by Dec. 15, your coverage starts on Jan. 1. The final deadline to sign up or change plans for 2027 coverage is Jan. 15, 2027, for coverage starting Feb. 1.
If your state runs its own exchange, your dates may be different. The chart below shows the states with their own deadlines. If your state isn’t listed, then the federal open enrollment timeline applies.

title: Microsoft reports progress with restoring global outage; email access improving
text:
Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
A global Microsoft outage this week disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide and highlighting the risks of depending on one of just a few major providers of essential technology.
Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. As the outage entered its second day Friday, Microsoft said it saw “encouraging recovery progress.” But the company also warned that “intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery" may persist for some users.
“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us," Microsoft wrote in a social media update.
The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.
Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”
The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.
Microsoft has scrambled to recover services
A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn't send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays.
On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.
Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff's office in Colorado's Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.
Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.
And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook. If the situation dragged on, the trouble could “impact the production timeline,” he said.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.
OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.
Outage has parallels with 2024 shutdown
Some have drawn parallels to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.
Governments and institutions in Western Europe, in particular, have been trying to reduce their reliance on services provided by a few big U.S. tech services in their continuing push for “digital sovereignty.” This week's outage renewed some of those calls.
British lawmaker Chi Onwurah, who chairs the Science and Technology Committee in Parliament, said the Microsoft outage “only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the U.K.’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services.”
She said her committee has previously warned that the U.K. is “hugely dependent” on a small number of U.S.-based technology providers, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing.
Florian Druckenthaner, a spokesperson for Germany’s digitization ministry, said the government’s IT security agency believes German business was widely affected, but there were no reports of major disruption at the government level.
Regardless, Druckenthaner said, the outage shows “the significance of building up redundancies and alternatives. We are working on that.”

title: VFW Post 3335 hosts annual Patriot Strong Ceremony
Davis V. Goliath: a small town fight against big data
text:
TUCKER COUNTY, W.Va. — Data centers were on the ballot for the first time in a U.S. election, according to Ballotpedia, which counted 47 local ballot measures dealing with data centers in the midterms. Voters chose to curb data center development in their communities in 46 of them.
Residents of one West Virginia community said they were not given that choice.
Proposed data center
The small mountain town in Tucker County is home to the Blackwater River and twin ski mountains. Tourism is the town’s lifeblood, and a proposed 10,000-acre natural gas-powered data center now threatens it.
Jane Browning, owner of Ranger Jane, said tourism makes up most of her business.
“Tourism is 80 percent of my business, and if there’s no tourism, there’s no business,” Browning said.
If completed, the data center would be the largest in the world, measuring slightly smaller than Manhattan.
Governor and residents
West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey believes the project will be a boon for the state.
“We’re going to make sure that the water’s addressed, the environment’s addressed, that the power bills are lower, it’s going to get handled the right way,” Morrisey said.
Residents described the situation differently. One said, “It came out of nowhere, there was no warning, there was no opportunity to say no.” Another said, “We were never given a choice, never given a voice.” A third said, “There’s something here that we don’t know.”
Developer’s recorded comments
North Carolina-based developer Ted McGavran of Fundamental Data said on a hot mic in July why West Virginia was chosen.
“Up in West Virginia, we’re the guys that wrote the bill and got it through the Legislature. We can do pretty much whatever we want to do up there,” McGavran said.
Morrisey denied that claim.
The bill’s sponsor is West Virginia Speaker of the House Roger Hanshaw. Hanshaw also serves as the lawyer for Fundamental Data, the company behind the project. Multiple requests for comment have not received a response.
Morrisey maintains the state is acting in good faith and said, “Nothing’s been approved.”
Public filings show the project’s air permits were approved Aug. 15.
Federal legislation
The issue has reached Washington. Sens. Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse are introducing a data center permitting reform bill.
“When a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply. Cost, water resources, infrastructure and local economy. In order for them to make a good decision,” Sen. Heinrich said.

title: All flights at Portland Jetport delayed amid nationwide ground stop
text:
19 flights at Portland International Jetport canceled due to nationwide ground stop
The FAA has lifted the ground stop after several hours
19 flights at Portland International Jetport canceled due to nationwide ground stop
The FAA has lifted the ground stop after several hours
More than a dozen flights at the Portland International Jetport (PWM), Maine's largest airport, were canceled on Friday due to a nationwide ground stop that was issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and lasted for several hours.
The FAA grounded all flights nationwide shortly after 4 p.m. because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. The ground stop was lifted at 8:19 p.m.
The Jetport experienced 19 flight cancellations due to the ground stop, including six flights that were set to depart Saturday morning. As of 8:30 p.m., there were 12 delays at PWM. The Jetport did not receive any diversions during the ground stop.
PWM officials said that airlines would be making independent decisions on what flights would operate.
Airlines have issued travel waivers for passengers to re-book, and Jetport officials advised passengers to check with their airlines for flight information.
At 4:49 p.m., Jim Keithley of Maine's Total Coverage reported that the flight board was showing that five flights slated to depart from the Portland Jetport had been canceled.
"I think we're probably not going to make it to New York today, so our weekend trip might be ruined and that's sad," said Ivan Belanger, who was traveling with his 9-year-old daughter, Ramona. "As soon as we got to the airport, we saw the news report that there was a nationwide grounding of all flights, which is why we are outside of security. We decided not to go through just in case."
University of Maine student Emily Chiarello drove from Orono to the Portland Jetport, where she was set to fly to Charleston, South Carolina, to visit her best friend. Chiarello and her friend have plans to travel to Charlotte, North Carolina, on Saturday for a John Summit concert.
"So I guess that's not happening anymore tonight," Chiarello said.
Chiarello said she had already gone through security and was sitting at the gate when her mother texted her about the nationwide ground stop.
"Then shortly after, I heard it on the announcements. They just said, 'All flights are grounded and nobody's leaving,'" said Chiarello, who is going to try to get to Charlotte on Saturday for the concert.
Scarborough resident Angelica Rego said she had plans to fly to Miami to celebrate her birthday weekend with her friend.
"They told me all flights were grounded because there was a security communications issue, and to just hang out," Rego said.
Rego said she thought she was going to manifest a good outcome, because the last nationwide ground stop in January 2023 lasted approximately 90 minutes.
"So I was like, 'OK, we'll hang out.' My friend is at the airport in Virginia kind of doing the same thing," Rego said. "Then, we've been basically looking at places that are in between. I think I'm just going to go get in my car and go drive somewhere."
While the ground stop was active, Bangor International Airport (BGR) advised travelers to anticipate potential flight delays and monitor their airline's website or mobile app for the latest flight information.
More information about the ground stop
When the FAA grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, it caused hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited "extraordinary circumstances" caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Trump administration officials blamed the ground stop on "overloaded," "outdated" systems. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system overwhelmed it.
Asked whether Mullin could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, he said: "There's nothing completely certain right now. It doesn't appear that way." He said there are no "footprints" showing an attack and that it appears to be "mechanically driven," adding that officials were still looking for the cause.
Even with the order being lifted, the airlines will not be able to return to normal operations immediately because so many of their planes and crews are out of position.
Mullin had said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.
But much work remains. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground, and not put them in the air where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them," said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot.
Friday's ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: School police officer tells officer he was responding to a fight when he was pulled over for speeding
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A school police officer told the officer that he was responding to a fight when he was pulled over for speeding, but the school district said that is not the case.
Footage from Louisville Metro Police officer Kendrick Eaves’ body camera shows Jefferson County Public Schools police officer Andre Lamont Shaw in uniform driving a district car.
Eaves had stopped Shaw at about 5 p.m. on Sept. 23 for speeding. In the recording, Eaves told Shaw his radar clocked him driving 69 mph — 34 mph over the 35 mph speed limit.
“So?” Shaw responded.
“Yeah, you’re speeding,” Eaves said.
“So?” Shaw said again.
“You can’t be going that fast,” Eaves said.
“Says who?” said Shaw.
“The law,” Eaves responded.
Eaves said Shaw flashed his rear lights when he’d initially tried to pull him over, believing it was an attempt to avoid being pulled over.
In the video, Shaw does not give his driver’s license to Eaves when he asks for it and instead asked Eaves to call his sergeant.
“You think you’re above the law and you’re not,” Eaves said.
Shaw is seen calling someone, though it is not clear who. Then he told the person on the phone that Eaves is “talking about taking me to jail” and laughs. He also notes that the stop is being recorded.
Eaves later told Shaw he can get out of his car and give his ID, or he can go to jail for reckless driving.
“What was reckless about it?” Shaw asked.
“You’re going 69 (mph) in a 35 (mph),” Eaves responded.
“Says you,” Shaw said.
“Says my front radar,” Eaves responded.
When a Louisville Metro Police sergeant arrived on scene, Shaw told the sergeant he was responding to a fight.
However, Jefferson County Public Schools did not support Shaw’s account when asked about the traffic stop. Instead, they said he was going home when he was stopped.
In an email, district spokesperson Juliann Morris said, “Officer Shaw was on his way home from completing his shift.”
In the video, the sergeant asked Shaw why his lights and sirens were not on, and Shaw appears to say he doesn’t have any.
“All JCPS police vehicles have lights. Some have sirens,” Morris said, but the district would not provide specifics about Shaw’s car.
Local First Investigations asked the school district about the difference between its account and what Shaw claims in the body camera video.
“We cannot comment further at this time as this is an ongoing matter,” Morris’ said.
Shaw has not yet responded to a request for comment.
Shaw was given a speeding ticket after giving his license to the sergeant. He was cited for speeding 26 mph over the limit or greater, with his arraignment scheduled for Dec. 15.
According to the Jefferson County Board of Education’s policy, any traffic citation received during the year “shall be reported to the superintendent prior to the employee driving a Board-owned vehicle.”
The district did not say whether Shaw has faced any disciplinary measures.
“He does still have access to a JCPS vehicle,” Morris said in an email. “We are aware of the incident and will monitor as the case is adjudicated.”
Louisville Metro Police Department said in a statement that officers are “authorized to enforce all applicable laws within Jefferson County.”
“Department policy does not establish a separate set of criteria for traffic stops involving officers from other agencies,” the department said in a statement. “Those encounters are handled under the same legal authority and officer discretion applied to any other traffic stop.”
The police department said it is aware of the incident, but had no further comment.
Prior to joining Jefferson County Public Schools, Shaw was an officer with the Louisville Metro Police Department.
He is also in the middle of a lawsuit he filed with another officer in 2024 against the department, alleging a hostile work environment, discrimination and uneven punishment because of race and faith.
The case is ongoing.

title: Ten County Soccer Players Honored with 2026 Butch Shaw Awards
text:
More Than the Final Score: 10 County Soccer Players Earn 2026 Butch Shaw Awards
Success in high school sports isn't always measured by wins, goals, or championships. Sometimes, the greatest recognition comes from the way an athlete plays the game and the respect they show along the way.
Ten Aroostook County high school soccer players have been named recipients of the 2026 Butch Shaw Awards, an honor recognizing outstanding soccer players who demonstrate the sportsmanship and respect that have long been part of the game's tradition in northern Maine.
Presented by the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials, the awards recognize five girls and five boys from across Aroostook County.
2026 Butch Shaw Award Recipients
Girls
- Lilly Burtt – Central Aroostook
- Madisyn Cyr – Wisdom
- Emma Soucy – Wisdom
- Reece Doucette – Fort Kent
- Ava Ezell – Houlton
Boys
- Dominic Cyr – Fort Kent
- Bodey McPherson – Presque Isle
- Drew Lamereau – Easton
- Levi Cole – Fort Fairfield
- Cooper Willard – Houlton
For these ten athletes, the recognition goes beyond what they accomplished during the fall soccer season. The award reflects the importance of competing with respect, displaying good sportsmanship, and representing their schools and communities in a positive way.
The Man Behind the Award
The Butch Shaw Award carries a history that stretches back four decades, honoring a man whose influence on Aroostook County athletics extended well beyond the sidelines.
Clyde "Butch" Shaw, a native of Mars Hill, joined the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials in 1972. He was among the early officials helping establish soccer as the sport grew in popularity among middle and high school students throughout the County.
Shaw was also a well-known and respected varsity basketball and baseball coach at Presque Isle High School.
His approach to athletics was built around three words that became his motto:
"Hustle, Pride, Defense."
But beyond competition and performance, Shaw believed that respect and good sportsmanship were essential qualities for every athlete, coach, and official.
In July 1985, Shaw was diagnosed with leukemia. He passed away that October, leaving behind a legacy that would continue to influence generations of County athletes.
The following fall, in 1986, the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials established the Butch Shaw Soccer Award in his memory.
The award was created to recognize outstanding soccer players who exemplify the same qualities Shaw valued throughout his life.
His family's connection to local athletics also continues today. His son, Ryan Shaw, serves as the boys soccer coach at Easton High School. Shaw's daughter is Erica McCrum.
A Legacy That Continues
Forty years after the award was established, its message remains just as important.
High school sports provide plenty of opportunities to celebrate championships, individual achievements, and memorable performances. The Butch Shaw Award recognizes something that can be just as meaningful: the character an athlete brings to competition.
For the ten players selected in 2026, their names now become part of a tradition that has honored generations of Aroostook County soccer players.
Congratulations to all ten recipients of the 2026 Butch Shaw Awards for representing their schools, teammates, and communities with pride and sportsmanship.

title: Red Sox agree to deal with World Series champion Jake Bauers
text:
The Boston Red Sox have signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal that rewards the first baseman for his 2026 breakout season that included being named MVP of the National League Championship Series, according to multiple reports, including ESPN.
Bauers never had more than 372 at-bats and never hit more than 12 homers in his first six seasons. He considered retiring before emerging as a power threat to help lead the Milwaukee Brewers to the World Series title.
The left-handed hitting Bauers, 31, set career highs with a .266 batting average, .874 OPS, 26 home runs and 86 RBI.
He was a postseason star, including in the NLCS sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers. He hit a go-ahead homer off two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell to end an 11-pitch at-bat in a 6-2 victory in Game 3 at Los Angeles.
Overall, Bauers was 4 for 14 (.286) with a home run and six RBI on his way to being named NLCS MVP. He was only 2 for 21 with no homers or RBI in the Brewers’ World Series win over Tampa Bay.
It was not immediately clear how Bauers will fit into Boston’s lineup. Willson Contreras is established as the starting first baseman. Bauers and Contreras could share playing time at designated hitter and first base.
Bauers played for Tampa Bay, Cleveland, Seattle and the New York Yankees before finding a home with Milwaukee in 2024. His .235 batting average in 2025 was his career high before his 2026 breakout.
Bauers was drafted in 2013 by the San Diego Padres. He hit .202 for the New York Yankees in 2023 and then hit .199 in his 2024 debut with Milwaukee. He considered ending his playing career before learning his wife was pregnant. He says he returned because the family needed health insurance.
ESPN was the first to report the deal.

title: FBI seizes $1.2 billion in crypto tied to Binance theft
text:
FBI says US has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group
FBI says US has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group
The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.
The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Related video at the top: Better Business Bureau Most Dangerous Scams
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.
Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

title: Hold the elected accountable on accountability
text:
A Nov. 7 letter (“Democrats should forget about retribution and focus on America”) says that retribution is not what Democrats were elected to do. There is a difference between retribution and holding someone accountable for corruption and crimes committed.
Trump and the Republicans who enabled him have been hyper-focused on retribution and blatant self-enrichment. Fed up with this, more than half, and up to 90% (depending on the poll) of voters told pollsters that government corruption was a major factor in how they voted.
Many Democratic candidates promised to address the crimes of the Trump administration and its allies. They were elected because voters expected them to keep that promise. The letter writer argued instead for a “focus on America.”
If we let crimes against the American people go unanswered, what is America? What is America if we leave the many holes in our systems of governance that Trump exposed unfilled? It’s an America where we can expect the crimes of this administration will happen again. It’s an America where the focus on working people will be temporary at best, at risk of flipping to enrich billionaires once again.
I agree, though, that in equal measure, Americans elected Democrats so that they could focus on the needs of working-class Americans. Voters expect our elected officials to walk and chew gum — and will hold them accountable in two years if they fail to do so.
Nancy Fannon
South Portland

title: BAAJA will wreak havoc on historic preservation in Maine
text:
The U.S. Senate is considering legislation that could cause irreparable harm to Maine communities.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would undermine Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, one of our nation’s most important tools for ensuring that tribes, state and local governments and the public have a voice in federal decisions that affect their communities.
Federal urban renewal policies and the construction of arterial highways resulted in the destruction of historic areas in Maine communities. Section 106 was established so that before a federally funded project moved forward, the people who live there were heard. The law has not stopped progress. It has improved federal projects — while protecting Maine’s historic and archaeological resources.
Consultation through Section 106 more sensitively redesigned Route 1 in Camden and Thomaston, located and documented colonial forts in Richmond and Windham, and prevented the construction of a telephone tower on the iconic Monhegan Island Lighthouse. Looking ahead, it will help communities manage the impact from highway construction, transmission lines, communication towers and data centers.
BAAJA would leave those decisions to federal officials. This bill does more than streamline Section 106. It narrows what resources the law protects and weakens the voice of the tribes, states, communities and all Mainers.
To ensure the voice of the people can be heard in charting the future of Maine’s built environment, please urge Sens. King and Collins to demand substantial revisions to, or removal of, the bill’s historic preservation provisions.
Earle G. Shettleworth Jr.
Director of the Maine Historic Preservation Commission, 1976-2015
Maine State Historian 
Hallowell

title: Obituary: Dennis N. Witham Sr.
Obituary: Neil Winthrop Wallace
text:
BOCA GRANDE, Fla. – Neil W. Wallace died on Oct. 27, 2026, at the age of 92. He was predeceased by his wife Elise “Butch” Raymond Wallace of 61 years who died on May 22, 2019. He lived a productive and fulfilling life marked by a rewarding business career, significant philanthropic commitments, a wide range of outside interests, and, above all, a long and happy marriage and a close family he deeply loved and cherished. After graduating from The Lawrenceville School, Neil attended Princeton University, class of 1955, and then Harvard Law School, class of 1958. After a brief period of practicing law at Nutter McClennen and Fish, he and his brother, Monte J. Wallace, founded The General Investment and Development Companies (GID) in 1960. GID went on to develop, own, and operate commercial real estate, growing into a major company with offices and holdings in leading cities across the United States and internationally, including Brazil and India. GID invested extensively in multifamily properties including many high-rise multifamily properties that it either developed from the ground up or acquired and also had significant investment in industrial properties. These investments are located throughout the United States and some abroad. His philanthropic interests focused primarily on conservation, health care, and education. He donated substantial land to The Nature Conservancy and Mass Audubon. He joined the Board of Brigham and Women’s Hospital in 1969 and later became a Life Trustee, serving until his death. He received the Heritage Society Award in recognition of his extraordinary gifts of time, talent, and financial support. Together with his wife, Elise “Butch,” he endowed the STRATUS Center and a floor in the obstetrical unit. He also joined the Board of the Museum of Science in 1969 and later became a life trustee. In 2014, he received the Colonel Francis T. Colby Award, honoring those who have made a major impact on the museum. He was a significant sponsor of the Hall of Human Life, which led to the Human Body Theater being named in his and Butch’s honor. He also served on the boards of the Charles River School, Noble and Greenough School, and Broadmoor Sanctuary in Sherborn and Natick, and as an overseer of the Boys and Girls Club. In addition, he served on the boards of several companies listed on the New York and Canadian stock exchanges. He and his brother Monte also made major gifts to Princeton University, including Wallace Hall, the home of Princeton’s Social Science Department, and the Wallace Theater and Dance buildings in the Performing Arts Center. Among their other gifts to Princeton was funding to renovate The Moffett Labs for the Department of Biology. Although he loved light-tackle fishing and pursued it in remote and beautiful places around the world, his greatest passion was the sea. He sailed his sloop, Aurora, across the Atlantic and joined it for months at a time during its five-and-a-half-year circumnavigation of the globe, including extended time in the remote islands of the South Pacific. As beautiful as those journeys were, his cruises in Maine, where he had a summer home, held a special place in his heart.
Neil is survived by his three children, Bradford S. Wallace and his wife, Ann Fowler Wallace; Jonathan R. Wallace and his wife, Lisa McGovern; and Julia W. Bennett. He is also survived by his grandchildren, Marlana Wallace; Jacqueline Wallace; Malcolm Wallace, and his wife, Celia; Jonathan Bennett, and his wife, Laura; and Andrew Bennett, and his wife, Francesca; his two great-grandsons, Theodore Bennett and Dezi Wallace; and his brother, Monte J. Wallace, along with Monte’s children, John Wallace; W. Gardner Wallace; and Elizabeth Wallace Trase; grandchildren and great-grandson. He was predeceased by his son-in-law, Robert Bennett, Julia’s husband, who died of cancer in 2011, and by his sister-in-law, Anne H. Wallace, Monte’s wife.
A service celebrating Neil’s life will be held at 11 a.m., on December 15, at St. Paul’s Church in Dedham, Massachusetts.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Brigham & Women’s Hospital or Noble and
Greenough School.

title: Troy Jackson isn’t backing Chuck Schumer’s challenger yet, but an ally expects him to
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Maine union leader close to U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson said Friday there is a “98% chance” the Democrat will back Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in his leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York.
Jackson has not said publicly whether he’ll support Van Hollen. His team said Friday evening that he looks forward to speaking with Van Hollen in the coming weeks. He and several other progressives have already said they won’t back Schumer in a leadership vote set for December, after Democrats won control of the Senate on Election Day.
The leadership fight puts Jackson, who upset five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins, in the spotlight with the party’s left flank as he meets new colleagues and builds out a staff. It would also set him against independent Sen. Angus King, who endorsed Schumer on Thursday night.
Last week, during freshman orientation on Capitol Hill, Jackson met with Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Dave Sullivan, eastern territory vice president of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers. Sullivan said all three agreed the Senate needed new leadership.
The machinists union sent a letter to Schumer and the Democratic caucus Tuesday pressing for a “new direction.” On Thursday, it endorsed Van Hollen after he announced his challenge.
“As the people speak across the country, the tsunami of a blue wave clearly shows everybody, top to bottom, left to right, wants change,” Sullivan said in an interview Friday.
Van Hollen, 67, was weighing a 2028 presidential run before he turned to the leadership bid. Sullivan said the union sees him as a steady choice, calling him “levelheaded with a good track record.”
The union represents 600,000 workers, including Bath Iron Works shipbuilders, and paid Jackson $90,000 as a consultant from March 2025 through August. Its president, Brian Bryant, a former BIW pipefitter, said in the endorsement that the race is a fight over working people.
“[Sen]-Elect Jackson has already made clear that he believes it’s time for new leadership in the Senate,” Hilary Barrett, a Jackson transition aide and his former campaign manager, said in a statement. “The next Senate majority leader needs to be ready to do what’s right for working families and the people of Maine.”
El-Sayed has also backed Van Hollen, along with Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan and Sen. Tina Smith, both of Minnesota, and Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a longtime Jackson ally. Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas is among the Democrats who oppose Schumer but haven’t endorsed anyone to replace him.
Axios reported that Schumer has 14 public endorsements. He posted on X Thursday night that he welcomed discussion about the caucus’s future.
“I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said.
King pushed back on the case against Schumer in a statement, saying the leader’s plans for the new majority were “directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters.”
“He has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” King said. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

title: Manchester United hires Mauricio Pochettino, who tearfully leaves US job to revive former power
text:
Manchester United hires Mauricio Pochettino, who tearfully leaves US job to revive former power
Tears filled Mauricio Pochettino's eyes as he discussed quitting the U.S. national team for his dream job with Manchester United.
“A decision that in some parts, it’s a very sad decision, in other parts, we are professional and we need also to try to find the next step, to try and make your dreams come true,” he said.
Just three months after the U.S. Soccer Federation announced his contract to lead the Americans through the 2030 World Cup, Pochettino said Friday he will depart next week for Old Trafford. He will try to revive the 20-time English champions, in the relegation zone after 10 games of the Premier League season.
“They know that there’s not too many opportunities [that] can happen in your career like a side of Manchester United and, of course, when that arrives, it’s difficult to turn down,” Pochettino said during an emotional news conference at the U.S. team training camp.
He signed a 2 1/2-year contract and will take over on Wednesday, Nov. 18, ahead of the match at Liverpool four days later, becoming United's eighth permanent coach or manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
Pochettino choked up at a news conference, speaking while seated between USSF president Cindy Parlow Cone and CEO JT Batson.
“One of the most difficult decisions in our careers,” he said, crying and rubbing his hands as Cone put a supportive hand on his back.
He did not want to speak about the state of United. The English club said the 54-year-old Argentine was “renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players," and had “consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues.”
Pochettino's appointment came one day after Michael Carrick was fired for overseeing United's worst league start in 40 years. Manchester United is 18th in the 20-team league.
Pochettino's departure creates uncertainty about what's next for U.S.
Pochettino and his assistants will remain with the U.S. for the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.
“We recovered our motivation,” Pochettino said. “We recovered our capacity to dream big, the capacity to train players that really want to improve and really want to share good moments and players that really care about the federation and this country.”
Pochettino took over the U.S. team in the fall of 2024 and led the co-host Americans to the round of 16 at this year’s World Cup. The USSF is likely to inquire about Pep Guardiola’s interest and also could consider elevating Under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, a former national team defender. Cherundolo will lead a senior national team training camp next month with players mostly from Major League Soccer.
The Americans’ next game with the full player pool after Tuesday is likely to be in late March, so the U.S. could be deliberate with its search.
Going into his final two games, Pochettino led the U.S. to 21 wins, 12 losses and two draws — counting a penalty-kicks win over Costa Rica as a draw. He was the first long-term U.S. coach not to win any titles since Steve Sampson from 1995-98.
“What you’ve done with the men’s and the boy's program in two years has been unbelievable,” Parlow Cone said. “Not only have you contributed to their advancement, you’ve contributed to the entire federation being better.”
Batson and chief operating officer Dan Helfrich will lead the search, assisted by women’s national team coach Emma Hayes and former American defender Oguchi Onyewu, a USSF senior vice president.
Manchester United is paying a release fee to the USSF to terminate his contract.
“Those funds are used to help us hire great coaches, help us (with) youth national team programs, coaching education,” Batson said. “Those funds are available for us to invest to make the biggest impact on our goals.”
Pochettino said he told his U.S. players and staff of his decision in a meeting on Thursday.
“I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation,” Pochettino said. “And they know us, how committed we are for the next two games."
United wagers a coach with no major trophies can turn its fortunes
After coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in the Premier League, Espanyol in Spain and winning the French title with Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino takes a job that has proved to be too big for a succession of managers since Ferguson led the team to a record 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns during a nearly 27-year tenure.
United has not won the league since Ferguson’s last season in 2013 and has been overtaken by rivals Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Arsenal.
Champions League-winning coaches Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho failed to meet United’s expectations, while David Moyes, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Carrick also came up short.
Despite winning the French league with PSG in 2022, arguably Pochettino’s greatest achievement was turning Tottenham into a serial title contender in the Premier League and also leading the club to the Champions League final in 2019.
He has never won a major trophy in England, most recently losing the final of the English League Cup with Chelsea in 2024.
It is not known how much Pochettino will earn at United, as European soccer teams typically do not disclose the salaries of coaches and players. United has spent huge sums on coaches and executives over the past 13 years and paid well in excess of $100 million in severance payments alone.
Pochettino earned just over $5 million during his first seven months as coach of the U.S., according to the U.S. Soccer Federation’s tax filing.

title: 50 years after iconic film, a gathering of ‘Rocky’ fans in Philadelphia breaks a world record
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — The story of Rocky Balboa is one that audiences love and know well – of resilience, grit and persevering despite the odds.
Fans honored his legacy 50 years after the film with a Guinness World Record-breaking gathering of people dressed as Rocky on Friday at the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
The uniform? A black beanie, grey sweatpants and sweatshirt, and black high-top Converse sneakers.
A growing number of Rockys amassed in front of the museum steps Friday afternoon, cheering as stragglers showed up to aid the record-breaking attempt.
“What’s your name?” the announcer asked one participant. “Rocky Balboa,” they replied.
A minimum of 250 people needed to be there for the occasion, according to Guinness. The official record was certified with 570 participants, an announcer said.
The city organized a host of events this month to honor its fictional underdog boxer, including a sprint up the stairs that Rocky stormed up in the film, a rededication marking the permanent installation of the Rocky statue, and a meat market challenge where fans can recreate a scene in the film where he trained by punching slabs of frozen meat.
After the world record was confirmed, the group ran up the stairs to pose for a picture in front of the museum.
On Saturday, tourism officials said 45,000 runners from all 50 states and 75 countries will participate in a “Rocky Run” throughout the city.
The 1976 film written by Sylvester Stallone tells the story of a small-time boxer from South Philly who gears up to take on the heavyweight champion of the world, Apollo Creed, fighting in the city to celebrate America’s bicentennial. Though he ultimately loses the fight, Rocky proves himself and wins the heart of Adrian, the neighborhood pet store clerk.
The movie was shot for less than $1 million, and Stallone was an unknown actor who had written the script in a desperate bid to land himself work.
The film won the best picture Oscar and became the highest-grossing sports movie at the time. Its numerous spinoffs and sequels has helped it hold the record for most successful sports movie franchise, according to Guinness World Records.
Philadelphia held its inaugural Rocky Day in 2023 with Stallone in attendance, expanding celebrations to a weeklong Rocky Fest the next year. The city kicked off this year’s festivities with the release of Stallone’s memoir, “The Steps,” on Sep. 29.

title: Gardens Aglow opens Saturday at Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BOOTHBAY, Maine (WABI) - Gardens Aglow opens Saturday at Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay and runs through Jan. 2.
A mile-long path glows with more than 750,000 LED lights. Strung end to end, the lights would stretch about 65 miles, the distance from South Portland to Boothbay.
This year’s theme is “Gathered in Maine.” Organizers told WABI the theme has a double meaning.
Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens, explained the meaning.
“It is both about the gathering and harvesting that Mainers and the natural world are doing during the winter and this time of year. And then it’s also about how we all gather together this time of year,” Ostherr said.
“Many people will say, yeah, we come from Massachusetts, we came from New Hampshire. We came from up in Aroostook County and we’re spending the night. I mean, a lot of people make it a big event as part of their holiday season,” she said.
Ticket information
Ticket prices start at $20 for adults and are on sale now. Tickets should be purchased online or over the phone, 633-8000.
The gardens is competing again for a USA Today Readers’ Choice award in the best botanical garden holiday lights category. It is currently ranked No. 2.
People can vote once a day through Nov. 30 at 10best.usatoday.com.
Park and Ride to Gardens Aglow
The Boothbay Harbor Region Chamber of Commerce provides shuttles from downtown Boothbay Harbor to the gardens on weekend nights during Gardens Aglow.
Shuttles run continuously from 3:45 to 9 p.m. from the Boothbay Harbor Town Office to the entrance of Gardens Aglow.

title: Murder of man who was found dead on Portland sidewalk remains unsolved 36 years later
text:
Murder of Scott Sampson, who was found dead on a Portland sidewalk, remains unsolved 36 years later
On Nov. 13, 1990, the 26-year-old father of two died in front of what was then Pine Street Variety at 64 Pine St.
Murder of Scott Sampson, who was found dead on a Portland sidewalk, remains unsolved 36 years later
On Nov. 13, 1990, the 26-year-old father of two died in front of what was then Pine Street Variety at 64 Pine St.
Friday marks 36 years since a 26-year-old father of two was killed in Portland, a murder that remains unsolved.
On Nov. 13, 1990, Scott Sampson was found dead on the sidewalk in front of what was then Pine Street Variety at 64 Pine St. in Portland's West End.
Maine's Total Coverage spoke with Sampson's family members when they visited the scene of the crime.
"Being down here in this area is just, it's a lot," Kyle Sampson told his older brother, Shawn, during a video chat call.
"Yeah, it sucks," said Shawn Sampson, who lives in Canada.
Shawn was 5 years old and Kyle was 3 when their father was murdered. Their mother, Lisa Maheux, had separated from their father a couple of years earlier and moved to northern Maine. Maheux said Scott Sampson would make frequent trips to see his sons and bring them toys.
"It just breaks my heart, because these boys have been without a father for 36 years, and whoever did this just gets to walk around living their life," Maheux said.
There were no witnesses to the murder and it was not captured by security cameras, but there were a few people who gave accounts of the final hours of Scott Sampson's life.
The manager of the 7-Eleven on Congress Street said he remembered Sampson buying hot dogs and speaking with another man outside earlier in the evening.
Sampson's sister, Sandy Hill, said she remembers it all.
"The Portland police saw him jostling with someone and they never stopped, but they recognized my brother," Hill said.
The 7-Eleven is just a couple of blocks away from Pine Street Variety. Sampson's family members said that many people, including a beat cop, saw him and simply did nothing.
"The cop saw him lying on the ground and drove by, thought he was just some drunk," Maheux said.
"The store owner left him there when he locked up at midnight," Hill said. "It wasn't until a couple was walking their dog that they went and checked on him, found no pulse and called the Portland Police Department."
Sampson had been stabbed in the stomach and died alone. That fact continues to eat away at his family to this day and leaves them aching for answers and justice.
"Somebody knows something. Nobody can keep a secret like this over these years," Hill said. "Nobody can."
Kyle Sampson recalled the last time he was at 64 Pine St. was in 2015, when he visited the site for the first time on the 25th anniversary of his father's death. At that time, Kyle Sampson was hanging flyers in the hopes that someone would come forward with answers. But those answers have yet to come 11 years later.
"There's a killer amongst us. He could be walking around in the same area. He could still be around here for all we know," he said. "It's disgusting to think that nothing's been done."
"My sons have had to live 36 years like this. The questions never get answered," Maheux said. "There are always more questions, no answers."
Scott Sampson's family has just two questions: Who? And why? Anyone who has any information about this cold case is asked to call Portland Police Detective Andrew Hagerty at 207-874-8602 or Detective Daniel Townsend at 207-874-8606. Information can be shared anonymously by calling 207-874-8584 and leaving a message on the department's Crime Tip Line. People can also text the keyword "PPDME" and a message to 847411 (TIP411).

title: Man United hires Mauricio Pochettino, who leaves US job with task of reviving former power
text:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ga. (AP) — Mauricio Pochettino was hired as Manchester United’s head coach on Friday, agreeing to leave his job with the U.S. national team to take on the challenge of reviving the fortunes of English soccer’s once dominant force.
Just three months after announcing a contract to lead the Americans through the 2030 World Cup, the U.S. Soccer Federation said Pochettino will depart next next week for Old Trafford. The 20-time English champion is in the relegation zone after 10 games of the Premier League season.
He has signed a 2 1/2-year contract and will officially take over on Nov. 18 ahead of the match at Liverpool four days later, becoming United’s eighth permanent coach or manager since club great Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
United said the 54-year-old Argentine was “renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players,” and had “consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues.”
Pochettino’s appointment comes one day after Michael Carrick was fired for overseeing United’s worst league start in 40 years, with one of the biggest teams in world soccer languishing 18th in the Premier League.
Pochettino and his assistants will remain with the U.S. team for the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.
“There is tremendous talent in the U.S. player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of U.S. Soccer,” Pochettino said in a statement.
Pochettino took over the U.S. team in the fall of 2024 and led the co-host Americans to the round of 16 at this year’s World Cup. The USSF is likely to sound out Pep Guardiola’s interest and could also consider elevating Under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, a former national team defender. Cherundolo will lead a senior national team training camp next month with players mostly from Major League Soccer.
USSF CEO JT Batson and chief operating officer Dan Helfrich will lead the search, assisted by women’s national team coach Emma Hayes and former American defender Oguchi Onyewu, a member of the USSF staff.
“Mauricio has left a lasting mark on U.S. Soccer through his leadership, professionalism and commitment to our players and culture,” Batson said in a statement. “What we are most proud of goes beyond the wins. He and his staff raised standards, strengthened our culture and created clearer connections from the youth national teams to the senior team.”
After coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in the Premier League, Espanyol in Spain and winning the French title with Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino takes a job that has proved to be too big for a succession of managers since Ferguson led the team to a record 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns during a near 27-year tenure.
United has not won the league since Ferguson’s last season in 2013 and has been overtaken by rivals Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Arsenal.
Champions League-winning coaches Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho failed to meet United’s expectations, while David Moyes, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Carrick also came up short.
Despite winning the French league with PSG in 2022, arguably Pochettino’s greatest achievement was turning Tottenham into a serial title contender in the Premier League and also leading the club to the Champions League final in 2019.
He has never won a major trophy in England, most recently losing the final of the English League Cup with Chelsea in 2024.
