title: Women’s basketball game in Orono brings Oregon coach closer to goal
text:
ORONO — Kelly Graves’ quest to coach a basketball game in all 50 states has taken on a bigger life than he ever imagined or intended. When his Oregon women’s basketball team played Friday in The Pit against Maine, Graves checked off state number 45.
“If we can get it done, we’ll get it done,” Graves said after his team’s come from behind 79-72 win.
The states left on Graves’ to-do list are New Hampshire and Massachusetts, which he hopes to get with another trip to the Northeast next season, as well as three Mid-Atlantic states: Delaware, Virginia and West Virginia.
When Oregon joined the Big Ten a few years ago, Graves looked at the map and realized the new conference opened up a whole new area of the country for his travels. The states started to tick away. This week, his team visited Vermont before coming to Orono to face the Black Bears.
What made the trip even better was Graves knew his team would face a pair of strong mid-major opponents who have been at or near the top of America East in recent years.
“This has been a really good trip. It’s a long trip,” Graves said. “(Maine) is a good basketball team.”
And the atmosphere was top notch. The fans who packed The Pit were their usual loud and rowdy selves. The Ducks noticed.
“So loud. When they were coming out for warmups, it was so loud in here, but I love it,” said Brooklynn Haywood, Oregon’s freshman guard from Anchorage, Alaska. “It gets me hyped up. It helps me play better … I’m down for a cool experience anytime.”
Playing in an arena that’s a shoebox compared to the ones the Ducks see across the Big Ten was a good experience for his team, Graves said.
“I love it. It was awesome. I love gyms like this. I really do wish more Power 4 teams would go out and experience this kind of stuff. I think our kids have had a good time,” he said.
The Black Bears led at the end of each quarter except the fourth. While it would’ve been nice to knock off a Big Ten team that advanced to the second round of the NCAA tournament each of the past two seasons, this was the type of game that Maine wants to win in March a lot more than in November.
For the Black Bears, it was an opportunity to get better. Coach Amy Vachon routinely tries to schedule tough nonconference opponents to prepare her team for America East play over the second half of the season. Playing a Power 4 team isn’t new to Maine. Playing one in The Pit certainly is.
“I think it’s so great for women’s basketball to expose the people from Maine to what a Power 4 team looks like,” Vachon said. “To show Maine we can compete with a Power 4 team.”
The Big Ten, the Southeastern Conference, the Atlantic Coast Conference and the Big 12 make up the Power 4 conferences in women’s basketball.
Oregon is the third Power 4 opponent to visit Maine since the start of the 2018-19 season. On Nov. 15, 2018, former Black Bears coach and Maine native Joanne Palombo-McCallie brought her Duke squad to play the Black Bears at Bangor’s Cross Insurance Center. On Nov. 30, 2023, an Indiana team led by Gorham’s Mackenzie Holmes took on Maine in Portland at Cross Insurance Arena.
Each of those teams had strong, bowline knot ties to Maine, though. Oregon’s tie was simply Graves’ wanderlust and passion for travel.
When Vachon got the email from Oregon asking for the game, of course she said yes. To borrow a catchphrase from Oregon’s Nike benefactors, just do it.
The Black Bears are set to play at Oregon next season. Maine’s new arena is going up next to Alfond Stadium. Would Graves consider bringing the Ducks back to play there in a few years? He took a deep breath before answering.
“No,” he said.
He will be back for a vacation with his wife, Graves said. So while the game Friday wasn’t a win for the Black Bears, it was a win for Maine, and a win for women’s basketball.

title: Reports: Red Sox agree to 4-year, $58M deal with Brewers' postseason hero
text:
Boston Red Sox agree to 4-year, $58 million deal with Jake Bauers, reports say
Bauers was named NLCS MVP and helped the Milwaukee Brewers win their first World Series title
Boston Red Sox agree to 4-year, $58 million deal with Jake Bauers, reports say
Bauers was named NLCS MVP and helped the Milwaukee Brewers win their first World Series title
The Boston Red Sox have agreed to a four-year, $58 million contract with free agent Jake Bauers, who played a big role in the Milwaukee Brewers' championship run, according to multiple reports.
Bauers, 31, has played seven major league seasons and had his best year in 2026, setting career highs with a .266 batting average, 26 home runs and 86 runs batted in. The first baseman also ranked second in the National League with a .389 on-base percentage.
He was named MVP of the NL Championship Series, batting .286 with a homer and six RBI in Milwaukee's four-game sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers. The Brewers would then go on to defeat the Tampa Bay Rays in five games to win their first World Series title.
Bauers could slot in at designated hitter for the Red Sox, who got great production out of first baseman Willson Contreras this past season. Contreras batted .275 with a career-high 27 homers and 81 RBI in his first season with Boston, and is a finalist for the American League Silver Slugger Award at first base.
There is expected to be increased activity in the early stages of the MLB offseason, as the collective bargaining agreement between the league and the MLB Players Association is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1.

title: Ketamine infusion therapy could offer hope for chronic pain patients
text:
(Aging Untold) — Millions of Americans live with chronic pain. The epidemic is often hidden behind closed doors as patients suffer in silence, according to research published in the “Journal of Primary Care & Community Health.”
Chronic pain, such as back pain, arthritis and headaches, including migraines, is often described as aching, burning, shooting or throbbing.
For those who cannot get relief from traditional pain management methods, some in the medical community are promoting ketamine infusion as a possible solution. The treatment works by slowing down pain-sensing nerves that send messages to the brain.
Elanor Koch of Nebraska said she has seen improvement since starting the therapy.
In 2020, doctors found a tumor on her cervical spine that had eroded and compressed her spinal cord by more than 60%.
“Before, I would wake up in pain and live life in pain, and I’d only have so much in me I could give a day until I would push myself into a flare that would leave me in bed for a handful of days,” Koch said.
She went through neck fusion surgery, then had to relearn to walk and use her left arm. Still, she experienced debilitating pain.
“Couldn’t get a hold of or a grasp on how to manage my pain in a way that felt safe or effective,” Koch said. “Opioid pain therapy didn’t feel like a good long-term solution, and other alternative pain-management areas were not working.”
Finding relief through ketamine treatment
In 2023, Koch found ketamine infusion therapy at Mind and Body Wellness Center.
The off-label treatment is said to help the brain process thoughts and emotions more effectively.
“When I’ve went through ketamine, I had a perspective that I’d never been able to force myself into,” Koch said. “To see it for what it is and understand that that’s part of the experience of why we’re here and it didn’t feel like my pain was as daunting.”
During the hour-long sessions, patients experience dissociation.
“You’re not fully aware of your physical body and you’re kind of just hanging out in your head for a while,” Koch said.
After six treatments in one month, Koch said she experienced significant improvement.
“I was like pain free for three months,” she said. “I had minor flares every once in a while, but they weren’t long lasting, and they weren’t very common or close together.”
Koch requires maintenance infusions about every few months.
Cost barriers limit access
Infusions cost $400 to 500 per session and are not covered by insurance.
Dr. Stephen Salzbrenner at Nebraska Medicine said the price keeps more people from accessing the treatment.
“It’s pretty widely accepted in the scientific community that it’s effective and so it’s offered,” Salzbrenner said. “Now it’s not often covered by insurance ‘cause it’s not approved. If it was FDA-approved for depression, then insurance might cover it as a treatment.”
FDA-approved alternative available
Salzbrenner offers an alternative treatment that is FDA-approved and accepted by insurance for depression.
Esketamine is a nasal spray that’s chemically related to ketamine but has a distinct chemical makeup.
“It can happen within hours, it’s really pretty remarkable,” Salzbrenner said. “Because a lot of the traditional antidepressants we have take six weeks, eight weeks, before you really know if it’s going to help.”
Salzbrenner said it’s essential to combine the treatment with talk therapy.
“Therapy is really indispensable,” he said. “You can’t replicate that with a medicine.”
Koch agrees with that approach.
“I have a psychiatrist and a talk therapist,” she said. “I’m no longer taking any antidepressive medications. If my word counts for anything as somebody who could barely get out of bed two years ago, I’d say try it.”
Treatment not suitable for everyone
People with certain medical histories might not be good candidates for ketamine infusion, including those with mental health conditions such as schizophrenia, uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease, kidney or liver disease and substance use disorder.

title: Anna Bullett wins recount for Portland’s District 4 City Council seat
text:
Anna Bullett won the recount of votes cast for the Portland City Council District 4 race by 12 votes, the same difference as the original tally.
Jake Viola formally requested the recount Monday, three days after the Portland City Clerk’s office finalized the Nov. 3 election results. The original tally had Bullett narrowly winning, 3,421 to 3,409, with 917 additional blank ballots.
The recount found that 3,423 people marked their ballot for Bullett and 3,411 for Viola.
“I just want to express my gratitude to all the volunteers, both Jake’s and mine, who came out today to do this very long day under a high-pressure situation,” Bullett said minutes after city officials announced the tally. “But I’m filled with confidence knowing our count stands. That just tells me our elections in Portland are very solid.”
The city of Portland followed the recount rules in state statute and set by the Department of the Secretary of State. In accordance with state law, each candidate provided a minimum of six counters throughout the process. The volunteers and city staff examined and counted each ballot by hand in City Hall on Friday from 9 a.m. until the final tally just before 4:45 p.m.
Bullett was first elected to the City Council in 2023. She campaigned for a second term with a focus on issues such as pedestrian safety, substance use and mental health, and continuing to work collaboratively with city staff.
Viola vowed in his campaign to remedy the unintended negative consequences of municipal policies, like Portland’s needle exchange program and inclusionary zoning policy. He promised to be accessible and communicative to District 4 residents.
In the two other City Council races this election cycle, former mayor Kate Snyder won an at-large seat and restaurateur Ilma López was elected to represent District 5. Both elections were determined in rank-choice runoffs and were seen by supporters as a needed shift toward a more moderate City Council. Viola hoped to join this trend.

title: School police officer tells officer he was responding to a fight when he was pulled over for speeding
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A school police officer told the officer that he was responding to a fight when he was pulled over for speeding, but the school district said that is not the case.
Footage from Louisville Metro Police officer Kendrick Eaves’ body camera shows Jefferson County Public Schools police officer Andre Lamont Shaw in uniform driving a district car.
Eaves had stopped Shaw at about 5 p.m. on Sept. 23 for speeding. In the recording, Eaves told Shaw his radar clocked him driving 69 mph — 34 mph over the 35 mph speed limit.
“So?” Shaw responded.
“Yeah, you’re speeding,” Eaves said.
“So?” Shaw said again.
“You can’t be going that fast,” Eaves said.
“Says who?” said Shaw.
“The law,” Eaves responded.
Eaves said Shaw flashed his rear lights when he’d initially tried to pull him over, believing it was an attempt to avoid being pulled over.
In the video, Shaw does not give his driver’s license to Eaves when he asks for it and instead asked Eaves to call his sergeant.
“You think you’re above the law and you’re not,” Eaves said.
Shaw is seen calling someone, though it is not clear who. Then he told the person on the phone that Eaves is “talking about taking me to jail” and laughs. He also notes that the stop is being recorded.
Eaves later told Shaw he can get out of his car and give his ID, or he can go to jail for reckless driving.
“What was reckless about it?” Shaw asked.
“You’re going 69 (mph) in a 35 (mph),” Eaves responded.
“Says you,” Shaw said.
“Says my front radar,” Eaves responded.
When a Louisville Metro Police sergeant arrived on scene, Shaw told the sergeant he was responding to a fight.
However, Jefferson County Public Schools did not support Shaw’s account when asked about the traffic stop. Instead, they said he was going home when he was stopped.
In an email, district spokesperson Juliann Morris said, “Officer Shaw was on his way home from completing his shift.”
In the video, the sergeant asked Shaw why his lights and sirens were not on, and Shaw appears to say he doesn’t have any.
“All JCPS police vehicles have lights. Some have sirens,” Morris said, but the district would not provide specifics about Shaw’s car.
Local First Investigations asked the school district about the difference between its account and what Shaw claims in the body camera video.
“We cannot comment further at this time as this is an ongoing matter,” Morris’ said.
Shaw has not yet responded to a request for comment.
Shaw was given a speeding ticket after giving his license to the sergeant. He was cited for speeding 26 mph over the limit or greater, with his arraignment scheduled for Dec. 15.
According to the Jefferson County Board of Education’s policy, any traffic citation received during the year “shall be reported to the superintendent prior to the employee driving a Board-owned vehicle.”
The district did not say whether Shaw has faced any disciplinary measures.
“He does still have access to a JCPS vehicle,” Morris said in an email. “We are aware of the incident and will monitor as the case is adjudicated.”
Louisville Metro Police Department said in a statement that officers are “authorized to enforce all applicable laws within Jefferson County.”
“Department policy does not establish a separate set of criteria for traffic stops involving officers from other agencies,” the department said in a statement. “Those encounters are handled under the same legal authority and officer discretion applied to any other traffic stop.”
The police department said it is aware of the incident, but had no further comment.
Prior to joining Jefferson County Public Schools, Shaw was an officer with the Louisville Metro Police Department.
He is also in the middle of a lawsuit he filed with another officer in 2024 against the department, alleging a hostile work environment, discrimination and uneven punishment because of race and faith.
The case is ongoing.

title: Bessent blames Commerce's Lutnick for not restricting Nvidia chip exports to China
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in implementing controls over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China.
Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Megaspeed to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.
“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said. Commerce “has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website, play a prominent role in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang resigned Thursday after news that he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, according to The New York Times. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports. On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government. Messages seeking comment were sent to the Commerce Department.

title: Every voice helps make a symphony in the PSO Children’s Chorus
text:
“As soon as you hear everything come together, it’s like, whoa.”
That’s a quote from Allison Largay, age 12, a member of the PSO Children’s Chorus, describing how it feels when weeks of rehearsals finally come together on stage, and the voices of the chorus blend with the full sound of the orchestra for the first time.
This season marks the fifth year young singers will sing alongside the Portland Symphony Orchestra during the Magic of Christmas. Since it first started in 2021, the PSO Children’s Chorus has grown from 11 singers to 48, welcoming young musicians ages 9 to 16 from communities across southern Maine and New Hampshire. Under the direction of PSO Children’s Chorus Director Matt LaBerge, they develop their musical skills, find inspiration in the professional musicians around them and become part of a tradition that brings generations together through music.
While the rehearsals are filled with laughter and camaraderie, the young singers are also developing the skills and discipline to perform alongside professional musicians. Singers must audition and arrive prepared for weekly rehearsals. Not only do they have a central role in the PSO’s Magic of Christmas, but for the past several seasons, they have also been featured in select PSO Classical and Discovery programs. There is no fee to participate in the PSO Children’s Chorus and it is one of several free or low-cost youth, family and school programs the PSO offers.
For Allison and her twin sister Alexa, being part of the PSO Children’s Chorus has become a highlight of their musical journeys. Since joining three years ago, the sisters have experienced the excitement of performing alongside a professional orchestra, discovering new musical interests and building friendships with fellow young singers.
Through the chorus, the two young sopranos have started to learn classical vocal techniques, how to read music and what it takes to perform with a professional orchestra. Being part of the chorus and performing alongside professional musicians has inspired the girls to explore every aspect of professional music-making opportunities. Notably, Allison conducted the PSO during “Sleigh Ride” in Magic of Christmas, and Alexa performed a children’s solo with Opera Maine.
Alexa also discovered a new instrument after watching a harpist perform with the PSO.
“It was really cool to me,” she said. “I’d wanted to play an instrument, but I wanted to play something unique, and the harp sounded gorgeous.”
After performing with the PSO, she was inspired to begin studying the harp herself.
For LaBerge, watching the Largay sisters and other young students make serious connections with and find inspiration in professional musicians right in their community has particular resonance.
Growing up in South Portland, LaBerge began playing trumpet in fifth grade. He remembers attending the PSO’s Magic of Christmas concerts with his parents and being captivated by the performances.
He went on to study music at the University of Southern Maine, where professors became influential mentors. In his senior year, a professor who played with the PSO recommended him for an opportunity to narrate a piece during the Magic of Christmas.
LaBerge is now a regular narrator of other PSO productions, and after serving as assistant director when the children’s chorus was newly established, he became its director in 2022.
“I’m only here today because teachers and mentors saw something in me, had faith in me, took a chance on me, and most importantly, they gave me opportunities,” LaBerge said.
It’s this kind of confidence he hopes to impart on the young singers in the PSO Children’s Chorus, and a feeling Alexa and Allison experience often. Both said singing with the chorus feels different from their other auditions and performances.
“With a group, it’s less scary because you have a bunch of people who can back you up,” Alexa said. “You can stop to breathe.”
When the girls reflected on the nonmusical skills they had built, they had wise answers. Allison said she’s built up her confidence and perseverance, vital in a profession where auditions often end in rejection.
“There’s a lot more nos than there are yeses,” she said.
Alexa had learned to appreciate the experience while it was happening.
“Enjoy it while it’s going on and really live in the moment,” she said. “Because when 17 comes, I won’t be able to do this anymore.”
The sisters have plenty of ambitions. Both dream of performing on Broadway, while Allison is also interested in becoming a veterinarian. Alexa would love to play the harp with the Portland Symphony Orchestra someday.
LaBerge understands how much can change between childhood and adulthood. He once sat in the audience at Merrill Auditorium, imagining what it might be like to perform on that stage. Today, he watches from the wings as his own singers step into the spotlight.
“My favorite feeling in the world is watching these kids go from nervous and shy to just living their best lives,” he said.
Music offers young people countless ways to learn, grow and connect, building skills that will linger on through life. While some may become professional musicians, others veterinarians and still others something they haven’t even imagined yet, they’ll all carry with them the confidence to use their own voices and an understanding of what they can accomplish together.

title: Death Notice: Margaret “Chick” Susi Veilleux
Retired veteran finds new mission volunteering at senior center
text:
PHOENIX (InvestigateTV) — A Valley Army veteran is spending his post-military and post-retirement years volunteering at a Phoenix senior center, offering companionship and practical help to seniors who have few other resources.
Robert Lane can be found at the Desert West Senior Center in the Maryvale neighborhood Monday through Friday, from morning until late afternoon.
Lane enlisted in the Army in the late 1970s, shortly after the Vietnam War ended, as part of an effort known as Operation Babylift.
“They flew me and a couple guys out to Fort Smith, Arkansas, and we fed all the Vietnamese women and babies there,” Lane said.
He has continued feeding people since — now serving hotdogs and nachos at the senior center.
Lane also takes seniors grocery shopping, drives them to doctor appointments, and spends time with them at the center. It is all part of the Senior Companion Program, which is an AmeriCorps Seniors service through Northern Arizona University.
“Making them laugh and just the joy in their face, that’s what it’s all about,” Lane said. “Because sometimes, some of them have nobody. Nobody at home and nobody to take care of them.”
Lane has been a regular at the center for nearly four years, and his energy is infectious.
“He is a huge source of encouragement because he really lifts our spirits,” Daniel Flores said in Spanish. “He gives us everything we need and helps us a lot.”
Lane’s wife, Synthia, inspired him to begin volunteering and is also a fixture at the center.
“This is where we’re just going to plant it until there’s no more retirement (and) we’re totally out of it,” she said. “We’re just not ready to give up yet.”
Synthia said she is typically working in the office while her husband engages with seniors on the floor as a “social butterfly.”
Lane has also picked up some Spanish during his time there since many of the seniors only speak Spanish.
He occasionally performs as Elvis for the senior center crowd.
“You come on down to the senior center and you can see Elvis here saying, ‘You ain’t nothing but a hound dog,’” Lane said. “Thank you very much.”

title: Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments dismissed, saying agent lied to grand jury
text:
Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh are expected in court Friday to ask a judge to throw out the original murder indictments for killing his wife and son. Now they’re saying the chief investigator in the case lied to the grand jury.
Murdaugh is facing a retrial on the murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence, ruling that a court clerk improperly influenced jurors against him during his 2023 trial.
Even if the longshot request to dismiss the indictments is granted by Judge Debra McCaslin at Friday’s pretrial hearing, it may not stop or even postpone an April retrial for the disgraced lawyer. Prosecutors can seek another set of grand jury indictments as soon as next month, and defense attorneys said they won’t stop them.
But a ruling for Murdaugh would be another rebuke of the chief investigator, State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen.
A judge last year threw out a different murder case Owen was involved in because the dead woman’s mother told the agent about a suicide threat her daughter made days before she died that Owen never relayed to prosecutors or defense attorneys.
Owen abruptly retired in 2024, not long after he was honored as State Law Enforcement Officer of the Year.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.
Defense lawyers said that as prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.
Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property, which wasn’t the case.
Prosecutors said they had plenty of other evidence supporting the murder charges, and wrote that “a single mistake is not bad faith.”
Owen told grand jurors about the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh’s voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his denials. Owen also told them about the family’s mounting debts and how Murdaugh’s schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.
But Murdaugh’s lawyers have repeatedly pointed out how little physical evidence prosecutors have — no DNA or blood was found splattered on Murdaugh or any of his clothes, even though the killings were at close range with powerful weapons that were never found.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.

title: Ring doorbell camera captures the Brooklyn building collapse
text:
NEW YORK (Gray News) - A Ring doorbell camera captured the moment an apartment building collapsed in Brooklyn, killing eight people.
In the video, provided by James Williams, debris and dust are seen billowing up as the structure to the right of a landing gives way. People can be heard shouting as the video continues.
A photo taken by Yuki Iwamura for the Associated Press appears to show a different angle of the landing and the apartment where the Ring doorbell camera was. The photo shows contents of the apartment exposed after the exterior wall fell in the collapse.
The three-story building collapsed on Wednesday as construction workers were digging in an adjacent lot.
Two children, ages 9 and 10, were killed along with adults ranging in age from 22 to 31, according to the New York City Police Department. There were also 18 people injured, including four firefighters, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. The children were Colombian, as was one of the adults who was killed, according to the country’s consulate in New York.
The fire department reported rescue operations Thursday after the last victim was freed from the wreckage.
Investigators have not determined the cause of the collapse. In its wake, Mamdani has ordered inspections at about 100 building sites involving companies related to the project.

title: Former officer to be castrated after child rape conviction: ‘We will take his manhood’
text:
POINTE COUPEE PARISH, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A former police officer and volunteer firefighter will be castrated after receiving three life sentences following a conviction for raping multiple children.
According to Louisiana’s 18th Judicial District Attorney Tony Clayton, a jury in October convicted former New Roads officer Kedreyon K. Williams, 31, of three counts of first-degree rape of juveniles, as well as indecent behavior with a juvenile and possession of pornography involving juveniles.
The jury deliberated for just over 30 minutes before delivering its verdict.
The district attorney’s office said a rape conviction carried a mandatory life sentence, but it wanted to go a step further by recommending that Williams be physically castrated.
“He performed disgusting acts on children who could not defend themselves. He is a child predator, and he deserves exactly what he is getting and more. The castration is another layer of punishment for these horrendous crimes,” the DA’s office said.
At sentencing, District Judge Kevin Kimball added that it was the “worst case” of child sexual abuse that he had seen.
“If a man takes sexual advantage of a child, then we will take his manhood!” Clayton said. “We hope the families know that justice was served here and have some comfort in knowing he will never be able to prey on any children again.”

title: Maine Savings pledges $1 million to St. Joseph Hospital emergency department expansion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor’s St. Joseph Hospital is expanding emergency care, and Maine Savings Credit Union is the first business to pledge funds to the Called to Care campaign, committing $1 million.
Beginning in Oct. 2027, the St. Joseph Hospital’s emergency department will grow almost double in size, from 9,000 to 17,000 square feet. Construction is planned in three phases and is expected to conclude in 2029.
“On the average day, we see anywhere between 85 to 95 patients with that. There’s many days where we see more patients than that. And so, hallways are filled. Our waiting room is overflowing with patients,” described Amanda Layman, director of critical care at St. Joseph.
The project will increase the number of treatment rooms from 23 to 31 and include a new centralized nursing station and behavioral health suite, along with an expanded SAFE area, waiting room and vertical care unit.
These additions and expansions have naming opportunities available for businesses and individuals who would like to contribute to the Called to Care campaign.
Maine Savings Credit Union was the first business to seize one of these opportunities.
“My board simply said, ‘Let’s actually do something that makes a meaningful impact. Let’s be the first business in the area to say yes to this project, and let’s throw that first million dollars at it and say, we’re here to stay. We’re here to support our region,’” Maine Savings Credit Union CEO and President Vanessa Madore explained.
Madore also serves as chair of the St. Joseph Board of Trustees. She says Maine Savings’ $1 million pledge will fund the vertical treatment area, a “fast track” for patients with less serious injuries and illnesses.
“When we looked at how we as a financial institution go beyond banking to meet the needs of our members and our employees, we wanted to do something that spoke to the innovative nature of healthcare, and maximizing the space to care for the largest number of people possible,” said Madore. “The vertical treatment suite does just that.”
Layman said she has seen many patients with less serious conditions leave the emergency department before being seen because of long wait times.
“Our vertical treatment space is to help get those patients through the department in a timely fashion,” Layman said. “The mission of the St. Joe’s Hospital is to serve our community. And this is truly one of the best ways that we can do that is by renovating this emergency department.”
With various naming opportunities available, St. Joseph Healthcare is still looking for businesses and individuals to donate to help fill federal funding gaps.
Staff said construction may affect patient flow, but operations will continue normally.

title: ‘I literally was a walking stroke’: A growing need for organ donations among Black Americans
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (InvestigateTV) — Black Americans face a critical need for organ transplants, yet they experience longer wait times and lower donation rates.
In 2026, African Americans accounted for more than a quarter of those on the organ transplant waiting list.
But at the same time, they made up only about 12% of all donors and nearly a quarter of total transplant recipients nationwide.
Health experts say the need is driven by higher rates of conditions like diabetes and high blood pressure. If those conditions are unmanaged it can lead to organ failure, especially kidney disease.
In fact, kidney disease is often called a “silent killer” because people can live with the condition for years without noticeable symptoms.
If you’ve ever tuned into a College of Charleston men’s basketball game, you’ve heard Everett German’s voice. That’s because he’s their official play-by-play announcer.
“So I announce all the games on the radio and our local TV games. In my 20th year of doing that. So this is a place that I’m familiar and comfortable with here at TD Arena,” German said.
He calls the love for his play-by-play work the why behind his why. But about 20 years ago, he faced a season of shakeups.
“I’m an account executive, so I’m constantly staring, you know, at a computer screen. And just one day I just started having blurry vision. I mean like my eyes, I’m like, ‘Oh, maybe again it’s time for me to get glasses.’ Wear and tear, so forth and so on,” German said.
So he went in for a visit with his optometrist. German said even though his tests didn’t appear abnormal, the doctor recommended he get his blood pressure checked.
“My blood pressure was 220 over 160. I literally was a walking stroke and the only symptoms I had was blurred vision,” German said.
He was immediately admitted to the hospital. His kidneys were failing with only 12% function left. For about five years, he was able to manage his condition with medication. But once his kidney function dropped to 5%, he needed a new organ. So he reached out to those who knew him best.
“It was something I blasted out to all my family, kind of letting them know what was going on and you know if anybody had interest in terms of being tested to be a donor,” he said.
After a year of being on dialysis, on June 8, 2011, German got the gift of life in the form of a transplant. His youngest sister, Charlene, became his kidney donor.
“She knows that if the roles were reversed, I would do the same. And you know, when you have that brother-sister connection, it’s just something that’s unbreakable and she didn’t hesitate. She did the testing and everything and everything she needed to do on her end and then when the time came, she was here and came through like my true hero,” German said.
This is the kind of success story that We Are Sharing Hope SC wants to see more of, especially in communities of color. The federally designated organization facilitates organ, eye and tissue donations throughout South Carolina.
“We currently have over 1,900 people that are on the waitlist and over 56% of those are African-American. So, a lot of that is based on the lack of education around it and lack of trust,” Krystal Cau, director of communications for We Are Sharing Hope SC, said.
Cau said the organization actively works to dispel myths about organ, eye and tissue donations in order to offer clarity and establish trust with community members.
“One of the biggest things that we hear is if there is a heart on my license, you fall ill, you’re in an accident, the medical professional won’t help because an organization like Sharing Hope would want to retrieve organs. So there’s no truth to it,” she said.
German works alongside We Are Sharing Hope SC to share his story of kidney donation and to encourage others to register.
Cau explained the conversations surrounding organ donation can be scary, but they’re important.
“People don’t want to speak about death and what happens when we are no longer here. The fact of the matter is, is that it’s a decision that can change someone’s life. You can save up to eight people’s lives just by saying ‘yes’, and to enhance their tissue donations up to 75 people’s life. So the impact that that has alone is incredible,” she said.
It’s a kind of impact that’s giving German, a now 51-year-old husband and father of two, a second shot at life on and off the court.
“It’s just a new outlook on life. It just makes you more appreciative of the things I used to take for granted, you know,” he said.

title: Patriots’ A.J. Brown, Rhamondre Stevenson look ‘pretty good’ in practice
text:
MUNICH — New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back Rhamondre Stevenson have looked “pretty good” in practice, coach Mike Vrabel said Friday before both players were listed as questionable for the game against the Detroit Lions in Munich.
Brown is dealing with ankle and knee issues, and Stevenson is trying to overcome a knee injury in time for Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions in Munich.
Vrabel, speaking to the media at Bayern Munich’s facilities before practice, was asked to gauge Brown and Stevenson’s progress.
“Based on yesterday I think pretty good,” the coach said. “Again, still have to go through today and see where that goes.”
Stevenson, the team’s leading rusher, was limited in Thursday’s jog-through practice after the team arrived in Bavaria. He was injured in last week’s loss to the Packers and sat out practice Wednesday before their overnight flight.
“We’re just always looking for guys that are looking for ways in as opposed to ways out,” Vrabel said. “At this point of the season, 10 weeks straight without a bye, there’s pretty much nobody out there that’s 100%. We have to realize that, we have to recognize that, but we also have to find ways to do our job.
“Rhamondre is one of those players that’s looking for a way in,” he added.
Brown, the team’s top offseason acquisition, has just nine receptions for 101 yards so far this season as he’s battled through injuries. He’s been limited in practice this week.
“The more that we can get everybody back, I think the more that it contributes to what we feel like we want to be as a team,” Vrabel said. “One guy certainly doesn’t make the difference, but certainly the more that we can get guys back, it’s exciting, the pieces can start to build and come together.
“We’ll see where things go today and hopefully those guys that haven’t been with us or maybe got hurt last week could be available.”
Before traveling Wednesday night, the Patriots ruled out LG Ben Brown (knee), CB Carlton Davis III (knee) and RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness).
Henderson said last week that he spent several days in the hospital undergoing tests to determine the cause of unexplained neurological symptoms that have affected his strength and coordination.
“I talk to TreVeyon everyday,” Vrabel said. “Just like everybody else that’s not available, he’s working hard to get back. When that is, I don’t know., I don’t have a timetable.”
No babysitting
Vrabel reiterated that he wants his players to have the right attitude.
“We talk about a lot of things that require no talent or skill. We talk about competitive spirit, we talk about communication, we talk about toughness, we talk about our attitude,” he said. “There are a lot of things that you can do that require no skill that hopefully can help us win. Those are some qualities that we’re trying to build.”
Creating turnovers is key, he added: “We have to find some guys that can go take the ball away from the other team — tip a pass, hit a guy hard enough to knock the ball loose. … There’s a lot of ways to do it. It starts by hopefully affecting the quarterback.”
Players won’t be under lock and key in Munich.
“I’m not going to sit there and babysit them and make them sit in a circle and hold hands,” Vrabel said. “They’re grown men.”

title: Trump bluntly tells JD Vance to shift focus from Iran to targeting ‘corruption and crime’ at home
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president says is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month-old war, has been blunt in blaming the war — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections in the United States.
But Trump brusquely told the vice president in a social media post Thursday to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing — and perhaps more politically salient — issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said in the post. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
Trump earlier this week said he believed the war “militarily is effectively over,” and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign.
Democrats have promised intense oversight of Trump’s business dealings and other targets when they take control of Congress in January after voters identified corruption as one of their top concerns. Trump’s post about Vance and the Iran war was, in part, responding to a flurry of reports about Democrats’ plans.
But it also came after The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday evening that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official.
The vice president’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
The White House press office, in an email, responded to a query by highlighting that Trump made clear in his post that he sees no need to negotiate with Iran.
Vance blamed Trump’s Iran war for midterm losses
Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in U.S. military interventions overseas, was lukewarm in his defense of the conflict after Trump launched it and became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting when he headed up negotiations over the summer.
Following the Nov. 3 losses, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X in which he didn’t mince words about the political impact of the conflict.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance said. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
The vice president is considering whether to launch a 2028 run for the White House. Voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the war could weigh down those ambitions.
The president has yet to endorse a successor for the 2028 race. In a CBS “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, the president said he “may or may not get involved” in offering an endorsement.
Trump earlier this week said that he believed that mediation efforts led by Qatar are making progress and that it was unlikely he would need to make good on earlier threats to restart the full-scale bombardment of Iran after he was past the midterm elections.
The president said in an interview on “The Hugh Hewitt Show” on Thursday that he stood ready to restart strikes if necessary. “If something doesn’t work out, I would not hesitate,” he said.
Separately, in an interview with commentator Stephen A. Smith, Trump suggested he hasn’t ruled out carrying out strikes on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, if the U.S. detects signs of activity at the facility.
Waters around Iran remain treacherous
Oil shipments coming out of the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near prewar levels after Iran effectively choked the critical waterway for months, stemming the flow of crude and energy resources from its Persian Gulf neighbors.
But international tankers now are relying on U.S. Navy escorts to get the oil out of the strait. The U.S. military has recently carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses.
And while crude and liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf are climbing, there’s also been an uptick in attacks on ships trying to traverse the waterway.
The British military on Thursday reported at least two tankers were struck by projectiles in recent days while traversing contested waters near Iran.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, an agency that monitors maritime safety, said one of the tankers was struck Wednesday in the Strait of Hormuz, northwest of Ras al-Khaimah. The agency reported the crew evacuated safely and no casualties were reported.
In another incident from Tuesday, the UKMTO said a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Persian Gulf. Multiple people were taken ashore for medical assistance while the remaining crew was safe and accounted for, the agency said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week he pressed his Group of Seven counterparts during talks in Paris to “step up” and help protect ships from Iranian attacks but acknowledged making no headway on the issue.
At the same time, a Saudi-led coalition is mired in fighting with Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. That fighting has made it precarious to transport oil and other goods through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
Qalibaf claims the U.S. wants Russia to intervene
Meanwhile, Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said in an interview that the United States has asked for Russian President Vladimir Putin to facilitate direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran.
“It was the Americans who, during a visit to Moscow, spoke with Mr. Putin and asked him to speak with Iran so that, in any case, Iran would agree to speak directly with them,” Qalibaf told Al Jazeera in the interview. “Look, Russia and Mr. Putin, the Russian president, are friends of ours. We have strategic relations with Russia. We are very close, and we hold Mr. Putin in particularly high regard.”
The White House did not directly respond to a query about whether the U.S. has asked Putin to facilitate talks with Iran.
Qalibaf said the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, traveled to Russia and briefed Putin on details of the negotiations. “He informed him that we had conveyed our positions, which represent the legitimate rights and rightful demands of our people, to the Americans,” he said, adding that it is up to the U.S. side to respond.
“It is up to them to decide. If they are truly telling the truth and are sincere about negotiations, then they should respond and begin the process,” Qalibaf said. “But if they want to pursue the path of war, then naturally, we are fully prepared for that as well.”
___
AP writers Michelle L. Price in Washington and Elena Becatoros in Athens contributed reporting.

Participant on reality show ‘Below Deck’ arrested after teenager dies
text:
ISTANBUL (AP) — A participant in the U.S. reality TV show “Below Deck” has been arrested in Turkey over a fight in the resort city of Bodrum that left a 17-year-old dead, local media reported Thursday.
Joao Franco, 36, and his brother Carlos allegedly became involved in an altercation with shopkeepers in Bodrum last Saturday evening, according to the private Demiroren News Agency.
Franco, whom the agency identified as a yacht captain, appeared in the Bravo channel’s “Below Deck Down Under” and “Below Deck Mediterranean” from 2018, as well as “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.”
“Below Deck” follows the lives of crew members aboard luxury yachts as they interact with each other and their guests.
The brothers were intoxicated and an argument broke out when they started swearing, Demiroren reported. During the subsequent fight, teenager Muhammet Koyabakan fell and hit his head on the ground. He was taken to a hospital but died on Monday.
The Franco brothers, who are Portuguese nationals, were detained and later formally arrested.
News reports did not specify the charges against them, but Demiroren said they told police they were attacked and acted in self-defense. They denied hitting Koyabakan.
Bodrum, a port city on the Aegean Sea, is a favored spot for wealthy yacht owners. Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos are among the billionaires who have visited in recent years.

title: Driver whose truck accelerated on soccer field, killing 2, won't be charged, prosecutors say
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (AP) — A woman whose pickup truck accelerated onto the field of a Kansas youth soccer game, killing two people, had been taking a nap in the driver’s seat when the vehicle began moving and will not face criminal charges, prosecutors said.
The 34-year-old woman, who authorities have not identified, told detectives she awoke Oct. 17 to the screams of both her children inside the truck and people outside at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, according to a report by Sedgwick County District Attorney Marc Bennett. Ten other people were injured.
She told detectives she was disoriented and tried and failed to press the brake, according to the report released Thursday. Bennett said Kansas law does not support filing criminal charges.
“There is no evidence to support the conclusion that she knew the truck was still in drive, or evidence to explain what motive she would have had to do so,” the report said.
Authorities have said the woman had two of her children in the pickup truck with her when she drove from a parking space onto one of the soccer fields, striking multiple children and adults, according to police. Another one of her children was playing soccer on a different field.
The two people killed at the scene were Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson, Kansas, police said.
Ten others ranging from 5 to 68 were taken to area hospitals with injuries described as nonserious.
After the crash, the woman was released pending results of toxicology tests and a mechanical examination of the vehicle.
Investigators say they interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the driver and her two children who were inside the pickup at the time of the crash.

title: Investigation says understaffing and unexpected fire behavior led to firefighter deaths
text:
Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of highly trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June, according to a report released by the U.S. Department of the Interior.
The firefighters, working for the U.S. Forest Service and the newly created U.S. Wildland Fire Service, were part of an interagency response to the Knowles fire that merged with others to form the Snyder Fire on the Colorado/Utah border. The Rifle Helitack crew had been dropped in a remote area to work on a fire line, but became trapped when strong winds blew the fires in their direction and overtook them.
Their deaths came after the Trump administration revived a previously discredited policy to stomp out all wildfires quickly. Decisions on how to fight the Knowles fire were driven by the desire to prevent the spread of cheatgrass and protect sage-grouse habitat and a downwind community, the report said.
These factors “established an organizational posture to aggressively suppress new starts while small,” the report said. “This policy framing drove the decision to insert helitack firefighters onto small wilderness starts on a day with extreme fire weather conditions forecast.”
Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, and Sydney Watson were killed at the scene while Nathan Matthews sustained burn injuries and died on July 24. A fifth firefighter on the team sustained burn injuries but survived.
Ron and Lisa Hutcherson, Nick’s parents, said the crew should not have been sent out ahead of the fire because dangerous winds were in the forecast. After meeting with investigators and visiting the site, they said they believe the deaths were preventable and were caused by a failure of leadership and oversight.
“Telling us how the fire reached our son does not answer why he was still there,” Ron Hutcherson said in an email to The Associated Press. “Who was watching the bigger picture? Who was responsible for bringing those firefighters home while there was still time?”
Lisa Hutcherson added: “My son depended on the people responsible for tracking the fire threatening him and making the decisions needed to keep him safe. We want answers, and we want accountability.”
Communication breakdowns with trainees at the helm
The Serious Accident Investigation report detailed the circumstances that led to the decision to send out the helitack team and the many problems that led to their deaths.
Multiple lightning fires ignited on June 27 in Colorado’s Black Ridge Canyon Wilderness. The region was experiencing extreme drought conditions, and the winds were picking up.
An incident team orchestrated coverage of the various fires by calling in aircraft and crews. At one point, the official in charge ordered all aircraft to the Jones fire, but constant high winds challenged all pilots that day, with many saying it was the most difficult flying of their careers, the report said.
By the early afternoon, communication systems broke down, with many trainee dispatchers trying to coordinate operations. There was also confusion over who would track aircraft.
“Dispatchers simultaneously tracked up to 16 active aircraft, three emerging incidents, multiple new starts, county river evacuations, and non-stop media inquiries, leading to severe cognitive task saturation,” the report said. “Due to constant radio congestion and workload strain, dispatchers felt they were unable to transmit the mandatory scheduled 1000 Fire Weather Forecast broadcast across the zone.”
The incident commanders on the Snyder and Jones fires did not have clear information about the location of the firefighters on the Knowles and Gore fires to the east, the report said.
“Because no operational role was assigned to continuously map personnel location against the emerging fires’ trajectories, overhead did not recognize that firefighters were positioned directly in the fire’s line of advance,” the report said.
A large fire about eight miles to the west of the helitack crew was observed three and a half hours before the entrapment, the report said. In less than three hours, the fire ran over complex terrain and reached the five firefighters, who were forced to deploy fire shelters, because a helicopter was unable to reach them in time.
Family wants to know why the crew was exposed to deteriorating conditions
The Hutcherson family met with fire investigators in Grand Junction on Oct. 26 for a three-hour official readout of the report, they said. The review described a failure of lookouts, communications, escape routes and safety zones, they said.
An aging mobile radio system and software crashes compromised official channels during critical operations, the family was told. Overlapping transmissions and confused radio traffic forced firefighters to use cellphones to communicate.
The Knowles fire was in a remote location, the family said, so the central question remains: “What justified keeping this crew exposed as communications, observation, and extraction options deteriorated?”
Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of the nonprofit Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, said the problem can be traced back to the Trump administration’s full-suppression policy, which has prompted crews across the country to take unreasonable risks.
“It was outrageous to have a full-suppression policy on a lightning-caused fire in the wilderness to prevent the spread of cheatgrass,” Ingalsbee said. “The policy driving this aggressive attack of all fires is an obsolete paradigm that is just humanly or ecologically unsustainable. And unfortunately this crew paid the ultimate price, ultimate sacrifice.”

title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that caused global disruption
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that disrupted businesses, schools and governments around the world
A massive Microsoft outage that left people around the world without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools, and other staples of modern office life is nearly fixed, according to the latest word from the company.
Microsoft has apologized for the outage, which could end up costing billions in lost productivity. Microsoft said the outage was caused by a "technical issue" rather than any cybersecurity breach. "The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change," the company said.
Video above: Cybersecurity expert explains issues behind Microsoft outage
The company reported that queues of emails waiting to be delivered are "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels."
Problems started midday Thursday on the U.S. East Coast, and quickly spread around the globe. As many as 430 million users were reportedly affected at some point.
In the United States, some companies’ frustrated workers went home early on Thursday. In Australia, businesses couldn’t print invoices, and some schools couldn’t hold online classes on Friday.
And there was no quick fix. As of 10:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, the outage was still widespread, affecting untold millions of people.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," Microsoft said in a post on X around 1 p.m. ET on Friday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," the company added. "Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration."
The disruption has caused a wide range of reactions. Some U.S. office workers celebrated the email blackout and joked that they could start the weekend early. Others barely missed a beat, connecting with colleagues via Slack, phone and even the old-fashioned way: in-person.
But small businesses scrambled for Microsoft alternatives to communicate. Local governments alerted constituents to call instead of email.
The outage could cost $7 billion in lost productivity, according to an estimate by Anderson Economic Group, a Michigan-based think tank. Patrick Anderson, the firm’s president, said that perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million users on Friday have actually seen their operations disrupted in a way that caused an economic loss. And he said the cost will likely increase beyond this initial estimate.
In Australia, Friday began with a realization that the Microsoft cloud was unresponsive. The outage took out live feeds from courts, and schools texted parents to phone in any absences until email systems were restored.
Australia’s national broadcaster, ABC, reported people missing job interviews because they couldn’t connect to virtual meetings, and even some supply issues with distribution centers stocking supermarkets due to the outage.
At first, Microsoft said the connection issues were happening "in the Americas," but over time, it became clear the troubles were global.
Downdetector showed a peak of 130,000 reports about Outlook outages, but that figure understated the scope of the problem, since most people do not report their experiences.

title: Child star in ‘Kindergarten Cop’ dies at 43
text:
(Gray News) - An actor best known for starring in the movie “Kindergarten Cop” as a child has died.

According to Roeser, Cousins had suffered from liver disease.
“It brings me comfort to believe he is now in heaven with his mother, free from the pain he was carrying. Rest easy, Christian,” Roeser said.
Christian and his twin brother Joseph “Joey” Cousins shared the role of Dominic Palmieri in the 1990 action comedy “Kindergarten Cop,” featuring Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Cousins also appeared in the television series “Knots Landing” and “Intruders,” as well as in the film “Critters 3.”

title: Family Dollar to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it overcharged customers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHESAPEAKE, Va. (AP) - Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle state and federal allegations that it routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on its shelves, website and mobile app.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states filed federal charges against the company Thursday and announced the proposed settlement the same day. The settlement must still be approved by a judge.
According to the FTC’s complaint, consumers from across the country have been reporting price discrepancies at Family Dollar for years. In January 2025, for example, consumers from at least seven states reported that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” sale on a package of diapers, even though the price was advertised on its mobile app and on shelf tags.
One Michigan consumer took a picture of the “2 for $20” shelf tag and brought it to the register, but reported that the store manager said the price was wrong and quickly removed the shelf tag, the complaint said.
Over the last five years, state and local regulators have cited Family Dollar for thousands of pricing violations, resulting in fines of more than $3 million, the complaint said. It has also entered into multiple settlements with state attorneys general and consumer protection agencies over inaccurate pricing.
Family Dollar said Friday it will work with the FTC and state agencies to meet the settlement’s requirements and provide clear information to customers about how the settlement could impact them.
“We take our responsibility to deliver a positive shopping experience seriously,” Family Dollar spokeswoman Janella Escobar said in a statement. “We remain focused on strengthening pricing accuracy across our stores and maintaining our customers’ trust.”
Family Dollar, which is privately owned and based in Chesapeake, Virginia, has more than 8,000 U.S. discount stores. It reported revenue of $13 billion in its most recent fiscal year, according to a company statement.
The case is similar to one the FTC and 20 states filed last month against Dollar General, a rival bargain chain. That case is ongoing.
Under the proposed settlement, Family Dollar will be required to establish a $40 million consumer redress fund payable to eligible consumers. The company must notify customers about the fund through notices in stores and on its digital platforms.
The settlement requires Family Dollar to establish a $20 million discount program for its customers and pay $3 million to the states involved in the case. Those states are: Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
The settlement also requires Family Dollar to implement a pricing accuracy program that is independently assessed and annually certified.

title: Three Portland restaurants to close the weekend before Thanksgiving
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland restaurants Roma Cafe, Bramhall and Nosh Kitchen Bar to close the weekend before Thanksgiving
Three well-known anchors of the Portland food scene will be closing in less than two weeks.
Roma Cafe, Bramhall and Nosh Kitchen Bar, all of which are located on Congress Street, will shut their doors during the weekend before Thanksgiving.
Bramhall and Roma, which are neighboring restaurants, will have their final day of service on Saturday, Nov. 21. The last day Nosh Kitchen Bar will be open is Sunday, Nov. 22.
Matthew Kurt, a host at Roma, said the rent for the restaurants' spaces has kept going up, along with the operational costs. But Kurt noted that the owner of the restaurants, Michael Fraser, and his family are ready to relax after years of serving Mainers and countless people who have visited Portland.
"People come in and say, 'We've had our anniversary here, our wedding here, our birthday here,' so it has been a touching part of Portland for many, many, many years," Kurt said. "We're sad to see it go and we thank everybody for their patronage."
Kurt said the reservation list at Roma Cafe is filling up fast. He also said that Fraser and his co-owners are open to selling the restaurants.

title: Is Outlook down? Microsoft says it’s ‘seeing improvements’ but struggles to restore services
text:
HONG KONG (AP) — A global Microsoft outage this week disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide and highlighting the risks of depending on one of just a few major providers of essential technology.
Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. As the outage entered its second day Friday, Microsoft said it saw “encouraging recovery progress.” But the company also warned that “intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery” may persist for some users.
“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” Microsoft wrote in a social media update.
The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.
Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”
The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.
Microsoft has scrambled to recover services
A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays.
On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.
Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.
Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.
And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook. If the situation dragged on, the trouble could “impact the production timeline,” he said.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.
OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.
Outage has parallels with 2024 shutdown
Some have drawn parallels to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.
Governments and institutions in Western Europe, in particular, have been trying to reduce their reliance on services provided by a few big U.S. tech services in their continuing push for “digital sovereignty.” This week’s outage renewed some of those calls.
British lawmaker Chi Onwurah, who chairs the Science and Technology Committee in Parliament, said the Microsoft outage “only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the U.K.’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services.”
She said her committee has previously warned that the U.K. is “hugely dependent” on a small number of U.S.-based technology providers, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing.
Florian Druckenthaner, a spokesperson for Germany’s digitization ministry, said the government’s IT security agency believes German business was widely affected, but there were no reports of major disruption at the government level.
Regardless, Druckenthaner said, the outage shows “the significance of building up redundancies and alternatives. We are working on that.”
___

title: Former officer to be castrated after child rape conviction: ‘We will take his manhood’
text:
POINTE COUPEE PARISH, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A former police officer and volunteer firefighter will be castrated after receiving three life sentences following a conviction for raping multiple children.
According to Louisiana’s 18th Judicial District Attorney Tony Clayton, a jury in October convicted former New Roads officer Kedreyon K. Williams, 31, of three counts of first-degree rape of juveniles, as well as indecent behavior with a juvenile and possession of pornography involving juveniles.
The jury deliberated for just over 30 minutes before delivering its verdict.
The district attorney’s office said a rape conviction carried a mandatory life sentence, but it wanted to go a step further by recommending that Williams be physically castrated.
“He performed disgusting acts on children who could not defend themselves. He is a child predator, and he deserves exactly what he is getting and more. The castration is another layer of punishment for these horrendous crimes,” the DA’s office said.
At sentencing, District Judge Kevin Kimball added that it was the “worst case” of child sexual abuse that he had seen.
“If a man takes sexual advantage of a child, then we will take his manhood!” Clayton said. “We hope the families know that justice was served here and have some comfort in knowing he will never be able to prey on any children again.”

title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce, lawyer says, ending long marriage
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce from his wife, Angela, one of his lawyers said Thursday.
It comes nearly a week after Paxton, a Republican, lost his U.S. Senate race by double digits to Democrat James Talarico in one of the most expensive contests of the midterm elections that saw a wave of victories for Democrats across the country.
Angela Paxton, a state senator, cited allegations of adultery when she sought to end their 38-year-marriage. She filed the divorce after her husband had launched his run for Senate, posting on social media that she was doing so on “biblical grounds.”
Jared Julian, a lawyer for Ken Paxton, said the terms would remain private.
“From my observation, however, they share a mutual respect for one another,” Julian said. He added that both appeared to be looking forward “to the next chapters of their lives.”
An attorney for Angela Paxton did not immediately respond to phone and email messages Thursday. The finalized divorce was first reported by The New York Times.
After Paxton entered the race, some Republicans considered Paxton a potential drain on GOP resources because of legal, ethical and personal questions he has faced for years.
Angela Paxton had stuck by her husband through a decade of legal troubles that included state and federal corruption investigations and a 2023 state impeachment trial that publicly exposed an extramarital affair.
The Senate race that seemed like a longshot for Democrats when the year began became partly a referendum on Paxton’s history. Despite beating the long-seated incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, in a primary and gaining President Donald Trump’s endorsement, Paxton struggled to find traction in the general election against Talarico.
In October, less than a month before the election, Angela Paxton urged voters to back the Republican ticket but did not mention her estranged husband by name.
“It’s not as much about the individual players on the team. It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” she said in a campaign advertisement.
Democrat Nathan Johnson was elected attorney general and will take office in January.
