title: Food Waste Pile in Front of Commons Kicks Off “No Waste November”
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The food waste pile in front of Commons on Wednesday, Nov. 4, marked a unique start to “No Waste November.” The collaboration between Dining Services and the EcoReps evoked a visceral reaction among students and reminded them of the importance of sustainability.
Associate Vice President for Dining, Conferences and Campus Events Christine Schwartz said in an interview with The Bates Student that she and the EcoReps wanted to “really get people to think about how much food gets wasted.”
The rotting apple cores and napkins in the trash pile represent some of what she says dining staff often see at the dish drop-off station: “people have put full meals together, not eaten any of it, and [it] come[s] back through the dish room.”
The “No Waste November” event is the latest iteration of Dining Services’ efforts to draw attention to food waste. Last spring, Dining Services put up a food waste tracker to measure the amount (in lbs.) wasted each year.
When asked whether the food waste issues have worsened in previous years, Schwartz said that it tends to ebb and flow: “we are constantly course correcting.”
Dining Services prioritizes the use of food waste for other means whenever possible. Schwartz said, “82 percent of the waste produced by the operation is diverted from the waste stream.”
Most of it, she added, goes to pig farmers and compost.
Wasting food, Schwartz added, also causes a significant financial burden on Dining Services, especially as prices have continued to climb in recent years. She said the price of cilantro has tripled in the past few years; similarly, the price of tomatoes has doubled.
The signs that adorn the Commons doors near the dish drop-off highlight another problem facing Dining Services: the lack of dish returns.
Schwartz estimates that there are currently 10,000 mugs in circulation among students and faculty outside of Commons.
Custodial staff, who are not responsible for cleaning up dishes left in academic buildings, are frequently overwhelmed: “It’s not the custodians’ job to pick plates, forks, knives [and] spoons up.”
Throughout the interview, Schwartz showed pictures of half-eaten meals deposited in unorthodox places across campus.
One image of a bowl of pasta and meatballs with sauce still had a thin coat of cheese on the top layer, showing the Commons-goer did not even try to taste it. Looking at the image, Schwartz quickly tallied up the cost of the meatballs; each of the six was 78 cents. In total nearly $5 were wasted on the meal not counting the pasta and sauce.
Moving forward, Schwartz wants to see more awareness from Commons-goers. She said, “it’s about personal accountability.”
Under a Commons policy, custodial staff members who return dishes receive a free meal. Some students believe they’re helping staff earn those meals, but Schwartz said they are actually causing harm.
“We’re on the wrong side of that … they are feeling overwhelmed, and … it has reached a point where we’re almost in an untenable situation.”

title: Holden's 25 Days Of Kindness Has Logged Over A Thousand Acts Since 2017
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The 25 Days Of Kindness Campaign: Holden PD Has So Much Planned For This Season!
What started by a small-town police chief as a simple idea to spread kindness for 25 days in his community, has turned into a year-round campaign of kindness picked up by the new police chief in honor of his former mentor's memory.
The Town of Holden's "25 Days of Kindness" program has kicked into high gear for the holiday season, but since it's inception in 2017 by the late Police Chief Chris Greeley in who passed away in 2023, it has grown, leaps and bounds into a perfect example of the good community members, citizens, civic leaders and business owners can do if they work together to help those in need right where they live.
According to their website, in the almost a decade since they've been participating in this program, the 25 Days of Kindness has performed over a thousand acts of kindness and affected hundreds of Holden residents, both young and old.
"25 Days of Kindness was founded to continue the mission of Chief Greeley, a beloved figure in Holden, Maine, who dedicated his life to serving others. His unwavering commitment to kindness and community inspired us to create an organization that would carry on his legacy after his passing."
"Chief Greeley believed that one small gesture could change a life, and it’s this belief that forms the cornerstone of our organization. Since our inception, we’ve grown into a movement that reaches far beyond Holden, touching hearts across Maine and beyond."
Current Holden Police Chief, Eddie Benjamin, says the program has grown so much, it's become a year-round thing, with the initiative donating food baskets to folks experiencing food insecurity, to filling an oil tank of an elderly person who can't afford to by fuel, to paying mortgages and electrical bills, to making sure local kids get to experience the joy of opening a present from under the Christmas Tree.
What Chief Benjamin says is amazing is that no matter what's going on with the economy around the world, folks in Maine keep stepping up and donating to help their neighbors.
"As you know, oil is so expensive right now, but people are coming forward and they want to help. They have a little bit extra and they want to make sure everybody's covered for the winter...we just had a business owner (he wanted to remain anonymous) he just donated $10,000 and said he wanted us to use this money for elderly people who need heat this winter."
"The Food Pantry in Holden is very, very low on food right now, so I believe we are going to donate $3,000 to buy food and there's a business owner that's going to match that, so that will be $6,000 for the food pantry."
Benjamin says people usually reach out, family members and friends of those in need and let the town know there is a need, and the 25 Days of Kindness steps in to help meet that.
He says there are a number of fundraisers, throughout the year, that folks can get involved with if they'd like to raise money to go towards the program.
Next Wednesday, the Holden PD will host their 2nd Annual "Jail and Bail" event where they local business owners volunteer to go behind bars and ask folks to send the program money to "bail" them out.
On Thursday November 19th, he says Police Officers from Holden, Brewer and Ellsworth will join Rock Steady Boxing (a Parkinson's disease organization) in a workout fundraiser at Titan Athletics in Brewer.

title: Spielberg says he has the same enthusiasm as he did making 8 mm movies as a boy
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Decades of success haven’t dulled Steven Spielberg’s appetite for filmmaking. The excitement that first drew him to the camera is still very much alive.
Before being honored at the Museum of Modern Art’s film benefit, Spielberg looked back on his journey from an ambitious young filmmaker to one of Hollywood’s most admired directors.
“I still have the enthusiasm that I had when I was 12 years old making 8 mm movies, little Westerns at home. That has never gotten old. I’ve gotten older, but that hasn’t gotten old,” Spielberg told The Associated Press at Thursday’s gala.
Though Spielberg has received virtually every major honor in filmmaking, from Academy Awards to industry tributes, recognition from MoMA holds particular significance.
“The Museum of Modern Art was one of the first museums ever to recognize film back in the mid-’30s as an art form. Not just as a concession or some kind of a technological concoction, but a real art form,” Spielberg said on the black carpet.
One of the most successful and influential directors in film history, Spielberg has made more than 35 feature films. His work spans fantasy, science fiction, and historical dramas, along with deeply human stories that explore the world around us.
From “E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial” and “Close Encounters of the Third Kind” to “Jaws,” “Jurassic Park” and the “Indiana Jones” series, he has taken audiences to extraordinary places. He has also turned to history and human conflict in films such as “Saving Private Ryan” and “Schindler’s List.” The latter won three Oscars in 1994, including best director for Spielberg.
Spielberg rarely goes looking for a specific genre. More often, he says, the stories find him, sometimes arriving out of nowhere.
“Often the movies that I wind up directing are the films that sneak up on me from behind, like an idea, like ‘E.T.’ which just came out of the blue one day,” he said.
The 1982 film, about a boy who befriends a stranded alien, became a sensation and one of the most beloved films of its era. It also became one of Spielberg’s signature works.
That instinct to follow an idea wherever it leads speaks to the curiosity that continues to drive his work and his reluctance to repeat himself.
“I’m a bit like a chameleon. I kind of take the shape of the environment that I’m standing in front of. And so my favorite directors are the directors who were able to come out of a hole each time, a different hole each time, and didn’t make the same movie in the same style again and again and again,” he said.
Celebrity guests included Robert De Niro, Michelle Williams, Drew Barrymore, Emily Blunt and John Krasinski. Spielberg’s longtime friend Martin Scorsese was also there to celebrate the director. On a rainy New York Evening, Spielberg made his way to the entrance to greet Scorsese with a warm embrace when he arrived.
The evening opened with a surprise appearance by Tom Cruise, followed by a special tribute featuring Emily Blunt, Steve Martin and Martin Scorsese. Oscar winner Ariana DeBose performed “Somewhere” from “West Side Story.” Bruce Springsteen also performed an acoustic version of “Dancing in the Dark.”
The annual benefit raises funds for MoMA’s film collection, supporting the preservation and acquisition of important works of cinema, as well as the museum’s film exhibits. Chanel has sponsored the event since 2011.
In his acceptance speech, Spielberg reflected on the collaborative nature of the medium and people who have shared in his journey.
“Standing alone up here feels wrong. Filmmaking is collaborating. And when I get singled out on a night like this it reminds me that I have never stood alone,” he said.

title: Maine caregivers report confusion over medical cannabis reclassification
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine caregivers report confusion over DEA medical cannabis reclassification
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration is implementing a reclassification of medical cannabis under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and the change has caused confusion and uncertainty for Maine caregivers.
The Justice Department said the change is intended to support state-regulated medical marijuana programs while maintaining federal controls.
Shannon Lord, owner of Triple Goddess Wellness in Milo, is one of many Maine caregivers who say communication is lacking from the DEA about registration for medicinal cannabis.
“A couple of our vendors, a couple of other stores had gotten a hold of us and said, ‘Are you applying for the registration?’ And we said, ‘We don’t even know what’s going on,’” Lord told WMTW media partner WABI.
The reclassification gives caregivers the option to register with the DEA in addition to registering with the states where they sell.
“What was the point? I have no idea,” Lord said.
Supplier losses
Suppliers and businesses that registered with the DEA are no longer allowed to conduct business with those who did not register. The change is causing Lord to lose 90% of her suppliers.
“It’s business as usual for us, other than not being able to do business with people who registered,” Lord said.
Not being permitted to do business with registered suppliers will in turn affect Lord’s customers.
“Our patients have come to rely on what we carry. They like what we carry. They ask specifically for what we carry. And now they have to start all over again,” Lord said.
Federal registration concerns
Medical cannabis is still federally illegal. With the new registration, business owners would be registering an illegal business with the federal government, even though it is legal in Maine.
“There is not much of a trust factor here. Like I said, it’s like going back to 2010, when we had the federal marshals come to our house, pull up our driveway. We never knew if they were going to come back. We did not know if we were going to be the ones that got raided,” said Catherine Lewis, director of education for Medical Marijuana Caregivers of Maine.
Lewis also owns a small business and said the change will affect her customers as well.
“We are on a month-to-month basis as it is now, and it has been for so many of the small caregivers. There is an abundance of businesses out there. There’s only so many patients we can serve,” Lewis said. “I’ve heard so many people say, well, just let the free market determine what the free market can handle. Make no mistake, this is so far from a free market. This is a heavily regulated and skewed market.”
Letter to congressional delegation
Lord wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation asking for clarification on the change. She said Rep. Jared Golden responded and connected Lord with a hemp and agriculture aide.
“I did more than write a letter. I drafted a proposal to amend the Controlled Substances Act to allow Congress to have states continue to operate the same as they have been,” Lord said. “It clearly states in the rule that they did in April that the states are doing a great job and they’re doing what the feds would require anyway. So why duplicate a program that’s already working?”
Kristi Shaw, vice chair of Medical Marijuana Caregivers of Maine, supports the letter.
“Nobody knows what to expect. They’re not really laying out their vision of what this looks like other than, you know, making it easier for the bigger companies to succeed and us to go away,” Shaw said.
State and federal responses
The Maine Office of Cannabis Policy has been releasing guidance documents for caregivers across the state. They also provided the following statement from Alexis Soucy, director of media & stakeholder relations, Office of Cannabis Policy:
“The administration and enforcement of federal cannabis law is outside of OCP’s purview and jurisdiction, and we have not received any guidance from federal agencies regarding these changes.”
The DEA has not responded to a request for comment.

title: Standish town councilor resigns after 3 months in the role
text:
The Standish town councilor who was appointed to fill a vacancy has resigned after about three months on the job.
Jeff Lowe, who the council unanimously voted into an empty at-large seat in August, wrote in his resignation letter that he is leaving for health reasons, said Town Manager Tashia Pinkham.
Filling the vacant seat was controversial before Lowe’s appointment because the remaining council members were stuck in a 3-3 split over who to appoint, and town staff and members of the public accused them of voting along party lines. The seat was vacant because former Councilor Terry Christy moved to a nursing home and registered to vote in Windham without informing the town.
The Town Council discussed Tuesday whether to fill the newly vacant seat and will vote at its Dec. 1 meeting on how to proceed.
Council Co-Chair Brandon Watson said he thinks the council should appoint the runner-up candidate from those previously interviewed by the appointments committee in executive session. Councilor Ben Macri said he disagreed, but did not explain why to avoid disclosing what was discussed in executive session.
Macri said he thinks the seat could be left open until the June municipal election because the next person they appoint would join the council around the time when they form the proposed budget for the 2027-28 fiscal year. He also suggested appointing someone with budget experience.
“Being thrown into the budget process easily puts someone (in) way over their head,” Macri said. “I would much rather get somebody that has experience and possibly is not even interested in running again. We get that person for six months, help us through that, and then the election comes about.”
Macri and Councilor Lisa Struebing said if the council does appoint someone to the seat, they would like all councilors to again be invited to the appointments committee meeting to interview candidates. The councilors on the appointments committee initially did not invite all members to the first round of interviews in July, but invited them for the second round that led the council to agree on appointing Lowe.
Anthony Folsom, a former Town Council candidate who attends every town meeting, said he is interested in filling the open seat.
“I think I have a good handle of what’s going on,” Folsom said. “I have no desire to run again.”

title: Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at prediction market Kalshi
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at prediction market Kalshi
Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday.
Related video above: Republican requesting probe into Russian oligarch who partially funded Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding party
Kalshi described the decision as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr.'s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi's biggest competitor Polymarket.
But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections. Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family's investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets.
“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer," said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.”
The president's eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years.
At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry's efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts.
Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration.
1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket's latest fundraising round. It was this investment that started the conversation about ending Trump Jr.'s advisory role with Kalshi.

title: New England Republicans should stand up for their heritage
FAA grounds all US flights ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
text:
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Bangor International Airport was left with two commercial airplanes on the ground at gates that are unable to take off and a third inbound that will be delayed, a spokesperson said.
“We have been told flights en route to Bangor are continuing, but at this hour nothing will be taking off,” the spokesperson said.
Portland International Jetport said that it has seven aircraft on the ground in Portland and all flights are currently delayed. As of 4:35 p.m. the airport reported no inbound flights in the air destined to Portland.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”
“Everybody’s safe. There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying,” Mullin said.
There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA’s nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.
But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
Friday’s ground stop was different from the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
Story by Josh Funk, AP Transportation Writer. BDN writer Ethan Andrews contributed reporting.

title: Joe Biden's White House memoir is an unapologetic defense of four years sandwiched between Trump
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — As presidential memoirs go, Joe Biden’s is a relatively brief 480 pages. But Biden’s effort, set for a Tuesday release, serves the genre’s usual purpose of providing an unapologetic defense of his time in the White House.
Biden pulls no punches on Donald Trump, blasting him for his election denialism, his role in the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol and blanket pardons of the participants.
He also boasts about his lengthy legislative record and rejects criticisms that his policies intensified inflation and complicated the nation’s recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic.
He stands by the deadly U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan and credits himself with rehabilitating U.S. international alliances that grew strained under Trump.
Biden also defends running for a second term in 2024 despite concerns about his age, even if that decision presaged Trump’s second presidency.
Here are some highlights of how Biden depicts his White House years in “Promise Me, America,” including what the former president doesn’t say.
Biden has no regrets on 2024
Biden makes no apologies for seeking a second term, and he complains that “the press and pundits kept talking about how weak I was” despite no challenger emerging.
“The primaries sent no warning signs that I was in trouble,” he writes. “But that couldn’t derail the narrative setting in on my candidacy. That I was too old. That I was declining mentally.”
And then came one disastrous night on the debate stage in Atlanta.
Biden writes that he’d questioned his team about the need to debate Trump at all.
“It’s not that I was concerned about my ability to debate Donald Trump,” he says. “It was that he was so prone to lying with abandon, bullying the moderators, violating the rules, whining about even a hint of fact checking, that I didn’t know whether there would be any value in my giving a public platform to this behavior.”
But Biden does lament in detail “one of the lowest moments for me” when he gave a nonsensical answer when discussing the deficit.
“I lost my train of thought, saw that my time was running out on the clock, and rushed the final part of my answer by blurting out: ‘We finally beat Medicare,’” he recalls. “What I meant to say was, ‘We finally beat Big Pharma.’”
That’s a reference to a deal negotiating drug prices for Medicare recipients, “a historic achievement,” Biden writes.
“Ironically, this historic achievement wouldn’t lift my candidacy. It would help to sink it,” he writes. “What should have been a highlight of the debate became Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.”
Biden thought he still could have won
Biden insists the race was still winnable even after the debate.
“Was I old? Yes. Was I able to do the job? Yes. Were voters angry about inflation? Yes. Were they angry about immigration? Yes. All tough problems. But not insurmountable ones,” he wrote, adding that it was “personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me.”
However, Biden recalls Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer telling him “I might still have five Democratic senators still supporting me.”
He told Schumer “he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race.”
He went to sleep on the night of July 20 having worked on a draft statement announcing his decision to drop out.
“Believe it or not,” he writes, “I slept well that night.”
Biden reflects on Kamala Harris
Biden’s election and his fate as a one-term president is tied inextricably to Kamala Harris. Although she was among the Democrats who “took their shots at me” during the 2020 primary, Biden recalls being impressed by her.
Biden often mentions Harris among the small group of advisers in the room for seminal moments and decisions, and he describes their relationship as warm. He praised her performance after she replaced him on the 2024 ballot.
Harris “was a first-rate candidate,” Biden writes of her 107-day campaign. “She performed masterfully in her debate with President Trump. She was great on the stump. She was a fundraising machine. I was proud of her and the campaign she ran.”
Biden criticizes Netanyahu but defends aid to Israel
Biden said his hopes for permanent peace in the Middle East were “shattered” with Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
When the war began, Biden writes, he called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu several times that day. “I wanted him to know my determination to ensure that a day like this would never happen again,” Biden writes, while saying his approach was influenced by Netanyahu’s domestic politics and increasing right-wing posture.
“He and I could be direct with each other, but there wasn’t a ton of trust,” Biden writes.
He also defends providing assistance to Israel even though it became deeply controversial among Democrats. Biden explains that he believed he had to “support America’s interests and America’s allies” as president but says, “since Netanyahu’s return to power at the end of 2022, I felt that the work of protecting Israel meant protecting it both from its enemies and itself.”
Afghanistan was a ‘ticking time bomb’
Biden devotes an entire chapter to Afghanistan, framing himself as a longtime skeptic of the war, including as Barack Obama’s vice president.
Trump had previously committed to withdrawing American forces, and Biden says it was an “odd predicament” — an agreement for the Taliban not to strike U.S. forces as they pulled out by a deadline. Biden described it as a “ticking time bomb.”
The details were not what “I would have negotiated” but Biden agreed “it was time to end the forever war.” So, he set a Sept. 11 deadline and, he writes, worked to shore up President Ashraf Ghani’s forces to defend themselves against the Taliban. Yet over the course of August 2021 “the Afghan army simply melted away.”
During the withdrawal, a suicide bomber struck at Kabul airport’s Abbey Gate. Scores of Afghan civilians died, as well as 13 U.S. service members.
“It was devastating,” Biden writes. “I think about them, and their heroism and their families, every day.”
Biden boasts of legislative successes
Biden says his ambitious “American Rescue Plan,” a $1.9 trillion response to the pandemic, was necessary to jolt the economy.
But he had to navigate Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, who’d become a key swing vote in an evenly split Senate. Biden described calling Manchin to the Oval Office as the senator held out on the bill.
“We were both Catholic politicians from the old school. Proud. Stubborn,” Biden writes of Manchin. “I never considered myself a Lyndon Johnson–type president, who cajoled and threatened and even physically cowed legislators, but I was losing my temper. I told Joe that I needed him on this, and if he screwed me, I’d go to every county in West Virginia and tell them that Joe Manchin was why they weren’t getting any help. Joe came right back at me, reminding me that I wasn’t so popular in West Virginia.”
Manchin voted yes and the measure passed.
___
Barrow is a national politics reporter who covered Biden’s 2020 presidential campaign.

title: Thoughtful design and energy efficiency define this rebuilt Colonial in Cumberland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
• Peaceful Cumberland setting, surrounded by farmland and protected forestland, minutes from Yarmouth and Interstate 295
• Energy efficient, with updated insulation and a solar array supplying approximately 80% of the home’s energy needs.
• Nearly new construction, with 98% of the home rebuilt in 2021-2022, including major structural and mechanical systems
• En suite bathrooms in every bedroom and a primary suite with direct laundry access
18 Greely Road, Cumberland
Price: $1.15 million | Bedrooms: 4 | Bathrooms: 5 | 3,348 sq. ft.
Behind its classic Colonial charm, this Cumberland home is full of modern surprises. Nearly rebuilt from the ground up, it combines thoughtful design, energy efficiency and contemporary comforts in a peaceful country setting just minutes from town.
Approximately 98% of the structure is new, including the roof, trusses, windows, siding, floors, plumbing and electrical systems. A new foundation was also poured beneath the breezeway and barn. Updated insulation and a solar array that supplies roughly 80% of the home’s energy needs help keep operating costs low, while functional gas fireplaces provide additional warmth.
Inside, the kitchen, dining room, living room and deck connect naturally, creating an easy flow for everyday living and entertaining. The primary suite is especially well planned, with direct access to a walk-in closet and laundry room. Every bedroom has an en suite bathroom, with three walk-in showers and two soaking tubs throughout the home. Radiant floor heating adds comfort to the primary bath.
Outside, lilacs and evergreens frame a private, half-acre setting surrounded by farmland and protected forestland. A popular local farm stand is just down the road. Despite the serene surroundings, the property is minutes from downtown Yarmouth, Cumberland Town Landing and its beach, and major commuting routes including Rt. 88, Rt. 1 and Interstate 295.

title: Teen gets new wheelchair ramp after her previous one was stolen
text:
Teen gets new wheelchair ramp after her previous one was stolen
Less than a week after a Louisville, Kentucky, teen had her wheelchair ramp stolen from her home, the community stepped up and righted the wrong.
Brittney Harbin said she discovered the ramp was missing on Nov. 6 when she went outside to help her daughter, Cerenity, get to her school bus.
Cerenity uses the ramp to get safely in and out of her home in her wheelchair.
The family started a GoFundMe so they could get a new ramp installed for Cerenity.
On Thursday, the family shared good news: A new ramp had been installed for Cerenity.
"Thank you for the donations and the support," Cerenity said.
Her mother shared a video of Cerenity using her new ramp as she got off the bus after school.
"I wasn't expecting somebody to actually make it like this," the teen could be heard saying in the video as she saw the new ramp. "Did they make it that fast?"

title: Death Notice: Ernestine Marie Stoddard
Multi-day manhunt ends with SWAT team dismantling Oklahoma house 'piece by piece'
text:
A standoff after a multi-day manhunt ends with SWAT team dismantling Oklahoma house
A three-day manhunt in Oklahoma ended peacefully after law enforcement used heavy equipment to dismantle a house and arrest a man accused of shooting at sheriff's deputies and a homeowner following a botched burglary
A standoff after a multi-day manhunt ends with SWAT team dismantling Oklahoma house
A three-day manhunt in Oklahoma ended peacefully after law enforcement used heavy equipment to dismantle a house and arrest a man accused of shooting at sheriff's deputies and a homeowner following a botched burglary
A three-day manhunt ended Thursday morning peacefully when law enforcement arrested Michael Garrett after dismantling a house outside Rush Springs, Oklahoma, where he had been hiding.
Garrett, accused of shooting at Bryan County, Oklahoma, deputies and a homeowner following a botched burglary earlier in the week, was located in a home on County Road 1530, about nine miles east of Rush Springs, which is around 60 miles from Oklahoma City.
His mother, Tammy Garrett, said she wasn’t surprised to learn where her son had gone.
“It’s his safe place. It’s always. It’s, it’s a safe place,” Tammy Garrett said.
The Oklahoma Highway Patrol (OHP) confirmed Garrett’s location using a drone and began a standoff.
“We gave him several commands over the course of about six hours. We released gas into the residence, trying to coax him out of the residence to end this peacefully,” said Lt. Mark Southall, public information officer for OHP.
When Garrett refused to comply, authorities decided to use heavy equipment to bring the standoff to an end.
“We made a decision to pull an excavator and start dismantling the house piece by piece, until we finally cornered him where he had nowhere to go,” Southall said.
With no escape route left, Garrett was taken into custody. Aerial footage captured the moment he was escorted out of the house.
Although Tammy Garrett expressed sadness over the loss of the home, she said she was grateful for law enforcement’s efforts to ensure her son’s safety.
“We’re going to keep your son alive. And in that, he did that, you know, and that’s the main thing,” she said.

title: Texas executes man convicted in beheading of 3 children
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A Texas man convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading three young children in a squalid, windowless apartment in 2003 was executed Thursday evening, hours after Oklahoma put another man to death.
John Allen Rubio, 46, was pronounced dead at 6:47 p.m. after a lethal injection at the state prison in Huntsville. The killings of the baby girl and two toddlers so rocked the city of Brownsville on the U.S. border with Mexico that the apartment building was later demolished and the land turned into a park and community garden.
After a spiritual adviser prayed over him briefly, Rubio thanked friends and family for their “love and understanding” and said he was “not the same person I once was.” He thanked prison staff for teaching him how to find God and also expressed love for his common-law wife, Angela Camacho, who is serving life in prison for her role in the slayings.
“I want to say I’m sorry to my wife’s family,” he said. “I can’t change the past but I can tell you my life is going to be over. But that’s not going to make you happy.”
“I’m going to be with my kids in a little bit,” he added. “I’m ready to go to heaven to be with my lord and savior.”
As the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital began taking effect, Rubio took three breaths and began what sounded like snoring. All movement ceased afterward, and a physician pronounced him dead 21 minutes after the injection began.
Earlier Thursday, James Pavatt, 73, received a lethal injection at an Oklahoma prison for the fatal shooting of his girlfriend’s estranged husband in 2001. The victim was killed as he arrived to pick up his two young children before Thanksgiving.
Thursday’s executions were the 36th and 37th this year, with the U.S. on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year — a pace driven by Florida.
The death penalty has drawn renewed attention since the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September. And last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office in January — what experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
Texas victims included a 2-month-old girl
Rubio and Camacho were accused of killing 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the apartment they shared in Brownsville. Camacho drew a life sentence after pleading guilty.
An appeals court overturned Rubio’s first capital murder conviction, ruling Camacho’s statements were improperly admitted as evidence in his trial. At his second trial, Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity but again was convicted and sentenced to death.
According to court records, Rubio wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but treated them as his own.
At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world.
Defense experts diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, a finding prosecution experts rejected. The defense experts also testified his childhood — marked by violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution — damaged him developmentally.
Oklahoma advertising executive killed in garage
When the Oklahoma inmate Pavatt was asked if he had any last words before his execution, he shook his head no. As a chaplain read from the Bible, Pavatt appeared to mouth some words that couldn’t be heard.
Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the killing of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Pavatt attended the same church as the Andrew family and had been having an affair with Rob Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. She was convicted at a separate trial and is the only woman currently on Oklahoma’s death row.
Weeks before the shooting, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.
Pavatt and Brenda Andrew fled to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while reentering the U.S.
Also Thursday, former Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory in a 1997 murder and awaits sentencing in December. Glossip, who had been on the brink of execution three times, was released on bond in May after nearly 30 years in prison. He had been awaiting a retrial after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned his conviction.
____
Stengle reported from McAlester, Oklahoma.

title: Maine’s social clubs could get us going out again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Once you start looking, you’ll see them everywhere.
There’s the Eagles aerie on St. John Street in Portland and the American Legion Post on the Westbrook-Gorham line, Le Club Calumet on Route 104 in Augusta and, not far from the bridge to Mount Desert Island, the home of the Trenton Grange.
They have banquet halls and pool tables, holiday parties and bars with cheap drinks. They provide somewhere to socialize without spending a lot of money and to meet people with common backgrounds or interests.
They’re the all-important “third places” (after home and work) that we talk about today. Before there was a buzzword for them, joining these groups was just what many Americans did.
After a peak in civic participation in the mid-20th century, priorities changed (including people watching more TV) and membership began to decline.
Now could be the time for a comeback.
A post-pandemic desire for socialization away from screens, coupled with the soaring prices and financial strains that have made going out to restaurants and bars prohibitively expensive, have created the right conditions for these clubs to rebound.
That’s especially true in Maine, where there’s been an influx of new residents looking to make friends, which is harder to do when we spend so much of the year hunkered down indoors.
Memberships are generally low cost and low barrier; I recently learned that I could join my local VFW post with a $25 check and the obituary of my grandfather, a World War II veteran.
Last month, a friend who belongs to the Elks Lodge in Augusta brought me to its sports lounge on a Friday night, when a cover band played to a packed crowd and people sipped on pumpkin espresso martinis.
Earlier this fall, I visited the Woodfords Club in Portland to check out the revived candlepin bowling league and found a lively all-ages scene, with people swing dancing in the main hall and chatting on couches in the lobby.
Back when it was an old boys’ club, there were as many as 500 members and a five-year waiting list, according to rental manager Dave Magee. Today, membership — which costs $200 annually for an individual or $380 for a family — is around 120-130 people.
Renting out the space to catering businesses, church groups and couples getting married pays the bills, Magee said, but the club could always use more members.
It just needs to be discovered by the people looking for more places to go.

title: Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor steps down from the band
text:
Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor steps down from the band
Duran Duran’s Roger Taylor has stepped down from the band due to a deterioration in his tinnitus.
The drummer of the group, which enjoyed massive global success in the 1980s, is also retiring from playing the drums “after careful consideration and medical advice,” Duran Duran announced on its Instagram page on Thursday.
“This is one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make,” Taylor said in the post. “Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I’ll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they’ve shown us over the years. But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse, and I’ve reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors.”
Tinnitus is the perception of a ringing, buzzing or roaring when no external sound is present, according to the World Health Organization. Perceived in one or both ears or inside the head, it can be constant or intermittent. A range of factors cause tinnitus, including exposure to loud sounds.
More than 50 million adults in the U.S. are affected by the condition, which is associated with hearing loss, according to the American Tinnitus Association. It has no definitive cure but can be managed in a range of ways, including by protecting your ears from loud sounds.
In the statement, Taylor said he is “going out on a real high,” adding: “We’ve just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour, which followed our second headline show at BST Hyde Park, our induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, and a return to the studio with Nile Rodgers. I couldn’t have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I’ll treasure forever. I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John.”
The band was started by keyboardist Nick Rhodes and bass player John Taylor in 1978, with Roger Taylor — no relation to John — recruited to play drums the following year. Guitarist Andy Taylor, also not related, joined in 1980, as did singer Simon Le Bon.
A leading part of the New Romantic movement, the band’s biggest hits include “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex,” “Rio” and “A View to a Kill.”
Paying tribute to Taylor, Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and John Taylor said: “Roger is our brother. His drumming helped define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning and having him back with us since 2001 has been incredibly important to us all. We completely support his decision and wish him health and happiness. He will always be part of this family, while we continue exploring new and exciting projects with the band.”
Andy Taylor, who is no longer part of the band, revealed in 2022 that he has stage 4 prostate cancer. Unable to attend the group’s induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, he delivered the news in a letter he sent to be read out at the ceremony.

title: GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert loses Congressional race for re-election
text:
GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert loses race for re-election to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in Colorado, AP calls
Retired Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat, will flip Colorado’s 4th District, ending conservative firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert’s tenure in Congress, the AP called on Friday afternoon.
Video above: Republicans and Democrats select next leaders for new Congress
Boebert’s loss comes after she elected to run in a more conservative district last cycle in an effort to preserve her political future. But Laubacher, who served more than three decades in the Navy, capitalized on the national headwinds against the GOP and focused her campaign on affordability issues.
The win denies Boebert, an ally of President Donald Trump and one of the most outspoken conservatives in the House Republican conference, a fourth term. Boebert was first elected in 2020, after she upset a fifth-term Republican incumbent in a primary.
In that time, she has emerged as one of the most recognizable, and at times polarizing, faces of the GOP’s MAGA wing, drawing attention from both Democrats and Republicans. Former President Joe Biden, whom she heckled during his 2022 State of the Union address, once billed her as “one of the leaders of this extreme MAGA movement.” The 39-year-old has also been a source of frustration for Republican speakers Kevin McCarthy and Mike Johnson.
Trump endorsed Boebert days before the election, praising her in a Truth Social post as a “MAGA Warrior, who has been with us from the very beginning.” But the pair have also been at odds at times. She drew the president’s ire earlier this year when she campaigned with one of his most vocal Republican critics in the House, Kentucky’s Thomas Massie, in his primary. The appearance prompted Trump to call her “dumb” and "weak-minded" and he threatened to withdraw his endorsement.
Boebert also crossed Trump and House Republican leaders last year when she joined a Democratic push to force the release of the Jeffrey Epstein case files, resisting a White House effort to sway her vote. At the time, GOP leaders opposed the release of the files, citing the potential disclosure of the names of Epstein’s victims.
This wasn’t the first time Boebert faced a tough reelection fight. She won reelection in 2024 by over 11 points, but nearly lost her race in a different district in 2022. She beat Democrat Adam Frisch by only 546 votes.

title: Schumer or Van Hollen? Maine senators split on who should be Majority Leader
text:
Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen? Maine senators split on who should be Majority Leader
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that is why he is running.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race, which will be the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
Sen. King supporting Schumer
Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, said on Thursday that he plans to support Schumer.
“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible," King said.
“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen. Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”
Jackson won't support Schumer
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, said during his election campaign that he would not vote for Schumer.
Maine's Total Coverage spoke with Jackson earlier this week and asked him about who he thinks should be the Majority Leader and if he had spoken with Schumer since arriving in Washington for orientation.
"I mean, he knows my position. I think he's, you know, he's fine with it," Jackson said. "As far as who should lead, at this point, the only person that's even made an attempt was, Van Hollen. And, I haven't had a chance to speak to him. So, you know, I'm not going to just vote for him because he's an alternative. But I'm looking forward to people running to have the conversation and see what their thoughts are on leading this caucus."
In July, after Jackson became the Democratic nominee in the Senate race, Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand released a joint statement supporting Jackson.
"A champion for affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been," they said.

title: Netflix Announces ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Tour Dates
text:
Netflix Announces ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Tour Dates and Details
A previously announced KPop Demon Hunters live tour is official, with dates announced for the United States and Europe.
Besides the phenomenal popularity of the KPop Demon Hunters movie on Netflix, the concept — a K-pop girl group is secretly a trio of warriors who protect Earth from interdimensional demons — does lend himself to pop concerts. But how do you turn three animated pop stars into a live show?
According to a Netflix press release, “beloved animated HUNTR/X characters – Rumi, Mira and Zoey – will interact with the audience through cutting-edge performance innovations that bring this fan-favorite K-pop girl group to life like never before (yes, that also includes the animated characters of the Saja Boys and Derpy Tiger).” This does not entirely answer my question, but the email does also explicitly say “fans are invited to join the animated characters of HUNTR/X for a live K-pop Concert Event.”
The press release also says the the KPop Demon Hunters show is “more than a concert, this is a first-of-its-kind production that immerses fans in the storytelling with live-action stunts and performers, fan-favorite music and choreography, and special performances.”

Heading up creative director for the tour is Amy Tinkham, who has worked for Cirque du Soleil as well as Disney’s recent Worlds Collide Tour which featured stars of the movies Descendants and Zombies.
The tour kicks off on June 5 2027 in Baltimore, and will make stops all over the country, including dates in Chicago, Atlanta, Orlando, Phoenix, Las Vegas, and Los Angeles.

title: At Sing Sing prison, incarcerated men get preview of new PBS documentary on nation's justice system
text:
OSSINING, New York (AP) — As the lights dimmed inside the chapel at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility in New York, around 30 incarcerated men sat scattered across the pews, waiting to preview a new docuseries on the history of the nation’s criminal justice system.
Our Lady of Hope chapel was soon abuzz with discussion, as some learned new things about an American institution with which they already have a great deal of personal experience.
The four-part series, “Crime and Punishment in America,” is set to premiere Monday on PBS. It spends eight hours tracing how the justice system evolved, from the colonial period to present day, and viewers get to hear from legal scholars, formerly incarcerated people, victims’ families and corrections officers.
The U.S. maintains the world’s largest incarcerated population, with nearly two million people behind bars in prisons and jails. In 2024, each state incarcerated more people per capita than most countries, according to the Prison Policy Initiative.
“What are we hoping to accomplish with this?” film director Lynn Novick said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Digging into the history and revealing it will help us to have a different conversation about what justice means in this country.”
Prisoners ask, ‘What do we do with transformed people’
Novick developed the series with frequent collaborator Ken Burns, an acclaimed filmmaker with numerous PBS documentaries to his name. In 2019, the two partnered on “College Behind Bars,” which followed a Bard College program to provide a liberal arts education to incarcerated people.
Sing Sing was Novick’s sixth screening for prison populations in correctional facilities: Maine, Connecticut, California and Washington state prisons, as well as New York City’s Rikers’ jail, have hosted previews of “Crime and Punishment in America.”
Sing Sing prisoners were shown a 47-minute reel from the full series.
“I hope that as people see this documentary, that they are challenged to think about what we have to do differently,” said Michael Shane Hale, 54 and from Kentucky, who has served 32 years of a 50-to-life prison sentence.
Hale said the viewing public should no longer question whether it’s possible for prisoners to turn their lives around. The question, he added, should instead be “what do we do with transformed people?”
Post-screening panel elicits impassioned discussion
The conversation at Sing Sing was more animated than Novick had anticipated. Some of the prisoners gathered in the chapel were invigorated by news of California Gov. Gavin Newsom saying he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
Several prisoners inundated a panel of speakers with concerns about what rehabilitation through incarceration looks like for their families and for victims. Others drew connections between their crimes, mental illness and economic circumstances.
“Nobody is the sum of their worst mistake, right?” said José Colon, 44 and from the Bronx, who entered prison at age 17 and has been incarcerated for nearly 28 years. “No matter where you are in life, there’s always room for growth.”
John Rizzo, another Sing Sing prisoner, asked the panel what “rehabilitation” means to society.
“When we come in here, we’re tainted,” Rizzo said later in an interview with the AP. “When we go back out into society, when is the incarcerated individual going to be acceptable again?”
Rizzo has served 16 years so far on a conviction for conspiracy and attempted murder. He said he spends his time helping peers apply for prison jobs and studying for a bachelor’s degree in behavioral science that he intends to earn while incarcerated.
Reginald Dwayne Betts, a panelist and poet who served eight years for a carjacking at 16, agreed with Rizzo. He said people seemed to focus on his past when he returned to life after prison. “It was always, ‘Can you tell me more about your crime?’” he said.
Betts has created a documentary following his life and became known for his work installing libraries in the nation’s prisons.
Prison officer-turned-commissioner promotes screening as education
Daniel F. Martuscello III, the first former correction officer appointed commissioner of the New York State Department of Correction, said he agreed to screen Novick’s film because he sees it as an extension of the prison’s Rehabilitation Through the Arts workshops.
“It’s our obligation, not only as commissioners, but as people running the system, lawmakers, to make sure that we’re telling that story,” Martuscello said. “Because to not do so, it takes away from that transformation, and really, it degrades public safety.”
John J. Lennon is an incarcerated Sing Sing prison journalist and a recipient of a 2026 Guggenheim Fellowship, a prestigious and competitive grant to support scholars, artists and scientists for work “under the freest possible conditions.” In-prison programs, he says, are what allowed him to build a writing career after entering prison with a ninth-grade education.
He said New York, and the nation as a whole, has much more reform work to do.
“If you want accountability in America, then there has to be forgiveness on the table,” Lennon said. “There has to be mercy on the table.”

title: Fort Kent cast prepares for ‘Les Misérables’ performances
text:
FORT KENT, Maine (WAGM) - Actors preparing to perform “Les Misérables” in Fort Kent said learning the music and understanding the story behind each song are part of bringing the show to the stage.
The musical follows Jean Valjean, a former prisoner trying to build a new life while being pursued by Inspector Javert.
Playing Inspector Javert
Olorin Braun plays Javert, a character whose commitment to the law leaves little room for understanding.
“He’s a police inspector that genuinely believes in black and white. There is no gray, there is only the law, and the law is the thing that we must adhere to and be good,” Braun said.
Preparing for two roles
Shanelle Rossignol plays both Fantine and Cosette. Rossignol said cast members have helped each other understand the story and work through rehearsals.
“Because I have two characters, it’s like taking a lot of time to memorize both songs and both roles. And then of course there’s the beautiful set work and a lot of hours have gone into it and I’m really excited. It’s going to be amazing,” Rossignol said.
Work beyond performing
Troy Celik, who plays Jean Valjean, also helps with the set. Celik hopes to pursue Broadway someday. He said taking on the role has offered a chance to develop new skills.
“It’s helped me grow as an actor as well as a singer, and it’s just opened me up to so many things that I just didn’t know I could do before,” Celik said.
Cast from neighboring communities
The production also includes performers from neighboring communities. Samantha Chasse, who plays Eponine, is from Madawaska. She said joining the cast gives her access to an opportunity that is meaningful in a small community.
“We don’t really have a huge program in Madawaska, so being able to come here and be a part of something this big really means a lot because the arts is something that’s super important,” Chasse said.
Performance dates
“Les Misérables” opens Nov. 19 in the Fort Kent High School cafeteria. Performances are Nov. 19, 20 and 21 at 6 p.m. A final performance is scheduled for Nov. 22 at 2 p.m.

title: Rescues underway after tanker collides with cruise ship on Mississippi River
text:
New Orleans cruise ship collision: All accounted for, 32 hospitalized
Federal, state and local agencies responded to a boat collision on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, Louisiana, on Friday, Nov. 13.
A tanker struck the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage, prompting a massive search and rescue response.
Latest updates:
- All passengers aboard the American Heritage have been accounted for, officials said.
- LCMC Health is treating 32 injured passengers
- The Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck the docked cruise ship on the Mississippi River in New Orleans at about 12:30 p.m. The cause has not been confirmed.
- Hotel rooms have been secured for any passengers impacted by the cruise line collision
In what is being called "A miracle on the Mississippi," all passengers aboard the American Heritage cruise ship struck in New Orleans have been accounted for.
LCMC Health is treating 32 passengers who were injured during the collision.
Here is everything we know as emergency responders work to find those unaccounted for.
What happened:
The Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck the American Cruise Lines vessel at about 12:30 p.m. near 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, according to Port NOLA. The cruise ship had docked approximately two hours earlier and was beginning to disembark passengers.
About 129 passengers, along with crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision.
The crash happened near the Crescent City Connection on the New Orleans side of the river.
Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel responded to the scene to conduct rescue and response operations.
Passengers were brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building, located at 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, for triage and assistance, according to Port officials.
"Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders. This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the allision have not yet been confirmed. Additional updates will be provided as information is confirmed," the Port issued a news release.
The crash happened near the Crescent City Connection on the New Orleans side.
Injuries and passenger assistance:
LCMC Health said it is treating 32 injured passengers. Passengers were brought to the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triage and assistance, according to port officials.
Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser said he has secured 85 hotel rooms for passengers affected by the collision.
LCMC Health issued the following statement regarding the treatment of patients involved in the cruise line collision:
"University Medical Center New Orleans and other LCMC Health hospitals have received an estimated two dozen patients following the reported maritime incident. Our medical teams are currently evaluating patients and providing appropriate care while coordinating with emergency responders. As this remains an active situation, we will provide additional information as appropriate."
American Cruise Lines issues statement:
"American Cruise Lines can confirm that our riverboat, American Heritage was involved in a collision while it was docked in New Orleans. We are in close coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved. We will share more information as it becomes available."
River traffic and ferry service:
The Coast Guard closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 during the response.
The Regional Transit Authority also suspended ferry service across the river as a precaution.
Below is a statement from the U.S. Coast Guard regarding its response to the scene:
"The U.S. Coast Guard, in coordination with local response partners, is responding to a vessel collision involving a tanker and a cruise ship near mile marker 96 on the Mississippi River.
"The river is closed to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while responders assess the situation and conduct response operations.
"This is a developing situation. Additional information will be released as it becomes available."
President Trump briefed on collision:
President Donald Trump was briefed on the New Orleans boat crash, per a senior White House official.
"Thank you to the United States Coast Guard for doing such an incredible job of rescue and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana. Likewise, all of Law Enforcement and First Responders were fantastic! Incredibly, nobody was killed by this major collision. 32 people are in the hospital. Thank you to Governor Jeff Landry for your outstanding leadership during this very agonizing period of time."
Federal, state, local officials respond:
Mayor Helena Moreno issued the following statement regarding the response:
"Emergency crews are responding to a collision involving a cargo ship and a riverboat cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans. Multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing. Public safety agencies are coordinating response efforts, with the immediate priority being the safety and rescue of those involved. This remains an active and developing incident."
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry flew to New Orleans to help with the emergency response to the cruise line collision.
His office issued the following statement regarding the incident:
"We are aware of the incident on the Mississippi and we are in close contact with local officials and law enforcement. I am headed to New Orleans now."
Congressman Steve Scalise spoke with WDSU live on television regarding federal resources made available to the United States Coast Guard during the search and rescue operation in the river.
Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the following statement regarding resources for the search and rescue response in New Orleans:
"The United States Coast Guard is supporting the state of Louisiana and our local partners in responding to a vessel collision near mile marker 96 on the Mississippi River. We are throwing every asset we have to help rescue missing passengers. The Department of Homeland Security is coordinating closely with the state of Louisiana. Our prayers are with all those impacted by this terrible tragedy."

title: Puppy yoga pairs stretching with snuggling
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Downward dog has a new meaning in Charlotte, where yoga classes include puppies. The classes blend calm movement with play, rest and cuddle time.
What happens in a puppy yoga class
The puppies don’t follow the poses, but that is part of the appeal.
“Everyone loves puppies and everyone loves yoga, and it’s a great way to kind of bridge the two,” said Jessica Seisay, a yoga instructor who is one of thousands across the country hosting this type of workout.
First-time participant Taylor Manley said the class left her calm. A puppy just wanted to sit in her lap the whole time, she said.
“I was trying to relax with him, and he was gonna make me go to sleep with him,” Manley said.
What research says about animal contact
Studies show contact with animals can lower cortisol levels and raise serotonin and dopamine, chemicals that boost mood and reduce anxiety.
Taylor Terry, the breeder of the puppies in the class, said she sees the effect on people.
“A lot of people are actually dealing with anxiety and depression, so it’s definitely a good place to just like, decompress,” Terry said. “Every time you see puppies, you just get happy.”
The puppies benefit, too
Terry said the classes also help socialize the puppies. She said they start out unsure of the people in the room.
“After like 10 minutes, they’re just like, ‘Oh my God, this is so fun,’” Terry said. “They’re running around everywhere.”
By the end of class, she said, the puppies are socializing and “having a good time.”
Terry said some puppies also meet future families in class.
Aging Untold hosts weigh in
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose called puppy yoga “brilliant.”
“Yoga could do all those things, and puppies can do all those things for you. Combine them, you get the best of both worlds,” Ambrose said.
“Give me a yoga mat and a bunch of puppies and I don’t care if I stretch. I just want the puppies,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.

title: ‘General Hospital’ actor releases statement after son is charged in fatal hit-and-run
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Jack Antonio Sabàto appeared in court Thursday for a hearing in the case stemming from a hit-and-run that killed pedestrian Carl Simmonds.
Sabàto, 32, is charged with the felony crime of leaving an accident without assisting and a misdemeanor count of leaving the scene of an accident involving injury or death.
Statement from Sabàto’s father
Sabàto is the son of actors Antonio Sabàto Jr., of “General Hospital,” and Virginia Madsen, known for roles in movies like “Candyman” and “Sideways.”
In a statement posted to his Facebook page Wednesday, Sabàto Jr. offered condolences to the family and loved ones of the person killed, said his love for his children remains unconditional, and asked the public and media to respect his family’s privacy.
“I also wish to extend my heartfelt condolences to the family and loved ones of the gentleman who tragically lost his life. My thoughts and prayers are with them as well,” Sabàto Jr. said.
What the charging document says
According to the charging document filed Nov. 10, Anchorage police and firefighters responded around 5:48 a.m. Monday to a body on the sidewalk along Airport Heights Drive near the Blood Bank of Alaska.
Officers identified the person as Simmonds and found broken vehicle parts nearby.
Prosecutors said surveillance video from the blood bank shows a white Chevrolet Tahoe hitting Simmonds around 5:35 a.m. The charging document says no braking was observed before or after the collision.
Police traced a registered white Tahoe to Sabàto and found the vehicle at an Amazon warehouse around 12:45 p.m. with fresh damage to its front-right corner, according to the document. Officers obtained a warrant to seize the vehicle.
The document says Sabàto called police at 2:46 p.m. and reported that he had struck an animal. When officers spoke with him, he said he had been doing late-night DoorDash deliveries and was on his way home when something appeared in the road.
He said he knew he had hit something, but did not know it was a person, according to the charging document.
Prosecutors said Sabàto told officers he did not stop to check because he was scared and did not have insurance. He also said he called police after his girlfriend told him the Tahoe had been taken, according to the document.
Tuesday’s hearing
At Tuesday’s hearing, a defense attorney challenged the state’s characterization of the case and argued that Sabàto had contacted police and cooperated. The attorney also asked for lower bail and a no-driving condition, citing Sabàto’s lack of criminal history.
The court set bail at $5,000 cash performance and $5,000 unsecured appearance, meaning the second amount does not have to be posted, but could be assessed if Sabàto fails to appear.
The judge also ordered him not to drive, sit in a vehicle’s driver’s seat or possess vehicle keys.
The charging document said the Alaska Public Safety Information Network showed no prior state convictions for Sabàto.
Blood bank video and family
The Blood Bank of Alaska is checking with police and its board of directors to determine whether footage of the crash can be publicly released.
KTUU also reached out to Simmonds’ family, who declined to speak.
In a Nov. 9 Facebook post, Crystal Tickett asked for help finding Simmonds, saying he left Alaska Regional Hospital around 5 a.m. that morning. Tickett wrote that she filed a missing persons report. A spokesperson for Anchorage police said the department does not have a record of the report.
The judge set Sabàto’s next pre-indictment hearing for Dec. 3.

title: Judge rules that Hermon School Committee discriminated against church
text:
A federal judge ruled Friday that the Hermon School Committee discriminated against an evangelical church when it rejected an application to rent high school space on a yearly basis.
But in the 37-page decision, U.S. District Court Judge Lance Walker didn’t overturn the School Committee’s 4-1 vote to instead offer a month-to-month lease rather than a 12-month or six-month option. He granted Pines Church and its pastor, Matt Gioia, $1 in damages, plus other fees.
In reaching his decision, Walker wrote that the church’s religious association was a “substantial factor” in the School Committee’s decision-making, saying that the proceedings were replete with “undertones and overtones” of animus toward Pines Church and Gioia.
Gioia moved from Colorado back to Maine with his wife, Jess, and six children during the COVID-19 pandemic to start a church. The church quickly grew and began renting space at an Orono movie theater to accommodate around 150 congregants.
During a barbecue, Gioia met Hermon School Committee member Haily Keezer, who encouraged him to look into renting space at Hermon High School. Such arrangements aren’t unusual in Maine. In 2011, The Rock Church rented Peakes Auditorium at Bangor High School for Easter services. And other churches over the years have used school space to accommodate an influx of congregants during parts of the year.
Gioia found an ally in Superintendent Micah Grant, a self-described born-again Christian. Throughout the process leading up to the December 2022 vote, Walker wrote, Grant acted as a “guardrail” for the School Committee whenever its members risked crashing into a “constitutional bridge abutment.”
Grant supported Gioia’s vision for a year-long lease and repeatedly stressed to committee members a preference for that option and that allowing Pines Church to rent the auditorium and two classrooms wouldn’t amount to an endorsement of the church.
“I am convinced that, if anything, Grant’s conduct as to procedure supported and favored treating the Church equally to all other potential public users of public space, a point he repeatedly made to the Committee in an effort to get them focused and in league with the Constitution and the advice given to them by their own lawyer,” the judge wrote.
While he didn’t accept claims that the rejection of a year-long lease amounted to a policy of discrimination, Walker found at least three School Committee members — Stephanie Oiler, Christopher McLaughlin and Karen Shorey — exhibited “bad motives” throughout the process leading up to the final vote.
In particular, Walker faulted McLaughlin, the only committee member to vote against leasing space to Pines Church, for his “intrusive” questions into the church’s denomination and views on diversity, equity and inclusion; abortion; and sexuality and sexual identity.
Oiler raised a number of practical issues over the church’s use of school property. Walker wrote that Grant “definitely dispelled” concerns over cleaning, parking, snow removal and more. The judge found that, despite couching her concerns in practical considerations, Oiler’s attitude toward Pines Church was “anything but neutral.”
“This was made only more obvious by protesting far too much that this was not about the Church but instead fear, for example, of mass vomiting epidemics and the platoon of janitorial assistance that would be required to mop it up,” Walker wrote.
While Walker acknowledged that the arrangement Pines Church sought with the Hermon school system was novel — no other group renting its school space does so on an annual basis — he wrote that “novelty is not a basis to discriminate against religious organizations” and chastised the School Committee for its failure to follow the “sound legal advice” of its lawyers.
The committee’s actions violated Pines Church’s rights under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution and the Maine Human Rights Act.

title: Play at Waldo Theatre depicts fictional conversation between JFK and painter Jamie Wyeth
text:
WALDOBORO, Maine (WABI) - A famous portrait of President John F. Kennedy is inspiring a new play at the Waldo Theatre.
Writer Shannon Mullen decided to bring the story of the portrait to life, and she thought a play would be the best way to tell it. Her version, “An Addition of One,” depicts a fictional conversation between Kennedy and painter Jamie Wyeth, who was tasked with painting the late president after his death.
How the play began
Mullen said the idea came from an interview with Wyeth.
“He mentioned that he had done this posthumous portrait of President Kennedy. Jamie was only 20 at the time, and he said that the process had gotten so real to him of getting to know this martyred president, that he created a memory of having met him for about a half an hour,” Mullen said. “And I remember listening to my recording of the interview a few days later, is when I first really heard that, and I thought, ‘That’s a play. I have to hear that conversation, and I guess I’m going to have to write it.’”
The portrait
Wyeth was hesitant when he was given the opportunity to create a portrait of Kennedy.
“I turned it down thinking, ‘How can I do it if he’s not alive?’ But then I started thinking about it, as I was taken up as everybody was with Kennedy at that point,” Wyeth said. “And so then I went myself and decided to do this, and I created a painting which was very romantic and so forth, and then I felt the need to get some life into it.”
To draw inspiration, Wyeth used his creativity and also leaned on other members of the Kennedy family, in particular Kennedy’s two brothers.
The portrait is popular now, but it was not a hit when it first came out.
“The portrait was hated when it was first reproduced in Look Magazine, life-sized,” Wyeth said. “Because at that point, he was this demigod with blue eyes and blonde hair, neither of which he had. Now it’s sort of reversed. It’s now the national stamp of Ireland, it’s reproduced a lot, it’s in the Boston Museum.”
One performer, two roles
Mullen wrote and directed the play, produced it and is the only actress in it. She plays both Wyeth and Kennedy.
Mullen said a table reading led her to take both roles.
“At that table reading, we asked the small audience we had, ‘Did you mind that it was two women reading these roles?’” Mullen said. “A friend of mine read Jamie and I read Jack, and they said no, they found it liberating because, as I hoped, they weren’t focused on or distracted by the fact that I don’t look like Jack Kennedy or sound exactly like him. So after that I said, ‘I think I’m just going to do them both myself.’”
Speaker series follows the show
The roughly 45-minute show is followed by a speaker series featuring artists, journalists and writers who explore the play’s themes.
Waldo Theatre leaders said the interactive format and post-show Q&A build on the theater’s reputation for fostering a close-knit community.
“We’re trying to get as many different kinds of people through the door, and to develop a program that has, like, a lot of legs. Maybe it’s a centipede,” Cooney said. “We’re trying to bring everybody in the doors and offer programming that can speak to people, but also resonates long after.”
The show premiered November 7th and will continue this Saturday, November 14th and Sunday the 15th at 4 o’clock.
There will be an additional two shows November 21st and 22nd at the same time.
