title: Prostate health: These are the symptoms men should not ignore
text:
(Aging Untold) — The prostate can have a big impact on men’s health as they get older.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the prostate is a small gland that slowly enlarges with age, and men should not ignore the changes that come with it.
What the prostate does and how it changes
“It’s a small gland, but it plays a huge role in men’s health. And it sits right at the base of the bladder,” Rogers said.
How an enlarged prostate can affect daily life
As the prostate enlarges, it pushes in on the bladder, and men start to have a frequent need to urinate. Because the bladder is being pushed on, it may not empty all the way, Rogers said.
“You increase your chances of urinary tract infections because bacteria can just be sitting there,” Rogers said.
Rogers said the effects can reach beyond the bathroom.
“When you’re not sleeping well, because you’re going to the restroom all night, now you’re impacting the whole sympathetic nervous system that has other medical implications,” Rogers said. That includes insulin resistance.
Symptoms men should not ignore
The gland grows so slowly that many men tend to dismiss the signs, Rogers said.
“Because it’s so slow growing, a lot of guys, they just kind of ignore it,” Rogers said. “They should not ignore those symptoms or the hesitancy and nighttime urination.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck described the gland as being like a donut around a straw. When the donut is squeezed, she said, the straw, which represents the urethra, holds urine behind it.
“Don’t just get used to frequent urination,” Cradduck said. “Don’t just say, ‘Oh well, I’m a little older, so I go more frequently.’”
Signs that should prompt a call to a doctor: not getting urine out, getting up two or three times a night, feeling back pressure while going and getting frequent urinary tract infections, Cradduck said.
“Go to your doctor,” she said. “Go to a urologist.”
Prostate cancer can have no symptoms
An enlarged prostate can also be a sign of prostate cancer.
“Prostate cancer a lot of times is without any symptoms,” Rogers said. “So usually we take a look at everything that’s going on and don’t simply ignore it, but go seek medical attention.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said that because there may be no symptoms, men should be proactive.
“They could have cancer and not have any symptoms,” O’Rourke said.
“Really be proactive, because you’re not going to get a sign until maybe it’s too late,” she said.
Cradduck said prostate cancer does not have to be a death sentence, but it can be because it can metastasize.
She said people may hear “prostate cancer” and think it is common and not a big deal.
“It is a great big deal when it metastasizes and it spreads,” Cradduck said. “Why would you even allow that? Get yourself checked.”
Rogers said prostate cancer has different scores, including a Gleason score.
That is a grading system to evaluate the aggressiveness of prostate cancer, according to Mayo Clinic.
Many men will die with the disease, Rogers said, and some men can die from it, depending on how aggressive it is and what the score is.
What PSA is and what a high number can mean
O’Rourke shared that her husband’s PSA level was not where his doctor wanted it to be.
“He said, just eat more leafy green vegetables. And darned if that didn’t lower the PSA level,” O’Rourke said.
Prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, is a protein the prostate gland produces, according to the Prostate Cancer Foundation.
“It’s a protein, so because of that, many things can cause it to elevate,” Rogers said. “Just because it’s elevated doesn’t mean you have cancer. You can have an infection, prostatitis and things like that.”
She said doctors often look at the interval over time to see the percentage of increase. There are other measures and more specialized tests that can show whether a PSA reading indicates high-grade cancer.
Rogers said inflammation is a factor in many cases. She said she has seen a person’s PSA drop quickly after inflammation was addressed in another part of the body.
“It really is inflammation,” Rogers said. “But you want to make sure it’s not a mask for something.”
Talk about it and get support
O’Rourke posted a challenge to men to talk to one another.
She challenged men to ask each other whether they are getting annual exams, having trouble urinating, noticing changes in their sex life, not sleeping or feeling fatigued.
“Get support to go to the doctor to get it checked,” O’Rourke said.
“Be proactive, but get your support system with the other guys,” she said. “Don’t be too embarrassed to talk about it.”
Key takeaways
- The prostate sits at the base of the bladder and slowly enlarges as men get older. It acts like a hose clamp on urine flow.
- Don’t ignore urinary changes. Weak streams, frequent urination, hesitancy and nighttime bathroom trips should not be treated as normal. Talk to a doctor.
- Talk with a doctor. Prostate cancer often has no symptoms, so screening and early detection matter.

title: Open health insurance enrollment: What it means for your taxes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When you work for yourself, the stakes of open enrollment are much higher than they are for someone on an employer-sponsored plan.
Three decisions you make during the Open Enrollment Period (OEP) affect your tax return:
- Your income estimate: The Marketplace uses your income estimate to set your Advance Premium Tax Credit (APTC). Guess too low, and you’ll have to pay back the excess credit when you file your tax return.
- Your plan: Your premiums may qualify for the self-employed health insurance deduction. The right type of plan can also let you make tax-deductible contributions to a health savings account (HSA).
- Whether you enroll: Some states charge a penalty if you go without coverage.
So how does the ACA tie into your taxes?
Once you have Marketplace coverage, if you get an Advance Premium Tax Credit, it links your health plan to your tax return. When you file, you compare the advance credit paid during the year with the credit you actually qualify for. The numbers come from Form 1095-A.
You have to file a return if you received advance credit payments, even if your income falls below the normal filing threshold, Intuit TurboTax reports.
What’s changing for 2026-27 and why your premium jumped
The enhanced premium tax credits that made Marketplace plans cheaper from 2021 through 2025 expired at the end of 2025. As a result, average out-of-pocket premiums rose 58% in 2026, according to the KFF (Kaiser Family Foundation). Insurance companies also raised health insurance premiums by an average of 20% in 2026 and are proposing an average of 15% for 2027.
Without the enhanced credits, if your household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty level, you don’t qualify for a premium tax credit. Going even $1 over that line costs you the entire credit.
If your income is close to the line, deductions that lower your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) may help you stay eligible for an advance premium tax credit. Learn more about how the premium tax credit works and how to stay eligible.
How your plan choice shows up on your tax return
Form 8962 calculates the difference between the credit you received during the year and the credit you qualify for once you know your actual income for the year. If you’re a W-2 employee with steady paychecks, the gap is usually small. If you’re self-employed, your income might rise and fall from quarter to quarter, so the difference can be big.
Starting with 2026 returns (the ones you file in 2027), you repay any excess advance credit in full, with no cap. So if a strong fourth quarter pushes your household income over 400% of the federal poverty level, you repay the full credit.
To avoid a big bill at tax time, update your income with the Marketplace within 30 days of an income change. You might also consider taking less than the full advance credit and claiming the rest when you file your tax return.
The tax forms you’ll need
If you have a Marketplace plan, the federal platform or a state-based marketplace exchange will mail you Form 1095-A and post it to your online account by January 31 of the following year.
It lists your monthly premiums, the benchmark plan cost, and any advance credit paid on your behalf. All three numbers feed directly into Form 8962.
Check the form before you file. If it has the wrong household members, coverage months, or benchmark premium, ask the Marketplace for a corrected copy. Wrong numbers can affect your credit and trigger an IRS notice.
If your spouse has employer coverage, you may also receive Form 1095-B or 1095-C. You don’t have to wait for either one to file.
Don’t leave this deduction on the table
If you pay for your own health insurance as a self-employed person, you can generally deduct the premiums you pay for yourself, your spouse, and your dependents. You claim the deduction using Form 7206 and Schedule 1, and you don’t need to itemize.
With premiums rising, this deduction can be worth more when you file your tax return. Just keep two limits in mind. First, your deduction can’t exceed your net business profit. Second, you can’t take the deduction for any month you were eligible for an employer-subsidized plan, including one through your spouse’s job.
Driving, delivering, or freelancing through a platform?
In California and Massachusetts, app-based rideshare and delivery drivers may qualify for a health insurance stipend from their platforms.
You can receive a stipend and a premium tax credit at the same time, but the stipend counts as business income, so include it in your income estimate and on your tax return.
Exemptions, penalties, and what happens if you skip coverage
Congress cut the federal penalty for going without health insurance to $0 starting in 2019, so skipping coverage won’t affect your federal return. However, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia may charge a penalty on your state or district return.
If you skipped coverage in one of these states, you may qualify for a state exemption, for example, if your coverage gap was short or the coverage available to you would have cost more than a set share of your income.
Exemptions aren’t automatic. You have to claim them on your state return.
Missed the window or had a life change?
If you miss the enrollment deadline, you must qualify for a Special Enrollment Period to get coverage at a later date. Common qualifying life events include losing health coverage after leaving a job, moving to a new area, getting married, or having or adopting a child.
If you don’t qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you can still apply for Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) any time of year.
Quick reference checklist
During open enrollment
- Enroll by Dec. 15 for coverage that starts Jan. 1 (Deadlines for state exchanges may differ).
- Estimate your household income using net self-employment income, and include any platform health stipend.
- If you want to contribute to an HSA, make sure your plan is a high-deductible health plan (HDHP).
During the year
Update your Marketplace application within 30 days of a significant income or life change.
When you file your tax return
- Watch for Form 1095-A by Jan. 31 and check it for errors.
- File Form 8962 to calculate your premium tax credit and compare it to the Advance Premium Tax Credit you received.
- Report any health care stipends you received as business income.
Mark your calendar
Open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs from Nov. 1, 2026, through Jan. 15, 2027, on HealthCare.gov. If you enroll by Dec. 15, your coverage starts on Jan. 1. The final deadline to sign up or change plans for 2027 coverage is Jan. 15, 2027, for coverage starting Feb. 1.
If your state runs its own exchange, your dates may be different. The chart below shows the states with their own deadlines. If your state isn’t listed, then the federal open enrollment timeline applies.

title: Retired veteran finds new mission volunteering at senior center
text:
PHOENIX (InvestigateTV) — A Valley Army veteran is spending his post-military and post-retirement years volunteering at a Phoenix senior center, offering companionship and practical help to seniors who have few other resources.
Robert Lane can be found at the Desert West Senior Center in the Maryvale neighborhood Monday through Friday, from morning until late afternoon.
Lane enlisted in the Army in the late 1970s, shortly after the Vietnam War ended, as part of an effort known as Operation Babylift.
“They flew me and a couple guys out to Fort Smith, Arkansas, and we fed all the Vietnamese women and babies there,” Lane said.
He has continued feeding people since — now serving hotdogs and nachos at the senior center.
Lane also takes seniors grocery shopping, drives them to doctor appointments, and spends time with them at the center. It is all part of the Senior Companion Program, which is an AmeriCorps Seniors service through Northern Arizona University.
“Making them laugh and just the joy in their face, that’s what it’s all about,” Lane said. “Because sometimes, some of them have nobody. Nobody at home and nobody to take care of them.”
Lane has been a regular at the center for nearly four years, and his energy is infectious.
“He is a huge source of encouragement because he really lifts our spirits,” Daniel Flores said in Spanish. “He gives us everything we need and helps us a lot.”
Lane’s wife, Synthia, inspired him to begin volunteering and is also a fixture at the center.
“This is where we’re just going to plant it until there’s no more retirement (and) we’re totally out of it,” she said. “We’re just not ready to give up yet.”
Synthia said she is typically working in the office while her husband engages with seniors on the floor as a “social butterfly.”
Lane has also picked up some Spanish during his time there since many of the seniors only speak Spanish.
He occasionally performs as Elvis for the senior center crowd.
“You come on down to the senior center and you can see Elvis here saying, ‘You ain’t nothing but a hound dog,’” Lane said. “Thank you very much.”

title: Puppy yoga pairs stretching with snuggling
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Downward dog has a new meaning in Charlotte, where yoga classes include puppies. The classes blend calm movement with play, rest and cuddle time.
What happens in a puppy yoga class
The puppies don’t follow the poses, but that is part of the appeal.
“Everyone loves puppies and everyone loves yoga, and it’s a great way to kind of bridge the two,” said Jessica Seisay, a yoga instructor who is one of thousands across the country hosting this type of workout.
First-time participant Taylor Manley said the class left her calm. A puppy just wanted to sit in her lap the whole time, she said.
“I was trying to relax with him, and he was gonna make me go to sleep with him,” Manley said.
What research says about animal contact
Studies show contact with animals can lower cortisol levels and raise serotonin and dopamine, chemicals that boost mood and reduce anxiety.
Taylor Terry, the breeder of the puppies in the class, said she sees the effect on people.
“A lot of people are actually dealing with anxiety and depression, so it’s definitely a good place to just like, decompress,” Terry said. “Every time you see puppies, you just get happy.”
The puppies benefit, too
Terry said the classes also help socialize the puppies. She said they start out unsure of the people in the room.
“After like 10 minutes, they’re just like, ‘Oh my God, this is so fun,’” Terry said. “They’re running around everywhere.”
By the end of class, she said, the puppies are socializing and “having a good time.”
Terry said some puppies also meet future families in class.
Aging Untold hosts weigh in
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose called puppy yoga “brilliant.”
“Yoga could do all those things, and puppies can do all those things for you. Combine them, you get the best of both worlds,” Ambrose said.
“Give me a yoga mat and a bunch of puppies and I don’t care if I stretch. I just want the puppies,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.

title: Bangor Humane Society documentary premieres at Black Bear Cinemas
text:
ORNO, Maine (WABI) - Black Bear Cinemas held a red carpet premiere Thursday night for a documentary about the Bangor Humane Society.
Everyone was invited, including some four-legged guests.
About the film
“Humane: Inside Bangor Humane Society” follows the work being done at the shelter.
Director and producer Keith Travers and his wife, Danielle, spent more than a year filming the animals, staff and volunteers.
They used their own resources to make the film.
The couple and shelter staff said the documentary shows the love and compassion given to the animals. They said it also shows the work behind the scenes to help nearly 2,000 animals find new homes each year.
Shelter staff react
“Our staff and literally more than a hundred volunteers work tirelessly all year long. We’re there on holidays. We’re there on weekends. Sometimes we’re there in the middle of the night. And so being able to show every aspect of that work, at least in as much as you can with 45 minutes, is really exciting. And so I hope that folks are just able to walk away knowing that the animals in our care are loved. And they’re ready for the next step,” said Kathryn Ravenscroft, Bangor Humane Society Director of Development and Communications.
How to watch
The documentary will stream on the Maine Public Broadcast Network in December.
More details are available on the Bangor Humane Shelter’s website and Facebook page.

title: Keeping Maine Pedestrians Safe Is Everyone's Responsibility
text:
As the days get shorter, it's a good time to remind pedestrians and drivers about how to coexist safely.
Maine Pedestrians and Drivers Must Work Together to Keep Everyone Safe
This topic hits home with me because I drive to work early in the morning, when people are out walking before dawn.
More than once, I've encountered pedestrians in dark clothing with few or no reflectors to signal their presence to drivers.
Drivers also have responsibilities, as was proven by a fatal crash earlier this week when a driver struck a bicyclist in Pittsfield.
Road safety is everyone's responsibility, so drivers and pedestrians have to work together.
Safety Tips for Maine Pedestrians Who Often Walk on Dark, Rural Roads
The National Traffic Highway Safety Commission offers several tips for pedestrians:
- Follow the rules of the road
- Walk on sidewalks when they're available. If there's no sidewalk, walk facing traffic and as far from the vehicles as possible.
- Use crosswalks when available and don't cross mid-block.
- Look both ways before crossing the street and make sure the drivers can see you.
- Wear bright, reflective clothing and/or have visible lights to alert drivers to your presence.
- Watch for vehicles entering or exiting driveways or backing up in parking lots.
- Be alert to others' movements, whether they're in a vehicle or on a bicycle.
- Make eye contact with drivers whenever possible and wait for a clear, complete stop before crossing the street.
I would add another suggestion to build on that last tip: Don't assume drivers can see you just because you're standing or walking in a crosswalk.
Being a Responsible Driver Means Keeping Maine Pedestrians Safe
Drivers also have a responsibility to keep pedestrians safe on the roads.
Here are a few suggestions from the NHTSA:
- Slow down because speeding endangers drivers and pedestrians.
- Keep your eyes moving and look for pedestrians everywhere.
- Minimize blind spots and remember to check them.
- Use extra caution at night or in bad weather.
- Yield to pedestrians in crosswalks.
- Watch for pedestrians when turning, especially if you're turning right on a red light.
- Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk.
- Follow the speed limit, including the slower limits in school zones.
- Watch for pedestrians when backing up. Look around instead of relying only on your backup camera.
I would add that drivers need to minimize distractions. Put the phone down and pay attention when you're behind the wheel.
According to the Maine Department of Transportation, 182 crashes this year have involved pedestrians.
8 of those have been fatal.
If we all work together, maybe we can get those numbers down in 2027.

title: I’m the new Belfast reporter for the Bangor Daily News
text:
Hi, I’m Parker Garlough, and I’m the new Belfast reporter for the Bangor Daily News.
I look forward to telling stories that matter in Belfast and the rest of Waldo County. Whether I’m writing about an up-and-coming local musician or a verdict in a court case, understanding how a story serves readers will be at the top of my mind. I’ll strive to uncover hidden information, provide essential context and keep readers informed. I’m a strong believer in the importance of local journalism, and I’m excited to be a part of it in Belfast.
Before joining the Bangor Daily News, I was a local news reporter at the York News-Times in York, Nebraska. There, I covered topics including education, local theater and the decontamination process at a Superfund site. Being a new journalist in an unfamiliar place taught me a lot, and I am eager to discover what Belfast will teach me.
I grew up in Naperville, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago. I graduated from Emerson College in 2025 with a degree in journalism. While in college, I freelanced and interned at local news outlets, sparking a passion for local news that has propelled me into my current role.
If you have a news tip, please don’t hesitate to reach out. I’m always happy to hear more about interesting things going on in Belfast, problems that need to be solved or any question that’s on your mind. You can contact me at pgarlough@bangordailynews.com.

title: Dolly Parton’s last recorded song is released—It's a duet with Bono
text:
Dolly Parton’s last recorded song is released—It's a duet with Bono
The legendary voice of Dolly Parton is back for one last rodeo, months after her death.
Video above: The story behind Dolly Parton writing 9 to 5
U2 released their 16th studio album Friday, “Carnaval de Luz” (“Carnival of Light”), which ends with the song “Torn,” a duet between the Irish rock band’s lead singer, Bono, and Parton.
The 11-time Grammy Award-winning singer-songwriter, known for her ballads of love and heartbreak, opens the song with gentle hums, followed by soft then powerful vocals.
“I can’t deny this passion and desire, but I know it has to burn me,” Parton sings.
“Standing this close to the fire, what am I supposed to do?” she continues.
“And how am I supposed to choose? I love ‘em both and I just feel so torn.”
The song’s final lyrics, “Every heart is torn,” echo the sentiments of fans across the world after the beloved star died from cancer in August.
According to her official website, Parton co-wrote the country song about broken family ties with U2 and Irish singer-songwriter Johnny McDaid.
She recorded it in Nashville in June, making the duet her last recorded vocal performance before her death.
“Hope you like what I did. I did quite a few things. Take from it what you want and what you need, but I love the song, and I think it could be something really special,” Dolly wrote to Bono on June 2, an image shared by her official Instagram account in a joint post with U2 shows. “Thanks for including me in your life. I’ve always loved you and always will.”
”When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song. And you can hear that,” Bono told Rolling Stone for U2’s September cover story. “And I can’t even listen to it now.”
Asked how the song came about, in an interview on the “Today” show released Friday, U2’s lead guitarist, keyboardist and vocalist The Edge said, “We were trying out a lot of collaboration and one of the thoughts was that we might do something with Dolly.”
“We sent her this couple of — these kind of folk songs we were working on,” Bono said. “There was a song called ‘Lifelong’ I played to her over the phone.”
“She goes, ‘That’s a little too Irish for me. Just for where my voice is right now,’” Bono continued, trying to emulate Parton’s voice. “And then she said, ‘You know I got a song called ‘Torn.’ You can take it wherever you want, and maybe I’ll like where you take it.’”
“I think it’s probably the right song to finish ‘Carnaval de Luz,’” he added.

title: Bucksport Man's Complaint Visit Ends With Arrest And A Towed Car In Bangor
text:
Bucksport Man Visits Bangor PD To Lodge A Complaint, Illegally Parks Across 2 Handicap Spots, And Ends Up Arrested
There is an artform to taking a moment to pause and breathe when you are upset about something. A minute of reflection can often keep us from making regrettable mistakes in the heat of the moment.
Read More: Bangor, Maine Woman Charged After Knife Incident On Summer Street
Case in point, this incident that took place on Thursday morning at the Bangor Police Department.
Bangor PD says it all started just after 11:30 AM, when the School Resource Officer, Gerardo Mendoza, went to meet with a man named Gerald Vilardi from Bucksport, at the Bangor Police Station on Main Street.
The men planned to meet and speak about an incident that had occurred early in the morning at a nearby Bangor School, which had left Vilardi quite upset.
Distracted by his emotions, authorities say Vilardi made some mistakes of judgment which ultimately resulted in his arrest, starting with where and how he chose to park his vehicle.
"When Vilardi arrived at the station, he parked diagonally across two handicap parking spaces. During the conversation, Vilardi became belligerent and disorderly in the Police Department lobby. He was taken into custody and taken to Penobscot County Jail."
Vilardi's car was towed after he was cited for parking in a spot without the proper plate or placard displayed.
Following his arrest, he was charged with Disorderly Conduct and Refusal to Submit to Arrest or Detention.
Read More: Waldo County Man Dies In Pittsfield Bicycle Hit-and-run
We get it, people are stressed out about a lot of things these days. But taking a moment to calm down and focus your energy on addressing situations rather than reacting to them instantaneously could mean the difference between driving off in your own car after filing a complaint and watching your ride get towed from behind bars.
Good luck out there. May calmer heads prevail.

title: Survivors of the deadly Brooklyn building collapse recall shock, terror and grief
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — One man’s pregnant wife was pulled alive from the rubble, while two of his roommates perished. A woman living next door woke from a nap to bright daylight flooding her bedroom because her apartment wall was suddenly gone.
Survivors of the Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people wept as they recounted their terror and grief during a news conference Friday.
New York officials, from building inspectors to prosecutors, say they’re investigating what caused the three-story building to come crashing down as workers were digging at an adjacent construction site.
Those who lost family, neighbors and their homes demanded answers.
“As they’re taking me, evacuating me from the building, I could see my neighbors coming out on stretchers,” said Ciahola Lawrence, whose apartment building next to the one that collapsed had a shared wall ripped away, exposing an abyss of dust and debris below.
“We didn’t deserve this,” said Lawrence, who sobbed in her husband’s arms as she spoke with reporters.
Among the dead were two children, ages 9 and 10, according to city officials. Another 18 people were injured, including four firefighters.
‘I no longer knew where I am’
Mamadou Mouctar Balde stepped out to buy groceries Wednesday, leaving his pregnant wife and two roommates, 31-year-old Mamadou N’Diaye and 23-year-old Mamadou Barry, at home. Barry was cooking and N’Diaye was sleeping on the couch, he said.
He returned to find firefighters, police and neighbors gathering outside and assumed there had been a traffic accident. Then a woman told him a building had collapsed.
“I didn’t see my wife. I didn’t see my friends,” Balde recalled, a tear streaking his cheek. “I no longer knew where I am.”
First responders found the bodies of N’Diaye and Barry while combing the wreckage. Balde’s wife, Fatoumata Bah, was pulled alive from the rubble. He said she and their unborn child were doing OK.
N’Diaye and Barry were Guinean nationals who came to the U.S. about five years ago from Conakry, the capital of the West African nation. Their uncle said their family is heartbroken.
“We ask the city and the Guinean community to stand for us, to have a justice for this tragedy,” he said.
Other victims came from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Trinidad, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
New York police identified the others who died as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Edgar Sapon, 26; and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26.
Mayor says authorities will pursue ‘any evidence of criminality’
Ahmed Tigani, commissioner of New York’s Department of Buildings, said Friday that his office is conducting “an exhaustive investigation” of the Brooklyn collapse.
The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site next to the fallen building, Mamdani said, significantly raising an earlier count of sites subject to renewed scrutiny.
“I think it is always an outrage when eight New Yorkers lose their lives, when 18 New Yorkers are hospitalized, and when families are shattered as a result of all of this,” Mamdani said.
If investigators uncover “any evidence of criminality,” Mamdani said, “it is one that we follow through to the fullest extent of the law.”
One witness who works across the street said he watched bricks fall minutes before the disaster. A woman in a neighboring building said she and fellow residents blamed vibrations from the construction for cracks that appeared in their apartment walls.
Video shows survivor descending stairs suspended over wreckage
Lawrence said the construction work had been a source of constant disruption, producing noises so loud that “you would hear that thumping and movement in your soul.”
A security camera above Lawrence’s door recorded video of her apartment’s shared wall and the building next door collapsing in a clattering rumble and a thick cloud of dust. Inside her apartment, a closet filled with hanging clothes and bags was exposed to the outside.
The security video shows Lawrence leaving her damaged home with a firefighter, who held her hand as they descended a stairway overlooking mounds of wreckage below.
“This feeling is indescribable,” Lawrence said. “I was right there.”
Zariah Coleman, who lived in the building next to the one that collapsed, was concerned about her cat. She said Friday that she too had felt the building shake because of the construction.
“I just really hope they come and get our cat,” Coleman said in tears. “He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.”
Rescue operations ended Thursday after crews spent more than a day searching for victims beneath debris removed with power saws, pickaxes and an excavator.
Building records show there were four apartments on the upper two floors and a commercial unit on the ground floor of the collapsed building.
The surrounding blocks along Flatbush Avenue, a busy Brooklyn thoroughfare, are tightly packed with older brick buildings and a few newly built apartment complexes. A mix of Caribbean and Mexican restaurants reflects the diversity of the neighborhood.
Official says prior problems that halted construction were fixed
A one-story building was demolished earlier this year on the construction site next to the collapsed building. Records show a contractor, Mordechai “Marty” Waisbrod, notified the city that excavation would begin in September and would include rock blasting. The contractor has not responded to phone messages left and emails sent to one of his Brooklyn-based businesses.
Permit applications indicated plans to dig below 15 feet (4.5 meters).
A stop work order was issued in March after inspectors concluded the demolition site lacked adequate overhead protection such as netting to protect neighboring buildings and pedestrians, according to the city’s Department of Buildings.
In April, inspectors found that the demolition work had resumed in violation of the stop work order, the department said. Work was allowed to continue after the problems were corrected, Tigani, the city buildings commissioner said Friday.
“We’re looking at the entire history,” he said, “and if there are additional things we need to see, that will be part of the investigation.”
The Brooklyn collapse was the second high-profile structural problem with a building in New York in the past five months. In July, several buildings in Manhattan were evacuated after support columns buckled inside a skyscraper that once was the headquarters of Pfizer.
___
Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa, and Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. Associated Press journalists Jennifer Peltz in New York and Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

title: Cost of living is the top obstacle to financial security, survey finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than half of the adults surveyed by ConsumerAffairs define financial security as simply not living paycheck to paycheck.
The survey of 1,000 adults ages 18 to 64 found the goal is more basic than many might expect, according to Dayna Edens, public relations manager at ConsumerAffairs.
“Truly just making ends meet is now the new bar, the new goal set for being financially secure,” Edens said.
Four in 10 respondents say they have less than $1,000 saved, not counting retirement accounts or home equity.
“We’re truly just talking about money you would have to spend if you would need to take an ER visit or your transmission or your car goes out. Even scarier, 19% have nothing set aside at all,” Edens said.
Only 20% of respondents know the exact dollar amount it would take to feel financially secure.
Edens described what respondents said would make the biggest difference.
“And when we ask them, what’s the biggest change that would be able to make that difference there? The top answer is not paying off debt. It’s not buying a home or setting aside money for the future. It’s truly just covering enough expenses and then still having something left over,” Edens said.
The cost of living was the biggest obstacle to financial security, cited by 46% of respondents.
Financial experts featured in the report recommend building an emergency fund and paying down high-interest debt when possible. Edens said it is important to be realistic about your own financial situation.
“You may not necessarily be the issue right now. You know, cost of livings are high. Do what you can right now to stay afloat,” Edens said.

title: Scarborough changes tree clearing rules after cutting controversies
text:
The Scarborough Town Council passed amendments to the town’s ordinances last week to address concerns and complaints about tree clearing.
Councilor Karin Schupe said the council has consistently received complaints about tree cutting, and the orders it passed to address them have been years in the making.
The first order changes the zoning to include a requirement for a 20-foot streetscape buffer for most streets. Many of the primary roadways already had a 25- to 35-foot streetscape buffer, but other streets didn’t have any requirements.
The second order changes the process for code enforcement cases and site plan reviews.
It also establishes protections for certain types of trees, including “significant” and “heritage” trees. Significant trees are non-invasive trees with a minimum diameter at breast height of 24 inches, and they must be preserved or, if removed, replaced at a ratio of two and a half trees to one. Heritage trees have a minimum diameter of 60 inches or meet other criteria, and they must be preserved or replaced at a ratio of five trees to one.
The orders will only apply to commercial properties, not residential properties.
During the council meeting, residents and councilors made multiple references to the trees cut at Eight Corners to build the Nonesuch River Apartments a few years ago.
“I have yet to speak to someone who wasn’t shocked and horrified by how it looks,” resident Averyl Hill said at the council meeting before the vote. “Yet that massive clear-cutting without any tree buffer was and is permitted under our current ordinance.”
The environment and sustainability are high priorities for many Scarborough residents, who are proud of the town’s marsh, beaches and other natural landmarks.
“That’s what makes Scarborough special,” Schupe said.
Besides addressing conservation concerns, Schupe said, the tree amendments could act as a mechanism to ensure growth and development in Scarborough is done thoughtfully and in an environmentally friendly manner.
One of the Town Council’s goals in 2026 was to limit tree cutting for new commercial developments.
Outgoing councilor Lawrence Cain proposed a few amendments at the order’s second reading, which were all approved.
One of the amendments changed the size of a significant tree from 20 to 24 inches in diameter, reducing the number of trees that can be considered significant trees. Another amendment increased the spacing allowed between trees from 15 to 20 feet on buffer strips, increasing a property’s visibility. Cain also proposed an amendment allowing the planning board to decrease the required buffer by up to 10 feet for some new developments.
The goal, Cain said, was to give property owners more leeway and limit how much the town is restricting how they can use their property. Too many tree-based restrictions could devalue properties, he said.
Schupe and some residents raised concerns during the second reading about making significant changes to the orders, especially after they had already been through the conservation commission, the ordinance committee, the planning board and the Town Council multiple times.
Correction: An earlier version of this story misspelled Averyl Hill’s first name.

title: Nationwide Ground Stop: FAA Halts All Flights Over Communications Issue
text:
Ground Stop Ordered for All Airports Nationwide
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday for all all airlines and all airports (including those in our area) for what they're describing as "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
The FAA issued the stop at 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday afternoon. It is unclear how long it will be in effect, according to reports from ABC and other outlets.
“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the advisory states, “all airports are ground stopped.”
The FAA issued the group stop due to a communications issues that impacted all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, according to a post from Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy on social media. He said that FAA technicians are currently investigating the issue.
Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis, the FAA said.
In the moments leading up to the alert from the FAA airports across the country including Chicago O'Hare and Newark, NJ were reporting delays.
Ground stops of the entire airspace are very rare. The most recent one took place in Janaury 2023. That's when a pilot notification system went down resulting in a ground stop. Prior to that one was issued after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
This is a developing story.

title: LePage edges out Dunlap for 2nd District House seat
text:
The tight race for the U.S. House in Maine’s 2nd District has been won by former Gov. Paul LePage, based on ranked choice tabulations, which concluded nine days after election day.
The results announced by Secretary of State Shenna Bellows found that Republican LePage garnered 170,890 votes (50.81%) to state auditor and Democrat Matt Dunlap’s 165,432 votes (49.18%).
The race to succeed U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd District, went to a ranked choice count after election night results found that no candidate had received more than 50% of the vote, as required under the ranked choice system.
The early tally showed 170,263 first-choice votes (49.894%) for LePage; 164,845 first-choice votes (48.307%) for Dunlap; 123 first-choice votes (0.036%) for declared write-in candidates, and 6,017 blank votes (1.763%).
Maine is one of only two states, along with Alaska, that allows some statewide elections to use ranked choice voting. Maine voters approved adoption of the system in 2016.
Spanning more than 27,000 square miles, Maine’s 2nd District is the largest east of the Mississippi River and includes all municipalities and unorganized territories in 10 of Maine’s 16 counties: Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington.
The secretary of state’s office said results of the ranked choice count are technically unofficial until the tabulation is shared with Gov. Janet Mills. Official results will be posted on the secretary of state’s election results page within 20 days after the election.

title: Trenton man honored as namesake of Maine's first hybrid diesel-electric ferry
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND — The new ferry that will ply the waters between Rockland and Vinalhaven bears the name of a Trenton resident who worked for the Maine State Ferry Service for decades.
The Captain Almer Dinsmore was officially commissioned at the ferry service’s headquarters in Rockland on Thursday, Nov. 5, and its namesake was among those in attendance for the commissioning.
The 154-foot-long motor vessel Dinsmore, according to the Maine Department of Transportation (parent agency of the ferry service), “is the first hybrid diesel-electric ferry designed and built in New England.”
“The vessel’s hybrid diesel-electric design marks a new chapter for the Maine State Ferry Service,” according to the MDOT, “connecting its tradition of maritime service with a new approach to powering its ferries.”
According to the MDOT, the Nov. 5 event marked the vessel’s official introduction into service on the Rockland-Vinalhaven ferry route.
“It is a tremendous honor to have my name on this vessel,” said Dinsmore. “The most meaningful part of my career was serving the island residents and working alongside dedicated crews. I am proud that this ferry will carry that commitment forward for Vinalhaven and the people who travel there.”
Dinsmore was born in Harrington and raised in Steuben. He graduated from Maine Maritime Academy in Castine in 1968. After a decade at sea, he took a job as a relief captain on the Everett Libby on the ferry’s Swan’s Island run in 1978. In 1987, Dinsmore became the Libby’s permanent captain. He stayed with the ferry service until his retirement in 2013.
“His work reflected a lasting commitment to the residents and workers who depend on ferry transportation,” the MDOT said in a press release.
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine’s 1st Congressional District, which includes Knox County, spoke at the Nov. 5 event and said ferries “are more than a transportation system for islands but also a health and safety system.”
“If your daughter breaks her arm or if your grandmother has a stroke, there is no other way on a bad night to get across the bay,” Pingree, a North Haven resident herself, said.
She said there are some who think ferries are luxuries, but she said they are as important for island communities as roads are for other communities, including fueling their economies.
Pingree said she reminds other members of Congress that she is the only one in Congress who will start her day taking a ferry.
The congresswoman said it was time the fleet was modernized.
“While we are in a period of occasionally debating on whether climate change is real, there is no debate on the high cost of diesel,” she said.
She gave an example of the importance of the ferries to everyday life by saying she was planning to head over on the midday ferry to North Haven when she got a text from a “very busy daughter” asking if Chellie could take her grandson to a dentist appointment. So, the congresswoman ended up taking a later ferry.
“I’m very excited that we’re naming this for Captain Dinsmore. Once again, I can’t say enough about the brave captains who take us back and forth and keep our families safe, in all types of weather,” Pingree said.
The new ferry is nearly identical to the Captain Richard Spear other than the electric propulsion capability.
The Dinsmore will be stationed at the Rockland ferry terminal, where the charging station is located, and primarily service the Vinalhaven run. The ferry Captain E. Frank Thompson will also run on the Vinalhaven route but dock overnight on the island.
The Captain Spear, which now serves the Vinalhaven route, will be used for other routes to be determined. The new vessel will move the Captain Henry Lee out of the ferry service rotation. The Lee serves Swan's Island.
The Dinsmore was built in the Senesco Shipyard in North Kingston, Rhode Island, and designed by Gilbert & Associates. The total cost was $21.9 million, with $16.6 million coming from a federal transit authority grant.
The vessel is planned to be staffed by a crew of five: a captain, an engineer, two able-bodied seafarers and one deckhand.
The ferry can carry 250 passengers and 23 vehicles. The cruising speed is 11 knots with a top speed of 13 knots. There is an elevator to meet the Americans with Disabilities Act.
The exclusive electrical operations will be used mainly when the vessel is docked and loading passengers and vessels. The parallel hybrid system will be used during transit to and from Vinalhaven. The system is designed so it can operate with diesel only, if needed.
The life expectancy of the new ferry is 30-plus years.

title: How long is the nationwide ground stop going to last?
text:
How long is the nationwide ground stop going to last? An aviation expert weighs in
The Federal Aviation Administration ordered the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
The United States Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said that this is a telecommunications outage, and it's too early to say how long the ground stop will last.
"It's going to take some time," Mullin said. "This isn't going to turn around and be resolved within the hour ... Once again, everybody is safe; the flights are accounted for; there should be no fear [for] the public."
Mullin said President Donald Trump has been briefed on the situation.
Watch below: Homeland Security secretary gives update on ground stop
While the Homeland Security secretary did not put a timeline on when normal flights would resume, Massport's former director, Tom Kinton, said this won't be a quick fix.
"This is going to take days," he said. "You're going to have canceled flights, you're going to have crews out of position, which means it's going to take a long time to unravel, unfortunately."
Kinton also said that crew hours will become a factor as the ground stoppage continues.
"The vast majority of flights are stuck on the ground, which means eventually crews are going to time out, which means flights are going to be canceled, and now passengers are going to be scrambling to get on other flights leading into some of the busiest travel time this country experiences on an annual basis - before Thanksgiving and then, obviously, Thanksgiving week," Kinton said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Front-center airbags largely unavailable in U.S.
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores why critical vehicle crash safeguards remain a costly optional feature in the U.S.
Then, we examine the crisis of jails serving as de facto mental health facilities and the programs working to break the cycle.
Plus, meet a retired couple bringing rock ‘n’ roll and joy to seniors.
Sacrificing Safety?
Victims of car crashes often recall such events happening “in the blink of an eye,” when in reality, it takes less than half that amount of time.
Particularly when the impact is coming from the side.
A safety device designed to prevent that kind of injury was introduced more than a decade ago: Front-center airbags deploy from the seat or center console to keep a driver from hitting the passenger side door or to prevent a driver and passenger’s heads from colliding.
But those airbags are largely unavailable in the U.S.
Jails not built for long-term care
Experts say prisons and county jails have become destinations for people who need mental health treatment, not time behind bars.
According to multiple reports, three jail systems are among the largest mental health facilities in the country: Rikers Island in New York, Twin Towers Jail in Los Angeles and Cook County Jail in Chicago.
But some people are looking for solutions, hoping to bridge the gap between police and mental health services.
Organ donations for Black Americans
Black Americans face a critical need for organ transplants, yet they experience longer wait times and lower donation rates.
In 2026, African Americans accounted for more than a quarter of those on the organ transplant waiting list.
But at the same time, they made up only about 12% of all donors and nearly a quarter of total transplant recipients nationwide.
Army veteran volunteers
A Valley Army veteran is spending his post-military and post-retirement years volunteering at a Phoenix senior center, offering companionship and practical help to seniors who have few other resources.
Robert Lane can be found at the Desert West Senior Center in the Maryvale neighborhood Monday through Friday, from morning until late afternoon.

title: What you need to know about new child car seat standards coming Dec. 5
text:
(Gray Media) – A new update to child car seat safety standards is fast approaching, changing the requirements for newly manufactured seats.
Starting Dec. 5, 2026, updated federal testing standards will affect how covered car seats are tested for side-impact crashes and how child restraints are tested for frontal crashes.
What’s changing?
Side-impact protection: FMVSS 213a
Covered car seats must meet a federal side-impact performance standard designed to reduce injuries and deaths in crashes where a vehicle is struck from the side.
The test uses a simulated vehicle seat and door to assess how a child restraint performs in a side-impact crash. It’s meant to simulate the kind of collision often called a T-bone crash.
The standard generally covers portable child restraints recommended for a weight range that includes children under 40 pounds or a height range that includes children under about 43 inches. That doesn’t mean a seat is exempt just because it can also be used by larger children.
There are exceptions, including car beds, harness-only restraints and qualifying restraints made only for school buses.
Important date distinction: NHTSA issued the side-impact rule in 2022. Dec. 5, 2026, is its mandatory compliance date, not the date the original rule was first issued.
Updated frontal-impact testing: FMVSS 213b
A separate updated standard becomes mandatory for child restraints manufactured on or after Dec. 5, 2026.
The frontal-crash test will use:
- An updated test seat designed to better represent a modern vehicle’s back seat.
- A simulated lap-and-shoulder belt for testing most restraints, rather than the lap belt used in the older test for many seats.
Basically, the government is updating how it tests car seats for front-end crashes while adding a separate side-impact requirement for covered seats.
Do parents need to buy a new car seat?
Parents are not required to replace their existing car seats simply because of the deadline.
A seat purchased after Dec. 5 may have been manufactured before that date, so the manufacture date, rather than the purchase date alone, matters. Some manufacturers also complied with the newer standards early.
Parents should continue to check that the seat:
- Fits their child and their vehicle.
- Is installed and used according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
- Has not been recalled and is within the manufacturer’s stated usable life.
What about weight limits for forward-facing seats and boosters?
The Child Passenger Safety Board overview describes updated manufacturer labeling requirements:
Manufacturers must specify a minimum forward-facing weight of at least 26.5 pounds.
Manufacturers must specify a minimum booster-seat weight of at least 40 pounds.
These are not instructions to switch a child’s seat as soon as they reach those weights. NHTSA recommends keeping children in each stage as long as they fit within the seat manufacturer’s limits.

title: Hannah Bottigheimer working on memoir about parenthood, identity and caregiving
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Hannah Bottigheimer writes about family, motherhood, mental health, and the intertwined lives of a blended family.
Bottigheimer and her husband have seven children, six chickens, and three cats.
About “The False Finish Line”
The working title of her memoir is “The False Finish Line.”
This is how she describes it:
“‘The False Finish Line’ is a memoir about parenthood, identity, and the risk of losing yourself to caregiving.
My youngest child, Sarah, was fourteen when she became psychotic overnight. In the middle of the night, she woke me up, insisting she was having a brain bleed and that her lungs were collapsing. She believed I was Dr. Ellis Grey from Grey’s Anatomy. Across six psychiatric hospitalizations, she spent nearly a year and a half away from home. Each discharge felt like we had finally made it—until stability gave way to another crisis.
“I told myself that if we could just find the right treatment, our old life would return. That was the “false finish line”: the imagined endpoint around which I had organized my life. The pursuit of my daughter’s recovery became its own kind of captivity, raising a question I was afraid to ask: Could I build a future for myself without abandoning her?
“The challenge became learning to build a meaningful life—for both of us—without making recovery the condition for beginning.”
Essay newsletter
Bottigheimer also writes a newsletter, “Private Acts of Disobedience.” In it, she writes about family, motherhood, mental health and the lives of a blended family.
Reason for writing
Bottigheimer said her family entered a different reality when her daughter became ill.
“I wanted to write honestly about the terror of seeing my child suffer, the search for help, and the uncertainty of what would come next,” Bottigheimer said. “I also wanted to explore the tension between maternal devotion and an identity beyond caregiving: what we expect of mothers, and what those expectations cost us. Writing has helped me examine my own experience and share a story other families might recognize.
Where to find her work
“The False Finish Line” is not yet available for purchase. Information about her writing and updates is available at www.hannahbottigheimer.com.
She is on Instagram at @HannahBottigheimerWrites, as well as on Substack and LinkedIn.

title: ‘All fake’: Man accused of posing as decorated combat veteran, stealing more than $80,000
text:
HAMPTON BAYS, N.Y. (News 12 Long Island) — A man is in a New York jail after authorities said he posed as a decorated combat veteran and stole thousands of dollars from a veterans organization.
The Suffolk County district attorney announced the charges Tuesday.
David Agtsteribbe, the former finance officer for the Hampton Bays American Legion, is accused of stealing more than $80,000 from the group. Investigators said he lied about his service and claimed to be a Purple Heart recipient.
What investigators say about his service
Investigators said Agtsteribbe enlisted in the Army in 1986 and was court-martialed the next year. He pleaded guilty to stealing money from another soldier and received a bad conduct discharge, officials said.
“The exact price for a Purple Heart is someone’s blood, sweat and tears,” Suffolk County District Attorney Ray Tierney said. “That’s what it costs for an actual person to win a Purple Heart. It cost him nothing but lies.”
Tierney said Agtsteribbe also claimed to be a prisoner of war. During the time he claimed to be a prisoner of war, Tierney said, Agtsteribbe was an inmate in upstate New York for a grand larceny conviction.
Fake credentials
The district attorney said Agtsteribbe used fake military credentials. Tierney said he benefited from the lies through membership in veterans organizations and Purple Heart license plates.
“It’s all fake,” Tierney said.
Veteran responds
Ira Freiband, a veteran, said he is hurt and disappointed in Agtsteribbe.
“I’m hurt, more than angry. I’m hurt and I’m hurt, I’m disappointed. I’m disappointed in him,” Freiband said.
Agtsteribbe remains in jail. There has been no comment so far from the commander of the Hampton Bays American Legion.
“He was so good at it. He fooled everybody. He fooled this whole town. We weren’t the only ones that got fooled,” Freiband said.

title: Recommendation: Drift among Maine sturgeon
text:
Murray Carpenter of Belfast is a journalist and author of “Caffeinated” and “Sweet and Deadly.”
As the sturgeon swam slowly along in 3 feet of water, its spine was undulating, serpentine, its flexible tail swinging. The chain of pyramidal scutes along its olive back were conspicuous, pale protuberances. Puffs of mud shot from its gills every few seconds as it foraged along the tidal flat, looking like an ancient beast gliding over primordial ooze. In a way it was — sturgeon evolved 200 million years ago and swam Jurassic waters among dinosaurs.
It was a memorable sighting, enabled by clear estuarine water, high June sun and my vantage from a paddleboard above and just off to its right side as we both drifted up Midcoast Maine’s Passagassawakeag estuary on a flooding tide.
It seemed especially notable because in 30 years of floating, swimming, wading, fishing and generally mucking around in the estuary, I’d seen a sturgeon just once before this year. This year, I had five sightings, and they were at least two different fish — one pushing 4 feet, the other a bit smaller.
The estuary has long links to sturgeon.
In Wabanaki lore, it was known as a place to find sturgeon. The connection inspired artist David Hurley to paint a sturgeon that’s displayed at water’s edge in downtown Belfast. In his 1877 “The History of the City of Belfast,” Joseph Williamson devoted a lengthy passage to parsing the word Passagassawakeag, then wrote, “…sturgeon have never been numerous in our river. The last one seen was in 1869, near City Point.”
Until their populations crashed over a century ago, up to 7 million pounds of sturgeon were harvested annually along the Atlantic coast for their flesh and their roe — caviar. Since 1998, regulators have banned their catch.
Both species of sturgeon in Maine — shortnose sturgeon and the larger Atlantic sturgeon — have been federally protected under the Endangered Species Act since 2012. In an effort to better understand the fish and their habitat, the Maine Department of Marine Resources is now urging Mainers to document sturgeon sightings on an online platform, where it was easy to report my observations.
Over the decades, it’s been amazing to see sturgeon cavorting on recovering rivers in Maine. Shortly after reporting on the demolition of Augusta’s Edwards Dam in 1999, I floated the newly unshackled reach with my wife and our two young daughters. It was a treat to watch 6-foot Atlantic sturgeon leap near us, though we worried about what would happen if one landed on our canoe.
In 2008, I reported on a University of Maine team led by Gayle Zydlewski that found a population of sturgeon in the Penobscot River after a long search. In recent years, while surfing in southern Maine, I’ve enjoyed watching sturgeon leaping in the ocean. And I once drifted over a sturgeon as it moseyed along a rocky point on the north shore of Penobscot Bay’s Sears Island. Zydlewski’s research shows that the sturgeon move throughout the Gulf of Maine, and well beyond.
In a natural world that can feel like it’s unraveling at the seams, Maine sturgeon are symbols of hope and recovery, survival and resilience. And leaving aside these fanciful concepts, it is simply cool to be in the presence of such magnificent fish.
Twice this summer, I saw a sturgeon being tailed by a striped bass, likely ambushing crabs or shrimp flushed by the larger fish. And I once spotted a sturgeon in time to grab a bit of video, though it’s not clear if it’s a shortnose sturgeon or an immature Atlantic sturgeon.
The fish are reminders that whenever you venture outdoors and look around, you’re bound to see some fine aspect of the natural world. It won’t often be a bobcat, a harlequin duck or a humpback whale, but it will be something. Perhaps a late monarch butterfly feeding on asters, a broad winged hawk heading for wintering grounds in Colombia, a red fox in a field at dawn or a snapping turtle crossing the road.
These sightings put us in our place on the planet, sharing it with the creatures who came long before us. Like a sturgeon in a Maine estuary on a warm summer day.

title: Truck driver accused of killing mom, 2 young sons in crash as they were heading to airport
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) - A truck driver in Missouri is accused of killing a mother and her two young sons in a crash as they were heading to the airport.
Eldar Skander, 39, was charged Tuesday with three counts of involuntary manslaughter in the deaths of 35-year-old Olga Sorbalo and her sons, 9-year-old Luis Sorbalo and 6-year-old Samir Sorbalo.
On Wednesday, the of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Skander was “an illegal alien from Ukraine.”
Court documents allege Skander was driving a semi-truck at a high speed on northbound U.S. 71 around 3:20 p.m. when he hit three stopped vehicles.
A preliminary investigation found no signs that the truck’s emergency brakes had been applied, authorities said.
An officer found a tablet on the truck’s floorboard open to YouTube.
The tablet contained the truck’s driving log, and a dash camera may have recorded the crash.
Skander’s address in the court filing listed him as a Chicago resident. Jail records show he is being held at the Jackson County Detention Center with “an additional hold for ICE.”
KCTV has reached out to immigration officials for more information about Skander’s status.

title: Sudden FAA ground stop throws the sports weekend into chaos
text:
The Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights nationwide Friday threw the sports world into chaos, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations, and NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
The FAA issued a notice that said the ground stop was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy later said there was a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide, and that FAA technicians were investigating.
“There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying,” Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said.
Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, eighth-ranked Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games. The Utes play at No. 22 Arizona, the Longhorns visit No. 24 LSU and the Vols are traveling to Texas A&M in three of the bigger games of the weekend.
“The Southeastern Conference is aware of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop and the potential impact on team travel for this weekend’s competitions,” the league said in a statement. “We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses. The safety and well-being of student-athletes, coaches and team personnel remain our highest priority.”
The Longhorns posted on social media a short video of them boarding their plane before the stoppage began. If they ended up taking a bus to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, the trip for the 6:30 p.m. CT kickoff against the Tigers on Saturday would take about seven hours.
“We are grounded and waiting to see when we can leave,” a Texas team spokesman said.
Tennessee spokesman Bill Martin likewise said the Vols had returned to campus and were waiting for more instructions, while Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State and Purdue did the same from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at Iowa.
Other schools affected by the stoppage included No. 19 Ole Miss, Baylor, Washington, Kansas State and Minnesota.
Asked whether Kansas State had an alternative plan for its trip to Baylor, a school spokesman replied: “Nothing at this point.”
San Jose State’s football team had boarded a plane and was on the runway for its trip to Air Force for a game Saturday when the plane turned around and went back to the gate. The team returned to campus and was waiting to see what happens.
It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time. The Big Ten said in a statement that all of its officials had arrived for their scheduled games Saturday.
Several teams were able to take off before the stoppage went into effect, including all those traveling in the Atlantic Coast Conference; Missouri, which was flying to top-ranked Georgia; Duke, which was visiting fifth-ranked Miami; and No. 10 Texas Tech, which posted on social media images of its arrival for a game at Oklahoma State.
Meanwhile, the Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly Friday for games on Saturday. They had just boarded the team plane in New Orleans after playing the Pelicans earlier this week when their flight to Memphis was halted in place.
The Pistons flew earlier in the day to Miami. The Cavaliers, Bulls and Grizzlies play Friday night and were due to fly afterward.
The Cavaliers played in Miami on Friday night and were scheduled to play the Mavericks at home Saturday. Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said about 90 minutes before tip-off that his team was scrambling to find hotel rooms in Miami for Friday night, just in case.
“It’s part of it. You just adapt,” Atkinson said.
There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL on Saturday. The Panthers were among the majority that made it to their destinations before the stoppage began, but the Sharks were left waiting in San Jose to see whether they would be able to travel to Utah.
The FAA did not provide a timeline for restarting flights, leaving sporting events taking place beyond Saturday in limbo. That includes most of the Week 10 schedule in the NFL, along with men’s and women’s college basketball and other sporting events.
JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates were trying to get to South Carolina for their game Sunday against the top-ranked Gamecocks. The team had just boarded its flight at Los Angeles International Airport when the ground stop was issued. After a while, the decision was made to deboard passengers and the team returned to the Galen Center.
For some of the NFL teams, trips via bus would be manageable: Pittsburgh plays at Cincinnati, the Los Angeles Rams play at Arizona, Minnesota is visiting Green Bay and Buffalo is scheduled to play the Jets in East Rutherford, New Jersey.
Story by Dave Skretta, AP Sports Writer. AP Sports Writers Jim Vertuno, Aaron Beard, Tim Reynolds and Beth Harris contributed to this report.

title: Double murder suspect charged again after witnesses lead investigators to hidden remains
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A suspect in a July double murder in Brookwood, Alabama, has been charged with another murder after skeletal remains were found Tuesday behind a Tuscaloosa apartment complex, the Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit said.
On July 6, Brookwood Police were called to do a welfare check around 1 p.m. The woman who rented the home was out of the country and had a co-worker, 31-year-old Jose Felix Alvarez-Duenas, house and dog sitting.
The woman was unable to reach Alvarez-Duenas for some time between July 5 and 6. She accessed several doorbell cameras and saw a suspect, later identified as 24-year-old De’Kendrick Crawford, acting suspiciously.
When Brookwood Police got to the house, they found Alvarez-Duenas inside the entryway. They also found 22-year-old Jazmine Alexis Bates, a University of Alabama student from Chicago, and a dog, dead inside a closet. All had gunshot wounds.
The VCU took over the investigation. Crawford, the renter of the home, Alvarez-Duenas, and Bates reportedly worked together at Buffalo Phil’s in Tuscaloosa.
Crawford had an outstanding felony warrant for shooting into an occupied building in May 2026. In that incident, Crawford was terminated from a contractor job on campus of the University of Alabama, and as he drove away, fired several shots that hit an occupied office building near Coleman Coliseum, authorities said. Warrants were obtained in that case, and Crawford was said to be actively eluding law enforcement.
Based on the video and other physical evidence found on scene, a warrant for capital murder was obtained, and the US Marshals Task Force was contacted to assist.
Within hours, Crawford was found at a relative’s apartment in Northport. Crawford refused to exit, police said, and the apartment building was secured. After a tactical breach and search of the building, Crawford was found hiding in an attic crawlspace and was taken into custody approximately 10 hours after the victims were discovered.
In early November, the VCU said a witness came to authorities claiming Crawford told them that before he allegedly killed Alvarez-Duenas and Bates, he had also killed an unknown man at a different place in Tuscaloosa.
Investigators were able to find other witnesses who also said Crawford had told them differing accounts of this murder. From there, the VCU said investigators pieced together different details from witnesses, compared them to digital evidence, and corroborated some of the places and events Crawford said to witnesses.
On Tuesday, authorities found skeletal remains partially buried in a wooded area behind River Road Apartments.
“The remains were purposely hidden and were only found by the corroborated details Crawford provided to witnesses,” the VCU said.
Crawford was reportedly interviewed before he allegedly denied involvement again. He was charged with murder in the new case.
The VCU said they have not yet identified the remains of the alleged victim. They believe he is a Black man between 40 and 70 years old, and that he may have a Chevy Cruze that was often seen at 10th Avenue Apartments, but authorities do not know if he was a resident at that complex or not.
The remains are being tested by the Alabama Department of Forensic Sciences in hopes of identifying the victim.
Anyone who knows of anyone who fits this description to be missing or believes they have any information is asked to contact the VCU at 205-464-8692.

title: Oregon coach Kelly Graves to coach in 45th state at UMaine game
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine women’s basketball team hosts Oregon tonight in the teams’ first meeting. The game tips off at 7 p.m. Friday.
UMaine is 2-0 this season with wins over Siena College and Merrimack.
The game adds another state to Oregon head coach Kelly Graves’ list of places he has coached.
Graves’ 50-state goal
Graves has made it a point to coach a game in all 50 states.
On Wednesday, Oregon played Vermont in its first-ever game against an America East opponent. After Friday night’s game, Graves will have coached in his 45th state.
“I’m really into maps. I have a big map in my office. When we joined the Big Ten, I was thinking, gosh, I’m going to be going to new places, you know, that I’ve never coached before,” Graves said. “This is my 40th season. When I started putting push pins in my map, I go, dang, I’ve coached in a lot of places. So I decided, you know, maybe let’s see if we can try and cross off all 50.”
Graves said this road trip has been long, adding that Maine is about as far away from Oregon as the team can get. Despite making the trip for games, Graves said he still makes time to enjoy the states the team plays in.
“These are business trips, you know, but you still have a lot of downtime. I don’t need to rest like the players do, so I like to explore best I can,” Graves said. “I love getting on the campuses and walking campuses. That’s kind of been a tradition. That way, I kind of get a feel for the school and things like that.”
While Graves has more time, he said his players also get the chance to experience places they may not visit otherwise.
“Let’s face it, you know, our players don’t get to come up, you know, to a Vermont or a Maine very often,” Graves said. “I think, really good for them.”
‘A win-win for both teams’
Graves said he likes to take his team on the road to help with chemistry in the early season.
“I’ve always tried to take teams on the road early in the season because it’s great for team bonding as well you get to know each other better,” Graves said. “We take their phones away when we’re at meals and other things so that they just spend some time talking and getting to know each other better.”
Graves spent time coaching at a smaller school before making the jump to Oregon. He said he understands the struggle for those schools to schedule “bigger” schools.
“I don’t think enough power for coaches, quite frankly, go to these kind of schools, the smaller mid-majors. I was at Gonzaga for a long time as a head coach there, and it was really difficult to schedule some bigger schools,” Graves said. “I understand how that goes, so this is kind of a win-win in all different ways. I know we’re going to get great competition. It’s going to be a great crowd. Love the arena. I mean, I really do. This is a pretty cool place.”
Earlier in the week, Maine’s head coach said there was excitement leading up to the game.
“We’re excited. I mean, we’re just really excited for the opportunity. It’s not often that a Power 4 team will come to a mid-major in general. You know, never mind Maine. I mean, Maine’s far from Oregon. So we’re really excited that they’re coming here and hopefully we’ll have a great crowd and a great atmosphere,“ said Maine’s head coach Amy Vachon.
Business trip mindset
Graves said the game is more important than checking boxes and said Maine has a excellent team.
“They’ve got good balance. They have players that can attack the basket, score around the rim. They’ve got an excellent inside game,” Graves said. “And then, you know, a lead guard who’s really dang good, you know, and leads the crew.”
Graves said Maine’s three-point shooting could be a factor in the game.
“They can beat you from the three-point line. They’re making over 10 a game and, you know, at over 36%,” Graves said. “We’re not going to have the size advantage like we did the other night. You know, they’re long inside and then their guards are taller. It’s going to be a tough match.”
The matchup will be streaming on ESPN+. The world-famous Red Panda acrobat will perform during halftime the game.

title: NFL quarterback Sam Hartman named as star of next season of ‘The Bachelor’
text:
(Gray News) - The Washington Commanders’ Sam Hartman is set to be the next “Bachelor.”
“Sam Hartman will be looking for love this offseason,” the team said in a press release.
The 27-year-old quarterback will star in the next season of “The Bachelor,” which will be the hit show’s 30th season.
“I’m excited but also very nervous,” Hartman said Friday on “Good Morning America.” “I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl. Thirty is going to be pretty tough.”
Hartman said that he was hesitant at first about being on the show, even nearly turning it down, but said a conversation with former “Bachelor” and NFL player Jesse Palmer changed his mind.
“He kind of gave me the insight of what it is, what it’s not,” Hartman said. “And I think anybody in their right mind, if you get told, ‘Hey, you’ve got a chance to go find the love of your life,’ I know one thing, when people are saying, ‘I do,’ they don’t ask you where you met, they ask if you wanna do it forever, and I don’t see any problem with that.”
Hartman was signed as a free agent with the Washington Commanders in 2024. Prior to the NFL, he played four seasons of college football at Wake Forest before spending a season at Notre Dame.
As for what he is looking for when it comes to love, Hartman said that he is looking for someone with drive and a competitive spirit.
“Competitiveness and somebody that I want to be able to chase. Not chase in a way that, ‘You haven’t texted me back in a week,’ but chase in a way that they have a drive for something and motivates me to wake up every day to chase them.”

title: Decoding hidden meanings behind some emojis and acronyms
text:
(Aging Untold) — Certain emojis and acronyms beyond LOL and BRB used in text messages carry hidden meanings that parents and grandparents may not know.
Jill Story said it is tough to stay on top of the abbreviated language her three daughters use.
“They have a whole language that they use that I’m constantly having to, like, figure out,” Story said.
Story said some of the acronyms her daughters use are even more difficult to decipher.
Chart lists coded emoji meanings
A chart from For Working Parents went viral.
The group’s founder, a former vice principal, detailed what he described as sinister emojis, symbols that could represent something different from what parents might think. The meanings range from drugs to sex to extremism.
Mothers guess at meanings
Neither Story nor two of her mom friends knew that Code 9, or CD9, means “parents are around.”
Aside from a few good guesses, none of the mothers knew all of the potential secret meanings.
One of the mothers said she felt somber and shocked after learning what some of the messages meant.
GNOC: Get naked on camera
Screen Sanity co-founder offers advice
Tracy Foster, co-founder and CEO of Screen Sanity, an organization that helps parents navigate the digital world as parents raise children, said one acronym she feels strongly about is KYS. Foster said it stands for kill yourself.
Foster said it is up to parents to help kids understand the weight of their words, whether explicit or coded.
“You don’t want them to become desensitized,” Foster said.
Foster said parents can start by showing interest in what their children know.
“So often, if you just start to show curiosity and an appreciation for their knowledge, they’ll start to open up,” Foster said.
Story said every generation has a coded language.
“As a mom, I would like to be up on those things,” she said.
