title: Maine lobsterman forfeits excess traps after officials hide tracking devices on his boat
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Surry lobsterman was charged with exceeding lobster trap limits and overfishing in a neighboring fishing zone after state officials placed covert tracking devices on his boat.
Dakoda Gray, 38, is accused of fishing 17 traps over the 800 trap limit off Tremont, a Mount Desert Island town, and of submerging 124 traps more than he was allowed to in a neighboring lobster fishing zone where he wasn’t licensed, according to court records.
Maine Marine Patrol officers put secret tracking devices on Gray’s fishing boat, “Sweet Melissa,” after obtaining a search warrant signed by an Ellsworth District Court judge in August, according to court records.
Gray was charged in September.
The search warrant and subsequent tracking devices resulted from an investigation into whether Gray was using untagged lobster traps and fishing over the 49 percent limit in a non-declared lobster zone, according to court records. Lobstermen cannot use more than 800 traps, and have to have state-issued tags on the traps they are licensed for.
A lobsterman can fish no more than 49 percent of their total traps in a secondary lobster management zone, according to state law. Gray is accused of exceeding that limit.
Jeff Nichols, a Department of Marine Resources spokesperson, declined to provide additional information on the pending case. It was not immediately clear the nature of the probable cause that led to the search warrant.
Gray failed to appear in court in early November, which led to the forfeiture of the 124 traps he set in the neighboring zone to the state, according to Will Ashe, his attorney.
Ashe did not know any details surrounding the tracking devices, he said, adding that he had only been retained to represent Gray in the matter related to the trap limit violations.
Gray also faces a Department of Marine Resources administrative license suspension hearing, Nichols said.
The tracking device is one of several tools officers use to investigate marine fisheries violations, Nichols said.
Hancock County District Attorney Robert Granger did not respond to an inquiry about the case from the Bangor Daily News.

title: WATCH: Master carver engraves crystals from last year's New Year's Eve ball
text:
WATCH: Master carver engraves crystals from last year's New Year's Eve ball
Dropped in Times Square on New Year’s Eve, the Constellation Ball was created with 5,280 Waterford crystals that incorporated three different designs to represent life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026.
On Thursday, people were able to buy one of those crystals and get their names engraved on it as a memento. The crystals will be replaced with new ones to ring in 2027 with a theme yet to be announced.
It takes about three days to make each crystal by hand for the roughly 12-foot (3.7-meter) geodesic sphere that weighs 12,350 pounds (5,602 kilograms). The process involves the design, molding, kilning and the finishing of each crystal. Waterford, a longtime luxury crystal brand from Ireland, has designed the New Year’s Eve ball’s crystals for over 25 years. Some new crystals are swapped in every year.
Watch the video above to see how the crystals were engraved
Richard White, a master cutter for Waterford, flew to New York City to engrave the crystals that vary in size from 1.5 to 4 inches in diameter. White used a small electronic pen with a diamond tip to engrave names on the small crystal pieces Thursday.
“To be actually here and to be up close, personal with it, is a real excitement for me,” White said of seeing the completed ball.
Delfin Ortiz, general manager and senior vice president of One Times Square, the 26-story building from which the annual ball drops, said the crystals are part of “tomorrow's history.”
A New Year’s Eve ball was first dropped in Times Square in 1907. Built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr, the 700-pound (318-kilogram), 5-foot (1.52-meter) diameter ball was made of iron and wood and featured 100 25-watt light bulbs. Nine versions of the ball have been featured in the century-plus since that first celebration.
The only years no ball drop occurred were 1942 and 1943, when the city instituted a nightly “dimout” during World War II to protect itself from attacks. Crowds instead celebrated the new year with a moment of silence followed by chimes rung from the base of One Times Square.
One Times Square began offering crystals for purchase last year, though Thursday marks the first time they were engraved.
The prices of the crystals range between $140 and $195, depending on the size.

title: New Congress must focus on affordability, ending war in Iran and immigration
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Leslie B. Otten is the founder of American Skiing Co., and former vice chair of the Boston Red Sox. He is also the chair emeritus of Maine Adaptive Skiing and of Cromwell Center for Disabilities Awareness. He is a first generation American and was a Republican candidate for governor in 2010.
To the members of the incoming Congress:
In a few short weeks, you will take office as representatives of the American people. You were elected to serve the interests of the United States and its citizens. As you begin your work, I ask that you focus on the challenges that matter most to the people who sent you to Washington.
First, work toward ending the war in Iran. It was ill-conceived and poorly executed, and it has imposed significant economic pain on much of the Western world through crippling energy prices. Diesel fuel at $6.50 per gallon, nearly double what many paid before, affects everything from transportation costs to the food on our dinner tables. The war with Iran, which began on Feb. 28, has cost the broader U.S. economy $265 billion or more, equating to roughly $2,000 per U.S. household, according to estimates from Moody’s Analytics. Direct taxpayer spending by the Pentagon accounts for $47.1 billion of that total — or about $351 per household across roughly 134 million U.S. households.
There are no winning scenarios here, only outcomes that are less bad than others. We understand that. It is time to stop digging, accept the consequences and begin the process of resetting.
Next, address the tariff debacle. This policy was poorly conceived and erratically executed, succeeding primarily in disrupting supply chains and fueling inflationary pressure. As legislators holding the power of the purse, you have a responsibility to pursue trade policies that strengthen rather than weaken our economy, our farmers, our businesses and our working families.
Our way of life is not under imminent threat, and no administration should wield unchecked economic authority. The limits of executive power are defined by the Constitution and by laws enacted by Congress. Where those limits are unclear, Congress should make them clear.
We are a nation of immigrants, except for those whose families were here before the rest of us arrived. To grow and prosper, our country still needs people who believe in democracy, freedom of religion and economic opportunity. Immigration should be legal, orderly and consistent with our values. We must defend against illegal immigration and deport those here unlawfully who have committed serious crimes. Our borders should be secure and open only to those whom we choose to admit under fair and consistently applied standards.
For those who are here illegally but are contributing members of our communities and who otherwise meet those standards, there should be a fair and reasonable path to remain. Immigration enforcement may have a role to play, but it should not be defined by shock and awe. This is a problem that Congress can solve through honest compromise and clear-eyed purpose.
The things that matter most cost too much. We are talking about the basics: a home, a car, food, energy, education and healthcare. What happened to the American Dream? The average first-time homebuyer is now around 40 years old. Add a 30-year mortgage, and retirement becomes a goal to pursue at 70.
Too many Americans feel like they are standing outside looking in. Costs are rising faster than wages, and the cost of living has become the defining economic challenge of our time. Inflation is the battle that needs to be won. Wars and tariffs are not helping families afford food or shelter. Pass laws that support farmers, expand affordable and reliable energy production, help first-time homebuyers, lower the cost of education, and give working families a fair chance to get ahead.
Two final requests. First, end corruption in both the executive branch and Congress. It is un-American and contrary to everything we stand for. Second, reject revenge politics. Revenge appeals to our worst instincts. It is time to take the high road and solve real problems, not settling scores. History is usually harsh enough without our help. Americans can spend their time getting ahead or getting even, but they should not do both. Put retribution aside, correct course and govern for the greater good.
The American people have entrusted you with a great responsibility. We ask only that you meet it with integrity, courage and common sense.

title: Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado loses House seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher
text:
DENVER (AP) — Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeated Rep. Lauren Boebert for a Colorado U.S. House seat on Friday, ousting a three-term Republican and staple of conservative media.
Laubacher is a former Navy rear admiral. Her win in the 4th Congressional District race is just one of several surprising Republican losses in what’s shaping up to be the most lopsided election in half a century.
Boebert embodied this decade’s version of Republican politics. The telegenic owner of a gun-themed restaurant named “Shooters Grill” in the western Colorado town of Rifle, she catapulted to notoriety alongside President Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.
Once elected to Congress, she refused to pass through metal detectors at the U.S. Capitol and taunted Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar as part of the “jihad squad.” After barely surviving her first reelection campaign, Boebert moved across Colorado to a more Republican district.
Republicans carried the 4th District by more than 18 percentage points in 2024. But even that wasn’t safe for her in this year’s midterm elections.
Boebert acknowledged the widespread losses as she returned to the Capitol this week, saying, “We collectively failed.”
“It’s very clear,” she said. “The American people let us know we have failed in this governing experience for this Congress.”
In a video posted on her social media account Friday, Boebert said she called Laubacher to congratulate her on her victory and thanked the district’s residents.

title: Winthrop football beats Freeport for 2nd straight Class D South title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FREEPORT — Ross Fichthorn fought all season to have a game like this.
Fichthorn, in his second game back from a knee injury, scored on a 37-yard run in the fourth quarter to help Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale beat Freeport 13-3 in the Class D South football final Friday night at Joan Benoit Samuelson Track and Turf Field.
The second-seeded Ramblers (9-1) will defend their state title next weekend against the winner of the North final on Saturday between Winslow and John Bapst.
Fichthorn suffered a torn MCL and a partially torn patellar tendon in his right knee in the Ramblers’ season opener against Lisbon on Sept. 4. He ran for 103 yards on 12 carries Friday night.
“My (regular) season got taken away with this injury. I’m just so blessed to be back, so blessed to finally be here,” Fichthorn said. “(The knee) has been feeling great. … A lot of rehab work. I always had a positive mindset, I prayed a lot. I give all thanks to the Lord that I’m back.”
Top-seeded Freeport finishes 7-3. Senior quarterback Andrew Thomas ran for 79 yards on 10 carries before leaving because of an injury.
The Ramblers trailed 3-0 to start the fourth quarter. Fichthorn took a handoff from quarterback Porter Lavigne and initially headed to his right before cutting back to his left, where he found open field and made his way to the end zone. Lavigne’s extra point gave Winthrop a 7-3 lead with 11:48 left in the game.
“Freeport flows (to the ball) really well, they have some really tough players,” Fichthorn said. “I kept my eye on the cutback lane, I finally saw it and ran for that (end zone) pylon like it was no tomorrow.”
Tristyan Ortiz intercepted a pass by Freeport’s Sam Willard on the next series, setting the Ramblers up on the Freeport 45. Seven plays later, Ortiz scored on a 3-yard run to make it 13-3.
Willard took over at quarterback after the injury to Thomas.
Freeport drove to Winthrop 22 on the next possession, but Carter Rand intercepted a Willard pass to seal the win.
Winthrop’s only loss this season was to Freeport, 29-28 on Sept. 11 in Freeport.
“We worked real hard this year, coming off the loss to them,” said Rand. “We came back, had a great game plan against them like always, and got it done … We had a good shutdown defense all game, but after those three points, we just locked in.”
The first half was a defensive battle. Freeport stopped Winthrop’s rushing attack by putting eight defenders in the box, daring the Ramblers pass. Winthrop also struggled with penalties in the first half, including two personal foul penalties on defense late in the second quarter. The Falcons took advantage, getting a 34-yard field goal from sophomore kicker Bryson Jack.
“We just wanted to outphysical (Freeport) and make some things happen,” said Winthrop coach Joel Stoneton. “We told them at halftime, ‘Guys, they just went down the field on penalties. We’re shooting ourselves in the foot. Settle down, play ball. Let’s keep going.'”
Winthrop has seven state championships, including two shared Class C titles in 1968 and 1975. The Ramblers beat Winslow 41-14 last season for their first Gold Ball since 2000.

title: New Orleans cruise line collision: What we know
text:
New Orleans cruise line collision: What we know amid rescues, massive response
Emergency crews are on the scene of a boat crash near the Port of New Orleans.
According to the Port of New Orleans, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage while the cruise ship was docked on the Mississippi River outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place.
At the time of the incident, approximately 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage.
Rescues were underway for 12 people in the water.
Below is everything we know about the rescue operation and collision so far.
What we know about American Cruise Lines
American Cruise Lines is the largest U.S. river and small-ship cruise line.
The cruise line has over 25 ships operating solely in the U.S. and 100% owned and operated.
What we know about the crash
Multiple agencies are responding to a boat crash in the Mississippi River.
At 12:30 p.m. local time, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage while the cruise ship was docked on the Mississippi River outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place.
The American Heritage had docked approximately two hours earlier to begin passenger disembarkation, according to Port NOLA.
At the time of the incident, approximately 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage.
Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard, and emergency medical personnel are on scene, conducting rescue and response operations.
Passengers are being brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building, located at 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, for triage and assistance, according to Port officials.
"Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders. This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the allision have not yet been confirmed. Additional updates will be provided as information is confirmed," the Port issued a news release.

title: Family Legacy Continues with Damariscotta Jewelry Store
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tucked away behind Best Thai in downtown Damariscotta, a new jewelry store strives to have something for everyone.
Alexandra’s Fine Jewelry officially opened at 15 Courtyard St. on Monday, Nov. 9, commemorated with a ribbon-cutting with the Damariscotta Region Chamber of Commerce and Information Bureau.
Owner Alexandra Newell said she looks forward to expanding her business into a physical location. For the past few years, Newell has been making and selling her jewelry from home. Her at-home operation has been going on for years, first as a side gig alongside her day job and then full force once the COVID-19 pandemic started.
“My goal is that I will have kind of something for everybody,” Newell said.
As a second generation gemologist and jeweler, Newell said making and selling jewelry is “in my blood.”
Newell’s jewelry ranges from the everyday items like stud earrings to more fine jewelry like a diamond tennis bracelet. Newell said she thinks the area needed a local jewelry store that can carry gifts that are on the higher end of the price range as well as pieces that are less than $200.
Most of the jewelry in store is made by Newell. She said her love for creating things helps inspire different pieces and she hopes to meet the needs of all of her customers. Whether that is through working with someone on creating their dream ring or finding what she already has in stock, she wants to have a variety that is accessible to everyone.
Originally from California, Newell and her family moved to Maine when she was around 12 years old. Her parents would go on to operate Chambers Jewelers in Thomaston, which is still open and run by her stepmother today.
Newell’s love for jewelry started with her father, who was also a gemologist. She said she has fond memories of working alongside him as a little girl, helping design different pieces and working with gemstones.
“It’s kind of inevitable that eventually, I think, have come to this point in my life,” Newell said.
After working at the jewelry bench throughout high school, Newell went off to the Gemological Institute of America in Carlsbad, Calif. She said she always knew she wanted to go to school there and became a graduate gemologist in 2015.
“My dad was very excited about that and so now I’m the second generation jeweler and gemologist in the family,” Newell said. “I’m kind of carrying on his legacy of passion with gems and jewelry and all things pretty and sparkly.”
Before creating her own business, Newell worked at art galleries that sold high-end jewelry, starting at Springer’s Jewelers in Bath. She also did wholesale work for other local jewelers.
In the store, customers will find a lot of silver, two-tone, precious metal, and gold items. The materials Newell uses for her pieces are sourced from all over the country. Newell said because she has been in the industry for so long, she has been able to develop relationships with people everywhere from California to Massachusetts.
By having such a good relationship with her vendors, Newell said she is more educated about what she is selling her customers.
Newell enjoys working with people directly and building relationships with her clients, she said. By doing so, she is able to sit down with a customer and explain what needs to be fixed or educate someone about how to care for a specific piece.
“There’s so many different aspects with the industry and there’s never a dull moment,” Newell said.
Looking toward the future, Newell said she hopes to incorporate local artists in her business by displaying their work on her walls. Due to the amount of blank space there is in her storefront, it is the perfect place to highlight creative people in the community, she said.
“I just think there’s so many artists here and there are so many creative people, and it would be a great spot to just showcase their work,” Newell said.
For now, most repairs will be made at Newell’s home, but she said she will like to get to a point where she can do more servicing in store. She said she wants customers to be able to come in with a quick turnaround, where they can drop off a broken chain, leave to get a cup of coffee, and come back to it fixed.
“I think my hope is that because I’ve put so much time and effort into this as my career, I think it’s going to do really good,” Newell said.
For more information on Alexandra’s Fine Jewelry, call 975-9665, email [email protected], or find Alexandra Newell Jewelry on Facebook.

title: The Latest: Now Democrats have to figure out 'What's Next'
text:
Following a historic blue wave of midterm election wins, Democrats are gathering in Denver for a What’s Next conference hosted by a new group called Majority Democrats.
President Donald Trump wants Vice President JD Vance to talk less about the Iran war and more about corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states. Vance’s blunt post-election analysis blaming the war and its economic reverberations for the sweeping Republican losses was getting attention.
And the sweeping Democratic gains in Congress are teeing up an onslaught of expected investigations into the Justice Department, which has functioned for nearly two years as an extension of the White House, unchecked by a Republican-controlled Congress as it pursued investigations into Trump’s enemies, fired waves of career employees and defended the administration in ways that judges across the country repeatedly deemed legally dubious.
Here’s the Latest:
Trump praises Democrat Scott Colom for courting MAGA voters at his Mississippi rally
Trump on Thursday heaped praise on Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom for courting some of his hardcore MAGA supporters in the final days of the midterm election campaign, a rare example of the Republican president showing admiration for a Democrat.
When the president traveled to Corinth, Mississippi, last month to campaign for incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Trump denigrated Colom as a “Marxist radical,” a “fake” and a “shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate.”
But on Thursday, during an appearance on Stephen A. Smith’s “Straight Shooter” podcast, Trump acknowledged that Colom demonstrated chutzpah by showing up at the Trump rally to mingle with some of the Republican president’s staunchest “Make America Great Again” supporters.
“I heard it the other day, where I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line, telling everybody on the line what a good job he did,” Trump said of Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor who capitalized on the electorate’s discontent with the economy in his successful underdog campaign. “I give him a lot of credit for that.”
Democrats flock to Denver for a post-midterms introspection-turned-celebration
Fresh off the best electoral performance in half a century, Democratic officials and strategists converged on Denver Thursday to plot a further course for the party and revel in their gains.
The two-day What’s Next conference, hosted by a new group called Majority Democrats, was put on politicos’ calendars months ago as another stepping stone as the party charted its way out of its post-2024 political wilderness.
Now Democrats will have to figure out what to do with majorities in both chambers of Congress and control of at least 12 new state legislative chambers.
“The fever has broken. The fog has lifted,” said Mitch Landrieu, the former Democratic mayor of New Orleans. “And now it falls upon us to rebuild the foundation of this great nation and to fulfill the promise of America.”
Barely a week after voters repudiated Trump and his Republican Party, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico said Democrats must work with him. Voters are hungry for results and can’t wait two years for Trump to leave office, he said, urging Democrats to avoid both intraparty fights and excessive caution.
Trump’s Justice Department faces a new era of scrutiny under a Democratic-led Congress
The Justice Department has functioned for nearly two years as an extension of the White House, unchecked by a Republican-controlled Congress as it pursued investigations into President Donald Trump’s enemies, fired waves of career employees and defended administration stances that judges across the country repeatedly deemed legally dubious.
Now, sweeping Democratic gains in Congress have shifted the balance of power in Washington, teeing up an onslaught of expected investigations into those actions and others as well as scrutiny from the majority party that the current Justice Department had until now managed to skirt.
The department has, at least publicly, appeared unbowed by the altered landscape.
Attorney General Todd Blanche says the department will cooperate with Congress but has also insisted that “we will not back down” from the Republican president’s agenda. Meanwhile, a top aide told prosecutors on a call to prepare to be on “wartime” footing and a U.S. attorney publicly warned a top Democrat about planned congressional investigations.
Trump bluntly tells JD Vance to shift focus from Iran to targeting ‘corruption and crime’ at home
President Donald Trump on Thursday directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president says is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month-old war, has been blunt in blaming the war — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections in the United States.
But Trump brusquely told the vice president in a social media post Thursday to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing — and perhaps more politically salient — issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls.
Trump earlier this week said he believed the war “militarily is effectively over,” and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign.

title: Jails have become destinations for people who need mental health treatment
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Experts say prisons and county jails have become destinations for people who need mental health treatment, not time behind bars.
A 911 call in Michigan
In May 2024, Cynthia Marek called 911 in Ingham County, Michigan, seeking help for her son, Brandon Labrie, who was experiencing a mental health emergency.
Within seconds, the crisis escalated into a stabbing. Labrie was charged in his mother’s death.
His father, Steve Labrie, spent more than three decades as a registered nurse in state-run psychiatric hospitals. He said weeks before the attack, his son had attempted suicide by overdose.
Steve Labrie said the family was told at the time that Brandon would be placed in a long-term mental health facility. He said that never happened.
“I’ve seen a lot of things in my life. It was, in my opinion, preventable,” Steve Labrie said.
He said he does not know what type of mental health treatment his son will receive.
“My guess is, if he gets any, it’s minimal. I wish I had those answers. I wish I knew,” Steve Labrie said.
Jails not built for long-term care
Mental health advocates say stories like this reflect a national reality. In many places, jails have become de facto mental health facilities, even though they are not built or staffed to provide long-term care, advocates said.
According to the National Alliance on Mental Illness, 60% of people with a history of mental illness do not receive treatment while incarcerated. Once people are locked up, it is challenging for them to remain on medication regimens.
William Malcom runs mental health services for the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office in South Carolina.
“We are the largest mental health facility in Charleston County and we really shouldn’t be,” Malcom said.
He said what he is seeing is happening nationwide.
“I don’t think this is really unique to Charleston County. This happens all over the country,” Malcom said.
Malcom said that when communities do not have enough places to take someone in crisis, jail can become the default.
Some police departments and sheriff’s offices are exploring changes to how they respond to mental health calls.
Zach Andrews is the mental health officer for Shelby County, Alabama. He responds to crisis scenes and trains deputies in crisis intervention.
“People experience mental health crisis pretty often, and I think the ones that make the news are those severe cases where potentially it was not handled in the most appropriate situation,” Andrews said.
The approach involves sending a mix of officers and mental health clinicians or peer specialists to de-escalate calls involving someone in crisis, connect the person to treatment and avoid jail.
The first crisis intervention team model was developed in Memphis in the late 1980s. It now exists in more than 2,700 communities across the U.S.
“CIT training is vital. Because what it’s doing, it’s training law enforcement and equipping them with tools and strategies to be able to handle those intense situations,” Andrews said.
A program for people leaving jail or prison
For people already in the court system, a handful of states, including North Carolina, are trying a model called Forensic Assertive Community Treatment, or FACT.
The program provides mental health care, housing help, peer support and court oversight for people with severe mental illness who have been released from jail or prison.
Angel Nelson is a peer support specialist for the FACT team in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. She said she knows how fast a personal crisis can spiral.
“Just being without the things we need, like food, the necessities, I started shoplifting, to get what I need,” Nelson said.
Nelson said trauma at a young age forced her into survival mode, leading to theft, addiction and repeated jail time. She said she started abusing drugs at age 9 and committed her first crime a few years later.
She said the turning point came when a judge gave her a choice: extensive mental health treatment or a lifetime behind bars.
“The first time, I went to the store by myself and didn’t steal nothing. That was the most awesome feeling I had ever felt in my life. I get so emotional because I never knew I could do that,” Nelson said.
Nelson now guides FACT participants through experiences she knows firsthand. She said that type of accountability and treatment saved her life.
“I was diagnosed with anxiety and postpartum depression,” Nelson said. “I was even told in one of my abuse group that the stealing could have come from trying to take back what was taken from me. And that was my innocence.”
Update on Brandon Labrie’s case
In April 2026, Brandon Labrie reached an agreement to plead guilty but mentally ill to second-degree murder. The following month, a judge sentenced him to 25 to 50 years in prison.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. Help is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

title: Jay aims to draft solar ordinance by April town meeting
Belfast approves loan for bike shop to finish brownfield cleanup
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BELFAST, Maine — In early 2024, Chris Gardner knew the bike shop he runs in Belfast was outgrowing its location.
CG Bikes opened in 2019 at 39 Main St., sharing the first-floor retail space with Downshift Coffee.
Gardner began looking for a new home for CG Bikes and found an ideal space — a vacant 1,260-square-foot former gas station and auto repair garage — about a mile away.
“It allowed us to be on one floor, have our own parking lot,” Gardner said. “The visibility was really good. It just made a lot of sense. It seemed like the perfect spot for a bike shop.”
The paved lot outside has plenty of room for customer parking and the fleet of bikes Gardner rents daily during the tourist season. On warm days, he opens the two garage doors for easy access to his always-busy repair shop and the sales floor, which features new and used bikes, apparel, shoes and gear for hardcore and casual cyclists alike.
Gardner leased the space and wondered whether it could one day fulfill his long-term vision of owning the property where his business operates.
“It gives you something to build toward as a business owner. And it gives you stability and some ability to control your own costs,” Gardner said. “That’s not to say that I imagined that this might be for sale or knew it might be for sale, and it wasn’t.”
A year and a half after signing his lease, Gardner approached his landlord about buying the garage. The two worked out a deal, and Gardner began exploring what it would take to build a residence on the site.
“I knew it was a gas station. I knew tanks had been removed in the past,” Gardner said. “I just knew that through word of mouth and living here.”
An earlier environmental assessment of the site revealed a toxic soup below ground: petroleum hydrocarbons, volatile petroleum hydrocarbons, polychlorinated biphenyls and heavy metals, including arsenic, barium, cadmium, chromium, lead, mercury and selenium. The property’s Declaration of Environmental Covenants, administered through the Maine Department of Environmental Protection’s Voluntary Response Action Program, prohibits residential construction and allows only industrial or commercial activities on-site.
Before closing on the property, however, Gardner received a new U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Phase I Environmental Site Assessment through Belfast’s Brownfields Assessment Program, a key step opening a pathway to redevelop the site.
Belfast now has 46 brownfield sites in varying stages of assessment, review and cleanup, according to the U.S. EPA’s Brownfields Near You directory.
At a recent meeting, the Belfast City Council discussed and voted on two of those sites, including CG Bikes — formerly Blood’s Garage — at 34 Northport Ave.
“So, in addition to recently receiving our second cleanup subgrant application, we have received our first cleanup loan application,” Belfast Economic Development Director Thomas Kittredge told city councilors Nov. 4. “We received an application for a cleanup loan from Velo Garage LLC, or Chris Gardner, the owner of [a] 0.35-acre parcel at 34 Northport Ave.”
The city of Belfast is using a $1 million grant from the U.S. EPA to capitalize a Brownfields Revolving Loan and Subgrant Program. For-profit businesses can apply for loans, and nonprofit organizations can apply for grants, to clean up environmental contamination on their properties.
Gardner applied for $250,000 in loan funding through the program at a zero percent interest rate with deferred repayment. Under the cleanup plan outlined in his application, crews will excavate and dispose of contaminated soil off-site, install a vapor barrier and sub-slab depressurization system, and cap the remaining on-site soil with engineered cover systems approved by the Maine DEP.
In one of her final votes, outgoing Belfast Councilor Mary Mortier led a 5-0 approval of the loan.
“So, Chris Gardner’s a local entrepreneur and he has grown his business from a little tiny business in a leased space. And now he owns a building in a very visible place that he can put a sign out for people that drive into town on a main drag to park their car here and rent a bicycle and visit our area,” Mortier said. “This is exciting growth.”
Even with the city’s financing approved, however, Gardner said he has not yet committed to building a residence on the property.
“There’s still a lot to be figured out,” Gardner said. “We have to consider the housing market and whether this is the right time to do this project.”
If he decides to proceed with the redevelopment, Gardner can draw on the $250,000 loan to complete the brownfield cleanup required to meet state standards and make the site safe for his family.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that is why he is running.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race, which will be the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote, even before Van Hollen entered the race. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election and many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal.
Making the pitch for his reelection, Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer opened discussion on a broad plan for their first 100 days in power that included health care and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war.
“I’m going to win it,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.
In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.
“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
Divisions over Schumer have simmered over the last two years
While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025, when Schumer was put on the defensive after he sided with Republicans on a spending vote.
Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.
Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.
While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least two backers: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, and progressive standard bearer Bernie Sanders.
El Sayed posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.”
“I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”
Sen. Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, held a press conference Tuesday announcing he would not support Schumer. He posted Thursday night that the American people “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats.”
Van Hollen has not yet laid out his own agenda, but he has criticized Schumer for his ties to Israel and other special interests.
While Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, he has strongly criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza.
Schumer says he has broad support
Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week. Beyond the election wins, those who support him say being the leader is a difficult job, experience is necessary and Schumer has proven himself with legislative successes when they held the Senate under President Joe Biden.
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” posted Maine Sen. Angus King, another independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the leadership election.
“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” King wrote.
Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., also posted her support Thursday evening:
Cortez Masto said Schumer was key in “securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader.”

title: Creator of ‘We Do Not Care Club’ describes first video, response from followers
text:
(Aging Untold) — Melani Sanders is a social media sensation now, but there was a time when the creator of the popular “We Do Not Care Club” wasn’t one to be in front of the camera.
That changed one day when she decided that she had reached capacity. She was already tired and still had so much to do. Instead, she recorded a video from her car in the parking lot of her local Whole Foods.
In it, she announced a new club — the WDNC, the We Do Not Care Club — and asked if anyone wanted to join her.
After posting it to all of her social platforms, she learned that people did!
Now millions have watched Sanders’ videos that address perimenopause, menopause and life after menopause.
She described the community as “that sisterhood that we need.”
Her book, “The Official We Do Not Care Club Handbook,” is a New York Times bestseller, and Sanders has gone on a nine-city, sold-out tour.
“And I did everything scared,” she said.
How the club started
In an interview with Aging Untold’s aging well coach Katherine Ambrose and board-certified physician Dr. Rhea Rogers, Sanders said she had gone to Whole Foods for ashwagandha.
In the parking lot after that shopping trip, she looked in the mirror and thought of all the things she had to do, including laundry, cooking dinner and taking a book to the library.
“And then I just said, you know what? No, you don’t,” Sanders said. “I am at capacity. I’m tired. My body is tired.”
Sanders said she’d had a hysterectomy some months before and thinks her body went into shock.
“But at that moment, in that car, I was just tired,” Sanders said. “I had had it with myself. I had it with my family, with my friends. I just had it and I was over it.”
So she hit record to see if anyone wanted to join her.
In the 20 minutes between posting that video to all of her platforms and arriving home, Sanders was gaining hundreds of thousands of followers, she said.
Response from followers
Sanders said she was “a little confused” by the response. She has been a creator for years and has had viral content before, but she said, “this was just something different.”
Within a few weeks, millions of people were following Sanders.
She said she became scared and for a while, she turned off her computer. Then, she decided to read the comments.
“One of the main things that women were saying was, ‘me too, me too,’ and ‘thank you for speaking up, thank you for using your voice,’” Sanders said. “All of this is just with Melani just being Melani.”
That was enough in that moment, Sanders said, and over the past year she is “slowly coming to grips with I’m enough.”
Menopause and perimenopause experience
What has surprised Sanders most about the menopause or perimenopause experience is that nobody was talking about it, she said.
Sanders said she had a great surgeon for her hysterectomy but was not told anything about perimenopause or menopause. She had to figure it out on her own.
Community and announcements
A big part of the We Do Not Care Club is Sanders’ funny “special announcements.”
She said members send ideas for them in the comments.
“‘Everyone, we’re all putting the world on notice of what we ‘simply just do not care much about anymore,’” Sanders said.
Sanders said the support from the “We Do Not Care Club” gives her courage.

title: Going back to school in retirement can build brain health and new connections
text:
(Aging Untold) — Schooling does not end for some people in retirement. They are auditing classes, joining lifelong learning programs or training for a new job. The cost can be low or even free, but it still takes time.
Why learning later in life matters
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said she sees going back to college later in life as personal enrichment.
“Learning is a lifetime thing,” Cradduck said. “We all should participate in learning all along. You’re totally keeping your brain active, but you’re also building some relationships.”
Cradduck said classroom education puts older adults in a room with a lot of younger people.
“You’re letting them see what they have the potential to do and what they can still do,” Cradduck said.
New connections in the brain and in life
Dr. Rhea Rogers said this is a way of “establishing neuroplasticity.”
“It’s always about making new connections, be it in the brain, be it in life, be it socially,” Rogers said. “And all the different benefits of interacting with the younger people and the older people, they all have a benefit to show each other.”
“It’s never too late”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a story of an 84-year-old caregiver who wanted to further her career and become a certified nursing assistant.
“And she went to school, and she got her nursing certificate. She got written up in the paper,” O’Rourke said. “She wanted a different kind of job and wanted to be tasked with more difficult things to do.”
O’Rourke said she was so proud of the woman.
“If it is a dream of yours, here it is. It’s never too late,” she said.
Paying for it
Nearly every state offers older adults free or discounted tuition to audit or take classes at public universities, according to AARP.
“When you’re 65 and older, you can go to school for free. A lot of the universities and a lot of the colleges, you don’t have to pay for the degree. So if you’ve been struggling with whether to have school debt or not, you won’t have it. And you can still get the education,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers added that there may also be military benefits for veterans, including some who may be disabled.
More than a college campus
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said there is also a lot of good community education.
“There’s colleges that put on lifelong learning for seniors. There’s also a lot of professionals and organizations that put on education that’s very popular for active adults. Longevity is really changing how we view adult learning and opportunities,” she said.
O’Rourke said there were local colleges where she worked that had lifelong learning for older adults, and it was highly sophisticated. The waiting list to get in was three years long.
“It’s really going to help you stay sharp, give you more interesting things to discuss, new things. And also what a great legacy builder, showing people what their potential is, that you can just keep on going and keep learning and having fun,” Ambrose said.

title: Davis V. Goliath: a small town fight against big data
text:
TUCKER COUNTY, W.Va. — Data centers were on the ballot for the first time in a U.S. election, according to Ballotpedia, which counted 47 local ballot measures dealing with data centers in the midterms. Voters chose to curb data center development in their communities in 46 of them.
Residents of one West Virginia community said they were not given that choice.
Proposed data center
The small mountain town in Tucker County is home to the Blackwater River and twin ski mountains. Tourism is the town’s lifeblood, and a proposed 10,000-acre natural gas-powered data center now threatens it.
Jane Browning, owner of Ranger Jane, said tourism makes up most of her business.
“Tourism is 80 percent of my business, and if there’s no tourism, there’s no business,” Browning said.
If completed, the data center would be the largest in the world, measuring slightly smaller than Manhattan.
Governor and residents
West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey believes the project will be a boon for the state.
“We’re going to make sure that the water’s addressed, the environment’s addressed, that the power bills are lower, it’s going to get handled the right way,” Morrisey said.
Residents described the situation differently. One said, “It came out of nowhere, there was no warning, there was no opportunity to say no.” Another said, “We were never given a choice, never given a voice.” A third said, “There’s something here that we don’t know.”
Developer’s recorded comments
North Carolina-based developer Ted McGavran of Fundamental Data said on a hot mic in July why West Virginia was chosen.
“Up in West Virginia, we’re the guys that wrote the bill and got it through the Legislature. We can do pretty much whatever we want to do up there,” McGavran said.
Morrisey denied that claim.
The bill’s sponsor is West Virginia Speaker of the House Roger Hanshaw. Hanshaw also serves as the lawyer for Fundamental Data, the company behind the project. Multiple requests for comment have not received a response.
Morrisey maintains the state is acting in good faith and said, “Nothing’s been approved.”
Public filings show the project’s air permits were approved Aug. 15.
Federal legislation
The issue has reached Washington. Sens. Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse are introducing a data center permitting reform bill.
“When a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply. Cost, water resources, infrastructure and local economy. In order for them to make a good decision,” Sen. Heinrich said.

title: The US flu season is off to a very early start. It's targeting the South and West now
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. flu season is off to a very early start, and it’s quickly intensifying.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday posted its latest update, reporting that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before.
The CDC also said that more than 3% of doctors’ office visits last week were for flu-like illness, signaling that flu season is really underway.
Louisiana is seeing the worst of it so far.
Flu season “is taking off and it’s taking off in a direction that’s only likely to increase in the next month or two,” said Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist at the LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.
“If you haven’t been vaccinated, you should get vaccinated now,” he added.
The early-season flu activity is higher than what’s usually seen at this point of the year, though it’s not clear that will mean this season will be worse than others, according to CDC’s update.
But not a good sign: The flu hospitalization rate in mid-October was the highest seen that early in an autumn in more than 15 years, noted Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University, during a recent media briefing.
The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths so far this season are tied to flu infections.
The surge began in the nation’s South and West, and the states seeing high flu activity so far include California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington, according to the CDC.
It’s not unusual for Louisiana to be among the first to see flu season surges each year. That is at least partly due to low vaccination rates, high poverty rates and challenges people face in accessing healthcare, Lopez said.
Doctors expect accelerated spread of flu and other respiratory viruses as people travel and gather later this month for Thanksgiving.
“As we prepare to gather with family and friends over the upcoming holidays, getting vaccinated is especially important,” said Dr. Nicole Iovine, a University of Florida-affiliated infectious disease specialist, in an emailed statement this week.
People should not get vaccinated if they are currently suffering significant symptoms, because the body’s immune system is otherwise occupied. But people should get a flu shot even if they already had an infection this fall, because the vaccine protects against three kinds of flu virus, and it’s not unusual for more than one strain to circulate each season, Lopez said.
Last winter’s flu season surged in late December and infections were especially intense in some parts of the country. At the time, New York City health officials called it the most intense season in 20 years.
The season faded in the following months, and was basically over by late March. But that spring the CDC estimated there had been at least 32 million illnesses, 380,000 hospitalizations and 24,000 deaths that season.
This fall, most of the illnesses so far are caused by a version of an A H1N1 flu bug with mutations that have the potential to more easily slip through the immune system’s defenses. However, data so far suggests the current vaccine “can recognize” the circulating virus and work against it, said Andrew Pekosz, a Johns Hopkins University immunology expert, during a recent media briefing.
Health officials won’t know for months exactly how effective this year’s vaccine is. But “right now there is no cause for concern,” he said.

title: What to know about Westbrook’s Main Street overhaul plan
text:
WESTBROOK — People driving through the heart of Westbrook could begin to see some major changes in a few years as the city tries to make Main Street a more walkable and welcoming place.
More than 60 people attended a community meeting Thursday with the Maine Department of Transportation about the improvements. The project is still in the early stages of design, so the goal of the meeting was to share preliminary findings and gauge locals’ thoughts.
WHAT IS MAIN STREET LIKE NOW?
Joe Stilwell, senior project manager for Maine DOT, said Maine DOT identified Americans With Disabilities Act compliance issues, such as tree roots and cracks in the sidewalk, short curb tip-downs and steep landings.
Currently, on-street parking is poorly marked, cars are parked too close to crosswalks, people are driving too fast, and pedestrians have to spend a long time on crosswalks because the road is so wide.
WHAT IS THE PROJECT?
The project would improve large stretches of Main Street from William Clark Drive to the Westbrook Arterial to make it ADA compliant. A section of Main Street from Bridge Street to Vallee Square was reconstructed in the last few years, so it will not be improved as part of this project.
The project would widen sidewalks to at least 6 feet — and 10 feet in some areas — and add more crosswalks. It would add curb bump-outs to prevent people from parking too close to crosswalks, raised crosswalks and rectangular rapid-flashing beacons (bright lights that flash when a pedestrian pushes a button to cross).
By narrowing the street and adding raised crosswalks to slow cars down, the goal is to divert traffic to William Clark Drive.
“We can give some of that roadway space back to pedestrians,” Stilwell said.
WHAT COMES NEXT? WHEN WILL CONSTRUCTION BEGIN?
There will be another public meeting in fall 2027, when half the design will be completed. Thursday’s presentation represented the first 15% of the design process. Maine DOT is funding the project through the preliminary design phase. Then, Maine DOT and the city will get a cost estimate and seek out funding sources.
In the best-case scenario, construction will begin in the early 2030s.
People can submit comments about the project and see the current plans on the Maine DOT website.
HOW MUCH WILL IT COST?
Stilwell said the project could cost around $8 million to $10 million, but Maine DOT and the city won’t have a cost estimate or funding until later in the process.
WHAT DOES THE COMMUNITY THINK?
Some locals at the meeting were concerned about losing parking spots on the street. Maine DOT will try not to take away too many parking spots, but it’s difficult to tell now how many spots will be impacted, Stilwell said.
Others asked whether the project would include bike lanes. Stilwell said cars and bikes would share lanes and there would be striped travel lanes with shared lane pavement markings.
When asked what their highest priority was between bike lanes and on street parking, community members at the meeting seemed evenly split.
Vision Zero Maine — a citizen-led group of Mainers committed to creating safe streets — along with the Westbrook Active Transportation Task Force and concerned Westbrook residents, shared a list of recommendations for the Main Street redesign.
They are asking for protected bike lanes and a 20 mph speed limit, among other recommendations. Bike traffic will bring more people to downtown Westbrook, and the city should prioritize moving people safely over parking cars, they wrote in the recommendations.
“Bike lanes enable affordable, accessible, and climate-friendly transportation options that are aligned with the city’s integrated equity frameworks and initiatives,” the recommendations reads.

title: Training Helps Houlton Shelter Dogs Get Adopted
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - Thanks to a partnership with Purpose Pups, some Houlton shelter dogs are finding new homes. For one dog named Mosey, training helped lead to a new best friend.
Several dogs at the Houlton Humane Society have received training recently, and the shelter says it’s helping with adoptions. One dog, who had been at the shelter for nearly a year, has now found his forever home thanks to the shelter’s partnership with Purpose Pups. Mosey was adopted by Eileen Voisine about a month ago, after she lost her other canine companion. She says, with a little training, Mosey was a perfect fit and helped fill the hole the loss left in her heart.
“I lost my pup very suddenly that I’d had for many years. It was very lonely. I live alone and I wanted another dog. They had Mosey and so I decided to give him a try. I fostered him in the beginning and trained with Tyler and so after fostering him it was a very good fit. So, I adopted him. Training helps tremendously and these dogs need a home. I’m very happy that I was able to rescue a pup that needed a home,” said Eileen Voisine, Mosey’s adopter.
Mosey received his training from Purpose Pups, a dog training business working with the Houlton Humane Society to help shelter dogs get adopted. “We worked with them for about 8 weeks total and Mosey was one of the dogs that we worked with. Everybody asks me this one questions. They say, “Have you ever met a dog you can’t train?” and I said, “No, but I’ve sure met a lot of humans I can’t train.” Because at the end of the day it doesn’t matter if these dogs listen to me. It matters if they’re able to transition and generalize and go on to listen with their owners and my job is to empower owners and their dogs to work together as a cohesive team,“ said Tyler Jones, Owner and Head Trainer at Purpose Pups.
Shelter officials say the training has helped with several adoptions so far, including Mosey’s. CJ Virgie, the Manager at the Houlton Humane Society said: “It’s been going really well. We adopted 2 from here that were trained by Tyler, and we also sent 4 down to Waterville because we were so crowded and 2 have been adopted from there. Eileen has adopted from us for many years. The dog that passed actually was from here. She came, met Mosey, fell in love with him, but again he was tough on a leash. She knew that, knew that he was in training and then decided that yes, the training is working, and she definitely wanted to adopt him.”
Purpose Pups says it plans to continue its partnership with the Houlton Humane Society to help more dogs find homes. Anyone needing help training their own pups can visit purposepups.com. To learn about adoption, visit houltonhumanesociety.us. The Houlton Humane Society and Purpose Pups say that, with a little training and a lot of love, shelter dogs like Mosey can become a wonderful addition to a family.

title: Great Movies That Were Made Almost Entirely Without a Script
text:
10 Movies That Were Made Almost Entirely Without a Script
To have a good movie, you must first have a good script. Movies don’t exactly live and die by their scripts, but it’s an important part of the process. But what if — and walk with us here — there was no script? What then?? Can you even have a movie at all? We’d say yes, because there are more movies out there that successfully tested this theory than you might think.
For every filmmaker who likes to chain themselves to their detailed screenplay, meticulously planning out every second of footage, there’s another freer spirit who enjoys the opposite tactic, allowing the movie to take shape as it’s being made. Oftentimes this is done by allowing the film’s cast to improvise their own dialogue, perhaps giving them certain beats or pieces of information their characters need to know or say, and otherwise trusting them to do their thing.
None of these movies are absolutely 100% improvised — that would be a real feat, and probably not the best way to make a coherent two-hour feature film people would actually enjoy — but all of them play with the concept of improvisation to varying degrees. Some of these films had treatments but no screenplays, others had rudimentary screenplays with empty space for the actors to fill in on their own, and still others were built entirely around the actors’ performances, the plot later coming clear in the edit. However they did it, all of these movies were made in the moment, the cast and the audience sharing in the surprise.

title: Former lawyer accused of trying to hire someone to kill a person, authorities say
text:
KENTUCKY (WXIX/Gray News) - A former Kentucky lawyer is accused of trying to hire someone to kill a person, according to federal authorities.
Chase Cox, 33, faces one count each of use of interstate commerce facilities in the commission of murder-for-hire and making false statements to a federal agency.
A federal indictment alleges Cox tried to pay a hitman using USPS between Sept. 25 and Nov. 3.
When authorities asked him on Oct. 8 whether there was any reason to believe he would threaten the intended victim, Cox allegedly lied.
“No, I love [the victim] with all my heart, I would never put [him/her] in harm’s way,” Cox said, according to the indictment.
In June 2024, Cox was sentenced to six months in jail for breaking into his ex-girlfriend’s apartment.
Prosecutors said he stole her iPad, read her text messages to track her down and then broke the device.
A judge later suspended his sentence and granted him probation after Cox pleaded that he would “be successful in the community.”
Eight days after his release from jail, Cox hired a “felon friend” to vandalize his ex-girlfriend’s car.
Cox is being held at the Shelby County Detention Center, where he is serving a five-year sentence for violating his probation after testing positive for cocaine and alcohol.
U.S. marshals will bring Cox to federal court in Covington for his arraignment on Dec. 9.
If convicted on both counts, Cox faces up to 15 years in federal prison, a $500,200 fine and six years of supervised release.

title: Down the Rabbit Hole: Where children’s stories come to life
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — Reading is crucial for young children, helping them to build their vocabulary and their imaginations. But the joy and love of reading among kids is slipping away. Federal data shows fewer children are reading for fun today compared to years past. That’s also true for adults.
But The Rabbit hOle, a Kansas City museum based on children’s literature, aims to bring that love for literature back, by bringing your favorite stories to life.
Sprawling more than 40,000 square feet, life-size exhibits at The Rabbit hOle include classic titles such as “Madeline,” “Frog and Toad” and “Curious George.” Newer titles include “My Garden” and “I Want My Hat Back.” There’s even a total recreation of the “great green room” from the book, “Goodnight Moon”, complete with a bed, fireplace, an oversized rocking chair, and a moon that actually moves in the sky.
At each of the exhibits, you can find the book that correlates with it. It’s not unusual to see a child reading “The Fire Cat” or “I am a Bunny” in a tunnel or a chair situated in the exhibit.
Since opening in 2024, the museum has drawn more than 300,000 visitors from all 50 states and other countries, including Italy, Sweden and Singapore. The museum has roughly 45 exhibits.
One exhibit features a 16-foot giant panda named Stillwater from the book “Zen Shorts” by Jon J. Muth. The displays are made in house at The Rabbit hOle factory.
Founder Peter Cowdin and his wife Deb Pettid ran a bookstore for 28 years before opening the museum. Cowdin said while he did not grow up in a “rich environment of children’s books”, he fell in love with the stories as an adult. And the idea behind The Rabbit hOle had been brewing for years.
“We wanted to do something that celebrated children’s literature in a way that had nothing to do with marketing and sales, but had everything to do with the history and culture and the books,” Cowdin said.
“Creation and generative activity is really at the soul of the Rabbit Hole,” he said.
Reading competes with screens
Abbey Mecca visits the museum regularly with her three children.
“Reading is like a non-negotiable from the start. When they first come home, that’s just part of our culture,” Mecca said. “It’s not an option to not read at our house.”
Screens, including tablets and smartphones, compete for children’s attention.
In the 1980s, more than half of 9-year-olds read for fun almost every day. The latest data from the Nation’s Report Card (needs a new hyperlink, this is not correct) shows that figure is down to 37%.
The statistics get worse as kids age. Only 14% of 13-year-olds regularly read for fun, according to the data. The number of children who never or hardly read is also growing.
Meanwhile, 65% of children ages 8 to 13 watch TV daily and average 5½ hours of screen time a day.
Idean Bindell, a mother of three, said the museum helps keep her children interested in reading.
“It’s really made my kids fall in love with the art of storytelling and not just see that there’s just books on a shelf. They see every step of the process,” she said.
Cowdin said getting children off screens was not the museum’s goal, but he said it has been a result.
“I never run into a kid wanting to be on a phone or a tablet in here ever,” Cowdin said.
Part of the reason he thinks children are so captivated by the books and displays at the museum, is because It’s not turning reading into a chore or homework.
“There’s this sort of overreaction, in my opinion, of, you know, really drilling and reading as a skill rather than a pleasure. And so our counterbalance to that is that exactly The Rabbit hOle is really emphasizing the joy of reading,” Cowdin said.
Cowdin hopes the museum inspires more people to follow its approach to reading.
Admission and exhibit permissions
Cowdin and his wife needed permission for every exhibit.
The authors or their estates had to agree to give them the rights for free to keep admission costs affordable.
Tickets are $16 per person. Admission is free for children 2 and younger.

title: Hampden woman identified as passenger killed in Hermon crash
text:
HERMON, Maine (WABI) -Authorities have identified the passenger killed in a single-vehicle crash Monday night in Hermon as 37-year-old Ashley Benningfield of Hampden.
The Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office says the crash happened around 8:45 p.m. on Nov. 9 on Billings Road, near Bryant Road.
The driver was identified as Mark Benningfield, 38, of Hampden. Four people were in the vehicle, and the three surviving occupants were taken to the hospital with serious injuries, according to the sheriff’s office.
The sheriff’s office says the other passengers who were taken for medical treatment have since been released from the hospital.
The sheriff’s office and its reconstruction team continue to investigate the cause of the crash and any contributing factors. No further information was released.
