title: Winter is Right Around the Corner: Are You Ready for Ski Season?
text:
Every year Bates students eagerly await the first snowfall. It’s often hard to tell if it’s going to be a light dusting or a full-on New England storm, but we ought to enjoy it either way.
Skiing is one of the best ways to spend a Maine winter. Luckily, Lost Valley Ski Area is a short 11-minute drive from campus in neighboring Auburn. Bates students, faculty and staff ski for free after showing their school-issued ID, thanks to the college’s institutional membership. They also offer 15% off rentals and companion passes.
However, if you’re seeking to purchase your first pair of skis or if you’re in need of a new pair, Lost Valley will be running its annual ski swap on Sunday, Nov. 15 from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.. Community members are invited to drop off equipment that they’ve outgrown on Saturday, Nov. 14 from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m.. The following day anyone can come and shop for discounted gear. Equipment that’s not sold or picked up is donated.
This is a great opportunity, considering that Sunday River is set to open for the 2026/2027 season on Sunday, Nov. 15 and Sugarloaf will follow suit on Friday, Nov. 20.
When asked to comment on his excitement for the upcoming ski season Malin Adams ‘29 expressed, “as much as I love the warm weather, there’s nothing better than the first pow day and waking up early to go to the mountain.”
Last year, the snow coverage at both mountains was plentiful. Sunday River received 126 inches of snow, while Sugarloaf got 116 inches. Sugarloaf usually accumulates more snow than Sunday River, since it’s farther north and its elevation is notably higher, so this was a surprising change, therefore it’s probably a one-off.
According to Powder Magazine conditions this season are expected to be increasingly variable, but that’s also the norm for New England skiing. The best seasons still see rain, sleet, and ice, hence the term Ice Coast.
Other outlets such as Unofficial Networks were less optimistic, saying that New England mountains may have sparser snowpacks, due to it being an El Niño winter. At the same time, they note that El Niño winters have still brought hefty amounts of snow in the past. The term El Niño simply expresses the reality that climate cycles in the Pacific Ocean have the potential to impact broader weather patterns.
Nonetheless, there’s much to be excited about because winter in Maine is truly magical. Even if skiing is not your cup of tea, there are many other on-campus traditions to look forward to, including the Bates Outing Club’s (BOC) annual snowball fight, which occurs during the evening on the first big snowfall of the year, and of course puddle jump in February.
Greta Hendrickson’s ‘28 personal favorite is the Bates carnival. “It will be the first carnival since my freshman year and it will be a great opportunity to bring new friends,” said Hendrickson.
Batesies it’s time to pull out those winter jackets, hats, gloves and boots because winter is on the horizon!

title: How Maine’s 2-decade-old school consolidation effort continues to unravel
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Next year, the town of Kingfield will leave MSAD 58 to form its own school district. The move will allow the western Maine community of roughly 1,000 people to keep its elementary school building and operate its own district, which will serve about 80 students.
Kingfield was the only one of more than a dozen Maine towns to successfully withdraw from or reorganize its school district in the Nov. 3 election. At least 12 other communities considered similar changes, driven by concerns that their schools could close, that their local tax dollars were being spent on improvements at other schools in their district, or that they lacked control over school governance.
Kingfield voters overwhelmingly supported the ballot measure to withdraw from the district, with over 70% voting in favor.
The trend highlights a broader trade-off facing small towns: leaving larger districts can give communities more control over their schools, but smaller districts may struggle to provide the specialized services and academic support available in larger ones.
It is the latest chapter in a decades-long debate about how to govern rural school districts, since former Gov. John Baldacci signed sweeping school consolidation legislation in 2007, penalizing those that chose to go their own way.
In a state facing enrollment declines and aging school buildings with insufficient state funding available for improvements, that challenge is only expected to get worse.
“A lot of communities place a really big value on their schools, which is wonderful because schools, in my opinion, are the backbone of public education,” said Laura Columbia, superintendent of MSAD 58.
“But I think what’s really important for people to think about is: At what cost? At what point are we keeping buildings at the expense of not providing services to students?”
The challenges for smaller districts extend beyond student services to the cost of maintaining a certain level of funding, said Janet Fairman, a University of Maine professor and co-director of the Maine Education Policy Research Institute.
“The state’s funding formula gives (small districts) enough money based on a certain staff-to-student ratio, and when these communities choose to be smaller than that, they have to pay the difference,” she said. “That means they have to tax themselves more or they have to somehow come up with more revenue to cover the difference in cost.”
When a town decides to separate, Columbia explained that it can also strain the existing school district.
Most rural districts in Maine are already facing a yearslong staffing shortage, and starting next year, MSAD 58 will have to compete with the newly formed Kingfield district for the few special education teachers, bus drivers and occupational therapists in the area. Under the agreement, Kingfield will still send its students to the MSAD 58 high school, so Columbia expects staffing challenges to be most acute at the elementary level.
“People really like to have local schools, I think that’s kind of aligned with a lot of Mainers’ philosophy on local control,” she said. “But we have limited resources to start with in many of our rural schools, and so it can often stretch those resources even further when we have smaller districts in the same area.”
Financial repercussions
School districts are financially incentivized to leave their larger consolidated school units, according to Amy Johnson, a professor at the University of Southern Maine and co-director of MEPRI along with Fairman.
Most Maine districts, 109, are typical school administrative units, with more than one school. But there are also 81 districts that have only one school. This typically means these districts operate their own schools for younger grades and use a tuition model, under which the Maine Department of Education mandates towns pay tuition for their residents to go to another town’s public school, or an approved private school.
One-school districts enroll anywhere between 2 and 600 students, with the median student population being 129, according to MEPRI data.
That’s similar to the plan for Kingfield, where the new school will enroll about 80 students.
But there are also 59 school units with no schools. That means a town withdraws from a school unit and does not form its own, instead choosing to send all of its students to other districts under the tuition model.
“What they gain from that is they only have to pay for the costs for their students, and they only have a handful of students,” Johnson said.
These school districts have the lowest per pupil spending, according to MEPRI data.
A typical school unit spends about $18,000 per student, not including career and technical education. Costs jump up for a one-school district to about $21,000, because, as Johnson explained, “you’re not sharing any costs, you’re trying to be an entire school district with one school plus some tuition students.”
But zero-school districts spend the least, about $15,000 per student, which is the higher end of the state average for tuition. But even at that level, that tuition often does not cover the cost of special education or other services that their students may need, leaving the district accepting them to cover those costs.
“There is this real financial benefit to pulling out of a school unit and becoming your own district, because then you can pay less towards the cost of education because you have fewer kids,” Johnson said. “Because all they’re doing is taking their tax dollars and sending their kids elsewhere.”
Similarly, Kingfield’s withdrawal from MSAD 58 will create a financial burden for the district, Columbia said.
Not only will it reduce per-pupil state funding, but also because Kingfield’s local contribution to the district was relatively large because of the town’s high property values.
And because the roughly 60 students being pulled from the district are spread across multiple grades, Columbia said it won’t result in any reduction in staffing or classroom space, and their associated costs.
Towns attempting joint withdrawal
Three towns about an hour south of Kingfield also attempted to leave their consolidated district, RSU 10, to form their own smaller school unit.
Buckfield, Hartford and Sumner proposed forming their own district because RSU 10’s central office is about a 40-minute drive away. Buckfield voters approved the change, but since the other two towns did not, all three will stay with the district.
This is not the first withdrawal from that regional district. In 2017, four towns — Canton, Carthage, Dixfield and Peru — withdrew from the district to form their own.
In the case of the Buckfield-area towns, they did not want to spend tax dollars on improvements within the district that their students would not benefit from, said RSU 10 Superintendent Matt Gilbert.
“They’re the smaller communities within our district, and they also have the smallest tax base,” Gilbert added. “They were focusing on the desire for control of their tax dollars to be closer to home.”
If the three additional towns had withdrawn and formed their own school district, Gilbert said they would have had about 500 students, which may have been a challenge, “and they would have lost all the benefits that they get from being part of a larger district and the economy of scale that comes with that, like central office services and supports.”
In the aftermath of last week’s election, the withdrawal committee discussed an alternative budgeting model with Gilbert, under which they would have more autonomy over improvements to schools in their communities, but share administrative costs with the larger district.
That means if they want to build a track or add a foreign language program to a school in their community, they would not rely on approval from the entire district school board.
“We were all forced into this consolidation because of the threat of being penalized financially,” Gilbert said, referring to the 2007 reforms.
According to Johnson from MEPRI, school consolidation is a reality many towns have to face due to declining enrollments, aging populations and people moving away from rural areas.
Baldacci attempted to address this challenge by mandating that roughly 300 districts be consolidated to 80 — though that effort was not completely successful, as there are now more than 200 districts. Still, Johnson said it’s not realistic to expect all towns to be able to independently meet their students’ needs.
“In small communities, you don’t start with an economy of scale. If there’s only one school to begin with, it’s much harder to close because there would be nothing left,” Johnson said. “But it’s more expensive to operate that way, and it’s less efficient.”
Consolidation vs. local control
Mount Desert Island-area schools still operate under an alternative organizational structure or AOS. That model allows each of the 10 schools to pass their own budgets but share a superintendent.
The AOS model was offered as an alternative to Baldacci’s consolidation mandate, but there are currently only eight AOSs left in Maine, according to the Maine School Management Association.
Several towns and islands around Mount Desert Island considered consolidating into a regional school unit, but many communities last week rejected the plan.
Superintendent Michael Zboray said several communities were reluctant to give up control over their local schools.
“I tried to argue that all the same people that are caring for your school now will continue to be the people caring for your school, you’ll just have a larger pool of money to help in that care if something catastrophic happened to your building,” Zboray said, “rather than having to rely on the tax base just within your town.”
Zboray said at least some communities on the island as well as neighboring Tremont agree they will eventually need a consolidated school unit because of declining class sizes and lower enrollment in all schools except Bar Harbor.
“It’s a very challenging situation, and we can apply that to police departments, fire departments and school departments,” said Maine School Management Association Executive Director Eric Waddell.
Waddell said he heard from people all over the state struggling to maintain local services amid affordability challenges and declining populations.
“I don’t know what the answer is other than to find alternate revenue sources for funding schools other than leaning so heavily on local property taxes.”

title: Boija posts second straight shutout, UMaine hockey skates to 0-0 tie at UVM
text:
University of Maine goalie Albin Boija posted his second straight shutout as the Black Bears and the University of Vermont’s Catamounts skated to a 0-0 tie at the Gutterson Fieldhouse in Burlington, Vermont, on Friday night.
Vermont picked up the extra Hockey East point by winning the shootout 2-1 as Colin Kessler and Ethan Burroughs converted among the Catamounts’ four shooters and Max Scott was the only Black Bear to score.
Senior Boija finished with 20 saves including eight in the third period when the Catamounts outshot UMaine 8-4.
He had shut out UMass 2-0 last Saturday night and now has 13 career shutouts.
It is the first time in his career that he has posted back-to-back shutouts and the first time a UMaine goalie has done so since Victor Ostman during the 2022-23 season. It is just the seventh time a UMaine goalie has had back-to-back shutouts since 2000.
He has now gone 148 minutes and 13 seconds without allowing a goal.
Hockey East Rookie of the Month for October Jacob Oster had 23 stops for the Catamounts including 12 in the middle period when UMaine had a 12-6 advantage in shots on goal.
Each goalie made three saves in the five-minute, three-on-three overtime before the shootout.
UMaine is now 5-5-1 overall and 1-3-1 in Hockey East while UVM is 5-3-2 and 4-1-2.
The teams will conclude their series on Saturday at 5.
Vermont had a goal in the first period disallowed by a UMaine challenge for an offsides call.
The referees reviewed it and upheld UMaine’s challenge that a Catamount was offsides on the play leading up to the goal.
UMaine Director of Hockey Operations Nick Fonzi was monitoring the game on a video screen and made the call down to UMaine head coach Ben Barr to alert him of the offsides.
“Nick has been great on those all season,” said Barr.
Barr called the game a “hard-fought” contest.
“It was a good hockey game. Albin was great. It was very tight-checking. It was disappointing not to be able to find a way to get (a goal),” said Barr. “The guys worked hard but there are things we can be better at.”
Vermont coach and former University of Southern Maine hockey captain Steve Wiedler called the game a “real battle from start to finish.
“Neither team wanted to blink. It was just an old school Hockey East slug-it-out type of game. I’m proud of our guys for sticking with it,” said Wiedler.

title: Deven Young indicted on murder charge by grand jury in death of Sunshine Stewart
text:
Deven Young indicted on murder charge by grand jury in death of Sunshine Stewart
Deven Young, the Maine teenager who is accused of killing a paddleboarder at Crawford Pond in Union last year, has now been formally indicted on one count of intentional or knowing or depraved indifference murder by a Knox County grand jury. That indictment was handed down on Thursday.
Under state law, that charge carries a minimum sentence of 25 years to life in prison.
Last week, Young agreed to be tried as an adult in the case.
Young waived his right to a bind-over hearing during a status conference that was held in Knox County Superior Court.
A judge then confirmed that Young will be tried as an adult, and he was ordered to be held without bail at the Knox County Jail in Rockland. The Knox County Jail is a 72-hour holding facility, and the county's long-term incarcerated population is now housed at the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Another status conference in Young's case is scheduled for January.
Now 19 years old, Young was 17 when he was charged with the July 2025 murder of Sunshine "Sunny" Stewart.
Prosecutors and the defense team were expected to address issues related to the potential bind-over hearing, which would have determined whether Young would be tried as an adult or a juvenile.
The Maine Attorney General's Office has sought to have Young tried as an adult. A judge would have made that determination after a bind-over hearing, a proceeding in which the court considers evidence, including the seriousness of the alleged offense and evaluations of the defendant.
At a status conference in September, a judge expressed frustration with the delays in scheduling a bind-over hearing after Young's defense team said they needed more time to evaluate Young at the Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland. The judge originally had wanted to schedule a bind-over hearing in December.
However, the defense said their expert needed about three months to complete a report after meeting with Young, and the Attorney General's Office would then need time to review it. The judge then said the process could push the bind-over hearing into 2027.
Since Young will be tried as an adult, he could face a sentence of at least 25 years and up to life in prison if convicted.
Sunshine Stewart's death on a pond in Union
Stewart, 48, was found dead by Maine Game Wardens on July 3, 2025, on or near 100-Acre Island in Crawford Pond in Union, one day after she went paddleboarding.
Authorities said a medical examiner determined that Stewart died from strangulation and blunt force trauma.
Young was arrested in connection with the death and has been held at Long Creek Youth Development Center.
A judge ruled in April that Young is competent to proceed with the case, finding that he has a factual and rational understanding of the proceedings and is able to consult with his attorneys.
Much of the evidence in the case remains sealed because the prosecution began while Young was a juvenile.

title: Nationwide ground stop lifted after flights halted for hours across US, FAA says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.
Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
EN ESPAÑOL | Gobierno federal ordena la suspensión de todos los vuelos a nivel nacional
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.
A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Mullin says no sign of nefarious act
Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.
At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.
Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
The stoppage affected thousands of flights
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.
At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.
“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”
Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.
Sports teams stranded and cargo flights delayed
NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.
U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.
Past problems have also been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
___
Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
___

title: Experts discuss implications of Texas’ blue wave
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - After Texas flipped blue in the midterm elections, political observers are discussing what the longterm implications of the elections could mean for Democrats and Republicans in the state.
The GOP stronghold delivered numerous high-profile wins for Democrats including a U.S. Senate seat, the governorship and control of the state house. That’s led some to say that the state has turned blue.
“The scope and scale of the Democratic victories here is something that nobody was predicting,” said Joshua Blank, research director of the Texas Politics Project at UT Austin.
The victories came in the largest Republican state in the nation and ended Democrats 32-year losing streak for statewide races. Democratic National Committee leaders now say the political tides in Texas have turned in their favor.
DNC says Texas has gone blue
“I think by any definition of the metric, Texas has gone blue,” said Libby Schneider, DNC deputy executive director. “And I think what we saw last Tuesday was a referendum on Republicans having almost complete control for 30 years in Texas and not getting a whole heck of a lot of done for Texans.”
The party has been targeting Texas and other Republican-leaning states in the region as part of its new southern strategy. The strategy aims to gain ground as more people continue to move to those states.
“I think what it tells us is that especially as we reached 2032 and we reached the next census and population is moving to states like Texas and to the south, that it just sort of reinforces what we’ve long believed here under Ken Martin’s DNC, which is that the South is the future and now the South is the present,” Schneider said.
Cornyn disputes shift
Not everyone is convinced one election means the state’s politics have shifted.
“You know, Texas is not a blue state, and I don’t even think it’s a purple state,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) on Wednesday.
Presidential election outlook
One question is whether Democrats could win Texas in a presidential election year. Blank said that could take a lot of work.
“Democrats are certainly going to say that Texas is in play, because Republicans are going to have to spend a lot of money and time defending what really is a foundation piece of their electoral college strategy,” Blank said. “A much more open question is whether Democrats are willing to commit the kind of time and resources necessary to compete in a state like Texas.”
Blank said the state is more competitive now. He said it could be an uphill battle for Democrats because of the breakdown of registered party members.
“The idea that Democrats did in one election, what it took Republicans three to accomplish most of is a historical and unprecedented. So it makes the question more valid,” Blank said. “But it also leads us to remind ourselves that there are still more Republican voters in Texas. A big part of the Democratic win here was not just about overwhelming turnout, but it was also about overwhelming Republican disengagement. And when those Republican voters become reengaged, what does it look like? And that we just don’t know yet.”
Investment in other states
Democratic Party leaders also said they plan to invest more in other Republican states across the South, including Florida, Alabama and Louisiana.

title: FAA grounds flights nationwide, disrupting NBA, NHL and college football travel for the weekend
text:
(AP) - The Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights nationwide for several hours Friday threw the sports world into chaos, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams scrambling to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend.
Transportation officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications issues at regional air traffic control centers for the stoppage. It left some teams searching for hotel rooms, others rescheduling flights, leagues adjusting start times, and some teams had took the extraordinary step of chartering buses rather than waiting for the ground stop to end.
“We’re going to allow for general aviation, those larger movements, to take place as a priority. Smaller movements will take lower priority,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said after the ground stop was lifted Friday night in Washington.
No. 19 Mississippi’s football game at Oklahoma was moved from Saturday to Sunday at 1 p.m. EST because of travel issues. Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny was upset with the decision, saying the Southeastern Conference threatened Oklahoma with a forfeit it did not agree to the move.
“I understand that difficult decisions sometimes must be made under extraordinary circumstances,” Denny said in a statement on X. “Put simply, this decision isn’t fair to our athletes, our institution or to Sooner nation.”
Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, No. 8 Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games. The Utes play at No. 22 Arizona, the Longhorns visit No. 24 LSU and the Vols are traveling to Texas A&M in three of the bigger games of the weekend.
“The Southeastern Conference is aware of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop and the potential impact on team travel,” the league said. “The safety and well-being of student-athletes, coaches and team personnel remain our highest priority.”
Texas and Tennessee both returned to their campuses during the ground stoppage. Once it was lifted following more than four hours of uncertainty, the schools began making plans to fly out as soon as possible, allowing them to arrive before game day.
Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State with the SEC pushing back the Saturday start time from noon EST to 4:15 p.m. to give the Tigers a little buffer. Purdue likewise decided to board buses from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at Iowa.
Other schools affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and Arizona State.
The Big 12 said the Kansas-West Virginia game scheduled for 5:30 p.m. EST would be moved up to 3:30 p.m. since the Jayhawks arrived in plenty of time. That allowed the league to shift the Arizona State-UCF game from 2:30 p.m. EST to 5:30 p.m., giving the Sun Devils an additional three hours after their flight from Arizona to Florida was delayed.
Washington spokesman Kurt Svoboda said the Huskies returned to campus when their flight was grounded, but officials stayed in touch with their airline partners and the flight crew remained in place. The Huskies ultimately flew out late Friday for their game at Michigan State on Saturday, which will start at 5:30 p.m. EST, 75 minutes later than originally scheduled.
It was unclear whether any referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would have trouble reaching their games. The Big Ten said in a statement that all of its officials had arrived for their scheduled assignments Saturday.
Several teams were able to take off before the stoppage began, including all of those traveling in the Atlantic Coast Conference; Missouri, which was flying to top-ranked Georgia; Duke, which was visiting fifth-ranked Miami; and No. 10 Texas Tech, which posted on social media images of its arrival for a game at Oklahoma State.
NFL teams playing Sunday typically travel the day before their games. They were expected to fly as planned on Saturday.
In the NBA, the Cleveland Cavaliers played in Miami on Friday night but won’t fly home until Saturday morning and plan to land about eight hours before a home game against the Dallas Mavericks. NBA teams hardly ever fly in on the day of a game, but there have been some circumstances — often weather-related — where it has happened.
At least two other NBA teams had Friday night flights pushed to Saturday morning, but those teams aren’t playing Saturday night. Cleveland scrambled to get hotel rooms re-booked in Miami, after checking out of their hotel earlier Friday.
“It’s part of it. You just adapt,” Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said.
There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL on Saturday. The Panthers were among the majority that made it to their destinations before the stoppage began. The Sharks, who were left waiting in San Jose to see whether they would be able to travel, arrived later Friday in Utah.
JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates were trying to get to South Carolina for their game Sunday against the top-ranked Gamecocks. The team had just boarded its flight at Los Angeles International Airport when the ground stop was issued. After a while, the decision was made to deboard passengers and the team returned to the Galen Center.
In soccer, the Utah Royals already were in the Washington, D.C., area ahead of their National Women’s Soccer League semifinal against the Washington Spirit on Saturday. But the Kansas City Current were supposed to depart Friday for their semifinal against Gotham FC on Sunday in New York, and team officials were uncertain when their flight would be allowed to leave.
The U.S. national team’s match against Haiti on Saturday in Miami was unaffected by the ground stop. Both teams and officials already were in town for the first leg of the two-match CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinal series.

title: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote, even before Van Hollen entered the race. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election and many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal.
Making the pitch for his reelection, Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer opened discussion on a broad plan for their first 100 days in power that included health care and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war.
“I’m going to win it,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.
In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.
“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
Divisions over Schumer have simmered over the last two years
While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025, when Schumer was put on the defensive after he sided with Republicans on a spending vote.
While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least two backers: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, and progressive standard bearer Bernie Sanders.
El Sayed posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.”
“I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”
Sen. Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, held a press conference Tuesday announcing he would not support Schumer. He posted Thursday night that the American people “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats.”
Van Hollen has not yet laid out his own agenda, but he has criticized Schumer for his ties to Israel and other special interests.
While Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, he has strongly criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza.
Schumer says he has broad support
Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week. Beyond the election wins, those who support him say being the leader is a difficult job, experience is necessary and Schumer has proven himself with legislative successes when they held the Senate under President Joe Biden.
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” posted Maine Sen. Angus King, another independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the leadership election.
“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” King wrote.
Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., also posted her support Thursday evening:
Cortez Masto said Schumer was key in “securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader.”

title: Measles antibody test: What to know about checking your immunity
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (Aging Untold) — Measles is highly contagious, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says adults can get seriously sick. Complications are more common after age 20.
A simple antibody test, also known as a titer test, can show whether a person is likely protected.
What a measles titer test involves
Any Lab Test Now in Greenville, South Carolina, offers more than 8,000 tests that people can walk in and request, according to Madison Gault, clinical director.
She and her team help patients understand everything about their health, from genes to cholesterol levels to antibodies.
Gault said the measles titer is the test drawing the most interest.
Reporter Kari Beal received two doses of the MMR vaccine as a child and had the titer test done because she wanted to know her current immunity.
What the results mean
Beal said her measles antibody level was 300 and the minimum for immunity is 16.
She took the report to family doctor Nita Bijoor and asked if 300 was high. Bijoor said there is no established “really high” level.
“It means you have a good level,” Bijoor said.
The result probably reflects good nutrition and a healthy lifestyle, and that Beal’s body is mounting a good antibody response, Bijoor said.
How the test works, and its limits
A titer test measures immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies, which indicate past exposure to or vaccination against a virus like measles.
Bijoor said sometimes a memory of the virus can remain in the cells without showing high levels of antibodies.
“There can be false negatives,” Bijoor said.
She said a person with a low result may still have a good antibody response, so the test is not 100% foolproof. Bijoor said it is still the best test available.
Who the test is recommended for
Bijoor said she recommends the test for:
- People who do not know their immunity.
- People who think they have natural immunity.
- Vaccinated people in high-risk jobs, such as educators and health care workers.
“I think in the setting of an outbreak, it makes sense if a patient wants to be absolutely sure,” Bijoor said.
Symptoms and complications discussed
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold expert, said measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads when infected people cough or sneeze.
Signs include a high temperature and red, watery eyes, usually followed by a diffuse rash.
She said complications can include pneumonia and encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain, which can occur years after infection.
Rogers said the IgG marker represents past exposure while the IgM marker represents acute exposure.
A person with no antibodies may never have been exposed or may have lost immunity, she added.
Rogers said lab results should be reviewed with a doctor because people can make the mistake of looking at a range and assuming a result is normal.

title: Holden's 25 Days Of Kindness Has Logged Over A Thousand Acts Since 2017
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The 25 Days Of Kindness Campaign: Holden PD Has So Much Planned For This Season!
What started by a small-town police chief as a simple idea to spread kindness for 25 days in his community, has turned into a year-round campaign of kindness picked up by the new police chief in honor of his former mentor's memory.
The Town of Holden's "25 Days of Kindness" program has kicked into high gear for the holiday season, but since it's inception in 2017 by the late Police Chief Chris Greeley in who passed away in 2023, it has grown, leaps and bounds into a perfect example of the good community members, citizens, civic leaders and business owners can do if they work together to help those in need right where they live.
According to their website, in the almost a decade since they've been participating in this program, the 25 Days of Kindness has performed over a thousand acts of kindness and affected hundreds of Holden residents, both young and old.
"25 Days of Kindness was founded to continue the mission of Chief Greeley, a beloved figure in Holden, Maine, who dedicated his life to serving others. His unwavering commitment to kindness and community inspired us to create an organization that would carry on his legacy after his passing."
"Chief Greeley believed that one small gesture could change a life, and it’s this belief that forms the cornerstone of our organization. Since our inception, we’ve grown into a movement that reaches far beyond Holden, touching hearts across Maine and beyond."
Current Holden Police Chief, Eddie Benjamin, says the program has grown so much, it's become a year-round thing, with the initiative donating food baskets to folks experiencing food insecurity, to filling an oil tank of an elderly person who can't afford to by fuel, to paying mortgages and electrical bills, to making sure local kids get to experience the joy of opening a present from under the Christmas Tree.
What Chief Benjamin says is amazing is that no matter what's going on with the economy around the world, folks in Maine keep stepping up and donating to help their neighbors.
"As you know, oil is so expensive right now, but people are coming forward and they want to help. They have a little bit extra and they want to make sure everybody's covered for the winter...we just had a business owner (he wanted to remain anonymous) he just donated $10,000 and said he wanted us to use this money for elderly people who need heat this winter."
"The Food Pantry in Holden is very, very low on food right now, so I believe we are going to donate $3,000 to buy food and there's a business owner that's going to match that, so that will be $6,000 for the food pantry."
Benjamin says people usually reach out, family members and friends of those in need and let the town know there is a need, and the 25 Days of Kindness steps in to help meet that.
He says there are a number of fundraisers, throughout the year, that folks can get involved with if they'd like to raise money to go towards the program.
Next Wednesday, the Holden PD will host their 2nd Annual "Jail and Bail" event where they local business owners volunteer to go behind bars and ask folks to send the program money to "bail" them out.
On Thursday November 19th, he says Police Officers from Holden, Brewer and Ellsworth will join Rock Steady Boxing (a Parkinson's disease organization) in a workout fundraiser at Titan Athletics in Brewer.

title: Woman discovers her father on FBI's most wanted list after taking DNA test
text:
Woman discovers her father on FBI's most wanted list after taking DNA test
A North Carolina woman, adopted in the 1950s, took a DNA test. The results uncovered details about her biological father that she never would have expected.
The DNA results revealed Kathy Gillcrist's father, William Bradford Bishop Jr., was a mass murderer who was on the FBI's most wanted list.
"The more I hear about him, the scarier it is," said Gillcrist.
A collection of newspaper clippings and wanted posters lay scattered across her kitchen table as she shared her story with sister station WXII.
"You know, a lot of skeletons come out of the closet," she said. "I googled him, and the first thing that popped up was his wanted poster from the FBI."
Gillcrist was adopted in the 1950s and spent most of her life unaware of who her parents were — until she took a 23andMe DNA test 60 years later.
"I was here expecting some famous person," she said. "Maybe Ronald Reagan was my father, you know. But, no. It's a murderer wanted by the FBI."
Bishop is a fugitive, wanted for the murders of his wife, mother and three sons in Bethesda, Maryland, back in 1976.
He allegedly bludgeoned his family to death, drove their bodies to North Carolina, burned them and abandoned his car before vanishing.
"And I thought, 'Wow, this is absolutely horrible,'" said Gillcrist. "And I realized that I remembered when that happened. I was a freshman in college. I went to Boston and the murders took place in D.C."
In April of 2014, the FBI placed Bishop on the list of its 10 most-wanted fugitives.
"I was shocked," Gillcrist said. "I have to say, and it's not because I am a horrible person, but I laughed. Because of just how crazy it was. I was crazy to think it was probably some famous person — and it's a murderer."
Gillcrist said she took the DNA test in 2017 in hopes of discovering more about her family background.
"I sent it away and it takes about six weeks," she said. "And I checked the box that I was adopted and said I wouldn't mind getting further information."
Shortly after receiving her results, a cousin reached out, who she quickly grew close with. Around eight months later, her cousin, a genealogist, helped her discover who her father was.
"I still always thought maybe I was the daughter of a famous person, like a movie star," she said. "So I said, is he somebody famous? And she kind of laughed a bit because we both have a crazy sense of humor and she said, 'Well, kind of!' And she said, 'How about you google him?' And she told me his name, which was William Bradford Bishop."
Gillcrist grew even more intrigued by her biological father and his story, collecting information over the years, gaining access to his journal entries, and gathering stacks of notes and newspaper clippings — as well as wanted posters.
"It's been 50 years since the murders," she said. "The murders took place the first weekend in March."
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Gillcrist put pen to paper to share her story. She released a book called "It's In My Genes."
"You know, it's not a game," she said. "Science is real. And once you learn information that's true, you can't take it back. So, be careful is my message."
After releasing her book, she formed a relationship with the FBI and even received telephone tips over the years from people all over the world.
"The murder was never solved," she said. "They've never found Bishop. The case is not closed."
Bishop, if alive, would be 90 years old now. And, if ever given the chance to meet him, Gillcrist said she would certainly still have some questions.
"I would ask him if he knew he had a daughter," she said. "And how that might have felt. And, if he's still alive, what does he think about everything that has come forth about him. I guess I would ask what motivated him to do that. I don't know that he would even have an answer."
Gillcrist said there have been potential sightings of her father over the years, mostly in Europe. She said it has been a few years, though, since she has received any photo sightings from people thinking they might have seen him.
She said as long as she knew she would be safe, she would be open to meeting him if he's ever found.

title: New Hannaford store opens in Presque Isle at former Graves' Shop 'n Save
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New Hannaford store opens in Presque Isle, taking over Graves' Shop 'n Save space
Hannaford Supermarkets opened a new location in Presque Isle on Friday in the space that housed a local grocery store for more than 65 years.
The new Hannaford store is located at 797 Main St., which was the address for Graves' Shop 'n Save, which had served the Presque Isle community since 1959 and closed on Monday.
"This store has been part of everyday life in Presque Isle for generations and we're proud to build on that legacy," James Redman, store manager of the Hannaford in Presque Isle, said in a statement. "Our team looks forward to welcoming customers with fresh, quality food, everyday value and convenient solutions that make their lives a little easier. We're excited to be part of this community and to serve the families who count on us."
Hannaford said that in the coming months, customers can expect to see upgrades throughout the 35,000-square-foot space in an effort to enhance the shopping experience.
The independently operated Presque Isle Pharmacy, which is located inside the grocery store, remains open but will eventually transition to a full-service Hannaford Pharmacy in December.
"This pharmacy has proudly served the Presque Isle community for years," Wendy Boynton, director of pharmacy operations at Hannaford Supermarkets, said in a statement. "We know how important it is for our customers to feel welcome and supported when it comes to their health. As we look ahead to this next chapter, we're committed to continuing to serve the community with care."
The Presque Isle location is Hannaford's 189th store and the 69th in the state of Maine. The store is expected to employ about 80 Hannaford associates, including many of the people who had worked at Graves' Shop 'n Save for years.
The Hannaford in Presque Isle will be open from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Sundays.

title: This grassroots ‘village’ helped a single mom drive away with a new car
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, SC (InvestigateTV) - It’s not like an episode of Oprah, but for single moms like Caroline Reed, it feels pretty close.
She was gifted with a white car topped with a big red bow, all thanks to Amanda Todd and her village.
To understand the gift is to learn about the journey.
“My heart has always been to help single moms. Every single mom’s story is different,” said Todd.
Helping single moms like her friend Reed isn’t what Todd does; it’s who she is.
“Beyond support and encouragement, they need help with the more expensive items,” she said.
Todd created “Their Village Helpers for Single Moms” Facebook group and trusted her faith and her followers to raise money to buy them cars.
“I was like, do me a favor and take this challenge; let’s get a mom a car,” she said. “Find something in your house that you can sell on Facebook, then Venmo me the money or drop it off on my porch.”
The group also had yard sales, and Todd even shrimped for cash. She also launched her business, Color Connection, where she finds women’s most flattering colors for clothes and makeup. Every penny of profit fuels her mission.
They raised $4,000 to put their first mom behind the wheel, and now they’ve doubled that amount.
The group masked the surprise at Reed’s birthday dinner and took her outside for the big reveal. It was nothing but happy tears and complete shock for a mom who, like Todd, is always showing up for others.
This time, the community showed up for her, including Coastal Grand Auto Sales, which not only helped with the car but also sweetened the gift with a two-year warranty.
The women then took the car for a spin. Reed said the real gift isn’t the car itself, but the peace of mind that comes with every turn of the key.
“To get into a car that’s now yours and not have to worry about stopping on the side of the road or just not being able to pick up Zee, it’s just something I never thought I’d be able to have,” she said.

title: Cony football shuts out Fryeburg to defend Class B North crown
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
LEWISTON — The Cony football team was dealt a serious blow early against red-hot Fryeburg Academy, when their star player was again relegated to crutches after only two plays.
In Anderson Noyes’ place, however, the Rams’ receivers and defense dazzled — and Cony again sits on the throne of the Pine Tree Conference.
Cony defeated Fryeburg 28-0 in the Class B North championship game Friday at Don Roux Field, sending the Rams to next Saturday’s state title game against either Marshwood or Kennebunk at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
“It’s a bummer to lose Anderson, but we have so much depth, and we trust everybody,” said Cony quarterback Drew Lindquist. “It feels amazing, just the fact that everyone was doubting us, and now we’re here again.”
Lindquist completed 7 of 20 passes for 176 yards and three touchdowns for the Rams. Jacob Fifield caught four of those passes for 135 yards and two scores for Cony, which outgained the Raiders 278-109 overall and 225-45 in the first half.
On the second play from scrimmage, Noyes left the game for No. 2 Cony (9-1) after reinjuring his right leg — the initial injury prevented him from playing until Oct. 16. It was a setback offensively for the Rams, who were forced to punt on their first possession and stalled on the goal line on their second.
Yet Cony’s defense stifled No. 4 Fryeburg (6-5), and on their third possession, the Rams found a breakthrough. After Cony got the ball back just shy of midfield, Fifield took a screen pass 54 yards to make it 7-0 with 1 minute, 24 seconds left in the first quarter.
That was only the start of a sensational performance from Cony’s receiving corps. With 4:08 left in the first half, Landen Perry noticed a matchup advantage, changed his route, and made a remarkable toe-drag catch in the end zone on a 17-yard pass to put Cony up 14-0.
“We have (a play called) ‘Dinner,’ where he goes and runs a 10-yard corner, and then we have ‘Lunch,’ where he would take it to the post,” said Cony coach BL Lippert. “I called Lunch, but he runs a corner and makes a great catch. I asked him, ‘What was that?’ and he said, ‘Coach, I thought Dinner would be open.’ It was a good check at the line.”
It was only the first brilliant touchdown catch for a Cony receiver. The Rams got the ball back and drove down the field, and with 27 seconds left in the half, Fifield made a remarkable one-handed grab to push Cony’s lead to 21-0. Lindquist then snatched an interception to close out the half.
Cony’s defense continued its dominance after halftime as Fryeburg never got inside the Rams’ 40-yard line. The Rams rounded out the scoring with a 7-yard touchdown run by Perry with 6:15 left in the fourth quarter to seal their second consecutive regional championship.
During the week, Lippert expressed wariness about Fryeburg quarterback Marcus Sutton’s big-play ability, something Sutton showed in leading the Raiders past No. 1 Lawrence in the B North semis. Cony completely neutralized the senior, who completed just 8 of 24 passes for 86 yards and ran for 9 yards on five carries.
“(Defensive coordinator Kyle) Bishop has done an spectacular job, shutting out Skowhegan last week and shutting out these guys this week,” Lippert said. “Those are offenses that have put up a lot of points this year. We’ve got some really good leaders in Diesel (Cox) and Josh Lajoie inside. Without Anderson, that changes the secondary a little bit, but we’ve got senior leaders in there.”
Fryeburg’s loss brings to an end a season in which the Raiders showed resilience after a 2-4 start. After the last loss in that stretch, a 35-34 defeat to Kennebunk, Fryeburg rattled off four straight wins over Mt. Blue, Skowhegan, Messalonskee and Lawrence.
“We were at a low point, but we battled back and put four wins together, including that win last week,” said Fryeburg coach David Turner. “We were hoping to come out and play our best tonight, and we didn’t do that. Credit to them — they caused us problems, and we just couldn’t get anything going.”
Cony’s win was its second straight over Fryeburg in the Class B North championship game. The Rams defeated the Raiders 40-7 in last year’s game at Edward Little High School before falling to 40-20 Westbrook in the state final.
That means unfinished business for a Cony team that saw the winningest season in program history a year ago end with a heartbreaking defeat. It will be a tough task without a player Lippert feels might be the state’s best, but a performance like this one could earn the Rams redemption.
“I told (our seniors) yesterday that I think they have the most wins in Cony history, and I’m thrilled they get to culminate it with one more game for a state title,” Lippert said. “The South has traditionally won more than the North, so we have to play our best game. We’ll see what we can do.”

title: Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments dismissed, saying agent lied to grand jury
text:
Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments dismissed, saying agent lied to grand jury
Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh asked a judge Friday to throw out the original murder indictments for killing his wife and son, saying the chief investigator in the case lied to the grand jury.
Video above: Judge response to Alex Murdaugh claiming innocence
Murdaugh is facing a retrial on the murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence, ruling that a court clerk improperly influenced jurors against him during his 2023 trial.
Even if the request to dismiss the indictments is granted, it may not stop or even postpone an April retrial for the disgraced lawyer. Prosecutors can seek another set of grand jury indictments, and defense attorneys said they won’t stop them.
Judge asks an interesting question at the end of the hearing
Judge Debra McCaslin did not immediately decide on the defense request, promising a written ruling next week. But one of her last comments at the hearing may have indicated where she is going.
"If you had to go back to the grand jury, could you have it all done and ready to go by April 5?" she asked prosecutor Creighton Waters.
"Your honor, I'm always working ahead," Waters responded.
Throwing out indictments could be another rebuke of agent on case
A ruling throwing out the indictments would be another rebuke of the chief investigator in Murdaugh's case, State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen.
A judge last year threw out a different murder case Owen was involved in because the dead woman's mother told the agent about a suicide threat her daughter made days before she died that Owen never relayed to prosecutors or defense attorneys. She was found dead by the same method she told her mother she was going to use to kill herself.
Owen abruptly retired in 2024, not long after he was honored as State Law Enforcement Officer of the Year.
Prosecutors pointed out that while Owen is accused of hiding or not revealing evidence in that case, all the issues in the Murdaugh case involved evidence and reports the defense had at the original trial.
The grand jury heard several questionable assertions
Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.
Defense lawyers said that as prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.
Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property, which was not the case.
The grand jury may have heard about plenty of evidence, including the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh’s voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his claims that he wasn't at the kennels near where his wife and son were killed any time close to their deaths.
But defense attorney Jim Griffin said the false evidence of the blood of Murdaugh's son was the only thing anyone heard that could link him to the place and time of the killings.
"A phone call doesn’t put him there. The video doesn’t put him there," Griffin said. "The blood from his murdered son sprang through the air — it’s raining back on him — puts him there."
Prosecutors call it a mistake and cite other evidence against Murdaugh
Prosecutors said they had plenty of other evidence supporting the murder charges, and wrote in court papers that "a single mistake is not bad faith."
Along with the kennel video, Owen told the grand jury about the family's mounting debts, guns missing from the house that matched what could have been used in the killings and how Murdaugh's schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.
"This is what the agent understood at the time. And it’s ultimately not something that would cause a substantial effect on the grand jury or cast grave doubt when we look at all the other evidence that was presented," Waters said.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.
But Murdaugh's lawyers have repeatedly pointed out how little physical evidence prosecutors have — no DNA or blood was found splattered on Murdaugh or any of his clothes, even though the killings were at close range with powerful weapons that were never found.
"What we're asking, Your Honor, is to reboot — go back to square one," Griffin said.

title: The Latest: FAA grounds all flights nationwide due to communications problems
text:
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, an FAA notice said.
The ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” according to the notice.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue was affecting the regional air traffic control centers that direct planes between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating.
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
Here is the latest:
Aviation safety expert says issue appears similar to September regional outage
Former United Airlines pilot and aviation expert Steve Arroyo said the problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, except this time on a nationwide scale.
Arroyo said it could be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
First nationwide ground stop since January 2023
A key FAA computer system malfunctioned, temporarily grounding all flights nationwide and touched off a cascading air traffic jam.
Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

title: Massachusetts man gets more than 5 years for fatal Maine Turnpike crash
text:
A Massachusetts man will spend the next few years behind bars for a deadly crash on the Maine Turnpike more than two years ago.
Oguzhan Cildir, 26, of Brighton, Massachusetts, was sentenced Tuesday to 15 years in prison with all but 5.5 years suspended, as well four years of supervised release, at the York Judicial Center in Biddeford, according to the York County district attorney’s office.
Cildir pleaded guilty to manslaughter, aggravated assault, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon and aggravated driving to endanger, the district attorney’s office said Friday afternoon.
Cildar was driving a black Toyota Prius south on Interstate 95, near mile marker 20 in Wells, about 8:41 a.m. on April 26, 2024, when he cut across lanes of traffic and went into the breakdown lane, hitting multiple vehicles and causing a pileup.
That crash left 53-year-old Gloria Cascio of Albion dead and her passenger, Vincent Cascio, seriously injured.

title: Ex-Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleads guilty to lesser charge in 1997 killing
text:
Ex-Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleads guilty to lesser charge in 1997 killing
Former Oklahoma death row prisoner Richard Glossip, who spent nearly 30 years incarcerated and was on the brink of execution three times for a 1997 killing, pleaded guilty to a lesser charge Thursday.
Glossip had been sentenced to death over the killing in Oklahoma City of his former boss, motel owner Barry Van Treese. Van Treese was beaten with a baseball bat in what prosecutors have alleged was a murder-for-hire scheme.
Another man, Justin Sneed, admitted robbing and killing Van Treese, but testified that he did so after Glossip promised to pay him $10,000. Sneed was the state’s key witness against Glossip and was sentenced to life in prison.
The U.S. Supreme Court previously threw out Glossip’s conviction, and he was released on bond in May to await retrial. His longstanding claims of innocence have drawn support from Kim Kardashian and other prominent figures.
With Glossip's plea to a lesser accessory charge, the murder charge was dismissed, said Don Knight, Glossip’s attorney. He said Glossip will be sentenced in December, when he could be released or sent back to prison for another 15 years.
"I'm grateful for all my attorneys and all their hard work, and I'm grateful to you standing by my side," Glossip said.
WATCH: Richard Glossip pleads guilty to accessory charge in 1997 murder case
“We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society by spending nearly 30 years on death row, during which time he was served three last meals and came within minutes of being executed for a crime he did not commit,” Knight said.
Accepting the plea to a lesser charge “was a difficult decision for me and, more importantly, the Van Treese family. We both recognize that this path ensures a conviction related to Mr. Van Treese’s killing and gives us the best chance to secure additional prison time for Glossip,” Drummond said.
By pleading guilty to being an accessory, Knight said Glossip acknowledged the prosecution’s allegations that he helped place plexiglass over a broken window at the motel. Van Treese’s body was inside the room, but Glossip did not know it was there and never saw it, Knight said.
The prosecution also said Glossip did not immediately tell police that Sneed had told him he killed Van Treese. Knight said Glossip did not believe that was true at the time.
“He had nothing to do with the murder, none of the planning, or carrying it out,” Knight said.
During his time on death row, courts in Oklahoma set nine different execution dates for Glossip, and he came so close to being put to death that he ate three separate last meals. In 2015, he was even held in a cell next to Oklahoma’s execution chamber, waiting to be strapped to a gurney and die by lethal injection.
But the scheduled time for his execution came and went. Behind the walls of the Oklahoma State Penitentiary, prison officials were scrambling after learning one of the lethal drugs they received to carry out the procedure didn’t match the execution protocols. The drug mix-up ultimately led to a nearly seven-year moratorium on executions in Oklahoma.
Van Treese’s family had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to leave Glossip’s conviction and sentence intact.
Glossip’s case attracted international attention after actress Susan Sarandon — who won an Academy Award for her portrayal of death penalty opponent Sister Helen Prejean’s fight to save a man on Louisiana’s death row in the 1995 movie “Dead Man Walking” — took up his cause in real life. Glossip’s case was also featured in the 2017 documentary film titled “Killing Richard Glossip.”

title: Cost of living is the top obstacle to financial security, survey finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than half of the adults surveyed by ConsumerAffairs define financial security as simply not living paycheck to paycheck.
The survey of 1,000 adults ages 18 to 64 found the goal is more basic than many might expect, according to Dayna Edens, public relations manager at ConsumerAffairs.
“Truly just making ends meet is now the new bar, the new goal set for being financially secure,” Edens said.
Four in 10 respondents say they have less than $1,000 saved, not counting retirement accounts or home equity.
“We’re truly just talking about money you would have to spend if you would need to take an ER visit or your transmission or your car goes out. Even scarier, 19% have nothing set aside at all,” Edens said.
Only 20% of respondents know the exact dollar amount it would take to feel financially secure.
Edens described what respondents said would make the biggest difference.
“And when we ask them, what’s the biggest change that would be able to make that difference there? The top answer is not paying off debt. It’s not buying a home or setting aside money for the future. It’s truly just covering enough expenses and then still having something left over,” Edens said.
The cost of living was the biggest obstacle to financial security, cited by 46% of respondents.
Financial experts featured in the report recommend building an emergency fund and paying down high-interest debt when possible. Edens said it is important to be realistic about your own financial situation.
“You may not necessarily be the issue right now. You know, cost of livings are high. Do what you can right now to stay afloat,” Edens said.
