title: Sales and prices of Maine homes drop by 6% in October
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Realtors across Maine reported fewer sales and lower prices in October, compared with the same time period a year ago.
Comparing October 2026 to October 2025, sales of single-family existing homes dropped 6.58% from 1,656 to 1,547 and the median sales price decreased 5.63% to $402,500 according to Maine Listings.
“As we move into the fourth quarter, buyer demand has softened as mortgage interest rates are shaping market dynamics,” said Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors and an associate broker at Oberg Insurance & Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
For buyers, there are more homes are on the market compared with a year ago, while sellers are facing more competition from other listings.
The dip is seen in a month-by-month comparison, too. After reaching a record high of $436,000 in June, Maine’s median sales price for a home dropped in July to $427,000.
By September, the median price was down to $415,000.
Mortgage rates at 3-year high
Mortgage interest rates are hovering at their highest levels in three years.
As of Nov. 12, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11%, down from the previous week when it averaged 7.18%, according to the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., known as Freddie Mac. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.24%.
The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.45%, down from the previous week’s average of 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%.
County trends
For Cumberland County as a whole, the median price decreased by 7.63% from $622,500 to $575,000, while the number of units sold fell by 10.71%, from 364 to 325.
But there were significant variations throughout the communities. Brunswick and Casco saw increases in the number of units sold and the median sales price. Brunswick’s sales increased by 36.84% and the median sales price rose by 11.97%, from $480,000 to $537,450. Casco had three more sales compared to last year and saw a 106% jump in the median sales price, from $265,000 to $547,000.
Other communities experienced drops. Falmouth had a decrease of 11.76% in units sold, and the median price slumped by 38.35% from $1.395 million to $860,000. In Portland, the number of units sold dropped from 50 to 38 compared to last year, and the median sales price decreased by 8.1%, from $617,500 to $567,500.
“As this month’s statistics remind us, the housing market really varies from town to town,” said Yvonne Myer, president of the Greater Portland Board of Realtors.
York and Piscataquis counties saw the biggest decline in number homes sold year-over-year. York dropped 18.9% from 819 to 664 and Piscataquis 14.6% from 123 to 105. Pricewise, Franklin County saw the biggest gain of 22.4%, from $290,000 to $355,000, although the number of units sold dropped 10.5% from 133 to 119.
National, Northeast numbers
At the national and regional levels, the numbers are mixed.
In the U.S., single-family home sales decreased by 8.6% in October and the median price was relatively flat, rising 0.4% to $421,900, according to the National Association of Realtors.
In the Northeast, October year-over-year sales decreased by 4.1%, while the median price was up 3.2% to $519,600.

title: DA chooses not to press charges against driver who killed 2 on soccer field during youth match
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - The driver of a pickup that hit and killed two people and injured nearly a dozen others at a sports facility last month will not face charges.
Sedgwick County District Attorney Marc Bennett and Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan provided the update this week on the investigation.
Sullivan said they met with the families of the victims privately before publicly announcing the decision.
Nick Schafer, 35, and 6-year-old Cole Adrian, both of McPherson, were killed in the crash.
Police said the driver drove to the Stryker Complex from Garden City with her children, who were playing soccer at the facility that October day.
The driver was not identified, other than being called “she.”
Bennett said the driver reported that the pickup was not her usual vehicle. She was sleeping in the vehicle just prior to the crash and believed she had put the pickup into park.
While she was either asleep or falling asleep, one of her children put the sunshades up. Soon after, the pickup jumped the curb and went onto the field of play.
Bennett said he considered six possibilities as reasons for the crash:
- A medical emergency.
- Impairment or intoxication.
- A vehicle mechanical malfunction.
- An intentional act.
- One of the children or the woman, while she slept, inadvertently put the vehicle into drive.
- As the driver pulled up to the curb, she was confused about the gear the car was in.
Bennett ruled out the first four possibilities. He said he did not reach a conclusion about the other two.
He said for charges to be filed, the act had to be intentional, knowing and/or reckless.
Bennett determined that not only was there no evidence that the act was intentional, but in fact there was evidence that it was not done on purpose.
“This is not a crime, and I cannot charge this driver with a crime,” Bennett said.
According to Bennett, though the crash may have appeared to be an act of negligence, negligent homicide is not a chargeable offense in Kansas. He said that the collision did not meet the standards for vehicular homicide, a misdemeanor in Kansas.
Sullivan said the woman had no confrontations at Stryker that day. She hysterically expressed regret following the incident.
Police noted that they reviewed 60 videos and 41 emergency calls, interviewing more than 100 witnesses.
One of the first witnesses who communicated with the driver was an off-duty law enforcement officer. That officer recorded the interaction.
To determine the driver’s condition, a blood sample was taken. There were no impairing substances in the blood. The driver’s medical records were also subpoenaed.
Bennett said the philosophy going into the investigation was to “know everything that was knowable.”
Sullivan said medical records and videos offered no evidence that the driver was impaired.
“Every lead was examined. Every piece of evidence was reviewed,” Sullivan said.
No mechanical issues were found with the vehicle. Sullivan said that if the vehicle had been left in park, it would not have been able to clear a curb, enabling it to approach the soccer fields.
That left questions about the exact circumstances behind who put the vehicle into drive and when and how it was shifted.
“There are some questions that we may never be able to answer with complete certainty,” Sullivan said.

title: Horses caught on camera boarding city bus
text:
DETROIT (WXYZ) - A video of a horse briefly boarding a Detroit city bus has gone viral, and the horse’s owner is sharing his side.
Ellessia Drew said she was near 7 Mile and Strasburg on Saturday evening when she recorded the video with her cell phone.
Witness reacts to video
“I was taking like, oh my god, like what about the people on the bus? What if the horse used the bathroom on a bus, like what’s going on?” Drew said.
“You never know in Detroit. Especially on 7 Mile,” said resident Alan Houser. “7 Mile right up there, anything can happen on 7 Mile.”
Owner explains why the horse was there
Jordan Williams, co-founder of Urban City Cowboys, said he was in the city helping with a fundraiser, taking kids on rides. Afterward, he said, he saw the bus and wanted to take a quick video.
“It wasn’t like I was tracking down the bus; I was like, ‘Oh, there’s the bus. Oh, there’s the bus stop, well it looks like it’s lining up for me,’” Williams said.
Williams said the bus stopped and the driver was shocked to see the horse and spoke to him through the door. He then walked the horse in and out of the bus.
Williams said there was no harm done. He said he has done the same on multiple DDOT buses over the years.
“We’ve been on the Jefferson, we’ve been on the Chalmers, we’ve been on the Conners, and now on the 7 Mile,” Williams said.
DDOT response
Detroit Department of Transportation said service animals are allowed on its buses, but horses are not. The agency said it is speaking to the driver and investigating the incident.
In a statement, DDOT said: “We are taking appropriate steps to address this incident as it is not consistent with DDOT policy and potentially creates an unsafe and uncomfortable ride for our passengers.”
Williams said he hopes the city can see he was just horsing around.
“Only in Detroit and on 7 Mile,” Williams said.
City officials said they will retrain all bus drivers and educate residents about their efforts to provide safe, reliable service.

title: The FAA says airplane departures can resume
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.
The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
The nation’s top homeland security official attributed the problem to a telecommunications outage and said there was no indication the communications failure was related to a cyberattack. The consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers.
“It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt.
Friday’s restrictions were imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” according to an FAA notice. The agency was investigating a communication issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide, said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening. Meanwhile, some flights within Alaska and Hawaii were not impacted, Alaska Airlines said.
Top official says no sign yet of nefarious act
Mullin told reporters at the White House that there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now.”
“Everybody’s safe. There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying,” Mullin said.
At least 827 flights have been diverted so far as a result. As of 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
The airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted included Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST, raising the likelihood of more cancellations and flight diversions.
United Airlines and American Airlines said flights already in the air will continue.
“It will be all hands on deck across America to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this nationwide ground stop,” American said in a statement on the social platform X.
At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday afternoon, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board.
Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there.
“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”
Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend’s baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago.
They had boarded a flight to Denver from O’Hare International Airport when they were told to get off the plane.
“We did see them taking luggage off our plane and others, so we’re assuming it’s going to be a pretty substantial delay,” Curtis said.
They were unsure whether to get a hotel room or keep waiting out the delay at the airport. With care already in place for their two young children at home, they might stay the weekend in Chicago, he said.
Sports teams stranded and cargo flights delayed
NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it is prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.
U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods – from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.
Despite the nationwide FAA ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon on its latest test flight.
The government has been working to overhaul outdated technology
There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA’s nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.
But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
Story by Josh Funk and Will Weissert Associated Press. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; and Alex Veiga in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

title: The race to become next Attorney General
text:
The race for an open seat to become Maine's next Attorney General
Attorney General Aaron Frey will term out at the end of this year.
The race for an open seat to become Maine's next Attorney General
Attorney General Aaron Frey will term out at the end of this year.
Sen. Anne Carney, D-Cape Elizabeth, and Yarmouth attorney Tim Shannon are set to face off in the race for the open seat for Maine's attorney general.
Attorney General Aaron Frey is set to term out at the end of the year and the legislature will elect the next AG after they are sworn in on Dec. 2.
Carney is the current chair of the legislature's judiciary committee and said this experience, along with being a litigator and a legal aid attorney, helps her understand the attorney general's office "from every side."
“This is a pivotal moment for Maine," Carney wrote in an email. "The Trump administration disregards the Constitution and tramples on individual freedoms. Our state has failed to recognize the inherent rights and sovereignty of the Wabanaki Nations. And every day, Mainers risk financial ruin at the hands of scammers who flood our phones and inboxes with calls, texts, and emails. Maine needs an attorney general who is ready to get to work on day one and produce results. That’s exactly what I’ll do."
Shannon is not a state legislator but is a former Yarmouth Town Councilor. He said he has been having "robust conversations" with state lawmakers who will ultimately make the decision of who to elect to the position.
Shannon ran for this position against Frey eight years ago. He considers himself a progressive Democrat.
"It's an important office in the best of times, and these are not the best of times," Shannon said, talking about standing up to the Trump Administration.
"The attorney general's office is the largest law firm in Maine it has one client, the people of Maine."
The winner of this race will need 111 legislative votes.

title: 'TrumpCare' and commemorative plaques — how Democrats are pitching deal-making with the president
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed has proposed “TrumpCare,” a golden insurance card providing universal healthcare, dangling the president’s name on the ambitious Democratic plan.
James Talarico has suggested Donald Trump could become a man of history like Lyndon B. Johnson, who was seen as a master of congressional dealmaking.
And even Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become the House speaker in January, has left the door open to working with the other side of the aisle “wherever and whenever possible” to deliver for the American people.
Democrats who swept into power by riding voter backlash to Trump are now pitching ways to collaborate with the president, playing to his vanity and his love of making deals to propel their own agenda.
The offers coming from the Democrats carry both practical and political applications — a strategy to show that the party is serious about the hard work of legislating and also an acknowledgment that Trump’s signature is needed for new laws.
Trump himself has said he doesn’t want to spend the final two years of his presidency simply vetoing bills from the Democrats in control of Congress. It was only a few short years ago, during his first term, that Trump stunned Republicans by cutting deals with the Democratic leaders he called “Chuck and Nancy” — Senate Leader Chuck Schumer and then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
Democrats appeal to Trump’s vanity
Before the next Congress begins in January, Democrats are trying to entice Trump with the prospect of timeless glory to a president fixated on making his mark on Washington.
All he has to do, they say, is work with them to deliver sweeping policies like Medicare for All.
“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed, who won the U.S. Senate race in Michigan after Trump branded him a terrorist sympathizer, wrote on social media.
He attached mock-ups of a gold-colored card, with Trump’s name and signature far more prominent than the small text reading “Medicare for All.”
Universal healthcare has long been anathema to Republicans, although Congress — and even the Republican president himself — will face pressure to deal with rising costs.
About 6 in 10 voters nationally said the federal government should play a bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare than it does now, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
The costs of expanding Medicare to cover more people would depend on the scope, and Democrats have considered plans that include dropping the eligibility age to below 65 or including children and young people. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that various so-called single-payer options could increase federal subsidies for health care from $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion by 2030, while the total out-of-pocket costs for patients would decline.
Trump’s willingness to slog through extended negotiations with Democrats is an open question, and his past promises of dealmaking have been hit and miss. He reiterated Thursday he is willing to work with Democrats.
“I’m going to be vetoing a lot of things that they’re going to send me initially that are bad for the country, and I think eventually they’re going to call in, they’re going to say, ‘Let’s make a deal,’ and we’ll be able to make deals on healthcare, on drug prices,” the president told commentator Stephen A. Smith in an interview.
Trump’s choice of Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff may foreclose some of those opportunities, however. Jeffries described Miller as a “stone-cold racist” and said he has “zero interest” in working with him.
The pitches from Democrats keep coming
The pitches from some of Democrats’ most high-profile new arrivals in Washington will help shape the party’s approach for the rest of Trump’s presidency.
Talarico, the Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas, described the ways that Johnson is memorialized on Capitol Hill and remembered for shaping civil rights and social services as a senator and president.
“If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality,” Talarico said Thursday at the What’s Next conference in Denver, where many Democrats gathered to plot their way forward.
Talarico made his pitch to Democrats as much as to Trump. After getting the fulsome repudiation of Trump they’ve been seeking for a decade, the party’s base voters may not be eager to see their newly elected leaders standing with him for a bipartisan signing ceremony at the White House Rose Garden that he paved over to create a patio resembling his Mar-a-Lago resort.
However, Talarico said Americans are counting on bold changes before the next president takes office after Trump’s second term ends.
“Some of these reforms may not pass until 2029, but the American people cannot wait two years for change,” he said. “So we must work with President Trump.”
The eagerness to work with Trump is notable from El-Sayed and Talarico, who were among the president’s most frequent targets as he hop-scotched the country for Republicans ahead of the midterms. He singled them out for especially personal attacks, questioning El-Sayed’s loyalty to the United States and labeling the Texan as “Talafreako.”
___
Cooper reported from Phoenix.

title: Microsoft explains what caused global outage, Outlook to go down for millions of users
text:
REDMOND, Wash. (Gray News) - Microsoft has apologized for a global service outage that has disrupted millions of users this week.
The tech giant took to social media on Friday to offer an apology to its users while explaining the cause of the outage that appeared to have started on Thursday.
“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” Microsoft shared.
The Microsoft outage disrupted business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and left multiple businesses across the world without access to Outlook emails and other platforms.
On Friday, Microsoft said it was making headway as it worked to restore services.
“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” the company said.
According to Microsoft, the outage was related to a technical issue that was not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” Microsoft said.
The company added that it has been restoring services gradually while validating stability at each stage, a process that has taken longer, but it has helped ensure a stable restoration.
The total number of people affected by the outage was not immediately shared, but the company stated earlier this year that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

title: Will Maine's extreme drought impact the look of your Christmas tree?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Will Maine's extreme drought impact the look of your Christmas tree?
Maine Christmas tree farmers are worried the drought could take away some of the holiday magic.
Will Maine's extreme drought impact the look of your Christmas tree?
Maine Christmas tree farmers are worried the drought could take away some of the holiday magic.
Christmas tree farmers are saying "bah humbug" to the forecast as their growing season finishes in an extreme drought.
For people shopping for trees, the impacts this year will be minimal. Some trees might be slightly duller in color, but with proper care, they should last just as long as trees from other years.
The real impacts will come when younger saplings are ready to be harvested in a couple of years.
John Weston is a seventh-generation farmer and current owner of Weston's Farm. He said that young trees need moist soil to develop a robust root system.
"When the ground is saturated and wet all around the tree, it's going to be much better. You'll have a more nutrient uptake. You'll just have a better-looking overall tree," Weston said.
Farmers can add water to the soil through drip irrigation or overhead watering, but it doesn't soak all of the soil, which is what encourages root development. It also costs money and labor.
Not having rain when it's young makes for a weaker overall tree in looks and health.
"The color of the needles, the amount of new growth that the tree will put on. It also weakens the tree, so if you happen to have more insect pressure that year or disease pressure, the tree just isn't able to withstand it the way it normally would," he said.
In a typical year, Weston expects to lose about 15% of saplings. Due to the drought, he said this year he's lost closer to 25%.
It's not just too little rain; too much rain has hit his farm recently as well.
In 2024, Weston said the Saco River had flooded over its banks and into his farm. It caused significant damage to trees that had been growing for years, and the ones that survived now have taller trunks after lower branches were taken out.
"The bigger comment is climate change. We're finding, as farmers in general, that it's affecting both ends of the spectrum," Weston said, referring to extreme droughts and floods impacting his farms.
Weston has adjusted by slowly moving his tree farms to higher elevations. It also allows him to irrigate his saplings, which helps during droughts. While it has made running a tree farm more difficult, he says it has to be done.
"We're now at the stage where we're pretty much guaranteed that we're going to have to be dealing with either a drought or a flood throughout the life of the tree," he said.

title: Edgecomb selectmen consider road name change
text:
In 2024, Roy Potter became Edgecomb’s full-time fire chief. He also became the 911 addressing officer. On Nov. 10, he reported a significant number of the town’s roads were improperly listed. Potter believed the situation must be addressed because public safety agencies need properly listed addresses. “I have set standards to follow. The state sets guidelines for doing my job. If I can’t get the backing of the selectboard to do my job, then I’m not going to be the 911 addressing officer.”
Selectmen sought Potter’s opinion because of a question about the name of a town road. Potter objects to Off-Shore Road’s name because it conflicts with emergency management system standards. The agency will often use “off this road or street” in directing emergency responders, he said.
If an emergency call directs a response to Off-Shore Road in Edgecomb, he believes that would create confusion. Virginia Campbell has lived at her Off-Shore Road residence for the past five years. She told selectmen the road was once a “750-foot driveway,” with one resident. It now has two residents and, despite Potter’s protestations, she doesn’t want to change the name.
She told the selectboard a previous board five years ago approved the name.
“We came up with a name and gave it to the 911 officer at the time. Roy (Potter) was fire chief, he shot down all the names as being too similar to others,” she said. “We went back to the drawing board and presented more names a couple months later, but Roy said those were too similar.”
The disagreement was decided by a previous selectboard who ultimately sided with Campbell. “We both presented our cases and in the end I was granted the name,” she said. “So my personal feeling is my road name should stand.”
Selectmen didn’t make a decision following the two presentations.
In other business, selectmen are considering forming an advisory capital reserve committee. Chairman Forrest Carver envisions the committee to establis, develop and maintain a long-term capital improvement and funding strategy for the town.
Selectmen reached a consensus that the new committee should have five members with staggered terms. Selectmen are still considering who should serve on the board.
Selectmen approved ADP as the town’s new payroll company. Selectman Cara Gaffney believes the change will improve municipal efficiency. “A professional service eliminates payroll accounting variances and ensures complete audit compliance and protects the town’s financial liability,” she said.
Selectmen voted, 3-0, to contract with RHR & Smith for auditing services for Fiscal Years 24, 25 and 26. The new firm starts on Jan. 1.
Selectmen meet next at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 24 in the conference room.

title: Enforcing immigration laws with unvetted, poorly trained thugs is deadly mistake
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
If further evidence was needed that ICE, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, needs to be overhauled, or even dismantled, it came this week in a report on the incomplete background check and training of the officer who shot and killed a young father in Biddeford.
The New York Times reported on Wednesday that ICE hired, armed and deployed David Brouillette without reviewing a background check that could have revealed his violent past and racist views. Because he had some experience, albeit limited and troubled, with law enforcement agencies, he was allowed to skip a training course in Georgia and did online training instead.
On July 13, he fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a traffic stop in Biddeford. Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old father from Colombia, was not the target of that day’s ICE operation. He was authorized to work in the U.S. and had a pending asylum case, according to his family and lawyers.
The Department of Homeland Security says an investigation of the shooting is ongoing, although no information about the review has been publicly released. His family identified Brouillette as the shooter. The agency declined to confirm his identity. Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey is also undertaking an investigation of the shooting.
The new information from the Times, which includes emails and numerous interviews with Brouillette’s family, reiterates that ICE is not a legitimate police force. Police departments vet their recruits, train them and do not let them roam the streets wearing masks and hiding their identities.
As we wrote in April, ICE needs a more targeted mission. It needs more oversight and accountability, and its agents need to be better trained.
Six months later, this is even more clear. We have little hope that it will happen, but an overhaul of ICE, with an emphasis on accountability and oversight, should come now, from this Congress, before more people are killed.
Brouillette, who worked briefly as a corrections officer and security guard in Maine, was hired late last year as ICE quickly ramped up its operations as part of the Trump administration’s mass immigrant deportation agenda. A whistleblower had warned of an “unprecedented lowering of standards,” which could undermine ICE and public confidence in the agency.
To justify the huge ICE buildup, President Donald Trump said the agency was going after the “worst of the worst.” That’s not what happened.
In January, ICE launched the offensively named operation “Catch of the Day” in Maine, with a supposed list of 1,400 targets. When ICE ended its enhanced operations at the end of the month, it said it had arrested about 200 people.
Data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, shows that the agency arrested 11 people with criminal convictions in Maine. Most of the people who ICE detained in Maine were held on immigration violations, which generally are civil, not criminal, matters.
Although the enhanced operation ended, ICE activities in Maine are continuing.
In July, Brouillette, a poorly trained and loosely vetted agent with long-standing racist views, his family told the Times, was part of an ICE operation in Biddeford searching for a resident who had been ordered removed from the country. Instead, they targeted Durán Guerrero, rammed his car and fired shots into his vehicle.
According to the Times investigation, law enforcement experts agree that Brouillette, who has mental health issues, possible brain trauma and a reported history of domestic violence, should not have been hired by any law enforcement agency, including ICE.
We can secure our borders and manage immigration in an orderly way without unvetted and poorly trained masked, armed agents harassing and killing innocent people. We’ve done it before and must do it again.
Congress can — and must — end this reign of terror by forcing a pause on ICE operations while questions are answered and requirements for restraint and transparency are put in place.

title: 11-month-old found buried alive in dog crate went home to family the same night
text:
BATESBURG-LEESVILLE, S.C. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) — An 11-month-old boy who was buried alive in a dog crate was released from a South Carolina hospital and is back home with his family after he was dug out of a grave.
Koah Sharp was rescued nearly 24 hours after he was reported missing. He is expected to make a full recovery, according to his medical team.
Koah’s disappearance led to a large law enforcement effort that ended with the arrest of his 25-year-old father, Michael Comer.
The grave
On Wednesday, Koah’s grandfather took WRDW to the grave in a wooded area off Parthenon Road in Lexington County. The area has trees spaced apart, sparse brush and ground covered in pine straw.
The hole has been filled in. The grandfather used a pointed finger to show the edges of the 2-foot-by-2-foot grave, then pulled aside the pine straw to show the dirt below.
Koah was found Tuesday, buried inside a dog crate a foot below the surface, crying “at the top of his lungs,” Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said.
Koon said the wire dog crate was wrapped in a towel that trapped enough air for Koah to survive for about 24 hours. He said the 45-degree outdoor temperature likely slowed the boy’s metabolism.
Koon said “a lot of things were going in Koah’s favor,” including the large response from law enforcement, the searcher who noticed the disturbed ground, the 45-degree outdoor temperature and the towel that created the air pocket.
“The Good Lord looked down on him,” Koon said.
How it unfolded
According to authorities, Comer had Koah for about four days after getting out of jail for other offenses.
Authorities were told of messages Comer sent to Koah’s mother in which he reportedly threatened to keep the child or gain custody, said he felt like killing himself and planned to move to New York.
On Monday, Comer’s mother was caring for the boy in Gaston, according to authorities. She left to run an errand, and another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Authorities said Comer left Gaston around 9 a.m. and was in Batesburg-Leesville around noon. Koon said that is probably when Koah was buried.
A relative filed a missing-person report by 3 p.m. Authorities said Comer went to several locations Monday without a car, which made it difficult to determine where the boy might be.
“We found some video of Michael in and around Batesburg-Leesville with no baby,” Koon said. “So certainly, we got worried, hoping and praying that he dropped the baby with another person. As the day went on and nobody came forward, it was certainly more and more concerning.”
Arrest and charges
Around 10 p.m. Monday, authorities found Comer, without Koah, in a shed that did not belong to him. He was arrested and charged with burglary.
Charges related to Koah were added later: attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child and custodial interference.
Bond was denied for Comer on Thursday morning.
A month earlier, Comer was placed on probation after pleading guilty to aggravated breach of peace. Court records also showed he was arrested earlier this year on a domestic violence count and a weapons-related count.
His next court appearance is set for Dec. 10.
The search and rescue
A South Carolina Law Enforcement Division helicopter logged several flights in the area of Parthenon Road on Monday night and early Tuesday.
Authorities focused on the area where Comer’s father lives.
Around 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, one of about 100 searchers noticed a disturbed section of ground about 50 yards into the nearby woods. Crime scene technicians checked the area.
“You could hear little Koah crying,” Koon said. “As you can imagine, the race was on. Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out.”
Koah was taken to a hospital around 2 p.m. Tuesday. He went home that night.

title: Bucksport Man's Complaint Visit Ends With Arrest And A Towed Car In Bangor
text:
Bucksport Man Visits Bangor PD To Lodge A Complaint, Illegally Parks Across 2 Handicap Spots, And Ends Up Arrested

title: UMaine women’s basketball hangs tough, falls to Oregon 79-72
text:
The University of Maine women’s basketball team fought valiantly against Oregon on Friday night at UMaine’s Memorial Gymnasium, but a fourth-quarter run for the Ducks proved too much to overcome as Oregon escaped with a 79-72 win.
Maine led by as many as 11 near the end of the first half and held a lead late in the third quarter, but an offensive onslaught from the Ducks in the final frame proved enough to give Oregon the win.
Maine was paced by sophomore Lala Woods, who went 6-13 from three-point range en route to a team-high 21 points. Sophomore Maddie Fitzpatrick continued her hot streak to begin the season for the Black Bears, finishing with 19 points, nine rebounds, and five assists.
Maine drilled 14 three-pointers in the contest and shot 47% from distance. That wasn’t enough to overcome how poorly the Black Bears shot from inside the arc, however, as the Black Bears went just 11 of 31 on two-point shots.
In contrast, the Ducks made just six of 26 three-point attempts but went 27-38 from two-point range.
Oregon standout Katie Fiso did as she’s done throughout her whole career for the Ducks, beating defenders off the dribble and finishing several tough layups near the cup on the night. The junior guard finished with 32 points to lead the Ducks. Freshman guard Brooklynn Haywood poured in 24 points off the bench for Oregon.
The game, which was played in Maine because of Oregon head coach Kelly Graves’ desire to coach a basketball game in all 50 states, sees UMaine fall to 2-1 on the season.
The Black Bears have a quick turnaround, staying at home for a Nov. 15 matchup vs. Brown. That game is set for a 1 p.m. tip.

title: High school athletes can capitalize on NIL, lawmakers look to protect young players
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - Name, image and likeness, or NIL, continues to dominate headlines and forever change the game for student athletes.
While the federal government tackles the college landscape, some states have enacted laws to protect high school students and their families.
In Louisiana, lawmakers recently passed legislation seeking to protect K-12 student athletes interested in signing NIL deals. Young players in the state can legally enter into big money contracts, but the new laws also look to add transparency and accountability.
A star recruit
At Tad Gormely Stadium, members of Brother Martin’s High School football team endured double session practices in Louisiana’s punishing summer heat ahead of the 2026 season.
Among them is Easton Royal. Most football scouts rank him as the number one high school wide receiver in the entire nation.
At 17 years old, the Brother Martin senior is considered a prime college football recruit. Royal said versatility is the strongest part of his game.
“There’s not one way that you can really stop me. I feel like, just give me the ball and put it in my hands,” said Easton Royal.
Putting the ball in Royal’s hands is what the Brother Martin Crusaders have consistently done the past three seasons, helping them maintain a top ten state divisional ranking.
Mark Bonis has been Brother Martin’s head football coach since 2009.
“He’s been with me since eighth grade. So, he becomes part of your family. He’s definitely one of the best we’ve ever coached, but what I’m really proud of is his growth and maturation from eighth grade all the way to senior year,” said Bonis.
Coach Bonis said Royal’s game highlights are impressive because of what he puts into practice.
“When you’re talking about one of the best players in the country and you’re having to pull him off the field from practice to me, that says a lot about him, but also sets the standard for your football program,” said Coach Bonis.
Royal is currently committed to the University of Texas, but still has time to change his mind. There’s no shortage of social media speculation about the possibility of him staying in state and playing for LSU.
Royal is on the verge of entering the world of paid collegiate athletes and potential big money endorsement deals.
But he doesn’t have to wait until college to earn NIL money. Royal said he is getting offers that could be life changing for his family.
“It would mean a lot because my mom, she’s right now a single mother with three boys, and we all eat a lot. And we’re boys. We’re kind of crazy, so she put in a lot of hard nights, working three jobs, working overnight, being tired. So being able to have the NIL would really help her so she can stop working as much as she does,” Royal said.
From NIL deals to where he’ll eventually play, Royal said he’s trying to stay grounded about all the attention.
“If I’m in a room, you won’t really know who I am unless somebody else brings it up. That’s just the type of person I am, and that’s how I keep myself humble. Because I have all this ability, but it can be taken away,” said Royal.
Royal may not talk much about any NIL deals, but since 2021, when the NCAA first allowed college athletes to monetize their name, image and likeness, the conversation and debate has trickled down to the high school level, and even lower.
For Coach Bonis, he believes Royal deserves NIL money, if that’s what he chooses.
“Personally, I think it’s a great deal. If anybody’s going to capitalize on someone’s name image and likeness then I believe that person, the player, should reap the benefits of that. Now, I disagree, and people confuse the two, with pay to play. I’m not a proponent for pay to play,” said Bonis.
Changing the game
John “J.T.” Curtis Jr. is the winningest high school football coach in Louisiana history. In his 57 years of coaching, Coach Curtis said he’s never witnessed the kinds of changes and situations NIL is generating.
“No longer do we use the term student athlete. All we hear about is NIL. You and I are here talking about NIL, not about a young man who is entering into college or entering into high school and their education and the importance of that education. Now it’s all about what can you do for me,” said Curtis, who is the head football coach at John Curtis Christian School.
Curtis said the deals are even “trickling down into junior high school and rising freshmen.”
One of his his biggest concerns is with sports agents, or people who present themselves as one. Curtis said he worries about agents taking advantage of teenagers and families who may be unfamiliar with the business side of sports.
“I’ve coached players who went to be professionals, and those pro agents are usually getting 3% to 5% the earnings of the player,” Curtis said. “I have heard, I have not seen, but I’ve heard through resources that some of these agents pitching deals to high school athletes and getting as much as 20% to 25% of a person’s NIL contract, and of course, that’s upfront money.”
Adding student protections
Patrick Connick, a Republican state senator in Louisiana, acknowledged that some younger students were “being approached by so-called agents” who reportedly had no qualifications or expertise.
Ahead of Louisiana’s spring legislative session, Connick, Coach Curtis and a committee of lawmakers worked on crafting bills to address the growing influence of NIL on young athletes.
Connick sponsored one NIL law that took effect in August. Among its provisions is a requirement for agents who represent student-athletes in the state to register with the Louisiana Attorney General’s office. Those agents must also complete training and pass background checks.
“These guys are young. Sometimes their family members, they see dollar signs, but we can’t let the agents take advantage of these kids. That’s the whole purpose of what this legislation is about,” said State Senator Connick.
For Royal, there’s one person he turns to for guidance on NIL and all other matters in life.
“My mom. We make the decisions, but she also has her close circle of people that she also goes to as well to help us make decisions like about agents and things of that nature,” said Royal.
Another NIL law sets up guardrails for K-12 student-athletes and their parents or guardians. One guideline requires parental consent for a minor to sign an NIL deal. Connick said the number of student-athletes in the state affected by NIL is unclear, but more regulation of it was needed.
“The whole purpose is to protect these young kids who have the potential of earning a lot of money at a very young age and we got to watch out for that,” Connick said.
While Louisiana’s new laws aim to protect high school athletes, they also place some limits on them. For example, student athletes cannot profit from marketing deals that involve drugs, alcohol, tobacco, gambling, or weapons.
Whether at the high school or college level, NIL can be polarizing. Brother Martin Coach Mark Bonis argues high school is where true amateur athletics still lives, and NIL can benefit student athletes, their families and even their schools from all the exposure.
“You see a young man, you see a family that’s worked for things for years and years, and you see the sacrifices that they’ve made. You want to make sure that they are receiving everything that they have earned,” said Coach Bonis.
Some, like Coach J.T. Curtis, said the injection of money NIL could weaken the integrity of scholastic sports.
“When big money comes in the front door, everything goes out the back door unless you have your values in the right place,” said Coach Curtis.
Ultimately, it may come down to the athlete and their loved ones. Even Coach Curtis admitted that if any of us or our families had these kinds of opportunities, debates about NIL would be of a different nature.
“It’s easy for me to be judgmental and say the pie in the sky, it’s all about your education and so on, but when you’re confronted with the numbers, then that’s a different thing,” Coach Curtis said.
Royal said money is a factor, but it’s not the sole reason why he’s on the football field.
“Being here at Brother Martin, Coach Bonis, they work us, it’s not easy. We’re practicing at Tad Gormley in the heat, so you really got to love it to want to be able to continue to play it for the rest of your life. And I feel like I really love the game of football,” Royal said.
It’s one teenager’s love for a game that increasingly requires adult decisions.
NIL across the country
As of November 2026, about three dozen states allow high school athletes to make deals.
Other states strictly prohibit compensation for NIL. These deals have caused some families to move states to capitalize on their skills.

title: Teen accused of killing paddleboarder in Union indicted on murder charge

title: Former nonprofit employee who helped foster children arrested on child endangerment charges
text:
WACO, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) — An employee of a nonprofit group that helps abused and neglected foster children navigate the court system was arrested Wednesday with his wife after authorities searched their Texas home and found the conditions in which they and their two children were living.
John Moorman, 51, director of advocacy at CASA of McLennan County, and his wife, 48-year-old Leslie Moorman, were expected to be released Thursday from the county jail on $5,000 bonds each. Both were arrested on state felony charges of endangering a child.
Employment status
John Moorman, a former Child Protective Services worker, was placed on administrative leave Wednesday from his job, said CASA Executive Director Ashlee Knutson.
“Moorman is no longer employed by CASA of McLennan County,” Knutson said Thursday.
CASA, or Court-Appointed Special Advocates, recruits, trains and supports volunteers who assist children in the foster care system.
Knutson said the arrests of John Moorman and his wife had nothing to do with his role as a CASA staff member.
“Anyone who serves a CASA program goes through a comprehensive, multi-layered background screening process – whether they are a staff member, volunteer, or board member,” Knutson said in a statement. “The process includes FBI fingerprinting as well as child protective services, national sex offender registry, and criminal background checks. Because these background checks are fingerprint-based and given the responsibility CASA programs hold, ongoing monitoring continues once someone begins serving in any of these roles.”
Search warrant at China Spring home
According to arrest affidavits, Waco police investigators served a search warrant Wednesday at the Moormans’ home in the 10000 block of Barton Creek Drive in China Spring. Authorities had received a “CyberTip concerning child sexual abuse material,” the affidavits state.
During the execution of the search warrant, officers “immediately noticed a foul odor commonly associated with human or animal excrement, such as feces and urine,” the affidavit states.
The detective wrote that while going through the home, investigators found trash, food, feces, soiled diapers and other materials ‘throughout the entire residence in a way that made it impossible to walk through without stepping on it."
The affidavit alleges that while there was food in the refrigerator, the kitchen was not in a state in which anything could be cooked and “there were bugs throughout the residence.”
The affidavit also alleges there was a rat’s nest in the kitchen and officers saw rodents in a child’s room.
“In the (detective’s) training and experience, the state of the residence presents a clear and present danger to the welfare of the children,” according to the affidavit.
Children placed with family
Child Protective Services workers took custody of a 15-year-old boy and a 6-year-old girl and placed them with other family members, said Cierra Shipley, Waco police spokesperson.
Investigators also seized “technology” from the Moormans’ home as the investigation continues, Shipley said.

title: ‘All fake’: Man accused of posing as decorated combat veteran, stealing more than $80,000
text:
HAMPTON BAYS, N.Y. (News 12 Long Island) — A man is in a New York jail after authorities said he posed as a decorated combat veteran and stole thousands of dollars from a veterans organization.
The Suffolk County district attorney announced the charges Tuesday.
David Agtsteribbe, the former finance officer for the Hampton Bays American Legion, is accused of stealing more than $80,000 from the group. Investigators said he lied about his service and claimed to be a Purple Heart recipient.
What investigators say about his service
Investigators said Agtsteribbe enlisted in the Army in 1986 and was court-martialed the next year. He pleaded guilty to stealing money from another soldier and received a bad conduct discharge, officials said.
“The exact price for a Purple Heart is someone’s blood, sweat and tears,” Suffolk County District Attorney Ray Tierney said. “That’s what it costs for an actual person to win a Purple Heart. It cost him nothing but lies.”
Tierney said Agtsteribbe also claimed to be a prisoner of war. During the time he claimed to be a prisoner of war, Tierney said, Agtsteribbe was an inmate in upstate New York for a grand larceny conviction.
Fake credentials
The district attorney said Agtsteribbe used fake military credentials. Tierney said he benefited from the lies through membership in veterans organizations and Purple Heart license plates.
“It’s all fake,” Tierney said.
Veteran responds
Ira Freiband, a veteran, said he is hurt and disappointed in Agtsteribbe.
“I’m hurt, more than angry. I’m hurt and I’m hurt, I’m disappointed. I’m disappointed in him,” Freiband said.
Agtsteribbe remains in jail. There has been no comment so far from the commander of the Hampton Bays American Legion.
“He was so good at it. He fooled everybody. He fooled this whole town. We weren’t the only ones that got fooled,” Freiband said.

title: Maine home sales, median price fall in October
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Maine Realtors reported fewer sales and lower prices in October, according to the Maine Association of Realtors.
October sales and median price
About 1,500 sales of single-family existing homes were reported by Maine Listing. Sales dipped 6.58% when comparing October 2026 to October 2025.
The median sales price decreased 5.63% to $402,500 over the same period. The median sales price indicates that half of the homes sold for more and half sold for less.
“As we move into the fourth quarter, buyer demand has softened as mortgage interest rates are shaping market dynamics,” said Judy Oberg, 2026 president of the Maine Association of Realtors and associate broker at Oberg Insurance & Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
“Statewide, buyers have more homes to choose from than last year and more room to negotiate. Sellers are facing more competition from other listings and that’s reflected in the median sold prices,” Oberg said.
National sales
Nationally, existing-home sales fell 8.6%, according to the National Association of Realtors.
“With more homes on the market, work with a knowledgeable local Realtor to negotiate a competitive offer. Move-in ready homes, priced strategically, are selling,” Oberg said.

title: Maine awarded second round of rural health care funds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The federal government awarded Maine a second round of funds to improve the rural health landscape.
Maine will receive $190.4 million from the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The funding comes nearly a year after a similar award in December 2025.
Maine will use the money to expand community-based services and accelerate regional planning.
“Expanding that work in year two, particularly in the areas of workforce and regional planning, will be vital to the future stability of rural health care in Maine,” Jeffrey Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said in a news release this week.
During the Rural Health Transformation Program’s first year, Maine put all of money toward health care workforce training, electronic medical record modernization and rural hospital efficiency.
Priorities for the second year include expanding community-based services, continuing health care recruitment and training efforts, modernizing technology and accelerating regional planning.
Proposed additions would support Tribal traditional healing services and expand electronic medical record investments to eligible county jails to improve continuity of care as people return to their communities.
“Our next phase builds on the foundation established through our initial work with providers, communities, and partners across Maine,” said Kristen McAuley, the program’s director. “Our focus is on helping people get the care they need, supporting the workforce that delivers it and developing coordinated services that can be sustained beyond the program’s funding.”
Year-two plan
Maine plans to add school-based health centers in rural communities, support new mobile health units where needed and continue integrating primary care into behavioral health clinics.
Other initiatives will:
- Help rural employers recruit and retain health care workers and expand career exploration and training for students and current workers.
- Invest in telehealth and modernize electronic medical records, including in county jails ready to provide MaineCare-covered services before release.
- Improve transportation coordination and helping residents navigate health coverage. A new proposal would help Tribal communities offer traditional healing services through MaineCare.
- Initiate regional planning sooner than originally planned, bringing local partners together to identify essential services and guide future investments; and continue efforts to improve hospital efficiency and advance payment models that support coordinated care.
“Year two of Maine’s Rural Health Transformation Program is an opportunity to turn our shared vision for rural health care into meaningful, lasting improvements for the communities we serve,” said Darcy Shargo, Maine Primary Care Association’s CEO. “Maine’s federally qualified health centers, serving one in six Maine people, are essential to this effort.”

title: This off-season Asian fusion takeout spot on MDI caters to locals
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An Asian fusion takeout spot on Mount Desert Island is one of few businesses that is only open during the winter, catering nearly exclusively to locals.
Word Up Take Out, located behind the Southwest Harbor Public Library, opened for its second season on Tuesday, offering a buffet of Asian fusion-inspired to-go options, including Korean BBQ beef bowls, pad thai, crab rangoon and General Tso’s chicken.
Other than local ski resorts, the takeout spot is one of few — if not the only — coastal Maine eatery that solely opens over the winter. Most MDI restaurants are only open for the region’s busy tourist season, between May and October, though some stay open year-round, like the Thirsty Whale Tavern and Geddy’s in Bar Harbor.
Owner Robert Higgins is occupied during the tourist season with the waterside Chart Room in Hulls Cove, where he is a chef and partner.
“I did it last winter in large part because I am the chef and partner at the Chart Room and in the winter, I would chill out and not do much, and it drove my wife nuts,” Higgins said Thursday. “So I decided I needed to do something before it went bad, so I opened this. For as long as I’ve lived here I’ve heard people complain about [how] nothing is open in the winter, and it’s true.”
The takeout spot is hoping to fill a void in wintertime dining options. It also joins a growing number of MDI restaurants that provide diverse foods.
“I’m pretty sure I’m the only person in a long way that only opens for winter,” Higgins said.
The restaurant’s latest menu includes ramen, jalapeno poppers, pickle fries, egg rolls and sandwiches. The spot is open Monday thru Friday from 11:30 a.m. until 6 p.m.
“I tried to keep it open last summer but it was a disaster,” Higgins said. “It didn’t even occur to me that I am the main ingredient to all this and it doesn’t work without me.”
The seasonal eatery may extend its hours to weekends as early as next week, Higgins said.
Most orders are completed online, though customers can also grab a meal by visiting the shop’s takeout window.
Higgins was born in Millinocket but has lived in Southwest Harbor for roughly eight years. He opted for Asian fusion food because he loves it, he said, adding that he incorporated sushi in last year’s menu but that the time commitment it required wasn’t worth it.
“The last two days, people have been thanking me when they come to the window, and I thank them, too. Without them, we’re nothing,” Higgins said. “We’re here for you.”

title: Measles antibody test: What to know about checking your immunity
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (Aging Untold) — Measles is highly contagious, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says adults can get seriously sick. Complications are more common after age 20.
A simple antibody test, also known as a titer test, can show whether a person is likely protected.
What a measles titer test involves
Any Lab Test Now in Greenville, South Carolina, offers more than 8,000 tests that people can walk in and request, according to Madison Gault, clinical director.
She and her team help patients understand everything about their health, from genes to cholesterol levels to antibodies.
Gault said the measles titer is the test drawing the most interest.
Reporter Kari Beal received two doses of the MMR vaccine as a child and had the titer test done because she wanted to know her current immunity.
What the results mean
Beal said her measles antibody level was 300 and the minimum for immunity is 16.
She took the report to family doctor Nita Bijoor and asked if 300 was high. Bijoor said there is no established “really high” level.
“It means you have a good level,” Bijoor said.
The result probably reflects good nutrition and a healthy lifestyle, and that Beal’s body is mounting a good antibody response, Bijoor said.
How the test works, and its limits
A titer test measures immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies, which indicate past exposure to or vaccination against a virus like measles.
Bijoor said sometimes a memory of the virus can remain in the cells without showing high levels of antibodies.
“There can be false negatives,” Bijoor said.
She said a person with a low result may still have a good antibody response, so the test is not 100% foolproof. Bijoor said it is still the best test available.
Who the test is recommended for
Bijoor said she recommends the test for:
- People who do not know their immunity.
- People who think they have natural immunity.
- Vaccinated people in high-risk jobs, such as educators and health care workers.
“I think in the setting of an outbreak, it makes sense if a patient wants to be absolutely sure,” Bijoor said.
Symptoms and complications discussed
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold expert, said measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads when infected people cough or sneeze.
Signs include a high temperature and red, watery eyes, usually followed by a diffuse rash.
She said complications can include pneumonia and encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain, which can occur years after infection.
Rogers said the IgG marker represents past exposure while the IgM marker represents acute exposure.
A person with no antibodies may never have been exposed or may have lost immunity, she added.
Rogers said lab results should be reviewed with a doctor because people can make the mistake of looking at a range and assuming a result is normal.

title: Mass. man to spend years in prison for deadly, multivehicle crash on Maine Turnpike
text:
Massachusetts man to spend years in prison for deadly, multivehicle crash on Maine Turnpike
A man from Brighton, Massachusetts, will spend 5.5 years in prison for causing a crash that killed a man and involved multiple vehicles on the Maine Turnpike in 2024.
Oguzhan Cildir, 26, was sentenced on Tuesday to 15 years in prison, with all but 5.5 years suspended, followed by four years of probation.
Cildir pleaded guilty to manslaughter, aggravated assault, two counts of reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, and aggravated driving to endanger.
Video in the media player above is from the day of the crash.
The crash happened at 8:41 a.m. on April 26, 2024, at mile 20 southbound on the highway in Wells. Police say Cildir was driving a black Toyota Prius southbound on Interstate 95 when he cut across several lanes of traffic, entered the inside breakdown lane, hitting a silver Toyota Sienna minivan and a white Toyota Tacoma pickup. Police say the truck rolled over several times. The driver of the truck, 53-year-old Gloria Cascio of Albion, died at the scene.
A passenger in the pickup, 60-year-old Vincent Cascio of Albion, was flown to Maine Medical Center in Portland with serious injuries. A LifeFlight of Maine helicopter landed on the highway to take Cascio to the hospital.
At noon that day, traffic was still backed up all the way to Biddeford, more than 10 miles from the crash scene.

title: Republicans score rare blue-to-red flip in Maine during midterm landslide
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (AP) — As Republicans dig out from under a midterm landslide, they can point to a single bright spot on the nationwide congressional map. That’s Maine’s 2nd congressional district, the only seat that went from blue to red without the help of redistricting.
It was far from a resounding victory. Even though President Donald Trump won the district by 9 points two years ago, it took a former Republican governor, Paul LePage, to squeak out a victory over Matt Dunlap, the Democratic state auditor.
The Associated Press called the race Thursday after officials finished the ranked choice voting process to determine the winner.
LePage and Dunlap were competing to replace Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat who is retiring from Congress.
The only other seats that went from blue to red are Texas’ 32nd congressional district and Tennessee’ 9th congressional district, but both of those flips were enabled by redistricting efforts that made the electorates far more conservative.
Meanwhile, Democrats have flipped 44 seats, and a handful of races have not yet been called.
Dunlap conceded last week and LePage declared victory, and he’s been in Washington for orientation for new members.
“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine,” said Brent Littlefield, a spokesperson for LePage.
Maine only has two congressional districts. The 1st is heavily Democratic and includes Portland and wealthy coastal towns. The 2nd includes a few small cities and vast rural and forested areas, and is home to industries such as logging, potato farming and lobster fishing. It’s more conservative than most of New England.
Golden had found success in the 2nd by running as a moderate Democrat who was willing to break with his party. However, he announced last year that he would not run for a fifth term, saying he had “grown tired of the increasing incivility and plain nastiness that are now common from some elements of our American community.”
As governor from 2010 to 2018, most of LePage’s two terms predated Trump’s presidency, but he aligned himself with the president toward the end of his time in office. The two shared a brand of brash, conservative populism, with LePage once saying he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular.”
However, LePage also criticized Trump’s tariffs on Canada, a key trading partner for Maine, and expressed support for legal immigration. When he declared victory last week, LePage vowed to make the state’s interests a priority in Washington.
“If it is good for Maine, I will work hard to make it happen. If it is bad for Maine, I will oppose it,” he said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Front-center airbags largely unavailable in U.S.
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores why critical vehicle crash safeguards remain a costly optional feature in the U.S.
Then, we examine the crisis of jails serving as de facto mental health facilities and the programs working to break the cycle.
Plus, meet a retired couple bringing rock ‘n’ roll and joy to seniors.
Sacrificing Safety?
Victims of car crashes often recall such events happening “in the blink of an eye,” when in reality, it takes less than half that amount of time.
Particularly when the impact is coming from the side.
A safety device designed to prevent that kind of injury was introduced more than a decade ago: Front-center airbags deploy from the seat or center console to keep a driver from hitting the passenger side door or to prevent a driver and passenger’s heads from colliding.
But those airbags are largely unavailable in the U.S.
Jails not built for long-term care
Experts say prisons and county jails have become destinations for people who need mental health treatment, not time behind bars.
According to multiple reports, three jail systems are among the largest mental health facilities in the country: Rikers Island in New York, Twin Towers Jail in Los Angeles and Cook County Jail in Chicago.
But some people are looking for solutions, hoping to bridge the gap between police and mental health services.
Organ donations for Black Americans
Black Americans face a critical need for organ transplants, yet they experience longer wait times and lower donation rates.
Army veteran volunteers
A Valley Army veteran is spending his post-military and post-retirement years volunteering at a Phoenix senior center, offering companionship and practical help to seniors who have few other resources.

title: Aging Untold: How to reset when stress becomes chronic
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore when everyday stress can become chronic and how it may affect your body.
Then, we meet older adults returning to college and look at the challenges and rewards of learning later in life.
Plus, in one Michigan town, a familiar thumbs-up has become a small gesture that brings big smiles to the community.
Stress is part of life for lots of people, but chronic stress can have physical effects.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said stress becomes chronic “when you can’t turn it off.”
The Aging Untold experts are sharing signs of chronic stress and tips on how to calm your body down, including box breathing and the SEEDS method.
Taking classes after retiring can be low-cost or even free.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she sees going back to college later in life as personal enrichment.
Dr. Rhea Rogers said learning new things later in life is a way of “establishing neuroplasticity.”
Some medical professionals are promoting ketamine infusion as a possible solution for patients who cannot get relief from traditional pain management methods.
Elanor Koch of Nebraska said she has seen improvement since starting the therapy.
She said a tumor eroded and compressed her spinal cord by more than 60%, and she would wake up in pain. A flare would leave her in bed for days.
Then, Koch said she found ketamine infusion therapy and experienced significant improvement after six treatments in one month.
People with certain medical histories might not be good candidates for ketamine infusion, including those with mental health conditions such as schizophrenia, uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease, kidney or liver disease and substance use disorder.
On most days, 78-year-old George Doxtader can be found on a bench at the corner of State and Main streets in Eaton Rapids, Michigan, giving a thumbs-up to greet passersby.
People in the community look forward to seeing him.
“It just makes them happy to see his smiling face and his thumbs-up,” Pastor Jenny Rouble of First Congregational Church said. She said Doxtader is a friend and a blessing to the community.
What many might not know is that Doxtader suffered two major health events decades ago and has paralysis on the right side of his body. And sometimes, he has trouble speaking.
