title: Maine school board member held without bail following new drug charges
text:
Eddington school board member held without bail following new drug charges
An Eddington mother and school board member was ordered to be held without bail after pleading not guilty to new drug-related charges.
Brittany Wood, 36, turned herself in to Penobscot County Sheriff’s deputies Wednesday night after a multiday search, according to WMTW media partner WABI. She pleaded not guilty to drug possession, falsifying physical evidence and violating conditions of release.
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office said deputies found Wood with what turned out to be illegal drugs during a traffic stop over the weekend. Wood said in court Thursday that she had a prescription for the drugs.
A judge ordered Wood to be held without bail because she was already out on bail on aggravated assault charges. Those charges stem from allegations that her then-9-month-old baby nearly died from exposure to drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, in May.
Despite the judge’s caution, Wood addressed the court.
“I don’t know why the state feels that I would need to be held away from my children, my family, my responsibilities. I’m doing everything right. I have extreme circumstances. I’m cooperating. I’m working. I’m doing everything that everybody’s asking — DHHS, law enforcement, everyone in the whole world. And I’m doing the best I can,” Wood said.
School board status
Wood remains an elected member of the Regional School Unit 63 School Board. Under board policy, she could be removed if she misses three consecutive meetings.

title: Trading company and art gallery to open in Houlton
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The first and most important art piece placed in a new gallery, opening later this month in Houlton, is a self portrait of the curator’s late father, Summer Dulinsky said.
By mid-morning Thursday, the Mustard Seed Trading Co. a curated gallery store and art gallery, was buzzing with a steady stream of artists and well wishers, as curator Dulinsky hung the final pieces for a preview show on Friday, Nov. 13.
Her father, Fred Hachtmeyer, who passed nine years ago, was an artist and an inspiration for Dulinksy’s first show in her gallery located on Houlton’s historic Market Square. But just as she lovingly points to her father’s piece, she does the same for the 11 other artists in this first show that she describes as a year of art, taking the viewer through northern Maine’s seasonal changes.
“There are so many crazy-talented people here,” she said.
This New Mexico transplant, who has worked as a creative consultant to many budding entrepreneurs since she came to Houlton in 2018, first opened the Mustard Seed space next door to the new gallery as a birthplace for creative exploration and the telling of artistic tales.
Her latest invention with its historic exposed brick wall and massively high ceilings is a place to honor and highlight created works from paintings, photography, wood, sculpture and textiles to pottery, restored vintage furniture and more, she said.
As a creative consultant who loves home decor, Dulinsky initially thought the trading company gallery would be more home decor items with a smaller art gallery in the rear of the elongated 640-square-foot space.
But she flipped her focus onto showing more art in the larger part of the gallery which can accommodate massive paintings. Not to mention a long line of artists hoping to get a chance to show their works in this hip gallery, reminiscent of those historic enclaves in New York City’s Greenwich Village.
The thought process behind it is: living a beautiful life, living it well, Dulinsky said.
“You don’t always have to have a million things to do that, but maybe it is that one big splurge. But at the same time, I want it accessible,” she said. “I love the places that have a $1,600, or $2,000 painting, and there’s also a $20 print of something else.”
And that is how she has planned the space that will accommodate seasoned and emerging artists but also have other items often found in gallery shops, such as prints of the originals, greeting cards, perhaps even T-shirts or bags with the art on them.
“Maybe I come in and I only have 10 bucks or maybe I’m not even shopping,” she said. “But I deserve as much reverence from the person who works there and respect and care as someone who comes in and has tons of money.”
Jane Torres, executive director of the Greater Houlton Chamber of Commerce, worked with the Aroostook County Historical and Art Museum in Houlton to put two large historic pieces on loan in the gallery, with one from A.H. Fogg dating to 1902. With the museum board’s approval, Melanie Bickford, co-owner of Petals and Pine in Ludlow, has been restoring the giant wood pieces for the gallery.
On Thursday, Dulinsky told the story of the first show that she said travels through the seasons with a vast array of works in varying styles, brushstrokes and hues, alongside very large black and white photographs of winter.
“It’s all about living a beautiful life,” she said, adding that she wants everyone to feel welcome and to come into the gallery to look at all the art pieces and other artisans’ works. “Not everyone can pay $650 for painting, but man, it’d make an incredible T-shirt or tote bag.”
Famed Maine artist Frank Sullivan, known for his muted landscapes, has a special place for two of his works in the gallery for the opening and preview show. Sullivan will be the first solo artist exhibition in January.
“It’s January 16th. I think around three in the afternoon or so, he’s going to be here to sign and talk about his book, ‘Drawing is Everything’,” she said. “And he’s going to actually have those drawings that people almost never see. He’s gonna have them here, I do believe, on exhibit.”
For the Friday preview show, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. at 37 Market Square, the artists will be available to talk about their works and there will be hors d’oeuvres and a celebratory toast, and a first glimpse of what’s to come, Dulinsky said.
During the upcoming holidays, the gallery will be open 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Thursday through Saturday and Sunday noon to 4 p.m.

title: This grassroots ‘village’ helped a single mom drive away with a new car
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, SC (InvestigateTV) - It’s not like an episode of Oprah, but for single moms like Caroline Reed, it feels pretty close.
She was gifted with a white car topped with a big red bow, all thanks to Amanda Todd and her village.
To understand the gift is to learn about the journey.
“My heart has always been to help single moms. Every single mom’s story is different,” said Todd.
Helping single moms like her friend Reed isn’t what Todd does; it’s who she is.
“Beyond support and encouragement, they need help with the more expensive items,” she said.
Todd created “Their Village Helpers for Single Moms” Facebook group and trusted her faith and her followers to raise money to buy them cars.
“I was like, do me a favor and take this challenge; let’s get a mom a car,” she said. “Find something in your house that you can sell on Facebook, then Venmo me the money or drop it off on my porch.”
The group also had yard sales, and Todd even shrimped for cash. She also launched her business, Color Connection, where she finds women’s most flattering colors for clothes and makeup. Every penny of profit fuels her mission.
They raised $4,000 to put their first mom behind the wheel, and now they’ve doubled that amount.
The group masked the surprise at Reed’s birthday dinner and took her outside for the big reveal. It was nothing but happy tears and complete shock for a mom who, like Todd, is always showing up for others.
This time, the community showed up for her, including Coastal Grand Auto Sales, which not only helped with the car but also sweetened the gift with a two-year warranty.
The women then took the car for a spin. Reed said the real gift isn’t the car itself, but the peace of mind that comes with every turn of the key.
“To get into a car that’s now yours and not have to worry about stopping on the side of the road or just not being able to pick up Zee, it’s just something I never thought I’d be able to have,” she said.

title: Wiscasset, Boothbay Region school districts’ leaders denounce firm’s report as wrong, misleading
text:
Wiscasset Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson said she knew nothing about Dirigo Strategic Advisors' June 2026 report, "Maine School Budget Analysis Tool Pilot," prepared for Maine Policy Institute and its Maine Education Initiative, until she heard about it recently from Alternative Organizational Structure 98 Superintendent of Schools Robert Kahler.
Kahler didn't know Boothbay Region schools were referred to in it, either, until someone mentioned it to him at a Maine School Management Association conference.
And Wiscasset School Committee Chair Tracey Whitney shared her multiple concerns Nov. 10 about Dirigo's report. Andersson provided Wiscasset Newspaper with it on request Nov. 11.
According to the discussion in the Nov. 10 Wiscasset school committee meeting, after Andersson learned about the report, she sent Whitney it; then Whitney asked Andersson to send it to the rest of the committee. "I felt that it was really important that we address (this) because this is out in the world (and) one part of it is now being used as marketing to other schools ... to do this same pilot," Whitney said.
Andersson, in the meeting, and Kahler, in a phone interview Nov. 12, said the report includes wrong information about their school systems.
Kahler said the report also makes it sound like the pilot tool helped pare the AOS school budget.
"It's a wildly inaccurate statement. And if anyone wanted to go back and look at the very hard work that the trustees did, that the school committee did and that my administrative team did," they could see that, Kahler said. "I know I don't recall seeing that tool used at all. I know I didn't use it during the budget season."
After he looked at the report, he contacted its makers and told them of his surprise and disappointment, and was told they don't need permission because the data included is public information.
Andersson said the data does come from public information, namely numbers on Maine Department of Education's data dashboard, but she said: "The data dashboard runs ... 18 months behind. She said Dirigo's report compared Wiscasset data with a "peer group" of school systems she doesn't consider similar to Wiscasset, including Mount Desert Isle, Winthrop and Islesboro. She said Wiscasset budget numbers are used that date to a January budget draft "that never got off the table," and the report gets wrong Wiscasset's cost per student.
"It's slick," Andersson said of the report. "It's fancy. It's slop, but to someone who didn't know that, they might think it was really the truth," Andersson said.
Wiscasset Newspaper has sought comment from the documents' makers.
Andersson added in the meeting, because the material is "faulty by any sort of measure" and has been around since last spring, it is "probably partially to blame for a narrative, that the quality of education here is not worth the amount of money ... It's disappointing that this may have influenced a couple of budget votes. We'll never know."
The town rejected school budget offers in June and September and passed a third offer Nov. 3.
Whitney said the report suggests Wiscasset's school committee played a part it did not play in the report — a report she said doesn't put Wiscasset in a good light.
"This was nothing that we as a board had approved. We hadn't voted on it. Never came before us. But we do figure prominently in this report."
Whitney said it appears a couple of then-committee members "acted ... without board knowledge (and) worked with this outside group" last spring, on different parts of the report. "The board did not approve this to begin with. The board never saw these reports up until I saw them (from Andersson). I'm concerned about the validity of the report seeing that no one ever worked with our finance group, (and) some of the numbers in here were pulled from budgets that weren't done yet."
The executive summary’s cover page states: “Prepared by Dirigo Strategic Advisors April 2026 DRAFT - FOR BOARD REVIEW, Prepared for: Brycson Grover, Board Member, Jonathan Barnes, Vice Chair.”
The cover page for a “research brief” reads in part: “Teacher Compensation & Staffing Peer Analysis, Wiscasset School Department, Prepared in Advance of FY 2027 Collective Bargaining. Prepared for: Wiscasset School Board; Board, Administration and Legal Counsel Prepared by: Dirigo Strategic Advisors. April 2026. DRAFT - FOR BOARD REVIEW.”
A note at the bottom of that page reads: “This document is prepared by Dirigo Strategic Advisors for informational purposes only. It represents research findings drawn from Maine Department of Education public data, verified Supabase DOE tables. the Maine School Budget Analysis Tool (maineschoolbudgetanalysistool.com), and Maine Revised Statutes. This document is not legal or financial advice, does not represent a negotiating recommendation, and should be reviewed in consultation with district administration and legal counsel. Dirigo Strategic Advisors is a strictly neutral research firm and holds no position on any bargaining outcome.”
The documents also claim Dirigo delivered “ongoing support” for then-Wiscasset School Committee Vice Chair Jonathan Barnes and then-member Brycson Grover.
Responding to email questions Nov. 11, Grover said: "I have not seen that exact report that you sent me before now, but there was parts of it that I have reviewed.
"I reviewed the information that had been provided to me during that time period. As a former school committee member, I have always made an effort to educate myself and review as much information as possible to improve my knowledge and understanding of the school budget, operations, and how different parts of the school district functions.
"I believe it is our responsibility as elected or appointed school committee members to remain engaged, ask questions, and seek information from all available sources. We cannot fulfill that obligation to provide the best quality education for Wiscasset students by simply accepting what is presented to us. It requires asking tough questions, educating ourselves, and taking the initiative to better understand the issues facing our district. That is how we should make educated, informed decisions and help our school district thrive, grow, and become something we continue to be proud of.
"I find it frustrating that there seems to be an issue with me seeking information. The information in these reports is public information and accessible to anyone. I don’t feel any board member have the ability to control what outside individuals or organizations choose to do with publicly available information or how they choose to analyze it. If board members are upset with the information that is displayed in the report I encourage the board to invite who did the report to do a presentation on it. It wouldn’t hurt in my opinion.
"As far as informing the rest of the board, I did not see a reason why an independent review of public information would require formal notice to the entire committee. Seeking information and educating myself does not automatically create an obligation to bring every independent analysis or resource I review before the full board. I also think it is unfortunate that the focus seems to be shifting toward placing blame on former board members rather than addressing the actual information and questions raised in the report."
Wiscasset Newspaper has also sought comment from Barnes.
In the meeting, member Christopher Hart said the report "does represent or (it) suggests that there was school committee endorsement of this project, of this product."
"And we're sitting here publicly and saying that isn't true," member Doug Merrill said.
When resident Chet Grover pressed those at the table for more specifics on what they said was wrong in the report, Hart said that, for one, it says Wiscasset has a pre-K through eighth grade campus and a nine through 12 one, Hart said. Wiscasset has pre-K through five at one campus and the rest at the other.
If the financial data it starts with is wrong, including about a budget draft used, the report's analysis can't be right, Facilities and Maintenance Director Buzz Johnson observed from the audience. When another audience member asked if he'd read the report, Johnson said "No, I don't have time for that kind of garbage."
The committee and Andersson reasoned there was no point to give the report further discussion.
Said Merrill, "We acknowledge it's there and we disagree with it strongly, and move on. It's inaccurate, but if you dwell on something like this, then you're giving it credence."
"And we don't want to give it legitimacy," Whitney agreed.
Merrill also said going to court over the report whose makers "had every legal right to produce" would "waste a lot of resources."
"I don't know about their legal rights, because it is riddled with inaccuracies," Hart said, but he agreed going to court is "not enticing at all."
Everyone has already acknowledged Wiscasset's test scores need improving, Vice Chair John Merry said. "We're working on that in our workshop (sessions), right? And I say we continue to do that."
"Absolutely," Whitney said.
Also Nov. 10, the committee nodded hiring Sarah Stephens as Wiscasset Middle High School's nurse. She was to start Nov. 16, Andersson said.
In a written statement the committee received, Stephens said she graduated from University of North Alabama and was commissioned into the Army Reserves as a nurse. "I moved to Maine after graduating to be close to family and absolutely love it here. Currently I still serve and provide fully funded care to communities in need with my unit during summers," Stephens wrote. "I have a variety of nursing backgrounds including dementia care; medsurg; pre-op/recovery room and most recently occupational health; certified in both adult and pediatric advanced care. I have four 'fur-children' and a supportive husband. I look forward to becoming part of the community and getting to know and care for the students at Wiscasset Middle High!"
"She's got quite a background," Merry noted.
WMHS resource room educational technician III Cheryl Dilts is retiring, effective next July 1, after 48 years in education, "including 20 wonderful years here at Wiscasset Middle High School," Dilts wrote. "I am very deeply grateful for the support of the administration, my fellow staff and teachers, plus the entire Wiscasset community throughout my years here at Wiscasset Middle High School. It has been an extreme honor to serve this school and our students. Thank you for all your guidance and support over the years."
Committee members accepted Dilts' retirement with regret. Whitney added appreciation and thanks for Dilts' years of service, and congratulations on her retirement. Dilts and her husband plan to get a camper and take it on a trip to Alaska, Andersson said.
Whitney read aloud from a card she said Wiscasset Elementary School Principal Stacy Clements handed her, from everyone at WES. Whitney read, "To the school board: Thank you for thinking of us."
And according to a parent in public comment, WMHS' changes this school year, toward keeping students where they are supposed to be, are working, and the school's atmosphere has completely changed.

title: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, with rival chipmakers itching to take advantage of the uncertainty and others wondering if the downfall of one of AI’s biggest cheerleaders will dampen the mood around the civilization-altering technology.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, was the very public face of a company that dominates the market for computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, Huang predicted Nvidia will be grappling with a $1 trillion backlog in orders for its chips by the end of the year, doubling his estimate from a year earlier.
A linchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street’s most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms.
Some of Nvidia’s biggest rivals, such as Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, saw their shares advance Thursday following Huang’s departure as investors predicted that its customers will look to diversify their suppliers. In the end, analysts say, this might not be a bad thing.
“This could turn what has effectively been a monopoly into a horse race again, as competitors rush to meet growing demand,” said Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at the global consultancy West Monroe. “Nvidia did not create that demand, and a shift in this part of the market could ultimately diversify the supply chain, create more choice for customers and strengthen the broader AI industry in the years ahead.”
Competitor chipmakers and designers see opportunity
Nvidia carved out an early lead in tailoring its chipsets known as graphics processing units, or GPUs, from use in powering video games to helping to train powerful AI systems. Demand soared as tech companies scrambled for more chips to build and run AI systems.
In annual filings, Nvidia has identified competitors including Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, Intel, Broadcom and cloud services companies like Google, Amazon and Microsoft. While these other players are established and respected within the industry for their chips, they have been trying to catch up to Nvidia.
Nvidia has had an advantage from the start and as soon as a competitor releases something just as good, Nvidia has put out the next better chip, said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer of International Services Inc. “Nobody’s just sitting still,” he said.
While some competitors saw bumps to their share prices Thursday, “their gains are going to be smaller than Nvidia’s losses,” said Chester Spatt, a finance professor at Carnegie Mellon University. But Spatt said he also anticipates chip purchasers could also become “much more reluctant to concentrate their purchases with a single source.”
The incident is also sure to prompt elected officials to seek stronger export controls on American-made chips, but that could be a boon for Chinese chipmaker Huawei, another Nvidia competitor. Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, said she suspects Chinese AI firms could accelerate efforts to secure overseas computing capacity ahead of tighter controls.
“Chinese chipmakers have already rallied on Nvidia’s troubles, but China’s AI developers depend heavily on Nvidia’s ecosystem,” she said. “This could be both an opportunity and a headache for China.”
Huang has had an outsized role as AI evangelist
While Huang is not the only face of AI — OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google’s Demis Hassabis and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton are among the others — he’s been an influential one. A celebrity-level industry evangelist with President Donald Trump’s ear and support, he has advocated for a light touch on AI regulation and has been bullish about AI’s potential to transform society, creating faster economic growth and more scientific breakthroughs.
“Jensen Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, which now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it,” said Asa Hiken, a senior analyst for research firm eMarketer. “And given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself.”
Lee, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the resignation fallout will ripple across the AI ecosystem.
“Obviously Nvidia’s technological leadership won’t disappear, but Huang had played an outsized role as its chief strategist, dealmaker and — very importantly — political advocate, with close access to both Washington and Beijing,” she said. “This happens at a critical juncture when markets are already questioning the sustainability of massive AI spending.”
Nvidia’s ‘circular financing’ deals spread the risk
Huang’s relationships across the tech landscape translated into Nvidia’s numerous partnerships and investments into companies that purchase its chips. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO turned interim CEO, has been a key force behind that strategy, but that approach is under closer scrutiny as the scandal and resignation have rattled the market.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, closed down almost 7% on Thursday. Nvidia holds a nearly 13% stake in the company.
Leadership within companies across the tech sector likely spent much of Thursday in meetings aiming to figure out a “backup plan” for some of their financing, Aldebert said. He described the circular financing practice as “incestuous.”
Many experts will be keeping a keen eye on what Huang’s departure and its fallout mean for pending public debuts of AI companies like Anthropic’s pending IPO, valued at $1.3 trillion.
It also comes in the wake of midterm elections marked by hostility toward data centers, ushering in many Democrats promising aggressive stances on AI regulation.
“This is all very interconnected and I think that we’re going to see a lot interesting dynamics happening the next month as it plays out,” said Greenstein, of West Monroe.
___
AP Business Writer Mae Anderson contributed to this story from New York.

title: Grateful for the opportunity to serve Scarborough and Gorham
text:
To the people of Scarborough and Gorham: I am deeply grateful to have been elected to represent our community in the Maine State Senate and honored by the trust placed in me. For the past six years, I have had the privilege of representing my hometown in the Maine House. As I begin work as a state senator, I remain committed to the same principles that have guided my public service: listening, working across differences and standing up for what everyone in our community deserves.
Throughout this campaign, I knocked on thousands of doors and had countless conversations about the challenges we face and they will guide my priorities: making everyday life more affordable, building an economy that works for everyone, protecting our rights and our environment and easing the burden of property taxes.
To everyone who volunteered, knocked on doors, made phone calls, put up a sign, wrote or recorded a message of support, or simply answered their door for a conversation: I am so grateful. And to everyone who cast a ballot, regardless of whom they supported: I am thankful for your participation in our democracy. Whether someone voted for me or not, I will work hard to earn their trust, listen to their concerns and remain accessible and accountable to them.
Scarborough and Gorham residents can reach me at [email protected]. I want to hear from everyone about the issues, policies, priorities and funding that our community believes I should be advocating for.
Rep. Sophie Warren
Scarborough

title: All people accounted for following cruise ship collision in New Orleans
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A tanker lost its steering and slammed into a docked American Heritage river cruise paddleboat near the Port of New Orleans on Friday.
Rescue efforts were underway immediately, with officials saying later in the day that all passengers were able to be accounted for.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 32 people needed hospitalization, but no critical injuries were reported, calling it “a miracle on the Mississippi.”
EN ESPAÑOL | Buque cisterna choca contra un crucero atracado en Nueva Orleans
Video from the scene following the reported collision showed boats and rescuers scrambling to get people in life jackets and out of the Mississippi River.
Moreno’s communication team said multiple people were rescued from the scene.
According to the Port of New Orleans press secretary, a tanker collided with an American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage around 12:30 p.m.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard the American Heritage, Port NOLA said.
Luggage and other debris could be seen floating in the river. Survivors were taken to a Port of New Orleans building next door to the dock.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the river was closed to all vessels near the site while the rescue efforts were ongoing.
“Our hearts are with the passengers, crew, and families affected by this afternoon’s collision between a passenger vessel and a tanker on the Mississippi River in New Orleans,” the Coast Guard said.
The river cruiser was docked on the Mississippi River outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with it, officials said.
The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers and was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it will also be joining the investigation.

title: BAAJA will wreak havoc on historic preservation in Maine
Brooklyn building collapse raises questions about city oversight and safety precautions
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Thousands of building construction projects are underway in New York on any given day. The deadly collapse of a building next to one of those work sites has raised questions about the city’s oversight and the safety precautions taken by contractors.
While the investigation is ongoing, some New York officials on Friday called for the hiring of more inspectors by the city’s Department of Buildings. The probe, meanwhile, is likely to focus not only on the building that fell but on an adjacent excavation site and its contractors, who had faced previous lawsuits and complaints.
Eight people were killed Wednesday when the three-story structure containing residential and commercial units in Brooklyn collapsed. It fell into a pit dug by workers excavating the site of another building that was recently demolished. Neighbors had reported feeling vibrations from the construction site, and at least one witness saw bricks falling from the building just moments before it collapsed.
Officials cite a shortage of building inspectors
Though it remains unclear how often the excavation site had been inspected, some city officials said Friday that more help is needed.
The Department of Buildings has a vacancy rate of around 9% — 168 of its 1,855 authorized positions — according to the city’s comptroller dashboard.
“We must, and we will, ensure that every single one of those positions is immediately filled,” said New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, a Democrat. “This is an unspeakable, horrendous tragedy, and we must meet this moment.”
Democratic City Council Member Farah Louis called for aggressive oversight.
“Grief without accountability is not enough,” Louis said. “Buildings do not simply collapse without systemic failures.”
The city has ordered inspections at more than 160 sites in New York that are associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition site where the building collapsed, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
It’s also bringing in an engineering consulting firm to provide an independent report, which Mamdani described as “standard practice for this kind of a tragic incident.”
New York lays out rules for excavation projects
All contractors doing excavation work must notify New York’s Department of Buildings 24 to 48 hours in advance, according to guidelines posted on the department’s website.
A contractor on this site provided notice Sept. 9 that work would begin the following day and include rock blasting.
Permits are required for most work, which must also meet submitted plans. All projects are required to have proper precautions, such as shoring, bracing and “regularly checking walls for cracks,” the city’s website says.
If any of the work violates any rule, regulation or law, the city’s building commissioner may issue a stop work order. The Buildings Department may also conduct random audits of excavation projects to inspect shoring, groundwater, excavation depth and other things that could affect safety.
“Department site monitoring does not relieve engineers and contractors of their professional responsibilities,” the city’s website says.
Contractor has faced previous lawsuits and concerns
Contractors involved in the demolition and excavation of the property next to the collapsed building had faced previous complaints and alleged violations.
In March, the city issued a stop work order after inspectors concluded the building was being demolished without adequate overhead protection. In April, inspectors found that the demolition work had resumed in violation of that order, the department said, but work was allowed to continue after the problems were corrected.
The general contractor, Townhouse Builders Inc., which also operates as Promont, was accused in a lawsuit of causing extensive damage to an adjacent building during renovation work in Manhattan in 2016. Townhouse denied the allegations in court papers, and the suit appears to have been settled out of court.
Townhouse was also accused in a lawsuit of damaging and compromising the structural integrity of adjacent buildings while performing excavation, pile driving and steel beam installation for a six-story hotel project in Brooklyn in 2016.
The damage included a breached wall, shifting, settlement and cracking, according to the lawsuit, which accused Townhouse of failing to perform a physical inspection prior to excavation and failing to properly support the property’s walls.
Townhouse’s lawyers reached agreements four times to delay their deadline to submit a written answer to the claims but never did. Nothing has been posted to the docket since 2022.
The owner of Townhouse did not respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.
Excavation can raiserisks for nearby buildings
The investigation into Wednesday’s building collapse should look into whether the designs that were submitted were adequate and, if they were, whether the contractor doing the work made a mistake, said Abi Aghayere, a professor of civil engineering at Drexel University who studies structural systems and why they fail.
“With an old building like this, the room for error is very, very, very, very slim,” Aghayere said.
There are four main possible causes for failure in a project that involves excavating adjacent to an existing building, he said. One is that vibration caused by the work could transmit to the nearby building and weaken the structure, he said.
A question investigators will need to look into is whether the integrity of the building that collapsed was being monitored during the work, Aghayere said.
Two other possibilities are that the shoring in place for the excavation work was not strong or stiff enough, he said. A fourth cause could be seepage of groundwater that caused the soil under the existing building to shift, destabilizing the property, he said.
Everyone — tenants, building owners and landlords — has a responsibility to report anything unusual they see, particularly in older buildings, Aghayere said.
“You might see a crack, don’t take it lightly,” he said. “That crack might be that building just crying out and saying, ‘Help, help. I’m about to go.’”
___
Lieb reported from Jefferson City, Missouri; Bauer from Madison, Wisconsin; and Brook from New Orleans. Associated Press writers Jennifer Peltz in New York and Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

title: Former lawyer accused of trying to hire someone to kill a person, authorities say
text:
KENTUCKY (WXIX/Gray News) - A former Kentucky lawyer is accused of trying to hire someone to kill a person, according to federal authorities.
Chase Cox, 33, faces one count each of use of interstate commerce facilities in the commission of murder-for-hire and making false statements to a federal agency.
A federal indictment alleges Cox tried to pay a hitman using USPS between Sept. 25 and Nov. 3.
When authorities asked him on Oct. 8 whether there was any reason to believe he would threaten the intended victim, Cox allegedly lied.
“No, I love [the victim] with all my heart, I would never put [him/her] in harm’s way,” Cox said, according to the indictment.
In June 2024, Cox was sentenced to six months in jail for breaking into his ex-girlfriend’s apartment.
Prosecutors said he stole her iPad, read her text messages to track her down and then broke the device.
A judge later suspended his sentence and granted him probation after Cox pleaded that he would “be successful in the community.”
Eight days after his release from jail, Cox hired a “felon friend” to vandalize his ex-girlfriend’s car.
Cox is being held at the Shelby County Detention Center, where he is serving a five-year sentence for violating his probation after testing positive for cocaine and alcohol.
U.S. marshals will bring Cox to federal court in Covington for his arraignment on Dec. 9.
If convicted on both counts, Cox faces up to 15 years in federal prison, a $500,200 fine and six years of supervised release.

title: Maine home sales fall for 3rd straight month
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine saw home sales fall for the third straight month in October.
Buyers closed deals on 1,547 homes last month, down 6.6% from 1,656 in October 2025, according to the Maine Association of Realtors.
Meanwhile, the median sales price for a Maine home fell 5.6% year over year to $402,500.
That comes on the heels of a 4% year-over-year drop in September and a 10% slump in August but after a stellar July that saw home listings exceed 6,200 for the first time since December 2019 and 77 daily sales, making it the eighth best July for home sales since 2000.
Judy Oberg, the president of the Maine Association of Realtors and an associate broker at family-owned Oberg Insurance & Real Estate Agency in Bridgton, on Thursday attributed dampened buyer interest to mortgage rates, which stood at 7.1% for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage this week. Although national mortgage rates have fallen four straight weeks, they remain higher than the same time last year, according to Freddie Mac.
“Statewide, buyers have more homes to choose from than last year and more room to negotiate. Sellers are facing more competition from other listings and that’s reflected in the median sold prices,” Oberg said.
Maine isn’t alone in seeing a sales slump. Nationally, home sales fell even more sharply (8.6%) in October, while the median sales price nudged up just 0.4% to $421,900, according to the National Association of Realtors.
In the Northeast, sales dropped 4.1% year over year, but the median sales price jumped 3.2% to $519,600.
On the county level in Maine, the most significant increase in median home prices for the three-month period ending Oct. 31 was in Franklin County, where it rose 22.4% to $355,000, compared with the same time last year. Hancock (10.9%), Lincoln (10.8%), Waldo (6.4%) and Knox (5.6%) counties also saw notable increases in sale prices for that three-month period. The highest median home price during that period was in Cumberland County, where it reached $600,000, down about 1.4% from the same time a year ago.
The median home price fell most sharply in Washington (14.5%), Oxford (4.7%) and Penobscot (1.4%) counties for that three-month period. Aroostook had the lowest median home price overall ($168,250).
On the sales front, Penobscot County saw the largest sales bump for the three-month period ending Oct. 31, increasing about 3.1%. It was followed by Waldo (2.7%), Lincoln (2.4%) and Washington (1.5%) counties. Sales fell most sharply in York (18.9%), Piscataquis (14.6%), Franklin (10.5%), Kennebec (10.3%) and Sagadahoc (8.2%) counties during that period.

title: DA chooses not to press charges against driver who killed 2 on soccer field during youth match
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - The driver of a pickup that hit and killed two people and injured nearly a dozen others at a sports facility last month will not face charges.
Sedgwick County District Attorney Marc Bennett and Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan provided the update this week on the investigation.
Sullivan said they met with the families of the victims privately before publicly announcing the decision.
Nick Schafer, 35, and 6-year-old Cole Adrian, both of McPherson, were killed in the crash.
Police said the driver drove to the Stryker Complex from Garden City with her children, who were playing soccer at the facility that October day.
The driver was not identified, other than being called “she.”
Bennett said the driver reported that the pickup was not her usual vehicle. She was sleeping in the vehicle just prior to the crash and believed she had put the pickup into park.
While she was either asleep or falling asleep, one of her children put the sunshades up. Soon after, the pickup jumped the curb and went onto the field of play.
Bennett said he considered six possibilities as reasons for the crash:
- A medical emergency.
- Impairment or intoxication.
- A vehicle mechanical malfunction.
- An intentional act.
- One of the children or the woman, while she slept, inadvertently put the vehicle into drive.
- As the driver pulled up to the curb, she was confused about the gear the car was in.
Bennett ruled out the first four possibilities. He said he did not reach a conclusion about the other two.
He said for charges to be filed, the act had to be intentional, knowing and/or reckless.
Bennett determined that not only was there no evidence that the act was intentional, but in fact there was evidence that it was not done on purpose.
“This is not a crime, and I cannot charge this driver with a crime,” Bennett said.
According to Bennett, though the crash may have appeared to be an act of negligence, negligent homicide is not a chargeable offense in Kansas. He said that the collision did not meet the standards for vehicular homicide, a misdemeanor in Kansas.
Sullivan said the woman had no confrontations at Stryker that day. She hysterically expressed regret following the incident.
Police noted that they reviewed 60 videos and 41 emergency calls, interviewing more than 100 witnesses.
One of the first witnesses who communicated with the driver was an off-duty law enforcement officer. That officer recorded the interaction.
To determine the driver’s condition, a blood sample was taken. There were no impairing substances in the blood. The driver’s medical records were also subpoenaed.
Bennett said the philosophy going into the investigation was to “know everything that was knowable.”
Sullivan said medical records and videos offered no evidence that the driver was impaired.
“Every lead was examined. Every piece of evidence was reviewed,” Sullivan said.
No mechanical issues were found with the vehicle. Sullivan said that if the vehicle had been left in park, it would not have been able to clear a curb, enabling it to approach the soccer fields.
That left questions about the exact circumstances behind who put the vehicle into drive and when and how it was shifted.
“There are some questions that we may never be able to answer with complete certainty,” Sullivan said.

title: FDA’s new warning about GLP-1s and blindness explained
text:
FDA’s new warning about GLP-1s and blindness explained
About 15% of Americans have taken GLP-1s, so recent headlines linking the diabetes and weight-loss treatment to blindness caused some alarm across the country.
On Nov. 9, the Food and Drug Administration announced it would be requiring GLP-1 manufacturers to include warnings about a rare but serious eye condition that can cause partial blindness.
The warning follows research showing that these medications may increase the risk of an optic nerve condition among people who take the drug compared to those who don’t.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
Warning labels will be added to the safety information of all GLP-1s including, Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound and Mounjaro.
But scientists have not confirmed that GLP-1s cause the vision loss — they just know that studies have shown an association. Doctors still aren’t sure how these drugs could have this effect on the body.
“The FDA is making this warning out of an abundance of caution,” said Dr. Scott Kahan, a weight-loss medicine specialist.
We looked into the vision condition the FDA is warning about, and the study findings that triggered the label.
What is this condition that causes partial blindness?
Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, happens when blood flow to the optic nerve is blocked or reduced.
It is painless, sudden and typically permanent. It doesn’t usually present as total blindness; it causes blurring or vision loss in part of a person’s field of view.
It generally affects just one eye, but 15% of people who develop it in one eye go on to develop it in the other. There is no known treatment.
Among the general population, the condition is rare — 1 out of every 200,000 people are affected. But it becomes more common after age 50, when 2 to 10 of every 100,000 people develop it.
The link between this condition and GLP-1s is especially hard to tease out because the risk factors for such vision loss already overlap with the conditions that GLP-1s are prescribed to treat, including diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol and sleep apnea.
That means some people on GLP-1s may have already been at risk for such vision loss prior to the medication.
What research prompted the FDA to look into this?
The study that triggered the FDA’s interest was published in 2024. It analyzed medical records for almost 1,700 patients who were seen at a neuro-ophthalmology clinic in Boston between 2017 and 2023. The analysis included only patients with diabetes, or those who were overweight or had obesity.
Researchers compared the incidence of NAION among patients who had been treated with the GLP-1 semaglutide with those who hadn’t.
Among the 169 diabetic patients who were treated with semaglutide, 17 developed the vision loss condition, a rate four times higher than the cohort that didn’t use GLP-1s. Among 254 patients who took semaglutide to treat obesity, 20 developed the vision condition, seven times higher than those who didn’t take GLP-1s.
Because these records originated at a clinic for people with neuro-ophthalmological issues, the rate of people with NAION was much higher than it would be for the general population. Still, the findings raised concerns about whether GLP-1s may be increasing the risk of this rare eye condition. So the FDA took a closer look.
What did the FDA find?
The FDA conducted a meta-analysis of 126 clinical trials conducted in the development of these drugs. The analysis included 134,253 patients — around 78,200 who were assigned the GLP-1s as treatment and around 56,000 patients who either got a placebo or alternate non-GLP-1 medication for lowering blood sugar.
Among those patients, the FDA identified 10 probable cases of the vision loss condition in the GLP-1 group, and five among patients who received a placebo. That works out to about a 1.7 times higher risk among people taking GLP-1s.
This research, based on more robust randomized clinical trials, reinforced that GLP-1s may be associated with a higher risk of the vision condition but also demonstrated how rare this condition is at the population level.
After reviewing other observational studies in patients with Type 2 diabetes and finding similar results, the FDA concluded there was enough of a risk to merit a warning label.
What does this mean for patients?
Kahan said that because GLP-1s are widely prescribed, awareness of even rare risks may become more pronounced.
“The risk appears to be real albeit quite rare,” Kahan said. “There has been a perception that these medications are miracle cures, but it’s important to be mindful of risks, which are inherent with any treatment, including GLP1 medications.”
Kahan said the new warning won’t change how he prescribes these medications, but hopes it will alter the conversation around these medications and lead to smarter prescribing.
Patients should be informed of the risks, and talk with their doctor about preexisting eye conditions. If you are currently taking GLP-1s and are worried, consult your doctor first — and don’t suddenly stop the medication without guidance.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Here’s what’s behind the spiking Penobscot County budget
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rising health insurance costs, deferred maintenance and fully funding the county jail are driving Penobscot County’s proposed 23% budget hike.
The county’s budget has risen sharply in recent years. Last year, commissioners approved a 15.6% jump. Next year’s budget is set to rise by $6.7 million, with all but one county department projecting higher expenses. Revenues are expected to only rise by $355,000.
The final budget has not yet been approved.
The county isn’t alone in seeing rising healthcare costs, staff salaries and maintenance expenses. It’s a common trend in many of the proposed budgets for Greater Bangor communities. But the county is left to deal with rising operating costs for the Penobscot County Jail, forcing its budget to outpace climbing expenses in many local communities.
This is the second year the county will fully fund the jail, which has drained approximately $11 million in unbudgeted costs since 2022. Next year, about $2.1 million is set to be added to the jail’s budget.
The county’s budget advisory committee last week scrutinized much of next year’s proposed budget but did not discuss cutting jail funding. Members then approved the budget without changes in an 8-5 vote.
Penobscot County Commissioner Dan Tremble voted against the budget, saying it would make taxes too high for residents.
“What we have not done is to adequately fund the county, and we’ve underfunded, underfunded, underfunded, hoped, hoped, and just kicked it down the road,” Commissioner David Marshall said at a budget meeting last month.
Personnel costs are also a significant driver of the proposed $41 million budget. Costs for employee benefits, healthcare and salaries went up roughly $2.7 million. The spike also accounts for three new employees: a grant manager, a sheriff’s deputy and a maintenance worker who will be hired next year.
Interest payments on yearly loans, reserve accounts for departments and building maintenance also made up a sizable portion of the spike.
Funds put into reserve accounts will be used to buy supplies and any unforeseen maintenance, according to County Administrator Blair Tinkham. The $500,000 added to the sheriff department budget will be spent on outfitting deputies and buying more ammunition, which are at “catastrophic levels” after reserves were depleted, Chief Deputy John Knappe said.
Penobscot County Commissioners will hold a public hearing and vote on the 2027 budget on Nov. 18.
Correction: An earlier version of this report misstated the budget advisory committee’s vote tally.

title: Republicans score rare blue-to-red flip in Maine during midterm landslide
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (AP) — As Republicans dig out from under a midterm landslide, they can point to a single bright spot on the nationwide congressional map. That’s Maine’s 2nd congressional district, the only seat that went from blue to red without the help of redistricting.
It was far from a resounding victory. Even though President Donald Trump won the district by 9 points two years ago, it took a former Republican governor, Paul LePage, to squeak out a victory over Matt Dunlap, the Democratic state auditor.
The Associated Press called the race Thursday after officials finished the ranked choice voting process to determine the winner.
LePage and Dunlap were competing to replace Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat who is retiring from Congress.
The only other seats that went from blue to red are Texas’ 32nd congressional district and Tennessee’ 9th congressional district, but both of those flips were enabled by redistricting efforts that made the electorates far more conservative.
Meanwhile, Democrats have flipped 44 seats, and a handful of races have not yet been called.
Dunlap conceded last week and LePage declared victory, and he’s been in Washington for orientation for new members.
“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine,” said Brent Littlefield, a spokesperson for LePage.
Maine only has two congressional districts. The 1st is heavily Democratic and includes Portland and wealthy coastal towns. The 2nd includes a few small cities and vast rural and forested areas, and is home to industries such as logging, potato farming and lobster fishing. It’s more conservative than most of New England.
Golden had found success in the 2nd by running as a moderate Democrat who was willing to break with his party. However, he announced last year that he would not run for a fifth term, saying he had “grown tired of the increasing incivility and plain nastiness that are now common from some elements of our American community.”
As governor from 2010 to 2018, most of LePage’s two terms predated Trump’s presidency, but he aligned himself with the president toward the end of his time in office. The two shared a brand of brash, conservative populism, with LePage once saying he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular.”
However, LePage also criticized Trump’s tariffs on Canada, a key trading partner for Maine, and expressed support for legal immigration. When he declared victory last week, LePage vowed to make the state’s interests a priority in Washington.
“If it is good for Maine, I will work hard to make it happen. If it is bad for Maine, I will oppose it,” he said.

title: Husson women’s soccer facing No. 7 Tufts in NCAA Tournament
text:
The Husson University women’s soccer team from Bangor will be a heavy underdog when it takes on the nation’s seventh-ranked Tufts University Jumbos in Saturday’s 11 a.m. NCAA Division III Tournament game at Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, New York.
But head coach Dennis Mullins and his 10-5-2 Eagles will be prepared for the Jumbos, who are 13-1-3 and coming off their first loss of the season. Tufts fell 2-1 to No. 8 Williams College in the NESCAC championship game.
In the other semifinal, 12th-ranked Vassar (11-1-5) will take on Hartford (13-3-1) at 1:30 on Saturday.
The winners will meet at 1 p.m. Sunday.
“We’ve been training very hard,” said Mullins, who has guided the Eagles to their second North Atlantic Conference Tournament title in three seasons. “Tufts is very, very good. We’re going to have to be patient, stay organized for the full 90 minutes, and know we can win without having much of the ball.”
Husson has posted shutouts in nine of its last 11 contests including a 1-0 victory over Maine Maritime Academy in the NAC semifinals and a 2-0 win over Lesley University in the conference title game.
Husson held Lesley without a shot on goal on just four shot attempts and MMA to just two shots on goal on five attempts.
“We have good senior leadership, a well-varied attack and a lot of team chemistry,” Mullins said. “There has been a great vibe on the team and no individual drama.”
Senior Olivia Charles leads the team in scoring with 10 goals and five assists with sophomores Thea Gerfen and Jaquie Pangburn being the second and third leading scorers. Pangburn was a former standout at Bangor’s John Bapst Memorial High School.
Paige Dunn and Hailey Tarbox, both juniors, and fifth-year senior Marila Corletto have been the catalysts in the midfield, according to Mullins. Sophomore Jillian Long, senior Emma Nicholson and freshman Olivia Lizzotte have anchored the back line.
Mullins said Lizzotte, an Old Town High School grad, has been a valuable addition.
Junior Ella Hosford and senior Rylee Speed are also among the team’s top seven scorers.
Speed is the only member of the program who started in the Eagles’ 7-1 loss to New York University in the 2024 NCAA Tournament, although Charles and Corletto saw some playing time off the bench.
Biddeford sophomore Gabriella Smith has had an outstanding season in goal, according to Mullins.
Smith is 9-4-2 with an 0.87 goals-against average and a .759 save percentage.
Tufts and Husson were originally scheduled to play a regular season game at Tufts, but a storm forced the match to be cancelled.

title: Going back to school in retirement can build brain health and new connections
text:
(Aging Untold) — Schooling does not end for some people in retirement. They are auditing classes, joining lifelong learning programs or training for a new job. The cost can be low or even free, but it still takes time.
Why learning later in life matters
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said she sees going back to college later in life as personal enrichment.
“Learning is a lifetime thing,” Cradduck said. “We all should participate in learning all along. You’re totally keeping your brain active, but you’re also building some relationships.”
Cradduck said classroom education puts older adults in a room with a lot of younger people.
“You’re letting them see what they have the potential to do and what they can still do,” Cradduck said.
New connections in the brain and in life
Dr. Rhea Rogers said this is a way of “establishing neuroplasticity.”
“It’s always about making new connections, be it in the brain, be it in life, be it socially,” Rogers said. “And all the different benefits of interacting with the younger people and the older people, they all have a benefit to show each other.”
“It’s never too late”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a story of an 84-year-old caregiver who wanted to further her career and become a certified nursing assistant.
“And she went to school, and she got her nursing certificate. She got written up in the paper,” O’Rourke said. “She wanted a different kind of job and wanted to be tasked with more difficult things to do.”
O’Rourke said she was so proud of the woman.
“If it is a dream of yours, here it is. It’s never too late,” she said.
Paying for it
Nearly every state offers older adults free or discounted tuition to audit or take classes at public universities, according to AARP.
“When you’re 65 and older, you can go to school for free. A lot of the universities and a lot of the colleges, you don’t have to pay for the degree. So if you’ve been struggling with whether to have school debt or not, you won’t have it. And you can still get the education,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers added that there may also be military benefits for veterans, including some who may be disabled.
More than a college campus
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said there is also a lot of good community education.
“There’s colleges that put on lifelong learning for seniors. There’s also a lot of professionals and organizations that put on education that’s very popular for active adults. Longevity is really changing how we view adult learning and opportunities,” she said.
O’Rourke said there were local colleges where she worked that had lifelong learning for older adults, and it was highly sophisticated. The waiting list to get in was three years long.
“It’s really going to help you stay sharp, give you more interesting things to discuss, new things. And also what a great legacy builder, showing people what their potential is, that you can just keep on going and keep learning and having fun,” Ambrose said.

title: SpaceX’s attempt for a Starship double catch is thwarted when the booster ends up in Gulf
text:
STARBASE, Texas (AP) — SpaceX’s attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.
Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.
It’s the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk’s company missed out on a double catch.
The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.
Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday’s miss all the more surprising.
“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.
This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.
The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.
SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.
SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.
Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said ahead of Friday’s launch.
NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.
During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.
“We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.

title: Video shows people being rescued from frigid Mississippi River after NOLA cruise ship collision
text:
Video captures emergency responders rescuing people from frigid Mississippi River after tanker strikes cruise ship
Compelling video shows emergency responders in New Orleans springing to action to pull people from the frigid waters of the Mississippi River.
See the video in the player above
Officials say all passengers have been accounted for after a tanker slammed into the docked American Heritage cruise ship that, according to reporting from New Orleans sister station WDSU, had about 129 passengers, along with crew members, aboard at the time of the collision.
According to Port NOLA, the crash happened around 12:50 p.m. under the Crescent City Connection.
The collision is under investigation, but the situation prompted a massive search and rescue response from local, state, and federal authorities as passengers and crew plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over.
The Associated Press reports that dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 66-degree Fahrenheit river onto nearby ships.
The city's mayor said 32 people were taken to the hospital, but none of them had critical injuries.

main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Heating costs drop in Maine; Home heating oil back under $6
Home heating costs in Maine have dropped over the last week as oil prices fall.
According to an update from the Maine Department of Energy Resources on Friday, the average statewide price for heating oil in Maine, as of Nov. 9, was $5.84 per gallon. It was $6.01 a week earlier.
Heating oil prices have set records several times this fall, reaching $6.05 in October. 
According to the DOER, the average statewide price of $6.05 per gallon marked an 82% increase in price from a year earlier. The department also said that based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, Maine residents are estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank to capacity than they would have one year ago.
Kerosene on Nov. 9 was $6.77 per gallon and propane was $3.64. A week ago, kerosene was $7.01 and propane was $3.66. Kerosene had reached a high of $7.06 in October.
According to AAA, gas prices have dropped by 14 cents per gallon in Maine over the last week, with an average on Friday of $4.06.
State officials said Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other state and consumes significantly more per capita than other New England states. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, but the DOER noted that figure has declined steadily from 70% in 2010.
In September, projections from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association indicated that Maine households are expected to spend an average of $2,939 to heat their homes with heating oil this winter.
On Oct. 21, the U.S. Department of Energy announced that it will make up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in an effort to increase supply and bring down prices.
The latest heating fuel prices are available to view on the DOER website and are updated weekly during the heating season. The DOER is encouraging Maine residents to review the department's Winter Heating Guide for helpful tips and resources related to winter heating, including information about financial assistance for home heating and cost-saving home efficiency incentives.

title: Prostate health: These are the symptoms men should not ignore
text:
(Aging Untold) — The prostate can have a big impact on men’s health as they get older.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the prostate is a small gland that slowly enlarges with age, and men should not ignore the changes that come with it.
What the prostate does and how it changes
“It’s a small gland, but it plays a huge role in men’s health. And it sits right at the base of the bladder,” Rogers said.
How an enlarged prostate can affect daily life
As the prostate enlarges, it pushes in on the bladder, and men start to have a frequent need to urinate. Because the bladder is being pushed on, it may not empty all the way, Rogers said.
“You increase your chances of urinary tract infections because bacteria can just be sitting there,” Rogers said.
Rogers said the effects can reach beyond the bathroom.
“When you’re not sleeping well, because you’re going to the restroom all night, now you’re impacting the whole sympathetic nervous system that has other medical implications,” Rogers said. That includes insulin resistance.
Symptoms men should not ignore
The gland grows so slowly that many men tend to dismiss the signs, Rogers said.
“Because it’s so slow growing, a lot of guys, they just kind of ignore it,” Rogers said. “They should not ignore those symptoms or the hesitancy and nighttime urination.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck described the gland as being like a donut around a straw. When the donut is squeezed, she said, the straw, which represents the urethra, holds urine behind it.
“Don’t just get used to frequent urination,” Cradduck said. “Don’t just say, ‘Oh well, I’m a little older, so I go more frequently.’”
Signs that should prompt a call to a doctor: not getting urine out, getting up two or three times a night, feeling back pressure while going and getting frequent urinary tract infections, Cradduck said.
“Go to your doctor,” she said. “Go to a urologist.”
Prostate cancer can have no symptoms
An enlarged prostate can also be a sign of prostate cancer.
“Prostate cancer a lot of times is without any symptoms,” Rogers said. “So usually we take a look at everything that’s going on and don’t simply ignore it, but go seek medical attention.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said that because there may be no symptoms, men should be proactive.
“They could have cancer and not have any symptoms,” O’Rourke said.
“Really be proactive, because you’re not going to get a sign until maybe it’s too late,” she said.
Cradduck said prostate cancer does not have to be a death sentence, but it can be because it can metastasize.
She said people may hear “prostate cancer” and think it is common and not a big deal.
“It is a great big deal when it metastasizes and it spreads,” Cradduck said. “Why would you even allow that? Get yourself checked.”
Rogers said prostate cancer has different scores, including a Gleason score.
That is a grading system to evaluate the aggressiveness of prostate cancer, according to Mayo Clinic.
Many men will die with the disease, Rogers said, and some men can die from it, depending on how aggressive it is and what the score is.
What PSA is and what a high number can mean
O’Rourke shared that her husband’s PSA level was not where his doctor wanted it to be.
“He said, just eat more leafy green vegetables. And darned if that didn’t lower the PSA level,” O’Rourke said.
Prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, is a protein the prostate gland produces, according to the Prostate Cancer Foundation.
“It’s a protein, so because of that, many things can cause it to elevate,” Rogers said. “Just because it’s elevated doesn’t mean you have cancer. You can have an infection, prostatitis and things like that.”
She said doctors often look at the interval over time to see the percentage of increase. There are other measures and more specialized tests that can show whether a PSA reading indicates high-grade cancer.
Rogers said inflammation is a factor in many cases. She said she has seen a person’s PSA drop quickly after inflammation was addressed in another part of the body.
“It really is inflammation,” Rogers said. “But you want to make sure it’s not a mask for something.”
Talk about it and get support
O’Rourke posted a challenge to men to talk to one another.
She challenged men to ask each other whether they are getting annual exams, having trouble urinating, noticing changes in their sex life, not sleeping or feeling fatigued.
“Get support to go to the doctor to get it checked,” O’Rourke said.
“Be proactive, but get your support system with the other guys,” she said. “Don’t be too embarrassed to talk about it.”
Key takeaways
- The prostate sits at the base of the bladder and slowly enlarges as men get older. It acts like a hose clamp on urine flow.
- Don’t ignore urinary changes. Weak streams, frequent urination, hesitancy and nighttime bathroom trips should not be treated as normal. Talk to a doctor.
- Talk with a doctor. Prostate cancer often has no symptoms, so screening and early detection matter.

title: Sudden FAA ground stop strands teams and throws upcoming sports weekend into chaos
text:
(AP) - The Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights nationwide for several hours Friday threw the sports world into chaos, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams scrambling to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend.
Transportation officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications issues at regional air traffic control centers for the stoppage. It left some teams searching for hotel rooms, others rescheduling flights, leagues adjusting start times, and some teams had took the extraordinary step of chartering buses rather than waiting for the ground stop to end.
“We’re going to allow for general aviation, those larger movements, to take place as a priority. Smaller movements will take lower priority,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said after the ground stop was lifted Friday night in Washington.
No. 19 Mississippi’s football game at Oklahoma was moved from Saturday to Sunday at 1 p.m. EST because of travel issues. Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny was upset with the decision, saying the Southeastern Conference threatened Oklahoma with a forfeit it did not agree to the move.
“I understand that difficult decisions sometimes must be made under extraordinary circumstances,” Denny said in a statement on X. “Put simply, this decision isn’t fair to our athletes, our institution or to Sooner nation.”
Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, No. 8 Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games. The Utes play at No. 22 Arizona, the Longhorns visit No. 24 LSU and the Vols are traveling to Texas A&M in three of the bigger games of the weekend.
“The Southeastern Conference is aware of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop and the potential impact on team travel,” the league said. “The safety and well-being of student-athletes, coaches and team personnel remain our highest priority.”
Texas and Tennessee both returned to their campuses during the ground stoppage. Once it was lifted following more than four hours of uncertainty, the schools began making plans to fly out as soon as possible, allowing them to arrive before game day.
Auburn opted to take a bus to Mississippi State with the SEC pushing back the Saturday start time from noon EST to 4:15 p.m. to give the Tigers a little buffer. Purdue likewise decided to board buses from West Lafayette, Indiana, for its game at Iowa.
Other schools affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and Arizona State.
The Big 12 said the Kansas-West Virginia game scheduled for 5:30 p.m. EST would be moved up to 3:30 p.m. since the Jayhawks arrived in plenty of time. That allowed the league to shift the Arizona State-UCF game from 2:30 p.m. EST to 5:30 p.m., giving the Sun Devils an additional three hours after their flight from Arizona to Florida was delayed.
Washington spokesman Kurt Svoboda said the Huskies returned to campus when their flight was grounded, but officials stayed in touch with their airline partners and the flight crew remained in place. The Huskies ultimately flew out late Friday for their game at Michigan State on Saturday, which will start at 5:30 p.m. EST, 75 minutes later than originally scheduled.
It was unclear whether any referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would have trouble reaching their games. The Big Ten said in a statement that all of its officials had arrived for their scheduled assignments Saturday.
Several teams were able to take off before the stoppage began, including all of those traveling in the Atlantic Coast Conference; Missouri, which was flying to top-ranked Georgia; Duke, which was visiting fifth-ranked Miami; and No. 10 Texas Tech, which posted on social media images of its arrival for a game at Oklahoma State.
NFL teams playing Sunday typically travel the day before their games. They were expected to fly as planned on Saturday.
In the NBA, the Cleveland Cavaliers played in Miami on Friday night but won’t fly home until Saturday morning and plan to land about eight hours before a home game against the Dallas Mavericks. NBA teams hardly ever fly in on the day of a game, but there have been some circumstances — often weather-related — where it has happened.
At least two other NBA teams had Friday night flights pushed to Saturday morning, but those teams aren’t playing Saturday night. Cleveland scrambled to get hotel rooms re-booked in Miami, after checking out of their hotel earlier Friday.
“It’s part of it. You just adapt,” Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said.
There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL on Saturday. The Panthers were among the majority that made it to their destinations before the stoppage began. The Sharks, who were left waiting in San Jose to see whether they would be able to travel, arrived later Friday in Utah.
JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates were trying to get to South Carolina for their game Sunday against the top-ranked Gamecocks. The team had just boarded its flight at Los Angeles International Airport when the ground stop was issued. After a while, the decision was made to deboard passengers and the team returned to the Galen Center.
In soccer, the Utah Royals already were in the Washington, D.C., area ahead of their National Women’s Soccer League semifinal against the Washington Spirit on Saturday. But the Kansas City Current were supposed to depart Friday for their semifinal against Gotham FC on Sunday in New York, and team officials were uncertain when their flight would be allowed to leave.
The U.S. national team’s match against Haiti on Saturday in Miami was unaffected by the ground stop. Both teams and officials already were in town for the first leg of the two-match CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinal series.
___
AP Sports Writers Jim Vertuno, Aaron Beard, Tim Reynolds, Larry Lage and Beth Harris contributed to this report.
