title: All people accounted for following cruise ship collision in New Orleans
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A tanker lost its steering and slammed into a docked American Heritage river cruise paddleboat near the Port of New Orleans on Friday.
Rescue efforts were underway immediately, with officials saying later in the day that all passengers were able to be accounted for.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 32 people needed hospitalization, but no critical injuries were reported, calling it “a miracle on the Mississippi.”
EN ESPAÑOL | Buque cisterna choca contra un crucero atracado en Nueva Orleans
Video from the scene following the reported collision showed boats and rescuers scrambling to get people in life jackets and out of the Mississippi River.
Moreno’s communication team said multiple people were rescued from the scene.
According to the Port of New Orleans press secretary, a tanker collided with an American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage around 12:30 p.m.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard the American Heritage, Port NOLA said.
Luggage and other debris could be seen floating in the river. Survivors were taken to a Port of New Orleans building next door to the dock.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the river was closed to all vessels near the site while the rescue efforts were ongoing.
“Our hearts are with the passengers, crew, and families affected by this afternoon’s collision between a passenger vessel and a tanker on the Mississippi River in New Orleans,” the Coast Guard said.
The river cruiser was docked on the Mississippi River outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with it, officials said.
The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers and was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it will also be joining the investigation.

title: Death Notice: Dennis N. Witham Sr.
Here’s why some contestants have been forced out of Miss Universe competition
text:
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico because of visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration, while two others are struggling to obtain visas.
Representatives from Zambia and the Republic of Congo have withdrawn from the pageant, which takes place this month in the U.S. territory, after failing to secure visas. Contestants from South Sudan and Zimbabwe are still awaiting theirs.
The United States has imposed sweeping travel restrictions affecting dozens of countries, many of them in Africa, under proclamations issued during Trump’s second administration.
Last December, the administration expanded restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while maintaining a full suspension of entry for nationals of the Republic of Congo and South Sudan.
“She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves,” Miss Universe Zambia organizers said in a statement this week announcing the withdrawal of their representative, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka.
In the Republic of Congo, Georgina Kambongo made history when she was crowned the Central African country’s first Miss Universe representative. National organizers say her inability to travel to Puerto Rico is linked solely to Trump’s travel restrictions.
“American visa challenges have delayed that journey, but the fight is not over,” Zimbabwe’s representative, Roseanna Hall, said in a social media post. “After months of preparation, I am not giving up. I remain confident that God who began a good work in me will bring it to completion.”
In South Sudan, organizers said contestant Adut Deng’s participation remained uncertain despite months of efforts to secure the necessary travel documents and approvals.
“South Sudan deserves to be seen, heard, and represented. Our queen carries the hopes, dreams, beauty, and resilience of a nation,” organizers said in a statement.
The competition’s 75th edition is expected to attract up to 120 contestants. Delegates began arriving in Puerto Rico on Sunday for rehearsals and other preliminary activities.
A national costume competition is scheduled for Nov. 21, followed by swimsuit and evening gown segments the following day. The winner will be crowned on Nov. 24.

title: My First Semester: Thoughts and Reflections from a First Year
text:
To some sort of past and future version of me,
I have a fear of being cheesy, of being cringey, I think most of us do. In fact, I think the use of the word cringey is cringey in and of itself. This semester, I took a class called Modern Essays with Visiting Professor Jaed Coffin and in the small cramped basement of PGill, he assigned my class an essay, in the style of writers like George Orwell and Joan Didion we answered the question of “Why I Write.” Now, this was hard, I have a lot of reasons to write, a lot of people do. But the prompt included another part, most beautifully and affectionately named “eat the roadkill.” To explain: if you’re going to write about roadkill, you should probably eat the roadkill. If you’re going to do something, understand something, you have to fully do that something.
So I bought a journal, opened it, signed the date––9/20/2026––and ate my roadkill. I don’t like writing about myself. I enjoy journaling much less, it’s the most horrible form of writing. The words on the page don’t become thoughts, they become strings of cheesy cringe. But here we are. My most recent journal essay is from yesterday, it was about some books I’m looking forward to reading over winter break, how my coffee from Le Ronj was particularly good, and how I enjoyed breakfast with my friends; simple, easy, a small beginning. And now, in this odd letter, I’ve arrived at my worst fear. We’re nearing the end of the semester, my first semester at Bates. Time always finds a way to surprise me, but, in this instance, time and I got along. Of course, it’s unnerving to find yourself halfway done with your first year of college, but how thrilling that thought manages to be.
A few weeks ago, I drove home for the first time since arriving at Bates; it was a dream, filled with silence besides the drone of soft jazz playing as I took the Maine Turnpike through hues of blending fall foliage. A peaceful drive, only forty minutes, it passed in the blink of an eye and I was home for October break. An odd feeling washed over me. Shock, perhaps, that I was really home, but really, it was a realization of where I finally was, bringing new friends to see the sunrise on beaches only a five minute drive from home, giving them a crash course on the best spots in Portland. It’s odd, sometimes you can live, moving through life monotonously, and then, one day find it’s happening, and happening in every way your dreams desire. When I, without confetti, mind you, opened my acceptance letter from Bates, I knew, even if I denied it for a bit, that I had found my home. Or rather, it, and the admissions committee, found me.
Remember touring Bates? For me, it was quiet, during October break where students, much like myself now, left campus for reprieve. I remember fall was short last year, it was past peak autumn when I visited, and most of the trees were already dead, or maybe I just remember it that way. I didn’t like the school much, it wasn’t anything special, if I can be honest with myself. My tour consisted of three other students, none of whom I believe ended up here. But, anyways, it was quiet and I particularly remember trying to talk to the tour guide, who was passionate, keen to talk about Bates. When I think of what I saw, I only remember walking through PGill, past the Puddle, and the quad paired with the classic “why I choose Bates” spiel.
My parents and I got into our car, parked behind Milliken House, where I’ve now eaten one too many microwaved hot dogs, and they interrogated me about my feelings towards Bates after the tour. I said something like, “I enjoyed it, I’ll definitely apply, we’ll just have to see what happens.” They had a different experience than me: the parents on their tour had talked, my dad helped a couple girls with their cars license plates (entirely losing the tour), and my mom, so often as she does, just had a “feeling” about it. And thankfully, she was right.
When I moved into Bates, we took two cars. My dads car was filled to the brim with essentials and dorm decorations. My mom and I took only my plants in my own car, plants which, for the first time in my life, are still alive. After everything was moved into my dorm, where athletes and JA’s dragged my stuff up two flights of the Adams Hall stairs, into what is now affectionately called the “dingle” by my friends, I was at Bates. Thanks to the Bates class of 2030 page, I already had a couple friends, and those friends had some more friends, and roommates who shortly became the best group I’ve had the opportunity to start Bates with.
At Bates Beginnings, this past April, I had spent the day with a girl, Francesca, who by the end of the day committed to Bates; I would like to think I had a part in that. Fran reached out to ask if I knew any good spots in Portland to eat while she and her mom were visiting, and being the best local I could be, I, of course, recommended Flatbread Co. Another girl, Mary, reached out to talk about my trip to Scotland, the same trip that she embarked on just a couple of weeks later. Gabby, Mary’s roommate from Alaska, was the only person I found that was in the same First-Year-Seminar as me, which has been an experience to say the least. Amongst so many others, newfound friends, and soon to become friends (like my friend Ruby), I wasn’t so nervous anymore.
With Laufey and Hamnet posters on the wall, my Bates flag above my bed, string lights illuminating the room with my little sheep from Scotland, Duncan, on my bedside table, my dorm was decorated. It was a new home, with clothes organized, fans plugged in and a heated blanket shortly on the way in the mail for winter. I said goodbye to my parents and was left in my dorm facing the daunting schedule for Orientation. My friends and I jumped around, academic fairs where I introduced myself to future professors, Green Dot sessions amongst building community down-lows, and introductions on how to live at Bates. Most significantly was Pres. Garry Jenkins’ welcome speech, which focused on how, eventually we would all look back on this moment and realise how formative Bates would be, how much we would change. In other words, it would be an “evolution,” and I was more than prepared to start mine.
The Puddle, perhaps one of the most iconic parts of campus, is home to one of my new favorite sunny day spots for reading, work, and hangouts: the Amphitheatre. As the new first-year class anticipated meeting their leaders and group for AEOSP, we gathered all along the grass and the stones. Leaders flooded in in wigs and outfits, armed with intro songs, signs, and welcoming smiles.
We set off on our AESOP trip, Mt. Blue basecamping three, driving to Mt. Blue itself where we spent the better part of the day hiking. It was stunning and entirely worth it. The views were expansive, gorgeous. Filled with endless mountains, spanning off into the bright distance bringing only the ability to bask in its sublimity, the view reminded me of why I wanted to stay in Maine in the first place. We made our way to the campground, at the base of Mt. Blue with beyond camera-worthy images of the surrounding mountain range. At the shore of Webb Lake, we settled into the campground with the other Mt. Blue AESOP groups and prepped for a fun night of burrito bowls, s’mores roasted over a fire pit, and a far-too-big game of mafia.
The next day, we woke up early arriving at the base of Tumbledown Mountain, a hike I had been wanting to do for years. It was finally my time. Much different from the experience of Mt. Blue, we scrambled up rocks and giant builders, squeezing up and into crevices and formations to make our way up the loop, and we were rewarded with a view. There, at the peak surrounded by rolling mountains covered in lush bright greens and littered with evergreens, sat Tumbledown Pond. With my group of AESOP friends, armed with our bathing suits, we took a dip. The water froze us with each step, but we jumped in anyway. My sock fell in, leaving it wet and soggy, but we enjoyed our lunch–PB & J wraps–anyway, with serene mountains surrounding us.
Before we made the trip back to campus, we enjoyed a day at the glistening lake and made a quick stop at an ice cream shop, doing our best to savor what was our last bit of summer. Even though it was technically still August, I indulged in a cup of pumpkin soft serve with chocolate sprinkles, something now highly reminiscent of Commons. And then, we were officially back on campus. It wasn’t orientation anymore, we weren’t on AESOP anymore; I said I was ready to begin, that this was real––but this was real.
Imagine this: you’re at the Club Fair, it’s 8pm, and three tents are filled, lined, to the brim, with clubs, organizations, club, and sports mixed with volunteer organizations and acapella groups vying for first years all to sign up and try out what they were pitching. I joined so many clubs it was hard to keep them straight. I knew a few that I wanted to join: Snaggletooth, the Bates Student, the Cheese Club, the Bates Outing club, to name a few. There were some wild cards, but when are there not? Bates itself, in some ways, was one for me.
Before I knew it, I was attending Bates Votes meetings and volunteering my time to help eligible students register to vote, ensuring students’ voices could exercise their democratic rights on election day. I was sitting in Le Ronj with Snaggletooth, voting on submissions, interviewing percussion instructors for the music zine MOSH!, and tabling with them for Bates’ Halloween trick or treat. I was pitching articles to the Bates Student, attending Environmental Coalition meetings, trying cheese, drinking some tea, amongst so, so, many others. I soon found myself in WRBC, Bates’ Radio Station, at midnight on Friday nights with my two friends and co-hosts Mary and Gabby, jamming out to music that we loved and cheekily giving out PSA’s about bear safety and invasive cat species. In the dark illuminating light of the basement radio station, lined to the brim with old CD’s, records, and walls full of writing, I recalled the chaos of the club fair and how everything fell into place once again.
And it was time, too, for the part of college that I had nearly forgotten about; there was no time to think about how nervous I was, I was in the throes of my academic life. It was terrifying, to be frank, but I was eager. I was everywhere: drowning, positively, in Jane Austen’s books with Ruby, with abrupt switch-ups carefully perusing Shakespeare’s prose with Gabby, or picking apart essays with Mary and Fran and writing our own, or even debating the Anglo-Irish Treaty and the Simla Conference in my decolonization and British Empire course. I’ve written gothic tales and watched movies, I’ve picked apart scenes from the Matrix, comparing them to Kagemusha, and laughed about what they did to Fanny Price in the 1999 Mansfield Park, debating which adaptation of Emma could possibly be the best. I’m sorry Professor Nayder, but the 2020 version of Emma has my heart.
At first, I was intimidated by academics at Bates, especially professors; would I do well? How do office hours work? How do I schedule a WCAT session, and what even is a WCAT? Everyone talks about how great professors are, how much they care, how they take such an active role in our education. Of course, I knew that had to be true to a point, but at the same time I underestimated the reality of those statements. Throughout September and October, Gabby and I spent our Saturday mornings painting the porch of our FYS professor, Sanford Freedman. Smattered in light blue paint, we learned a lot, he gave immensely helpful advice on everything Bates. And it’s everything, thus far, that has made me realise I’m on the right track, there’s nothing to be frightened about. Bates is not perfect, Sanford was sure of making that clear, but nothing is; and nonetheless, it can remain special.
The other day I walked past a tour and felt like a fish in a bowl. It wasn’t the first time: at some point in late September I vividly remember sitting in a hammock with a friend by the Puddle and some parents excitingly taking aesthetic photos of us. A year after my own tour of Bates, on the opposite side of the picture, everything felt different. I was the one studying in PGill while prospective students walked by, I with the group lounging about the quad, pushing people on the swing, I was spending hours in the library, and eating at Commons surrounded by my friends. At the end of summer, before I started Bates, a woman approached me at the cafe I work at, because of my Bates sweatshirt, he asked if I was a Bates student. I said, “Yes, I’m going to be this fall,” and she smiled, telling me a story about her daughter and her friends who, some twenty years after graduating, still come together to make Commons-themed meals. I keep thinking about it, every time I sit at a table in Commons with my friends, surrounded by laughter, stories, and good food; and I wonder, if we too, will have some odd and slightly endearing tradition that will make us nostalgic for Bates.
These thoughts, these moments, this experience, this cringy letter is not just addressed to me: it’s for everyone. To the current students who felt the same; to the seniors, juniors, and sophomores who’ve already made this place feel like not just a college, but a community; to those who felt the opposite and left, or will leave. To all other first-generation students who are scared that a place like Bates won’t be for them, I, too, was terrified, but I think this place is alright. To alumni who miss their days here, to their kids who are here now, thank you for the community you’ve passed onto us. To all the parents who are facing a life without their kids at home, they’re okay here. To Bates professors who have only just started guiding me on my academic journey here, and for helping so many other students with theirs, thank you. To all future students, the current seniors at Scarborough High School, and schools all over, looking to apply here, submit the application: you never know what will happen. To all the students who have started this journey, this evolution, with me: thank you, it’s all working out isn’t it? And lastly, dear me, future me––I can’t wait to be you.
Just always do something,
Dakota D

title: Bangor Humane Society documentary premieres at Black Bear Cinemas
text:
ORNO, Maine (WABI) - Black Bear Cinemas held a red carpet premiere Thursday night for a documentary about the Bangor Humane Society.
Everyone was invited, including some four-legged guests.
About the film
“Humane: Inside Bangor Humane Society” follows the work being done at the shelter.
Director and producer Keith Travers and his wife, Danielle, spent more than a year filming the animals, staff and volunteers.
They used their own resources to make the film.
The couple and shelter staff said the documentary shows the love and compassion given to the animals. They said it also shows the work behind the scenes to help nearly 2,000 animals find new homes each year.
Shelter staff react
“Our staff and literally more than a hundred volunteers work tirelessly all year long. We’re there on holidays. We’re there on weekends. Sometimes we’re there in the middle of the night. And so being able to show every aspect of that work, at least in as much as you can with 45 minutes, is really exciting. And so I hope that folks are just able to walk away knowing that the animals in our care are loved. And they’re ready for the next step,” said Kathryn Ravenscroft, Bangor Humane Society Director of Development and Communications.
How to watch
The documentary will stream on the Maine Public Broadcast Network in December.
More details are available on the Bangor Humane Shelter’s website and Facebook page.

title: Casco ayahuasca sanctuary holds weekend session for veterans
text:
Pachamama Sanctuary, a self-described “spiritual retreat” in Casco, is hosting 20 veterans Nov. 13-15 for an ayahuasca retreat.
Jacob VandenPlas, a veteran from Wisconsin, said this weekend’s retreat is his second time at Pachamama. VandenPlas said he was hesitant prior to his first retreat in April, and spoke about how many veterans dislike the feeling of not being in control and being unable to defend themselves. He said going to the retreat helped counteract those feelings, and called it “one of the single most life-changing things that has ever happened in (his) life.”
“I still to this day don’t possess the vocabulary to truly articulate how impactful it was,” said VandenPlas.
Vines and Valor partnered with Pachamama to organize the weekend retreat. Troy Ulshoeffer, a retired Navy chief petty officer who founded Vines and Valor last year, said this is the organization’s third and largest retreat held at Pachamama. Ulshoeffer said Vines and Valor focuses on bringing healing to veterans through “holistic therapy.” The veteran-led organization leads two retreats per year, and raises funds to provide grants to cover the cost.
Ulshoeffer, who served in the Navy for 20 years, began to undergo “holistic therapy” in early 2024, after dealing with PTSD, addiction and the loss of his mother following his retirement from the military. Ulshoeffer has advocated for expanded veteran access to “holistic therapy” not only through Vines and Valor, but also testifying at the United States Capitol.
Ayahuasca is a hallucinogenic beverage originally used by Indigenous peoples in South America in the context of religious ceremonies. It’s made using DMT, a psychedelic drug which is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance by the federal government. Research is ongoing regarding the use of ayahuasca to treat mental disorders such as depression and substance use.
Ulshoeffer said the weekend will include ayahuasca ceremonies, as well as activities to build camaraderie among participants.
VandenPlas runs his own nonprofit, DC Farms for Vets, based in Wisconsin. He said that since his visit to Pachamama, he has been winding down his work there to put more effort into helping with Vines and Valor, and said he believes the organization is making a bigger impact than he ever could on his farm.

title: Family Dollar to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it overcharged customers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHESAPEAKE, Va. (AP) - Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle state and federal allegations that it routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on its shelves, website and mobile app.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states filed federal charges against the company Thursday and announced the proposed settlement the same day. The settlement must still be approved by a judge.
According to the FTC’s complaint, consumers from across the country have been reporting price discrepancies at Family Dollar for years. In January 2025, for example, consumers from at least seven states reported that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” sale on a package of diapers, even though the price was advertised on its mobile app and on shelf tags.
One Michigan consumer took a picture of the “2 for $20” shelf tag and brought it to the register, but reported that the store manager said the price was wrong and quickly removed the shelf tag, the complaint said.
Over the last five years, state and local regulators have cited Family Dollar for thousands of pricing violations, resulting in fines of more than $3 million, the complaint said. It has also entered into multiple settlements with state attorneys general and consumer protection agencies over inaccurate pricing.
Family Dollar said Friday it will work with the FTC and state agencies to meet the settlement’s requirements and provide clear information to customers about how the settlement could impact them.
“We take our responsibility to deliver a positive shopping experience seriously,” Family Dollar spokeswoman Janella Escobar said in a statement. “We remain focused on strengthening pricing accuracy across our stores and maintaining our customers’ trust.”
Family Dollar, which is privately owned and based in Chesapeake, Virginia, has more than 8,000 U.S. discount stores. It reported revenue of $13 billion in its most recent fiscal year, according to a company statement.
The case is similar to one the FTC and 20 states filed last month against Dollar General, a rival bargain chain. That case is ongoing.
Under the proposed settlement, Family Dollar will be required to establish a $40 million consumer redress fund payable to eligible consumers. The company must notify customers about the fund through notices in stores and on its digital platforms.
The settlement requires Family Dollar to establish a $20 million discount program for its customers and pay $3 million to the states involved in the case. Those states are: Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
The settlement also requires Family Dollar to implement a pricing accuracy program that is independently assessed and annually certified.

title: Trump bluntly tells JD Vance to shift focus from Iran to targeting ‘corruption and crime’ at home
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president says is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month-old war, has been blunt in blaming the war — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections in the United States.
But Trump brusquely told the vice president in a social media post Thursday to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing — and perhaps more politically salient — issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said in the post. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
Trump earlier this week said he believed the war “militarily is effectively over,” and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign.
Democrats have promised intense oversight of Trump’s business dealings and other targets when they take control of Congress in January after voters identified corruption as one of their top concerns. Trump’s post about Vance and the Iran war was, in part, responding to a flurry of reports about Democrats’ plans.
But it also came after The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday evening that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official.
The vice president’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
The White House press office, in an email, responded to a query by highlighting that Trump made clear in his post that he sees no need to negotiate with Iran.
Vance blamed Trump’s Iran war for midterm losses
Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in U.S. military interventions overseas, was lukewarm in his defense of the conflict after Trump launched it and became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting when he headed up negotiations over the summer.
Following the Nov. 3 losses, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X in which he didn’t mince words about the political impact of the conflict.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance said. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
The vice president is considering whether to launch a 2028 run for the White House. Voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the war could weigh down those ambitions.
The president has yet to endorse a successor for the 2028 race. In a CBS “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, the president said he “may or may not get involved” in offering an endorsement.
Trump earlier this week said that he believed that mediation efforts led by Qatar are making progress and that it was unlikely he would need to make good on earlier threats to restart the full-scale bombardment of Iran after he was past the midterm elections.
The president said in an interview on “The Hugh Hewitt Show” on Thursday that he stood ready to restart strikes if necessary. “If something doesn’t work out, I would not hesitate,” he said.
Separately, in an interview with commentator Stephen A. Smith, Trump suggested he hasn’t ruled out carrying out strikes on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, if the U.S. detects signs of activity at the facility.
Waters around Iran remain treacherous
Oil shipments coming out of the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near prewar levels after Iran effectively choked the critical waterway for months, stemming the flow of crude and energy resources from its Persian Gulf neighbors.
But international tankers now are relying on U.S. Navy escorts to get the oil out of the strait. The U.S. military has recently carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses.
And while crude and liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf are climbing, there’s also been an uptick in attacks on ships trying to traverse the waterway.
The British military on Thursday reported at least two tankers were struck by projectiles in recent days while traversing contested waters near Iran.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, an agency that monitors maritime safety, said one of the tankers was struck Wednesday in the Strait of Hormuz, northwest of Ras al-Khaimah. The agency reported the crew evacuated safely and no casualties were reported.
In another incident from Tuesday, the UKMTO said a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Persian Gulf. Multiple people were taken ashore for medical assistance while the remaining crew was safe and accounted for, the agency said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week he pressed his Group of Seven counterparts during talks in Paris to “step up” and help protect ships from Iranian attacks but acknowledged making no headway on the issue.
At the same time, a Saudi-led coalition is mired in fighting with Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. That fighting has made it precarious to transport oil and other goods through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
Qalibaf claims the U.S. wants Russia to intervene
Meanwhile, Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said in an interview that the United States has asked for Russian President Vladimir Putin to facilitate direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran.
“It was the Americans who, during a visit to Moscow, spoke with Mr. Putin and asked him to speak with Iran so that, in any case, Iran would agree to speak directly with them,” Qalibaf told Al Jazeera in the interview. “Look, Russia and Mr. Putin, the Russian president, are friends of ours. We have strategic relations with Russia. We are very close, and we hold Mr. Putin in particularly high regard.”
The White House did not directly respond to a query about whether the U.S. has asked Putin to facilitate talks with Iran.
Qalibaf said the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, traveled to Russia and briefed Putin on details of the negotiations. “He informed him that we had conveyed our positions, which represent the legitimate rights and rightful demands of our people, to the Americans,” he said, adding that it is up to the U.S. side to respond.
“It is up to them to decide. If they are truly telling the truth and are sincere about negotiations, then they should respond and begin the process,” Qalibaf said. “But if they want to pursue the path of war, then naturally, we are fully prepared for that as well.”
___
AP writers Michelle L. Price in Washington and Elena Becatoros in Athens contributed reporting.

title: Edgecomb selectmen consider road name change
text:
In 2024, Roy Potter became Edgecomb’s full-time fire chief. He also became the 911 addressing officer. On Nov. 10, he reported a significant number of the town’s roads were improperly listed. Potter believed the situation must be addressed because public safety agencies need properly listed addresses. “I have set standards to follow. The state sets guidelines for doing my job. If I can’t get the backing of the selectboard to do my job, then I’m not going to be the 911 addressing officer.”
Selectmen sought Potter’s opinion because of a question about the name of a town road. Potter objects to Off-Shore Road’s name because it conflicts with emergency management system standards. The agency will often use “off this road or street” in directing emergency responders, he said.
If an emergency call directs a response to Off-Shore Road in Edgecomb, he believes that would create confusion. Virginia Campbell has lived at her Off-Shore Road residence for the past five years. She told selectmen the road was once a “750-foot driveway,” with one resident. It now has two residents and, despite Potter’s protestations, she doesn’t want to change the name.
She told the selectboard a previous board five years ago approved the name.
“We came up with a name and gave it to the 911 officer at the time. Roy (Potter) was fire chief, he shot down all the names as being too similar to others,” she said. “We went back to the drawing board and presented more names a couple months later, but Roy said those were too similar.”
The disagreement was decided by a previous selectboard who ultimately sided with Campbell. “We both presented our cases and in the end I was granted the name,” she said. “So my personal feeling is my road name should stand.”
Selectmen didn’t make a decision following the two presentations.
In other business, selectmen are considering forming an advisory capital reserve committee. Chairman Forrest Carver envisions the committee to establis, develop and maintain a long-term capital improvement and funding strategy for the town.
Selectmen reached a consensus that the new committee should have five members with staggered terms. Selectmen are still considering who should serve on the board.
Selectmen approved ADP as the town’s new payroll company. Selectman Cara Gaffney believes the change will improve municipal efficiency. “A professional service eliminates payroll accounting variances and ensures complete audit compliance and protects the town’s financial liability,” she said.
Selectmen voted, 3-0, to contract with RHR & Smith for auditing services for Fiscal Years 24, 25 and 26. The new firm starts on Jan. 1.
Selectmen meet next at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 24 in the conference room.

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: A Rock Solid Underdog Story
text:
‘I Play Rocky’ Review: A Rock Solid Underdog Story
I Play Rocky should be a disaster. A biopic about the making of Rocky is an exercise in redundancy. Rocky is already a biopic about Sylvester Stallone.
Stallone himself has said that for 50 years. In a 1977 interview, he told Barry Norman of the BBC that he created the character of underestimated club fighter Rocky Balboa as an outlet to express his personal hopes and frustrations about his life.
“I said ‘Jeez if i can take my plight as an actor and put it into a real underdog, that being a boxer, and tell my story — like I couldn’t get an agent and he couldn’t get a manager. I had no love in my life at the time and he didn’t either and so on and so forth,” Stallone explained. (“I have to do this because this is really my story. This is my autobiography,” Stallone added in the documentary The Rocky Saga when asked why he turned down more than $250,000 for his Rocky script in favor of $20,000 and the chance to play the character of Rocky.)
Stallone even told Norman in that 1977 BBC interview that he did contemplate writing something less allegorical and more openly confessional and dismissed it. “Say I had written [Rocky] about a struggling writer in California, in Hollywood,” he continued. “And here he is bumming around in his convertible with his sun tan, but his scripts aren’t selling. So what? At least he has a tan? It just doesn’t work.”
READ MORE: Every Rocky and Creed Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
The only reason I Play Rocky works is Anthony Ippolito. For years, film critics’ go-to biopic dismissal has been “[Actor looking for awards consideration] isn’t giving a performance; he’s just doing a bad SNL impression of [famous historical figure].” Ippolito’s work as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky is the opposite.
It possesses all the superficial hallmarks of a great Saturday Night Live impersonation; the look, the body language, the voice. (My god, the voice. No one else on Earth has ever sounded like Sylvester Stallone — and Ippolito sounds just like him.)
But Ippolito’s work goes beyond superficial mimicry. He embodies the plucky underdog energy that audiences fell in love with when they saw Stallone as Rocky in 1976. He captures Stallone’s wry humor, his wellspring of rage at his shabby life and rough upbringing, and the soulful sensitivity he put into his most famous fictional creation. It’s not just an impressive caricature. It’s a total spiritual embodiment.
Peter Gamble’s script follows Stallone before he became “Sly,” back when he still went by “Mike” because he struggled to pronounce Sylvester as a child. Mike desperately wants to make it as an actor in 1970s New York City, but no one can see past his tough-guy physique and gravelly speech patterns. Things get so bleak after a series of misfortunes that Stallone winds up sleeping in the street, where he’s dismissed as a “bum” — the insult that boxing fans will eventually hurl at Rocky— by a passing policeman. The only thing that finally pulls him out of the gutter is a gig in a shabby, softcore porn film.
Later, Mike supplements his acting income with a job at a movie theater, where he hits it off with the ticket seller, Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb). Even Mike’s dismissive, discouraging father (Matt Dillon) likes Sasha, and encourages his son not to screw the relationship. For her part, Sasha encourages Mike to embrace his real name and to bet on himself. If no one will give him an opportunity as an actor, she says, he should create one for himself as a writer.
A few years later, Stallone and Sasha are married and living in Los Angeles, where Stallone has a desk full of scripts no one wants. When a friend introduces him to producers Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell) and Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) he’s determined to finally break through. He sells them a screenplay he dashed off in three days, inspired by a fight between Muhammad Ali and “Bayonne Bleeder” Chuck Wepner, a massive underdog who managed to knock down the champ and survive into the 15th round. Winkler and Chartoff love the script — but hate Stallone’s request that he play Rocky himself. They offer him more and more money, but Stallone rejects each subsequent paycheck, insisting over and over “I play Rocky.” (Cue the Leonardo DiCaprio pointing meme.)
Once Stallone finally gets the producers to agree to his demands, he must make Rocky with a minuscule budget; if he goes a single day over budget, United Artists holds the contractual right to fire and replace him. So Stallone, like Rocky, must push through endless adversity to achieve his dream.
This is not exactly the most suspenseful business negotiation ever captured on film; everyone watching I Play Rocky knows how it ultimately turned out. (Spoiler alert: Sylvester Stallone was not fired as the star of Rocky.) Likewise, many of Rocky‘s most famous behind-the-scenes stories — like Carl Weathers (Stephan James) nearly blowing his audition by insulting the poor performance screenwriter they had play the scene with him (AKA Stallone) — have been told many times in various documentaries and DVD supplemental features. Rocky fans won’t find much new or surprising.
That’s why Ippolito’s performance is so key. Despite our knowledge of how Rocky turned out and where Stallone’s career went, he finds ways to get us invested in his story through sheer force of charisma. Like Stallone himself, he’s an undeniable (if unlikely) star. He’s also got the right touch for I Play Rocky’s lighter moments, which get a fair amount of emphasis from director Peter Farrelly, who has not completely forgotten his roots in broad comedies now that he mostly makes prestige historical dramas like the Oscar-winning Green Book.
I guess I didn’t learn the lesson of Rocky myself, because I had pretty much written off I Play Rocky before I saw it. What more needed to be said about this film and its extremely famous rag-to-riches backstage story? Not much. But it’s not what’s said here, but how it’s presented, with a level of warmth and uplift worthy of its source material. Unlike in Rocky, there’s no question whether Stallone will go the distance. But damned if we don’t pump our fists when he reaches the top of the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps anyway.
RATING: 7/10

title: Ring doorbell camera captures the Brooklyn building collapse
text:
NEW YORK (Gray News) - A Ring doorbell camera captured the moment an apartment building collapsed in Brooklyn, killing eight people.
In the video, provided by James Williams, debris and dust are seen billowing up as the structure to the right of a landing gives way. People can be heard shouting as the video continues.
A photo taken by Yuki Iwamura for the Associated Press appears to show a different angle of the landing and the apartment where the Ring doorbell camera was. The photo shows contents of the apartment exposed after the exterior wall fell in the collapse.
The three-story building collapsed on Wednesday as construction workers were digging in an adjacent lot.
Two children, ages 9 and 10, were killed along with adults ranging in age from 22 to 31, according to the New York City Police Department. There were also 18 people injured, including four firefighters, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. The children were Colombian, as was one of the adults who was killed, according to the country’s consulate in New York.
The fire department reported rescue operations Thursday after the last victim was freed from the wreckage.
Investigators have not determined the cause of the collapse. In its wake, Mamdani has ordered inspections at about 100 building sites involving companies related to the project.

title: New mercantile shop opens on Blue Hill’s Main Street
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new shop opened in a former realtor’s office in downtown Blue Hill this week.
Gingerfly Life, billed as “a store for the creative and curious,” is a new venture for former theme park designer Sarah Gibbon.
It’s another addition to downtown Blue Hill and aims to contribute to the community year-round, including with artistic offerings.
“I really want people to sort of feel like it’s a cabinet of curiosities that they can spend ages just looking around,” Gibbon said. “They don’t have to buy anything, just to come and be inspired and take the time to look.”
Her family has spent summers on the peninsula for decades, she said, and on a visit three years ago, she resolved to move if the chance ever arose.
After a career in theater and designing theme parks, most recently for Universal Studios, she had the chance to pursue another contract or come to Maine. She chose the latter.
Gibbon rented a place to live in the Stonington village of Oceanville last winter, where she joined the cribbage club and took an entrepreneurship class at the local adult education program that led to the idea of the mercantile.
“I thought, yes, this is my place,” she said. “This is where I want to be for the rest of my life.”
The shop space, tucked in the back of a professional building with a deck overlooking the local harbor, is the former office of the realtor Gibbon bought her house from. Local shop Bucklyn Coffee out front has been a driver of traffic to the store, and response overall has been “so wonderful,” she said.
Wares range from secondhand books to antique jewelry to tea to key chains to duck decoys to paintings to stationary supporting her love of physical mail. She’s also polling visitors to compile a list of things people wish they could buy locally that aren’t easy to find.
The goods are sourced from friends, local artists, English companies and Gibbon’s own collection. She had always hoped to have a store one day and purchased items on trips around the world, she said.
Gingerfly Life will evolve over time, but Gibbon aims to host art workshops and is considering starting an ‘arts club’ where people can use materials for a small fee.
Her original vision in that class was encouraging others to come to Maine for the restorative environment she experienced here, she said, possibly through retreats.
“But working with the folks who live on the island full time, it was like well, why don’t you think about people who actually live here first, Sarah, and then think about others afterwards?” she said. “… Really get to know your community.”
A mentor in the course advised her to live somewhere and see how the area speaks to her rather than coming in from away with a grand plan, she said, and the mercantile concept was born during a class brainstorming session.
Gibbon thinks of a mercantile as a source of things someone needs or might never think they’d need all in one place. The store was inspired by the general stores in Little House on the Prairie, one of the only television shows she saw growing up in South Africa.
“Gingerfly Life,” meanwhile, began as a made-up name with a friend. It came to represent what the state offered Gibbon when she first arrived, she said: a chance to appreciate her surroundings while really getting to know people and listen to them, compared to a corporate life rushing from meeting to meeting.
“So the gingerfly life is about taking a step back, but it’s still full of possibility,” she said. “… It’s almost like a dragonfly perching on a branch and then taking stock, and then it’s off to do something else.”
And, it turns out, opening a store isn’t that different from planning a theme park — it just happens at a smaller scale, with room for more of her own creativity.
“All my life I’ve been getting ready for a big opening and then it opens and the public comes in and then it’s kind of theirs,” she said, describing curating details and overdelivering on a concept. “So it’s been very similar with the shop.”
The store at 107 Main St. in Blue Hill is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Tuesday through Saturday.

title: Ten County Soccer Players Honored with 2026 Butch Shaw Awards
text:
More Than the Final Score: 10 County Soccer Players Earn 2026 Butch Shaw Awards
Success in high school sports isn't always measured by wins, goals, or championships. Sometimes, the greatest recognition comes from the way an athlete plays the game and the respect they show along the way.
Ten Aroostook County high school soccer players have been named recipients of the 2026 Butch Shaw Awards, an honor recognizing outstanding soccer players who demonstrate the sportsmanship and respect that have long been part of the game's tradition in northern Maine.
Presented by the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials, the awards recognize five girls and five boys from across Aroostook County.
2026 Butch Shaw Award Recipients
Girls
- Lilly Burtt – Central Aroostook
- Madisyn Cyr – Wisdom
- Emma Soucy – Wisdom
- Reece Doucette – Fort Kent
- Ava Ezell – Houlton
Boys
- Dominic Cyr – Fort Kent
- Bodey McPherson – Presque Isle
- Drew Lamereau – Easton
- Levi Cole – Fort Fairfield
- Cooper Willard – Houlton
For these ten athletes, the recognition goes beyond what they accomplished during the fall soccer season. The award reflects the importance of competing with respect, displaying good sportsmanship, and representing their schools and communities in a positive way.
The Man Behind the Award
The Butch Shaw Award carries a history that stretches back four decades, honoring a man whose influence on Aroostook County athletics extended well beyond the sidelines.
Clyde "Butch" Shaw, a native of Mars Hill, joined the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials in 1972. He was among the early officials helping establish soccer as the sport grew in popularity among middle and high school students throughout the County.
Shaw was also a well-known and respected varsity basketball and baseball coach at Presque Isle High School.
His approach to athletics was built around three words that became his motto:
"Hustle, Pride, Defense."
But beyond competition and performance, Shaw believed that respect and good sportsmanship were essential qualities for every athlete, coach, and official.
In July 1985, Shaw was diagnosed with leukemia. He passed away that October, leaving behind a legacy that would continue to influence generations of County athletes.
The following fall, in 1986, the Northern Maine Board of Approved Soccer Officials established the Butch Shaw Soccer Award in his memory.
The award was created to recognize outstanding soccer players who exemplify the same qualities Shaw valued throughout his life.
His family's connection to local athletics also continues today. His son, Ryan Shaw, serves as the boys soccer coach at Easton High School. Shaw's daughter is Erica McCrum.
A Legacy That Continues
Forty years after the award was established, its message remains just as important.
High school sports provide plenty of opportunities to celebrate championships, individual achievements, and memorable performances. The Butch Shaw Award recognizes something that can be just as meaningful: the character an athlete brings to competition.
For the ten players selected in 2026, their names now become part of a tradition that has honored generations of Aroostook County soccer players.
Congratulations to all ten recipients of the 2026 Butch Shaw Awards for representing their schools, teammates, and communities with pride and sportsmanship.

title: Navy has quietly fired some commanders and other officials, drawing congressional pushback
text:
Navy has quietly fired some commanders and other officials, drawing congressional pushback
The Navy has quietly fired or removed several top officers in recent months but broke with its usual practice of announcing those changes, drawing pushback from Congress.
Two Democratic lawmakers said Thursday that the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine last month after an underwater collision. Separately, the sea service in September fired the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East, according to a defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe sensitive personnel matters.
Dr. Brian Monahan, a Navy rear admiral and attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, also departed his post during a Navy investigation — with no public announcement or confirmation.
All three are a break from the Navy's longstanding policy to announce major removals of commanders and other highly visible officials. They also follow an increasing level of secrecy over military operations, especially in the Middle East.
"As a result of the Navy's failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy's commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress," Reps. Joe Courtney of Connecticut and Adam Smith of Washington wrote in a letter to Navy leaders.
The developments could set up a contentious confirmation hearing next week for acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao as he seeks to permanently take over as the top civilian official.
In a letter to Cao and the Navy's top uniformed officer, Adm. Daryl Caudle, Courtney and Smith said they had "deep frustration" over the Navy's failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee about the firing of the commander, second in command and top enlisted sailor of the USS South Dakota submarine.
The letter says they were fired after the submarine ran into something on the seabed, but the Navy would not offer public comment.
The Navy also on Sept. 27 relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, commander of the USS Michael Murphy destroyer, which has been deployed to support operations against Iran, due to a loss of confidence, the defense official said. She had been in the job less than a year.
Typically, the firing of someone like Cunningham would be announced by the Navy within days, but the service did not offer public comment even when asked about it.
On Thursday, Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California also confirmed the departure of Monahan, the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, but provided few other details.
The Navy has opened an investigation, according to a person familiar with the situation who was not authorized to discuss the matter and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
For nearly 18 years, Monahan held the top job in the Office of the Attending Physician, which is responsible for providing emergency medical assistance to members of Congress and the Supreme Court as well as congressional staff and visitors.
Monahan was sometimes in the news for discussing matters such as Sen. Mitch McConnell's health and for administering a COVID-19 vaccine to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
Restrictions on the military sharing information go beyond the Navy.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, has released few details on recent limited strikes on Iran and refused to comment on or specify damage to bases or equipment, usually citing the need for operational security.
Major satellite imagery providers with U.S. contracts have blocked or delayed public release of images in the region at the request of American officials. As a result, it took months to determine that Iranian drone and missile strikes damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment in the region, according to an Associated Press analysis.
___
Associated Press writers Ben Finley and Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report.

title: Horses caught on camera boarding city bus
text:
DETROIT (WXYZ) - A video of a horse briefly boarding a Detroit city bus has gone viral, and the horse’s owner is sharing his side.
Ellessia Drew said she was near 7 Mile and Strasburg on Saturday evening when she recorded the video with her cell phone.
Witness reacts to video
“I was taking like, oh my god, like what about the people on the bus? What if the horse used the bathroom on a bus, like what’s going on?” Drew said.
“You never know in Detroit. Especially on 7 Mile,” said resident Alan Houser. “7 Mile right up there, anything can happen on 7 Mile.”
Owner explains why the horse was there
Jordan Williams, co-founder of Urban City Cowboys, said he was in the city helping with a fundraiser, taking kids on rides. Afterward, he said, he saw the bus and wanted to take a quick video.
“It wasn’t like I was tracking down the bus; I was like, ‘Oh, there’s the bus. Oh, there’s the bus stop, well it looks like it’s lining up for me,’” Williams said.
Williams said the bus stopped and the driver was shocked to see the horse and spoke to him through the door. He then walked the horse in and out of the bus.
Williams said there was no harm done. He said he has done the same on multiple DDOT buses over the years.
“We’ve been on the Jefferson, we’ve been on the Chalmers, we’ve been on the Conners, and now on the 7 Mile,” Williams said.
DDOT response
Detroit Department of Transportation said service animals are allowed on its buses, but horses are not. The agency said it is speaking to the driver and investigating the incident.
In a statement, DDOT said: “We are taking appropriate steps to address this incident as it is not consistent with DDOT policy and potentially creates an unsafe and uncomfortable ride for our passengers.”
Williams said he hopes the city can see he was just horsing around.
“Only in Detroit and on 7 Mile,” Williams said.
City officials said they will retrain all bus drivers and educate residents about their efforts to provide safe, reliable service.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Cloud Coverage Builds Friday, With A Few Snow Showers Possible This Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. We had a decent day across the region today with sunshine making a return after several days of mostly cloudy skies and occasional rain and snow showers. Partly cloudy skies overnight tonight will once again allow temperatures to cool off into the upper teens and lower 20s. We’ll see more cloud coverage build into the region during the day tomorrow, with temperatures remaining slightly below average for this time of year. The coastal storm we’ve been watching over the past several days continues to look like a miss for our region, but we will still have to watch for some light shower activity heading into the upcoming weekend.
Temperatures overnight tonight look to be very similar to what we woke up to this morning, with lows for most locations falling back into the upper teens and lower 20s. Partly cloudy skies are expected for the majority of the overnight hours, with light northwesterly winds around 5 to 10 mph. I would anticipate another chilly start to the day tomorrow, with temperatures taking a little longer to rebound given the increased cloud coverage we’re expecting during the daytime hours.
As we head into the end of the work week, expect more cloud coverage to build into the region throughout the day tomorrow. An area of low pressure making its way off the New England coastline looks to remain far enough to our south that the majority of the precipitation associated with this system will miss us entirely. The latest forecast guidance continues to illustrate this trend nicely, with even portions of Downeast Maine now looking to miss out on much of the precipitation from this system. High temperatures tomorrow look to top off in the mid to upper 30s for most locations, with a few lower 40 degree readings possible across southern portions of Aroostook County.
Heading into the overnight hours tomorrow night, we’ll be watching for the potential of a few flurries developing across portions of the region. While the coastal storm itself looks to miss us, an area of low pressure in the upper levels of the atmosphere will still be making its way into Northern Maine heading into the upcoming weekend. Temperatures won’t cool off quite as much tomorrow night as what we’re expecting tonight, with the increased cloud coverage helping keep low temperatures in the mid to upper 20s for most locations.
We’ll continue to watch for some light shower activity during the day Saturday, primarily in the form of snow showers during the morning hours, before some rain showers begin to mix in as temperatures warm up heading into the afternoon hours. I don’t anticipate everyone seeing shower activity during the day Saturday, with some of the better chances for seeing snow showers remaining across the higher elevations of northern and western Aroostook County. High temperatures Saturday look to be very similar to what we’re expecting tomorrow, with highs in the mid to upper 30s and a few lower 40 degree readings across southern locations.
Taking a look at the latest snowfall potential from our NextGen model, you can see that the higher elevations of northern and western Aroostook County still have the best opportunity to see some accumulating snowfall from this weekend’s shower activity. For those of us living along the Route 1 corridor, I don’t expect much, if anything, in the way of accumulating snowfall. Some of the higher elevations could see a coating of snow, with the potential for an inch in a few locations if we’re able to get some heavier snow showers to develop. Those traveling along Route 11 north of Ashland Saturday will want to keep an eye out for the potential of some slick spots if those heavier snow showers do develop. Ultimately, this is a much quieter forecast than what we were looking at earlier this week.
Temperatures look to remain fairly consistent heading into the upcoming weekend, with highs in the upper 30s through Sunday for most locations. The good news for those of you not quite ready for the colder temperatures to stick around is that we’re looking at a gradual warming trend heading into the new work week. Sunshine makes a return to the region Monday and Tuesday, helping temperatures rebound back into the mid to upper 40s by the middle of next week. These readings will once again be above average for this time of year. Unfortunately, with a quieter stretch of weather ahead of us, we’re not looking at much in the way of additional relief from our ongoing drought situation either. For more details on what to expect heading into the upcoming weekend, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader, saying voters ‘called for change’
text:
Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader, saying voters ‘called for change’
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a statement that "the American people called for change" and that is why he is running.
"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."
Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
It will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades. The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators will not say publicly how they will vote. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election, and Schumer recruited many of the party's winning candidates and raised money for them.
Schumer has been talking to Democratic senators since the election and forming an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer laid out a broad plan for their first 100 days in power.
"I'm going to win it," Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.
In a statement after Van Hollen's announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.
"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."
Divisions among Democrats preceded the race
While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen's run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025, when Schumer was put on the defensive since he sided with Republicans on a spending vote.
Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.
Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.
While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least one backer: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week. He posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need "bold leadership."
"I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience," El-Sayed wrote. "We need both right now. Which is why I'm proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority."
Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., also called for new leadership at a press conference Tuesday, though neither endorsed a specific candidate.
Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week.
Maine Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the leadership election, issued a statement after Van Hollen's announcement: "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?"
"Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible," King wrote.

title: Experts discuss implications of Texas’ blue wave
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - After Texas flipped blue in the midterm elections, political observers are discussing what the longterm implications of the elections could mean for Democrats and Republicans in the state.
The GOP stronghold delivered numerous high-profile wins for Democrats including a U.S. Senate seat, the governorship and control of the state house. That’s led some to say that the state has turned blue.
“The scope and scale of the Democratic victories here is something that nobody was predicting,” said Joshua Blank, research director of the Texas Politics Project at UT Austin.
The victories came in the largest Republican state in the nation and ended Democrats 32-year losing streak for statewide races. Democratic National Committee leaders now say the political tides in Texas have turned in their favor.
DNC says Texas has gone blue
“I think by any definition of the metric, Texas has gone blue,” said Libby Schneider, DNC deputy executive director. “And I think what we saw last Tuesday was a referendum on Republicans having almost complete control for 30 years in Texas and not getting a whole heck of a lot of done for Texans.”
The party has been targeting Texas and other Republican-leaning states in the region as part of its new southern strategy. The strategy aims to gain ground as more people continue to move to those states.
“I think what it tells us is that especially as we reached 2032 and we reached the next census and population is moving to states like Texas and to the south, that it just sort of reinforces what we’ve long believed here under Ken Martin’s DNC, which is that the South is the future and now the South is the present,” Schneider said.
Cornyn disputes shift
Not everyone is convinced one election means the state’s politics have shifted.
“You know, Texas is not a blue state, and I don’t even think it’s a purple state,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) on Wednesday.
Presidential election outlook
One question is whether Democrats could win Texas in a presidential election year. Blank said that could take a lot of work.
“Democrats are certainly going to say that Texas is in play, because Republicans are going to have to spend a lot of money and time defending what really is a foundation piece of their electoral college strategy,” Blank said. “A much more open question is whether Democrats are willing to commit the kind of time and resources necessary to compete in a state like Texas.”
Blank said the state is more competitive now. He said it could be an uphill battle for Democrats because of the breakdown of registered party members.
“The idea that Democrats did in one election, what it took Republicans three to accomplish most of is a historical and unprecedented. So it makes the question more valid,” Blank said. “But it also leads us to remind ourselves that there are still more Republican voters in Texas. A big part of the Democratic win here was not just about overwhelming turnout, but it was also about overwhelming Republican disengagement. And when those Republican voters become reengaged, what does it look like? And that we just don’t know yet.”
Investment in other states
Democratic Party leaders also said they plan to invest more in other Republican states across the South, including Florida, Alabama and Louisiana.

title: High school athletes can capitalize on NIL, lawmakers look to protect young players
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - Name, image and likeness, or NIL, continues to dominate headlines and forever change the game for student athletes.
While the federal government tackles the college landscape, some states have enacted laws to protect high school students and their families.
In Louisiana, lawmakers recently passed legislation seeking to protect K-12 student athletes interested in signing NIL deals. Young players in the state can legally enter into big money contracts, but the new laws also look to add transparency and accountability.
A star recruit
At Tad Gormely Stadium, members of Brother Martin’s High School football team endured double session practices in Louisiana’s punishing summer heat ahead of the 2026 season.
Among them is Easton Royal. Most football scouts rank him as the number one high school wide receiver in the entire nation.
At 17 years old, the Brother Martin senior is considered a prime college football recruit. Royal said versatility is the strongest part of his game.
“There’s not one way that you can really stop me. I feel like, just give me the ball and put it in my hands,” said Easton Royal.
Putting the ball in Royal’s hands is what the Brother Martin Crusaders have consistently done the past three seasons, helping them maintain a top ten state divisional ranking.
Mark Bonis has been Brother Martin’s head football coach since 2009.
“He’s been with me since eighth grade. So, he becomes part of your family. He’s definitely one of the best we’ve ever coached, but what I’m really proud of is his growth and maturation from eighth grade all the way to senior year,” said Bonis.
Coach Bonis said Royal’s game highlights are impressive because of what he puts into practice.
“When you’re talking about one of the best players in the country and you’re having to pull him off the field from practice to me, that says a lot about him, but also sets the standard for your football program,” said Coach Bonis.
Royal is currently committed to the University of Texas, but still has time to change his mind. There’s no shortage of social media speculation about the possibility of him staying in state and playing for LSU.
Royal is on the verge of entering the world of paid collegiate athletes and potential big money endorsement deals.
But he doesn’t have to wait until college to earn NIL money. Royal said he is getting offers that could be life changing for his family.
“It would mean a lot because my mom, she’s right now a single mother with three boys, and we all eat a lot. And we’re boys. We’re kind of crazy, so she put in a lot of hard nights, working three jobs, working overnight, being tired. So being able to have the NIL would really help her so she can stop working as much as she does,” Royal said.
From NIL deals to where he’ll eventually play, Royal said he’s trying to stay grounded about all the attention.
“If I’m in a room, you won’t really know who I am unless somebody else brings it up. That’s just the type of person I am, and that’s how I keep myself humble. Because I have all this ability, but it can be taken away,” said Royal.
Royal may not talk much about any NIL deals, but since 2021, when the NCAA first allowed college athletes to monetize their name, image and likeness, the conversation and debate has trickled down to the high school level, and even lower.
For Coach Bonis, he believes Royal deserves NIL money, if that’s what he chooses.
“Personally, I think it’s a great deal. If anybody’s going to capitalize on someone’s name image and likeness then I believe that person, the player, should reap the benefits of that. Now, I disagree, and people confuse the two, with pay to play. I’m not a proponent for pay to play,” said Bonis.
Changing the game
John “J.T.” Curtis Jr. is the winningest high school football coach in Louisiana history. In his 57 years of coaching, Coach Curtis said he’s never witnessed the kinds of changes and situations NIL is generating.
“No longer do we use the term student athlete. All we hear about is NIL. You and I are here talking about NIL, not about a young man who is entering into college or entering into high school and their education and the importance of that education. Now it’s all about what can you do for me,” said Curtis, who is the head football coach at John Curtis Christian School.
Curtis said the deals are even “trickling down into junior high school and rising freshmen.”
One of his his biggest concerns is with sports agents, or people who present themselves as one. Curtis said he worries about agents taking advantage of teenagers and families who may be unfamiliar with the business side of sports.
“I’ve coached players who went to be professionals, and those pro agents are usually getting 3% to 5% the earnings of the player,” Curtis said. “I have heard, I have not seen, but I’ve heard through resources that some of these agents pitching deals to high school athletes and getting as much as 20% to 25% of a person’s NIL contract, and of course, that’s upfront money.”
Adding student protections
Patrick Connick, a Republican state senator in Louisiana, acknowledged that some younger students were “being approached by so-called agents” who reportedly had no qualifications or expertise.
Ahead of Louisiana’s spring legislative session, Connick, Coach Curtis and a committee of lawmakers worked on crafting bills to address the growing influence of NIL on young athletes.
Connick sponsored one NIL law that took effect in August. Among its provisions is a requirement for agents who represent student-athletes in the state to register with the Louisiana Attorney General’s office. Those agents must also complete training and pass background checks.
“These guys are young. Sometimes their family members, they see dollar signs, but we can’t let the agents take advantage of these kids. That’s the whole purpose of what this legislation is about,” said State Senator Connick.
For Royal, there’s one person he turns to for guidance on NIL and all other matters in life.
“My mom. We make the decisions, but she also has her close circle of people that she also goes to as well to help us make decisions like about agents and things of that nature,” said Royal.
Another NIL law sets up guardrails for K-12 student-athletes and their parents or guardians. One guideline requires parental consent for a minor to sign an NIL deal. Connick said the number of student-athletes in the state affected by NIL is unclear, but more regulation of it was needed.
“The whole purpose is to protect these young kids who have the potential of earning a lot of money at a very young age and we got to watch out for that,” Connick said.
While Louisiana’s new laws aim to protect high school athletes, they also place some limits on them. For example, student athletes cannot profit from marketing deals that involve drugs, alcohol, tobacco, gambling, or weapons.
Whether at the high school or college level, NIL can be polarizing. Brother Martin Coach Mark Bonis argues high school is where true amateur athletics still lives, and NIL can benefit student athletes, their families and even their schools from all the exposure.
“You see a young man, you see a family that’s worked for things for years and years, and you see the sacrifices that they’ve made. You want to make sure that they are receiving everything that they have earned,” said Coach Bonis.
Some, like Coach J.T. Curtis, said the injection of money NIL could weaken the integrity of scholastic sports.
“When big money comes in the front door, everything goes out the back door unless you have your values in the right place,” said Coach Curtis.
Ultimately, it may come down to the athlete and their loved ones. Even Coach Curtis admitted that if any of us or our families had these kinds of opportunities, debates about NIL would be of a different nature.
“It’s easy for me to be judgmental and say the pie in the sky, it’s all about your education and so on, but when you’re confronted with the numbers, then that’s a different thing,” Coach Curtis said.
Royal said money is a factor, but it’s not the sole reason why he’s on the football field.
“Being here at Brother Martin, Coach Bonis, they work us, it’s not easy. We’re practicing at Tad Gormley in the heat, so you really got to love it to want to be able to continue to play it for the rest of your life. And I feel like I really love the game of football,” Royal said.
It’s one teenager’s love for a game that increasingly requires adult decisions.
NIL across the country
As of November 2026, about three dozen states allow high school athletes to make deals.
Other states strictly prohibit compensation for NIL. These deals have caused some families to move states to capitalize on their skills.
