title: Man United hires Mauricio Pochettino, who leaves US job with task of reviving former power
text:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ga. (AP) — Mauricio Pochettino was hired as Manchester United’s head coach on Friday, agreeing to leave his job with the U.S. national team to take on the challenge of reviving the fortunes of English soccer’s once dominant force.
Just three months after announcing a contract to lead the Americans through the 2030 World Cup, the U.S. Soccer Federation said Pochettino will depart next next week for Old Trafford. The 20-time English champion is in the relegation zone after 10 games of the Premier League season.
He has signed a 2 1/2-year contract and will officially take over on Nov. 18 ahead of the match at Liverpool four days later, becoming United’s eighth permanent coach or manager since club great Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
United said the 54-year-old Argentine was “renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players,” and had “consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues.”
Pochettino’s appointment comes one day after Michael Carrick was fired for overseeing United’s worst league start in 40 years, with one of the biggest teams in world soccer languishing 18th in the Premier League.
Pochettino and his assistants will remain with the U.S. team for the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.
“There is tremendous talent in the U.S. player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of U.S. Soccer,” Pochettino said in a statement.
Pochettino took over the U.S. team in the fall of 2024 and led the co-host Americans to the round of 16 at this year’s World Cup. The USSF is likely to sound out Pep Guardiola’s interest and could also consider elevating Under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, a former national team defender. Cherundolo will lead a senior national team training camp next month with players mostly from Major League Soccer.
USSF CEO JT Batson and chief operating officer Dan Helfrich will lead the search, assisted by women’s national team coach Emma Hayes and former American defender Oguchi Onyewu, a member of the USSF staff.
“Mauricio has left a lasting mark on U.S. Soccer through his leadership, professionalism and commitment to our players and culture,” Batson said in a statement. “What we are most proud of goes beyond the wins. He and his staff raised standards, strengthened our culture and created clearer connections from the youth national teams to the senior team.”
After coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in the Premier League, Espanyol in Spain and winning the French title with Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino takes a job that has proved to be too big for a succession of managers since Ferguson led the team to a record 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns during a near 27-year tenure.
United has not won the league since Ferguson’s last season in 2013 and has been overtaken by rivals Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Arsenal.
Champions League-winning coaches Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho failed to meet United’s expectations, while David Moyes, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Carrick also came up short.
Despite winning the French league with PSG in 2022, arguably Pochettino’s greatest achievement was turning Tottenham into a serial title contender in the Premier League and also leading the club to the Champions League final in 2019.
He has never won a major trophy in England, most recently losing the final of the English League Cup with Chelsea in 2024.

title: With measles surging, the US is likely to lose 'elimination' status. Vaccines offer best hope
text:
With measles surging, the US is likely to lose 'elimination' status. Vaccines offer best hope
Babies are dying in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and New York. A high school closed in Pennsylvania. A Texas labor and delivery unit had to enact emergency protocols after measles was detected in a laboring mother.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed.
Measles is spreading in the U.S. at a pace not seen in over three decades. The highly contagious respiratory disease can cause a rash, cough, runny nose, fever, watery eyes and high fevers. It can lead to hospitalization and death.
With communities nationwide feeling the disease’s effects, the U.S. is on track to lose the sought-after "measles elimination" status it achieved 26 years ago.
The Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that coordinates public health efforts across dozens of countries, designates nations as having achieved measles elimination when robust surveillance shows they have ended "endemic" — or regular and sustained — virus transmission.
Elimination status means a country has not seen very large measles outbreaks and has not had uncontrolled domestic virus transmission for a year or more.
This is no longer true of the United States, data shows.
Measles cases skyrocketed in 2025 and 2026. This year alone, the country has already recorded more than 5,100 measles cases — the highest number seen in 35 years.
With case counts rising each week, experts say there’s only one way to end the spread: increased measles vaccination.
Any community with vaccine coverage below 95% is particularly vulnerable to outbreaks.
Measles is "exquisitely contagious," said Jennifer Nuzzo, a Brown University epidemiology professor who tracks measles. "The virus just has to show up, and then it explodes."
How many measles cases have U.S. health authorities recorded this year?
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had reported 5,182 measles cases and six deaths in 2026 as of Nov. 6.
The CDC says it counts only confirmed cases.
Other public health data aggregators have recorded higher case counts.
Johns Hopkins’ U.S. Measles Tracker reported 5,400 cases in 2026 as of Nov. 11. That total reflects lab-confirmed measles cases compiled from state and county health departments, county-level news releases and news articles.
Brown University School of Public Health’s Tracking Report newsletter tallied 5,478 cases and nine deaths as of Nov. 5 — eight confirmed by states and one confirmed by a local coroner. Its report pulls data from state health department websites and counts cases by the dates they were reported to health organizations. Other organizations often mark the cases by the date the measles rash is detected.
How many measles outbreaks have been documented this year?
With two months left in the year, the CDC reports 43 new measles outbreaks in 2026, defining “outbreak” as three or more related cases. The agency reported 48 outbreaks total last year and 16 in 2024.
The U.S. has recorded more than 100 new measles cases each week for 13 weeks straight.
How many states are seeing large measles outbreaks?
So far in 2026, 13 states have seen more than 100 measles cases, according to CDC data. In 2025, just five states surpassed 100 cases. At least six states are currently battling sizable measles outbreaks.
Pennsylvania’s outbreak is the largest this year by far among all states, with officials documenting more than 1,500 cases and six measles-associated deaths, according to state health department data as of Nov. 9. Hundreds more cases have been documented in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin.
Not everyone infected with measles seeks medical care, so these figures are likely undercounts. And states often record a measles-associated death if the person died while having measles.
Under the second Trump administration, the CDC has not recorded the same number of U.S. measles deaths as states, after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an antivaccine activist, publicly questioned whether evidence sufficiently demonstrated measles was the cause of death.
In the U.S., officials typically expect about one to two deaths per 1,000 measles cases. Given the nine measles-associated deaths states have reported this year, "there is reason to believe that we are far, far from totally enumerating the amount of infections," Nuzzo said.
Why is the U.S. likely to lose its measles elimination status?
The Pan American Health Organization commission that assesses measles and rubella elimination in the Americas was meeting Nov. 10-13 and expects to release its decision about the U.S. status on Nov. 17.
Many public health experts believe measles is once again endemic in the U.S.
In early 2026, Maimuna Majumder, a computational epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital, and other researchers analyzed the country’s measles data. Since then, Majumder said it “seems inevitable” that the U.S. would lose its elimination status.
The U.S. is currently seeing uncontrolled measles spread that has lasted for more than 12 months, and available evidence signals that the actual number of infections surpasses the recorded case totals, Nuzzo said.
"By every measure that matters, measles is no longer a rare condition in the United States," Nuzzo said. "It has returned to continual spread — spread that doesn’t require imported infections."
Dr. Jonathan Temte, a University of Wisconsin public health and community engagement professor emeritus, said losing this designation — one the United States helped define years ago — says a lot about how the country’s public health and medical systems are doing.
Measles elimination is a goal countries work toward, Nuzzo said: "It is a point of pride when you achieve it, and it is a point of embarrassment when you lose it."
Could the U.S. eliminate measles again?
Yes. Doing so starts with containing outbreaks.
Canada lost its measles elimination designation in 2025, but still managed to control measles spread in 2026 — declaring its multi-jurisdictional measles outbreak over in October. Brazil lost its elimination status in 2019 and regained it in 2024.
The U.S. was largely holding steady low case numbers from 2000 until 2019, when it recorded 1,274 cases. The 2018-19 outbreak was centered in New York City and surrounding counties, and officials responded by declaring a public health emergency, mandating vaccinations, closing schools with measles transmission, prohibiting unvaccinated children from attending school and doing public outreach, KFF reported. The New York outbreak was interrupted by August 2019 — less than 12 months after it began.
It's important that sick people stay home and unvaccinated people who’ve been exposed undergo a 21-day quarantine, but widespread transmission only ends with increased vaccination, Nuzzo said.
Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina, presented the country’s measles report to the Pan American Health Organization commission. Vaccination is key, he said.
"If we do not want an incurable and deadly disease to stalk our kids in schools, playgrounds and churches," Brewer said, adding, "We need to get more kids vaccinated."
It's uncertain how public health officials will respond should the U.S. lose its status. In a Tuesday interview with Reuters, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said she didn’t foresee the federal government altering its approach.
"We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states," she said.
PolitiFact Staff Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Is Outlook down? Outage hits companies as Microsoft struggles to restore services
text:
HONG KONG (AP) — A global Microsoft outage this week disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide and highlighting the risks of depending on one of just a few major providers of essential technology.
Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. As the outage entered its second day Friday, Microsoft said it saw “encouraging recovery progress.” But the company also warned that “intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery” may persist for some users.
“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” Microsoft wrote in a social media update.
The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.
Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”
The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.
Microsoft has scrambled to recover services
A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays.
On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.
Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.
Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.
And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook. If the situation dragged on, the trouble could “impact the production timeline,” he said.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.
OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.
Outage has parallels with 2024 shutdown
Some have drawn parallels to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.
Governments and institutions in Western Europe, in particular, have been trying to reduce their reliance on services provided by a few big U.S. tech services in their continuing push for “digital sovereignty.” This week’s outage renewed some of those calls.
British lawmaker Chi Onwurah, who chairs the Science and Technology Committee in Parliament, said the Microsoft outage “only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the U.K.’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services.”
She said her committee has previously warned that the U.K. is “hugely dependent” on a small number of U.S.-based technology providers, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing.
Florian Druckenthaner, a spokesperson for Germany’s digitization ministry, said the government’s IT security agency believes German business was widely affected, but there were no reports of major disruption at the government level.
Regardless, Druckenthaner said, the outage shows “the significance of building up redundancies and alternatives. We are working on that.”
___
Associated Press journalists Adam Schreck in Bangkok; Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Australia; Sheikh Saaliq in New Delhi; Mayuko Ono in Tokyo; Geir Moulson in Berlin; Menalaos Hadjicostis in Nicosia, Cyprus; and Pan Pylas and Brian Melley in London contributed.

title: UMaine football travels to Albany for CAA contest; MMA hosts Husson
text:
The University of Maine football team will try to salvage something from a miserable season starting Saturday in a familiar venue: Tom and Mary Casey Stadium in Albany, New York.
UMaine will take on Albany’s 25th-ranked Great Danes in a stadium where the Black Bears have won seven of the last eight meetings, including a 34-20 win in 2024.
UMaine will be looking to snap an eight-game losing streak, its longest in one season since 1967. UMaine is 1-8 overall and 1-5 in CAA conference play.
Albany is 6-4 and 4-2, respectively, and still has a shot at an FCS playoff berth. The Great Danes will be looking to rebound from a potentially costly 31-7 loss to Bryant.
UMaine is coming off its second bye week of the campaign.
“I’m really impressed with their team in all three phases,” said UMaine head coach Jordan Stevens. “It’s going to be a big challenge for us and one we’re really excited about.”
The Black Bears’ primary focus will be converting red zone scoring opportunities into touchdowns instead of field goals.
“We’ve been making a living on field goals, and that’s not where you want to be,” said Stevens.
UMaine has averaged 13.3 points per game, good for 122nd among 124 teams in the FCS. Only Bucknell (11.8 PPG) and Virginia Military Institute (8.8 PPG) are scoring less.
The UMaine defense has done its job for the most part, ranking ninth in the country and atop the CAA in red zone defense, stopping opponents from scoring inside the red zone 30.3% of the time. It ranks seventh in the country in third-down stops, allowing just a 29.9% conversion rate, and sixth in fourth-down defense (30.8%).
“Our defense has been outstanding, make no mistake about that,” said Stevens.
UMaine’s defense will face an Albany rushing attack averaging 175 yards per game, second-best in the CAA. Rahshan La Mons is Albany’s leading rusher with 789 yards on 136 carries, but he missed the Bryant game due to injury.
Joey Koch has gained 552 yards on 100 carries, and quarterback Kai Colon has 81 carries for 175 yards. Colon has completed 56.9% of his passes for 1,557 yards and 13 touchdowns with seven interceptions.
B.J. Norman is the leading receiver with 41 catches for 478 yards and seven TDs, and the defense, best against the run in the CAA (109 yards per game), features linebacker Dillon Dunathan (76 tackles, 4 sacks, 1 interception), safety/cornerback Victor Holt (65 tackles, 3 sacks, 2 INTs) and end Shawan Lewis, whose 9.5 sacks are fourth best in the country.
For UMaine, Caden Drezek has completed 52% of his passes, and Eddie Buehler has completed 54%. Buehler has thrown for 847 yards and four TDs, and Drezek, who has been getting most of the playing time lately, has thrown for 796 yards and three TDs. Buehler has thrown six interceptions, and Drezek has thrown three.
Rashawn Marshall has rushed for 581 yards on 133 carries, and Nick Laughlin (35 catches, 330 yards) and Evan Wallace (31 catches, 299 yards) are the leading receivers.
Defensively, linebacker Sam Oppenheimer ranks 11th in the country with 90 tackles and 13th with 46 solo tackles. He also has two interceptions. Linebacker Noah Carpenter has 70 tackles; strong safety Jeremiah McGill has 66 and end Chris Bacon has a team-high 3.5 sacks.
The six NCAA Division III football teams in the state will also play on Saturday.
Husson (4-5 overall and 4-2 in the Conference of New England) will take on in-state rival Maine Maritime Academy (0-9 and 0-6 CNE) in Castine at noon. MMA has lost 45 straight games dating back to 2017. Husson has won four of its last five games.
Brody Gibson has completed 56.9% of his passes for 1,323 yards for Husson; Jacob Lenz (36-for-404) and Caden Crocker (29-189) have been the leading receivers; Anthony Santacroce (124 rushes, 562 yards) and Daniel Ruiz Cantu (119-for-530) are the top rushers, and the defensive standouts have been J.T. Wright (63 tackles) and Erik Menger (60, four sacks).
Brayden Trombly has five interceptions, Melvyn Telisca has four, and Calvin Casavant has five sacks.
For MMA, Auston Harris has had an exceptional season on offense, leading the Mariners in rushing yards (545) and receptions (37). Harris has completed 53.6%of his passes for 1,284 yards. Ty Regis and Evan Flowers have each caught 24 passes for 340 and 208 yards, respectively.
Defensively for MMA, Lucas Houghton has 96 tackles, Matt Gagin has 84, and Connor Cuba has 76. James Boyer-Russell has a team-high three sacks.
Biddeford’s University of New England will travel to Henniker, NH, to take on New England College in the second annual Battle for Route 202. UNE has won four in a row.
Colby will visit arch-rival Bowdoin for a 1 p.m. game, and Bates will go to New York to take on Hamilton at noon.
In the CBB (Colby, Bates, Bowdoin) series, Colby would win the series with a win, since it has already beaten Bates 21-19. Bates beat Bowdoin, 10-7. A Bowdoin win would leave all three schools at 1-1.

title: Maine airports respond to FAA stoppage
text:
BANGOR, ME (WABI) - A nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration was lifted at around 8:30 p.m. Eastern time tonight.
The FAA initially issued the ground stop citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Cause not immediately clear
The cause was not immediately clear, although the ground stop came after frequency outages were reported in some parts of the country.
According to Reuters, nearly 7,000 flights have been delayed or canceled.
Duffy cites equipment failure
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was due to equipment failure and the communication issues that arose from it. He blamed outdated equipment and a lack of funding from Congress.
Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullen spoke with the press earlier tonight.
“And this is not going to get done overnight. You’re right. But when do you want to start it? America, when do you want to start building a brand-new system? Well, you have a team with President Trump that actually is building it right now, but we don’t have full funding. And so I think there’s no better time than the present to actually give us the money and let us finish the build. What went down was old. Right? It was the old legacy equipment. It failed. And, listen, it’s going to continue to fail. But my number-one job is America’s safety,” Duffy said.
Mullen: ‘The public was never at danger’
“The public was never at danger through this process. There was never any lives at risk. There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution. But I do understand the Internet traffic and where all these conspiracies start running towards. I just can’t say this enough. All your loved ones are safe. We are working to resolve the issue,” Mullen said.
BGR releases statement
Bangor International Airport officials tell WABI that their airline partners are still assessing the situation to determine how many have been impacted. Flights enroute to Bangor are continuing, but at this hour nothing will be taking off. Two commercial airliners are on the ground at gates but are unable to take off, and a third inbound that will experience delays.
Airport spokesperson Angel Matson said: “Bangor International Airport (BGR) is aware of the nationwide ground stop issued the evening of Friday 13, 2026 by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) following a communications issue affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers across the country.
“The FAA is actively investigating the issue, and BGR is monitoring the situation closely while remaining in communication with our airline and air traffic control partners.
“Passengers traveling through BGR should be prepared for potential flight delays or disruptions as the situation develops. Travelers are strongly encouraged to monitor their flight status directly through their airline’s website or mobile app and ensure that email and text notifications are enabled to receive the most current information.
“This is a nationwide air traffic control issue and is not specific to Bangor International Airport.
“The safety of passengers, airline crews, and airport personnel remains our highest priority. We appreciate the patience and understanding of travelers as the FAA works to resolve the issue and restore normal operations.
Additional updates will be shared as information becomes available.“
CNN contributed to this report.

title: St. Dominic Academy is alive and well in Auburn
text:
In late May 1897, rumors circulated that Mark Twain had died while in London. Contacted for confirmation, Twain replied, “The report of my death was an exaggeration.”
Twain’s feelings mirrored my own a few weeks ago when I read the Oct. 16 Sun Journal article headlined “A year after St. Dom’s closes, Auburn schools see big uptick in enrollment.” School officials say the two developments may be related.
St. Dominic Academy remains open and thriving. Contrary reports are indeed exaggerated. The academy continues to operate at its spacious Auburn campus, offering a Catholic education for young people from pre-K through eighth grade.
The academy’s record of providing Catholic education began in 1878 and continues to
this day, with key priorities still in place:
- Authentic Catholic doctrine.
- A calm, well-mannered environment.
- Weekly mass and confession.
- Partnership with parents, the child’s primary educator.
- Daily play and exercise.
- Cursive handwriting.
- Phonics-based reading instruction.
- Traditional classes in academic content knowledge.
- Art and music instruction.
The academy’s disciplined focus on academics and character is welcome at a time when local school achievement rates are averaging below the state average in both math and reading.
Parents naturally want what is best for their children. Many local families have found
what they’re looking for on Gracelawn Road. The school welcomes inquiries and visits throughout the year.
St. Dominic, the patron saint of the academy, prized education in his own day. His
academy in Auburn is proud to keep that tradition alive and well in the present.
Joseph McCleary
Portland

title: This woman and her dog have taken to the motorcycle life
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, SC (InvestigateTV) - Paige Parlato kicks her motorcycle alive, and her Doberman mix, Han, is ready to ride.
“He’s very laidback, he really likes to be where I’m at, but he really can have some energy if he wants to,” Parlato said.
Parlato and Han cruise weekly through the Grand Strand, turning heads everywhere they go.
“Normally, they’re in shock when he’s on the back, and they just want all of his attention,” Parlato said.
Parlato, a vet tech, adopted Han at 12 weeks old.
“He came in as a surrender with a broken jaw,” Parlato said. “The people couldn’t care for him, and I took him on in, and he’s been with me ever since.”
By day, the two clock in at the clinic.
“He goes, and he helps technicians learn new skills,” Parlato said.
The pair then turns to riding for their shared escape.
“Whenever he heard bikes, he associated them with friends,” Parlato said. “So whenever the bikes showed up, his friends showed up, and he got to play and have fun, and he was not scared of the sounds. He was out there with everyone.”
She recorded Han’s excitement for the open road before they suited up for safety. Han slipped into his adventure backpack and goggles before getting strapped onto Parlato’s back.
“We try to keep off the busier roads. Places where he can enjoy and we don’t have to go too fast,” Parlato said.
The pair posts their adventures on social media.
“It just makes people smile, so I want more people to see them; he makes people happy,” Parlato said. “I just enjoy being with him, and he enjoys being with me, so it’s just a happy experience all around.”
Han also enjoys hiking, rock hunting for fossils and paddleboarding.

title: Letter: Maine shouldn’t abandon popular vote compact
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Maine made a promise, and I don’t want us to be the first state to break it.
In 2024, Maine joined the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, agreeing that the candidate who wins the most votes across the whole country should become president. The compact now stands at 222 of the 270 electoral votes it needs to take effect, with Maine’s four among them.
Last year, a bill to pull Maine out of the compact passed the Maine House 76–71 and was long tabled in the state Senate. If it ever moves, Maine would become the first state ever to walk away from the compact — after giving its word.
Many believe the Electoral College is a relic of slavery. Smaller states need not worry about fair representation, because each state gets two senators no matter its population — that is already lopsided in favor of citizens in smaller states. And the Bill of Rights still applies to every American.
A Mainer’s vote for president should count the same as anyone else’s.
I have written to my own legislators and asked them to stand by Maine’s decision. I hope your readers will do the same.
Wilfred Langford
Stetson
